en: *Cheng weishi lun*, Scroll Four.
Verified by the Layman of Jintan, Wang Kengtang.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra* states that all sentient beings [possess this consciousness]... that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness.

The eighth is the *āhāra* (nutriment) that draws forth consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*). The preceding [seven] were discussed in terms of the stages of arising and ceasing, while this is discussed in terms of the stage of abiding;
therefore, it is mentioned next. First, a sutra is cited as proof. Next, the eighth consciousness is established as the *vijñāna-āhāra*. Then, a sutra is cited for its explanation.

"Nutriment" (*āhāra*) has the meaning of "sustaining and benefiting" and the meaning of "maintaining. Because the eighth consciousness sustains and benefits the physical sense organs and the body, it is considered nutriment. Therefore...
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "If one were separated from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the food of consciousness for sentient beings already born would not be established.
Why? Because among the six consciousnesses, it is impossible to find even a single one that can perform the function of food for sentient beings already born within the three realms.
As the Blessed One said, there are four kinds of food. The first is edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), the characteristics of which are as follows..."
What is its characteristic? It is transformation and decay (*vipariṇāma*). "Segment" (*kavaḍa*) refers to a divided portion; it is so called because it can be swallowed or sipped.

This characteristic of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) is grasped at the time of transformation and decay, not at the time of consumption; therefore, it is said that its characteristic is transformation and decay.

For it is only at the time when odor, taste, and tangibility undergo transformation and decay that they are able to nourish and develop the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Thus is the essence of this edible food.
It has the three objects—odor, flavor, and tangibility—as its substance. Question: Why do the two objects of form and sound not constitute its substance? Answer:

The visual and auditory consciousnesses apprehend their objects through "apprehension at a distance" (*viprakṛṣṭa-grahaṇa*); thus, the objects of form and sound do not come into contact with their respective faculties.

Consequently, they cannot support the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the faculties; therefore, they do not constitute its substance. The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body apprehend their objects through "apprehension by contact" (*saṃnikarṣa-grahaṇa*); as for the object and the faculty...

Therefore, it is able to support the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the sense faculties (*indriya*). For this reason, the three objects (*viṣaya*)—smell, taste, and touch—are specifically established as the substance of food (*āhāra*).

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "For this reason, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is comprised of three bases; namely, smell, taste, and touch are established as food, while the form base (*rūpa-āyatana*) is not so established.
This is because [the form base] only causes benefit or harm once it has reached the stage of transformation through taste, potency, digestion, and so forth."
There are certain types of edible food that cause harm at the time of consumption but provide benefit only when they have been transformed;

such is the case with bitter and acrid substances. There are also certain types of edible food that provide temporary benefit at the time of consumption but cause harm once they have been transformed;
such is the case with sweet and delicious things that are unsuitable for one's constitution. Therefore, it is only when [the food] has been transformed that...

It is established as food when it is being consumed, not at the time of its enjoyment. Furthermore, it is said: "Moreover, this edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) should be said to be comprised within the spheres of odor, taste, and tangibility.
Why? Because it is through odor, taste, and tangibility that, when properly digested and transformed, [the body] is able to be nourished."

That which undergoes improper digestion and transformation is what constitutes diminution. Other phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth do not undergo nourishment, diminution, or transformation;
therefore, they are said not to have the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).

If various substances, at the time of swallowing, cause the mind to rejoice and the sense faculties to become alert, at that moment they are not called edible food, but are merely called contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*). If...

Having been consumed, it is digested and transformed with ease, increasing joy and happiness; it is only at the time of such digestion and transformation that it is called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
If there is digestion and transformation that cannot nourish the sense faculties or bring about well-being, then although it has been digested and transformed, it is not called edible food.
Furthermore, if various edible substances do not produce delight at the time of swallowing, nor can they cause the sense faculties—
At that time of gratification, it is not yet called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*);

rather, it is when, at a later time, it has been digested and transformed into a state of well-being, thereby increasing happiness—that it is then called edible food. If there is digestion but no increase in happiness, it is not so named.
Although these are digested and transformed, they are still not called "food. As appropriate, one should formulate four logical permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*):
there may be a substantial object that is not food, namely those substantial objects that cannot nourish the sense faculties and the primary elements;
there may be that which is food but not a substantial object, namely the three foods beginning with contact (*sparśa*); and there may be that which is both food and a substantial object.

This refers to various types of material food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) that are capable of nourishing the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Alternatively, there are things that are neither material food nor sustenance;
namely, contact (*sparśa*), mental volition (*manas-karma*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), which cannot nourish the sense faculties and the primary elements.

In this manner, the remaining categories of contact, mental volition, and consciousness should each be analyzed according to their respective applications using the fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*). Second is the nutriment of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*); its characteristic is as follows:
What is it? Its characteristic is contact with objects. "Contact" (sparśa) refers to the act of contacting or encountering. It denotes the factor of contact associated with the six consciousnesses.
When one encounters external objects such as forms and other sensory fields—such as the sensations of softness, smoothness, cold, warmth, and so forth—a sense of joy and pleasure arises.

This contact is able to nourish and benefit both the sense faculties and the primary elements; thus, it is called the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*). This refers precisely to the moment of actual enjoyment.

As previously analyzed, because this contact (*sparśa*) pervades all states of mind, although it is associated with eight consciousnesses, its function as "nutriment" (*āhāra*) is most pervasive and predominant in relation to the six consciousnesses.
These six consciousnesses refer to the six—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and not to the sixth [mental] consciousness alone.
This is because the objects contacted by them have coarse and manifest characteristics, and thus they possess a distinct capacity [to provide nutriment].
Because it embraces pleasant and joyful sensations, and because it can produce a bodily equanimity that is conducive to benefit, this is the meaning of being preeminent.

Since the objects contacted by the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] are subtle, they are entirely unable to produce joyful or pleasant sensations; although they do produce the sensation of equanimity, [it is not preeminent].

However, because it is neither beneficial nor detrimental, this principle reveals that contact (*sparśa*) which gives rise to sorrow and suffering is not the "nutriment" (*āhāra*) of equanimity (*upekṣā*), as it does not provide sustenance.
Tonghui said: "For example, when one encounters a woman, that contact can sustain the body and thus receives the name 'nutriment.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the attachment to forms upon seeing them is called 'nutriment. How [could this be otherwise]?"

Is it not the meaning of nutriment by contact? Even if it were not nutriment by contact, why is it that when one watches theatrical performances and the like, one does not feel hunger even though one has not eaten all day?

Third is nutriment by mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*). What is its characteristic? Its characteristic is aspiration. It consists of desire (*chanda*) among the specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*) and volition (*cetanā*) among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*);
these two function together. Because it is able to aspire toward those desirable objects, it is [called nutriment] by way of this aspiration.

Because it is based on expectation. It serves as a basis for benefit, just as seeing water from afar prevents death from thirst, or as suspended sand satisfies hunger and the sight of a plum stops thirst;
what is recorded in historical accounts all serves as proof of this. Question: Why is desire not considered nutriment? Answer:

Because it benefits the faculties through deliberation (*vitarka*), and not through the power of desire itself. Question: Deliberation is also a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*) and is possessed by all eight consciousnesses. Of which consciousness is this [nutriment] the deliberation?

It can serve as nutriment. It is said: that which belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has a predominant significance as nutriment, because the sixth [consciousness] excels in its aspiration toward objects.
The *Utpatti-sarga-sūtra* states: "If there are sentient beings whose mental intentions provide nourishment and moisture, their sense faculties will increase."

Just as with fish, turtles, frogs, *kāraguda*, and other sentient beings whose sense faculties and life-force are moistened and sustained by mental volition (*manasikāra*), these take volition as their nutriment. Fourth is the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*). What are its characteristics?
Its characteristic is grasping (*upādāna*). Consciousness (*vijñāna*) refers here to the eighth consciousness, which possesses the characteristic of appropriation (*upādāna*).

Because it is sustained by the power of the first three kinds of nutriment, this consciousness now becomes predominant; its function is to nourish the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Therefore, although this consciousness pervades the essential nature of all consciousnesses, the meaning of "nutriment" applies most prominently to the eighth consciousness. Why is this? Because its characteristics are of a single class.
Furthermore, because it sustains excellence, and by virtue of this sustaining, the basis (the body) endures for a long time;
were it not so, it would be like a corpse, soon to rot and decay. Therefore, one must admit that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also nutriment, as it performs the function of benefiting the basis.
These three nutriments, when distinguished by the three periods of time, are such that edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) belongs to the past, and contact (*sparśa*) belongs to the present.

The mental factor (*manas*) belongs to the future. As for the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), its substance increases and flourishes due to the power of the preceding three foods, and because it conditions birth in the present and the future.
Furthermore, consciousness nourishes the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Thus, one should know that the food of consciousness extends across the three periods of time. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* asks: "What is food? How many are foods? For what purpose [are they]?"
Therefore, one contemplates food. This is because it is subject to transformation; that which is subject to transformation exists as an object;
that which exists as an object involves aspiration; that which involves aspiration involves grasping; and that which involves grasping is the meaning of "food.
Three aggregates, eleven elements, and five bases—partially—are food. One contemplates food in order to abandon attachment to the self that dwells by means of food.

Regarding the three aggregates (*skandha*): edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); the two foods of contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*cetanā*) are the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);

and the food of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*) is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Regarding the five bases (*āyatana*): edible food consists of the three bases of odor (*gandha*), flavor (*rasa*), and tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*); contact and volition are the base of mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*); and consciousness is the base of mind (*mana-āyatana*). Regarding the eleven elements (*dhātu*):

edible food comprises the three elements of odor, flavor, and tangibility; contact and volition are the element of mental objects (*dharma-dhātu*); and consciousness comprises the seven mental elements (*saptacitta-dhātu*).

The realms: namely, the mind-faculty realm (*manas-indriya-dhātu*) and the six consciousness realms (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*). These four are able to sustain the body and life-force of sentient beings so that they do not cease or perish;

therefore, they are called "nutriments" (*āhāra*). This concludes the definition of nutriment. As for the statement: "Edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is effective only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)," [it means as follows].

To exclude the first three types of nutriment: they are neither constant nor universal, and they do not serve as the support for sentient beings. Edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is functional only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);

since it is not used in the higher realms, it cannot be universal or constant. Although the two nutriments of contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*manasikāra*) pervade all three realms, they are subject to interruption;
therefore, they cannot be constant. [The phrase] "the evolving consciousnesses such as the eye" and so forth below serves to distinguish these from the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
It is intermittent and subject to transition, and it is not the support for sentient beings. What constitutes its intermittence? First, the mindless meditative attainments;
second, deep sleep; third, fainting; and fourth, the heaven of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*). Because these involve interruptions, it is not pervasive. What constitutes its transition?

This refers to the state of possessing mind, which—according to the supporting faculties (*indriya*) and the objects of perception (*ālambana*)—operates within the three natures, the three realms, and the nine [stages].

Since the earth and other elements undergo transformation, they are not eternal. Because they cannot universally and perpetually sustain the body and life, they do not possess the meaning of "consciousness as nutriment" (*vijñānāhāra*).
Therefore, for anyone who does not believe in the existence of the eighth consciousness, this one nutriment would have no basis;
would it not then contradict the Sūtra’s statement that "all sentient beings subsist by depending on nutriment"? [The opponent says: No.

They further argue: "In the state of non-consciousness (*acittaka*), although the six consciousnesses are absent, that which precedes entering meditative absorption is called the 'past,' and that which follows emerging from absorption is called the 'future.
Thus, the six consciousnesses are not non-existent, and therefore they possess the quality of being nutriment (*āhāra*).

To refute this, he establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "Past and future consciousnesses and so forth do not serve as nutriment in the state of non-consciousness, because they are [not present]."
It exists eternally, because it lacks both substance and function, like flowers in the sky and so forth. Furthermore, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states:

"Consciousnesses of the past and future, and so forth, are not non-existent during the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), yet they do not serve as nutriment (*āhāra*). Even if they possessed substance and function, they would not be subsumed under the present, because they lack the nature of nutriment, like empty space and so forth.
Again, a further counter-argument is proposed: "The meditative mind that induces [the state] acts as the nutriment that sustains the body for the one who has entered meditative absorption."

Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The various minds and mental factors of one who has entered meditative absorption cannot be called 'nutriment,' because the Sūtras do not so state, and because they have ceased to exist.

To refute this, a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established: "The mind and other factors of one who has entered meditative absorption do not serve as nutriment for sentient beings in a state of non-consciousness (*acittaka*), because at the time of abiding in that non-conscious state, those [factors] have already ceased; and it is already fully established that what is past is not nutriment."

Because they have already ceased and no longer exist, it cannot be said that the two attainments—the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—are dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, these states sustain beings such as those in the realm of non-perception; yet the four kinds of nutriment, such as edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), do not include the state of non-perception.

Moreover, since dissociated formations are merely conventionally established based on the temporal states (*avasthā*) of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), how could they possess the nature of nutriment?
Yes. If one investigates in this manner, it is certain that there are no six consciousnesses capable of performing the function of nutriment for those sentient beings;

yet you maintain that they exist, which is utterly unreasonable. Your insistence that the sixth consciousness still exists in states such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) will be refuted extensively in a later chapter.
Furthermore, the phrase "for them" refers specifically to those who maintain that the sixth consciousness exists in states such as the attainment of cessation. Moreover, you should...
Regarding the statement that when one gives rise to untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousness while born in the two higher realms, what serves as its nutriment:

if it were held that untainted consciousness and so forth serve as nutriment, then since untainted consciousness and so forth destroy the tainted (*sāsrava*), they could not function as nutriment for that body and life.
Nor can it be said that there are tainted seeds within untainted consciousness that can perform the function of nutriment; [this is because] untainted consciousness and so forth...
Because it cannot maintain impure seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
"Untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) and so forth cannot maintain impure seeds, because they destroy existence (*bhava*), just like *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that sentient beings of the higher realms sustain life with the body or sustain the body with life, such that these would be mutual food for one another; nor is there a lack of body among those comprised by the four nutriments (*catvāra āhārāḥ*).

Because of the life-force (*jīvita*). If it is claimed that body and life-force sustain one another and serve as mutual nutriment, then in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), since there is no physical body to sustain the life-force, and the life-force has nothing to sustain it, it would necessarily be extinguished and severed; how then could it function as nutriment?

Furthermore, it cannot be said that the homogeneous group (*nikāyasabhāga*) serves as nutriment, because the homogeneous group and such have no substantial reality (*dravya*); how then could they function as nutriment? For this reason, it is certain.

Knowing that there is a distinct ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) apart from the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which maintains the body and life-force so that they do not cease or perish, it is said that "all sentient beings subsist on nutriment.
Fearing that one might object, "If the Buddha also subsists on nutriment, he too must be a sentient being," it is stated:
"Sentient beings are established based solely upon the five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*); the Buddhas, however, have no appropriated aggregates."
All are empty; they do not fall into the outflows (*āsrava*), nor are they comprised within the category of sentient beings (*sattva*).

Even if the Buddhas were to manifest as classes of sentient beings, they would still subsist by means of food. One should know that these are all manifestations of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) and are not actual sentient beings who subsist by means of food.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Compendium of Abhidharma), Part III, states: "Furthermore, there are briefly four ways in which these four nutriments (*āhāra*) are established by way of differentiation:
first, the nutriment that sustains an impure basis; second, the nutriment that sustains a basis that is both pure and impure; third, the nutriment that sustains a completely pure basis..."
Fourth is the manifestation of dwelling in eating. Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "Kāśyapa, dwelling in the dharma of equality, one should go on alms-round in succession.
One should go on alms-round for the sake of non-eating. One should take morsel-food for the sake of destroying the characteristics of combination.
One should receive that food for the sake of non-acceptance. All of these are methods for breaking the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and accomplishing *nirvāṇa*.
This refers to the "subsisting on food," which is to say, manifesting as one who dwells subsisting on food.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the state of one dwelling in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), as well as the states of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*) and so forth, are to be understood by analogy with this.

The ninth [point] establishes that there is consciousness in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). The preceding [section] revealed the eighth [consciousness] by way of the process of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti-dvāra*);

this [section] reveals it by way of the process of cessation (*nivṛtti-dvāra*). First, a scriptural authority is cited: for a noble one who has entered the attainment of cessation, the activities of body, speech, and mind are all ceased.
Specifically, inhalation and exhalation are the application of the body; feeling and perception are the application of the mind; and vitarka and vicāra are the application of speech.

Regarding the preparatory stages (*prayoga*): these three preparatory stages are associated with the sixth consciousness, for they are all extinguished within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

As for why vitality (*jīvita*) does not cease: it is the capacity existing upon the seeds of the eighth consciousness that maintains the continuity of the physical and mental aggregates of a single lifetime without interruption;
this is termed "vitality. Regarding the statement "nor is it separated from warmth": warmth (*ūṣman*) is a characteristic of the eighth consciousness.

[This is] the analysis. These two factors are both inseparable from the eighth consciousness. Since within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the six groups of consciousness, as well as the preparatory applications of body, speech, and mind, are all inactive, yet vitality (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*) remain, it is clearly known that it is the eighth consciousness that serves as the basis for vitality and warmth.
Next, the eighth consciousness is established by the name "consciousness not separated from the body" (*asambhinna-kāya-vijñāna*). [It] abides in the meditative attainment of cessation.
If mental activity has already ceased, then the visual and other consciousnesses should all no longer exist.

If one does not allow for the presence of a certain subtle, constant, and pervasive consciousness that maintains life-force, warmth, and cognition, then based upon which consciousness could it be said that "consciousness does not depart from the body"?
The Hīnayāna proponent says: "The consciousness that does not leave the body arises again at a later time after the state of cessation;

it is not the eighth consciousness. He then establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "The consciousness abiding in the meditative attainment of cessation is the subject (*dharmin*); its thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is 'not separated from the body'; the reason (*hetu*) is:"
Because it arises again at a later time, it is like a tertian malaria. The Mahāyāna says: "If that were so, the sūtra should not have stated that 'mental formations (citta-saṃskāra) cease.

Your claim that consciousness (vijñāna) arises again at a later time after having ceased implies that mental formations would also arise again after they have ceased, because consciousness and perception (saṃjñā), etc., share the same arising and ceasing.
If you argue that consciousness arises again at a later time after having ceased, [then consider] life-span (āyuḥ)...

It would follow that heat and the sense faculties, like consciousness, would arise again after having ceased, which would lead to a great logical error. To refute this through formal reasoning (*pramāṇa*), one states:
The subject (*dharmin*) is "vitality, heat, and the sense faculties. The thesis (*pakṣa*) is: "They are not separated from the body. The reason (*hetu*) is:

"Because they arise again at a later time. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) should also be like consciousness; for we have observed that there are cases where vitality, heat, and the sense faculties have ceased and then arisen once more.

Therefore, one must admit that consciousness, like vitality and warmth, truly does not depart from the body; it is not like the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which cease and then arise again.

Just as a person on a day when a tertian fever does not manifest is not called a healthy person, because they possess the physical faculty (*kāyendriya*) that sustains the illness—this serves as an analogy for the eighth [consciousness] sustaining the seeds—so too is this analogy applied to the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
There is fundamentally no fault; the error lies merely in not believing that there is an eighth consciousness. Next, [the argument] refutes [the position] by means of insentient objects.

Furthermore, within this state, since the first six [consciousnesses] have already ceased, if there were no eighth consciousness to maintain this body, it would be like inanimate matter such as tiles or pebbles—devoid of cognition.
How, then, could one be called a noble being who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)? To refute this through formal logic (*pramāṇa*), one states: "Abiding..."
The state of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) does not belong to the category of sentient beings, because it is entirely devoid of consciousness, being comparable to shards or rubble.

Next, it is refuted by way of its lack of appropriation (*anupātta*): if there were no maturation (*vipāka*) to sustain the sense faculties, they would immediately decay and rot, resulting in the absence of vitality and warmth, like a corpse;
thus, there would be no possibility of recovery. How, then, could that consciousness arise again at a later time? The formal inference is as follows: [the mind] abiding in cessation...
In that state, the faculties, vitality, and warmth should all perish, for there is no longer anything to sustain them; they would be like a corpse.
As for the consciousness mentioned in the sūtras as not departing from the body, to what could it possibly belong? Why is it said that the final consciousness does not return to be born again?
Because once the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) has abandoned this body and transferred its support to another body, it never returns to be born here again.

This is not the case according to the principles of the body. Otherwise, the white bones of the world could all become flesh. Next, [the argument] is refuted by means of the lack of a sustaining [consciousness].

Furthermore, if at this stage there were no consciousness that sustains the seeds, subsequent consciousnesses would not arise, because they would lack their seeds. There must therefore be an eighth consciousness that sustains the seeds;

only then can [subsequent consciousnesses] arise, like a tertian malaria fever that begins to manifest again. Past and future [dharmas] do not [mutually...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated here.*

This accords with the Dharma. As established in the preceding chapter, the refutation of non-existent dharmas is fully proven. All dharmas, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, do not exist apart from consciousness;

nor do they possess the capacity to receive perfuming (*vāsanā*) or maintain seeds (*bīja*). Furthermore, none of these are the consciousness that maintains vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and the non-separation from the body.
Therefore, in this state, that which maintains vitality, warmth, and the non-separation from the body is not [any other consciousness] but the eighth.

To whom does this belong? To summarize and apply a single measure: within mindless states such as the meditative attainments of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth, consciousness must truly exist, because these states possess the faculties, vitality, and warmth, and are comprised within the category of sentient beings, just like states with a mind.

If one were to claim that the sixth consciousness exists in these states, this would be precisely what was extensively refuted in the preceding chapter. First, the refutation of the first six [consciousnesses] begins: "If one were to claim..."
To claim that consciousness is not separated from the body and is thus the sixth [consciousness] is logically untenable.
This meditative absorption is designated as "mindless" (*acittaka*) precisely because the sixth consciousness is absent. How could there be a sixth consciousness while it is also called "mindless"?

If you argue that "mindless" refers only to the absence of the five sensory consciousnesses and not the absence of the sixth, then all meditative absorptions should be termed "mindless. Why? Because [the sixth consciousness would be present in them].
Whenever one enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, necessarily do not arise.

Since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is included among the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), when the five consciousnesses are absent, the mental consciousness is also absent. One may formulate this argument as follows:

"In the state of cessation (*nirodha-avasthā*), the mental consciousness does not exist, because it is included among the six evolving consciousnesses, just like the group of the five consciousnesses. Furthermore, in this state, [the mind] is not separated from the body.
Consciousness is profoundly deep and subtle; its modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects of perception (*ālambana*) are all impossible to discern.
Therefore, one knows that the consciousness remaining at the stage of cessation is certainly not the sixth [consciousness]. To refute this, one establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*):

"The consciousness in this state is not the sixth consciousness, because its modes of activity and objects of perception cannot be known, just like vitality, warmth, and so forth. If there were anything knowable in the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), [the reason would be inconclusive].
As for "consciousness," it should be understood as being like the four dhyānas and eight samāpattis; it is not subsumed under this state. Why?

Because those who enter these meditative absorptions do so fundamentally to bring to rest cognizable consciousnesses that can be discerned, rather than entering these absorptions to counteract consciousness that is non-discerning.
Since such consciousness exists [in this case], it should not be this meditative absorption. To establish the formal argument (*pramāṇa*): the state of abiding in cessation is not [this absorption].
This stage is included [in the category of consciousness] because it possesses mental aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) that can be known; thus, it should be like other stages.
Next, regarding the presence or absence of mental factors (*caitta*), it is said to clarify whether the sixth consciousness exists or not:

"Furthermore, if the sixth consciousness exists in this stage, do those mental factors exist or not? If one says they exist, that contradicts the Sūtra, for the Sūtra states regarding this meditative absorption..."

Mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) are all extinguished. Since all mental factors (*caitta*) belong to the category of formations, it is called the "attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception" (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Because feeling and perception are among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), [the opponent] objects, saying: "In this state of meditative equipoise, there are three types of preparatory effort (*prayoga*):
first, bodily effort, which refers to inhalation and exhalation; upon entering the fourth dhyāna, bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*) are severed. Second, vocal effort..."
This refers to vitarka and vicāra. Upon entering the second dhyāna, verbal activity ceases. The three mental applications (manasikāra) refer to feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā).

Upon entering the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), mental activity ceases. Since the application for this attainment consists solely of aversion toward feeling and perception, only feeling and perception are extinguished within this state;
for these two mental factors (caitta-dharma) provide strong support to the mind, more so than other mental factors.

The Dharma alone is designated as "mental formations" (*citta-saṃskāra*). Now, when one speaks of the cessation of mental formations in reference to the cessation of feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*), there are still other mental factors (*caitasika*) present;

what contradiction is there in this? The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying: "If one merely feels aversion toward feeling and perception and thus causes only feeling and perception to cease, without causing the first six [consciousnesses] to cease..."
Regarding that which is called "cessation": even within the meditative attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), there is likewise only a revulsion toward perception (*saṃjñā*);

thus, it should be only perception that ceases, while the first six [consciousnesses] do not cease—this is what is termed the "attainment of non-conceptualization. Yet you do not admit that those [six consciousnesses] exist therein; why is this?

Since it is only the support provided by feeling (*vedanā*) and perception that strengthens the mind, when feeling and perception cease, the mind supported by them should likewise cease. Why then do you persist in this attachment?

"Is there a sixth [mental factor] in this state? The opponent defends the position, saying: "Just as when the inhalation and exhalation cease within the body, the body itself does not cease; how can you demand that the mental king (citta-rāja) cease along with its associated mental formations? When vitarka and vicāra—the formations of speech—cease, speech no longer proceeds. When saṃjñā, vedanā, and other mental formations cease, the mind (manas) still remains.

Therefore, your analogy is invalid. The master of the treatise refutes this: [The Master’s Refutation: This is not so. For example, when one is in a state of deep sleep, although the formations of speech such as vitarka and vicāra have ceased, the formations of the mind such as saṃjñā and vedanā have not ceased. Furthermore, when one is in a state of meditative absorption (samādhi), although the formations of the body such as inhalation and exhalation have ceased, the formations of the mind such as saṃjñā and vedanā have not ceased. Thus, it is not the case that because the formations of the body cease, the formations of the mind must necessarily cease. Moreover, if the formations of the mind were to cease while the mind itself remained, then the mind would be devoid of all mental factors (caitasika-dharma). Since this is logically untenable, your argument is incorrect. Furthermore, if the formations of the mind were to cease while the mind remained, then the mind would be like space, which is devoid of all characteristics. This contradicts the established doctrine that the mind is characterized by the presence of mental factors. Therefore, your analogy is invalid. The opponent might further argue: "If the formations of the mind were to cease while the mind remained, then the mind would be like a lamp whose light has been extinguished, yet the vessel remains. But this is not so. A lamp is a composite of the elements of fire and fuel; when the fuel is exhausted, the fire ceases and the lamp is extinguished. It is not the case that the vessel remains while the light has vanished. Therefore, your analogy is flawed. Consequently, it is established that when the formations of the mind cease, the mind itself also ceases. Thus, there is no sixth mental factor in this state. This concludes the refutation.

He said: "If it is as you say—that when bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*) cease, the body does not cease, and by analogy the mind does not cease—then it would also follow that when vocal formations (*vāk-saṃskāra*) such as vitarka and vicāra cease, speech likewise would not cease; yet you do not accept this.

Furthermore, formations with respect to phenomena are either pervasive (*vyāpin*) or non-pervasive; do not take them as mutual analogies, for that would contradict and undermine correct reasoning. If [the formations] were pervasive, then when they ceased..."

When that which is fixed by nature (*dharmatā*) ceases along with the universal factors (*sarvatraga*), it does not cease along with the non-universal factors. Thus, although the formations (*saṃskāra*) have ceased, the phenomenon (*dharma*) still remains.

What is meant by "non-universal"? It refers to inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*). Because these breaths do not pervade all phenomena of the body, there are cases where the breath has ceased while the body remains.
Vitarka and vicāra are universal factors with respect to speech; therefore, when vitarka and vicāra cease, speech also [ceases].

In meditative absorption, vitarka and vicāra cease. If one applies this analogy to feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā), then since feeling and perception have ceased, the mind (citta) should also cease.
This is because feeling and perception are universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-sarvatraga-dharma). To refute this through formal logic (pramāṇa), one states:

Feeling and perception are also subsumed under the category of universal mental factors with respect to the mind, because they are universal mental factors, just like volition (cetanā) and so forth. How could it be that feeling and perception have ceased while the mind remains?

Furthermore, [this is] refuted by applying the same logic to the mental factors (*caitasika*). Regarding "volition (*cetanā*) and so forth": volition is associated with desire; "and so forth" refers to the five mental factors beginning with desire.

Based on the statements from other sources, the ten universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viniyata*) factors are the *mahābhūmika* (universal) mental factors; the eleven beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are the *kuśalamahābhūmika* (wholesome universal) mental factors;
and the twenty-six beginning with greed (*lobha*) are the *kleśamahābhūmika* (afflictive universal) mental factors. Therefore, it says: "Since it is admitted..."

Volition (*cetanā*) and the others are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). When feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) cease, the other universal mental factors should likewise all cease.
Since the universal mental factors have ceased, the great wholesome ground factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*), such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, would also not exist;

for it is not possible for the remaining factors to persist once the universal mental factors have ceased. How, then, can it be said that only feeling and perception cease while the other mental concomitants (*caitta*) still remain? This being granted...

Volition (*cetanā*) and so forth are not absent in this state; therefore, sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are likewise not absent. Why is this? Because they are among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
Since volition and the others exist, contact (*sparśa*) must necessarily exist, because contact is the root of all mental factors (*caitta*).

Where there is contact, there must be sensation, because contact takes sensation as its object. Where there is sensation, there must be perception; these two dharmas, sensation and perception, are never dissociated.
Therefore, regarding these feelings (*vedanā*) and perceptions (*saṃjñā*) and the other mental states: if they do not exist, all are absent; if they exist, all are present.
How could it be logical to claim that only feeling and perception are extinguished, while the other mental states are not? Furthermore, he attempts to defend this by saying:
"Just as in the twelve links of dependent origination, feeling conditions craving (*tṛṣṇā*); this feeling only conditions craving after it has perceived an object that is desirable or pleasant. If...

When one perceives an object that is loathsome or repulsive, this feeling (*vedanā*) certainly does not take attachment (*rāga*) as its object. How could all feelings possibly take attachment as their object?
By this analogy, it is the same for the arising of feeling from contact (*sparśa*): when contact encounters an agreeable object, a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) arises.
When one encounters an object that is disagreeable to the mind, how could a pleasant feeling (*saumanasya-vedanā*) possibly arise?

Therefore, the principle you assert—that contact (*sparśa*) is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika-dharma*)—is not established. The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying: "Your defense is not valid, because there is a distinction [between the two]."

What is the distinction? It is that within the Buddha’s sūtras there is a specific differentiation: while it is only in the case of feeling conditioned by contact (*sparśa-pratyayā vedanā*) that there is a distinction between what is agreeable and what is disagreeable, there has never been a passage where it is distinguished that contact gives rise to feeling that is not felt. Therefore, wherever there is contact, there must be feeling;

wherever there is feeling, there must be perception (*saṃjñā*). This principle is certain, as these are among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). Thus, one knows that feeling and perception [are inseparable].

"Cessation. Thought (*cetanā*) and the others do not cease either. To refute this, one establishes the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*): Within this state of cessation, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) also do not cease, because thought and the other [mental factors] are present, just as in any other state possessed of mind.
If you admit that there is mind in this state, it contradicts the scriptural statement that "mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) have ceased" in this state;
furthermore, the cessation of feeling, perception, and so forth could not be established. If there were no mental factors (*caitta*) in this state, [the claim of cessation would be untenable].
If the dharma [of feeling] were absent, consciousness (*vijñāna*) would likewise have to be non-existent, because mental factors (*caitta*) are inseparable from the mind (*citta*).

Since the mental factors of the universal ground (*mahābhūmika*) cease when the ground itself ceases, if the universal factors ceased while the dharma did not, then feeling and the others could not be termed "universal ground" factors.
Furthermore, if the mental factors ceased while the mind did not, this consciousness would not be a "concomitant" (*samprayukta*) phenomenon. If...

If one grants that mind and mental factors are not associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), then this consciousness could not be said to share the same basis (*āśraya*), the same object (*ālambana*), the same time, and the same activity (*kāritra*) as the mental factors;
it would then be like form (*rūpa*) and so forth. To establish this, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows:
This consciousness would then lack a basis (*āśraya*) and an object (*ālambana*), and so forth; furthermore, it would not be "mind" (*citta*), just like dharmas such as form (*rūpa*).

Furthermore, in the sutra passage below, the preceding section refuted the primary mind (*cittarāja*) by means of mental factors (*caitta*), while this section refutes mental factors by means of the primary mind.

First, a sutra is cited to prove that where there is mind, there must necessarily be mental factors. Then, from the words "If in this meditative absorption... onwards, the intended meaning of the sutra is established and the opponent's false attachment is rebuked.

Even if they were to counter-argue that at other times the triad of sense-faculty, object, and consciousness possesses the power of conjunction to produce contact (*sparśa*), and that based on contact, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth can arise—this is not the case within meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

This is because, through the preparatory application (*prayoga*) preceding this absorption, one has cultivated a state of aversion toward coarse and agitated mental factors (*caitta*). Consequently, while in the state of absorption, these three factors lack the capacity to produce contact; since contact is thus absent...
It is not produced, nor are there feelings and so forth; since it lacks all mental factors (*caitta*), it should be called the "concentration that extinguishes mental factors.
Why, then, does the Sūtra state only that this concentration extinguishes feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*)?

Even if one were to argue that at the time of prior aversion, the mind takes feeling and perception as its objects, and for that reason the name "concentration that extinguishes feeling and perception" was established, the other mental factors would nonetheless be extinguished along with them.

If names were not established, then this mind-king (*citta-rāja*) would also necessarily perish along with them, because it coexists with the feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) that are to be abandoned, just as other mental factors (*caitta*) perish following the cessation of feeling and perception.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: the mind abiding in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) should also perish simultaneously [with its associated factors].

Because it is associated with that which is to be loathed, just like other mental factors (*caitta*). Generally, the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) possesses these two names.

Since the mind is ceased, there is no sovereign (*rāja*); since feeling is ceased, there is no object. Therefore, the two attainments together encompass both the sovereign and its mental factors. Below, this is refuted by means of the three natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, if there were a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within this attainment, among the three natures, what nature would it be? It could not be defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
Furthermore, it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Because it is necessarily wholesome, it is not defiled-indeterminate (*kliṣṭāvyākṛta*).
A defiled-indeterminate mind must necessarily possess mental factors (*caitta*), for such a state does not exist during the stages of non-consciousness (*acittaka*).

Since the original intention was to loathe defilement and cultivate the wholesome, one should not loathe the wholesome and give rise to defilement. Since the original intention was to loathe distraction and seek tranquility, one should not seek tranquility and give rise to distraction. Therefore...

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "This meditative absorption is not dissociated from body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) and is certainly not mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because [in this state] neither the wholesome, the unwholesome, nor the indeterminate natures can be established. If it were not unwholesome, it would necessarily be wholesome;

for even within the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), all unwholesome states are not permitted, let alone their presence in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Nor is it indeterminate."
If it were admitted that this [consciousness] therein is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), then it would follow that the *ālayavijñāna* is established.

Furthermore, this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is definitely wholesome; it is not unwholesome. What is this wholesomeness? If it were wholesomeness by association (*saṃprayoga-kuśala*), then the mind and its mental factors must necessarily be associated with shame (*hrī*), dread (*apatrāpya*), and the three roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) to constitute a wholesome nature. If they are not [associated with these],...

Regarding the nature of what is wholesome—namely, natural wholesomeness (*svabhāva-kuśala*), ultimate wholesomeness (*paramārtha-kuśala*), wholesome by motivation (*samutthāna-kuśala*), and wholesome by application (*prayoga-kuśala*)—there are thirteen wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*) in the two-volume *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya*. These constitute natural wholesomeness.
This is the first type of intrinsic goodness (*svabhāva-kuśala*). Regarding intrinsic goodness, it refers to the eleven mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth;
this is the sixth type of ultimate goodness (*paramārtha-kuśala*). Ultimate goodness refers to *tathatā* (suchness) and *nirvāṇa*.
This is the thirteenth type of goodness by outflow (*niṣyanda-kuśala*). Regarding goodness by outflow, it means:

For one who has already attained tranquility, by the dominant power of this [attainment], they give rise to superior qualities such as the supernormal powers (abhijñā), which are mundane and supramundane, both common and uncommon. This preparatory virtue is precisely that eighth preparatory virtue.

Regarding "wholesome by application" (*prayoga-kuśala*): this refers to relying upon and associating with virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*), hearing the true Dharma, attending to it correctly (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), and practicing the cultivation of pure wholesome dharmas in accordance with the Dharma.

If it is claimed that this consciousness does not correspond with the three roots of goodness, but rather corresponds with what is wholesome by nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*) and what is wholesome in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-kuśala*), this is also not the case; it contradicts one's own tenet (*svamata*).

Therefore, in terms of intrinsic goodness (*svabhāva-kuśala*), only shame (*hrī*), dread (*apatrāpya*), and the three roots of goodness (*trīṇi kuśalamūlāni*) are included in this category, because their essential nature is wholesome by itself, like excellent medicine that does not depend on association (*samprayoga*) or origination (*samutthāna*).

As for ultimate goodness (*paramārtha-kuśala*), only suchness (*tathatā*) and nirvāṇa are so designated because they are definitive; that is to say, true liberation, within which [nirvāṇa]— [The text continues: ...in nirvāṇa...
It is supremely peaceful; all sufferings are forever stilled, just as one who is free from illness.

If it is claimed that this mind is not virtuous by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), but is rather virtuous through its origination (*samutthāna*), being induced by the roots of virtue of application (*prayoga*) and not by the power of the roots of virtue such as non-attachment (*alobha*), this is also incorrect. It would also contradict your own tenet, because... [self...]

The fundamental [state] is the cessation attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*). It is characterized by a distaste for coarse movement, wherein perception (*saṃjñā*) and other mental factors do not function;

it is not induced by the application of effortful attention (*manasikāra*) or by roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*). If it were induced by roots of virtue through such application of effort, then, like other virtuous minds, it would not be designated as "arising together" (*samutthāna*).

The refutation by means of formal logic (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: "The mind that abides in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is a wholesome state of origination (*samutthāna-kuśala*), because it is induced by the roots of wholesome application (*prayoga-kuśalamūla*);

otherwise, it would contradict one's own tenet, just like other wholesome minds. Regarding the claim that a wholesome mind can arise immediately after a mind of any of the three natures, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"For example, immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, nine minds may arise: namely, the four minds of its own realm, two of the form realm, [two of the formless realm, and one of the untainted realm]."

Regarding the mind: at the time of entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and at the time of rebirth (*pratisandhi*), wholesome (*kuśala*) or defiled (*kliṣṭa*) minds arise. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is one [type].

At the stage of rebirth, a defiled mind of that realm arises immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but a wholesome mind of that [formless] realm does not arise, because it is extremely distant.

Furthermore, regarding those who are in training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), since a wholesome mind can give rise to minds of the three natures (*tridharmasvabhāva*), how can a wholesome mind [arise] from the aforementioned [defiled states]?

[Question: Does this [state] arise because it is induced by the roots of goodness of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*)? Therefore, the mind is virtuous. It must necessarily be due to the power of association with the roots of goodness.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "Alternatively, there are those who maintain that the concentrated mind is called 'virtuous' because it is induced by the roots of goodness of the preparatory stage, and not due to the power of association with the roots of goodness. This [view] contradicts that treatise’s position regarding the power of association.
It is contrary for the mind to achieve its establishment as virtuous. If that were so, this concentrated mind would necessarily be associated with the three roots of virtue;
and since it is associated with the roots of virtue, it must also necessarily be associated with feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), for there is no other cause [for such association].
Therefore, it is said that it is not without mental factors (*caitta*). If there were no mental factors, the mind itself would also not exist. Thus one should investigate.
The evolving consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, are definitely separated from the body at the time of entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

That which is not separated must necessarily be the eighth [consciousness]. This is because, when entering the attainment of cessation, one is precisely ceasing the previously distracted evolving consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, but is not ceasing the extremely tranquil apprehending consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*). Question: When entering the attainment of cessation, is it only the distracted evolving consciousnesses that are ceased?
Regarding the statement that "the cessation [samādhi] which utterly stills the *ālayavijñāna* is also a state of mental concentration; why then is it called 'mindless' (*acittaka*)?

The answer is found in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (or *Karma-siddhi-prakaraṇa*), which states: "The mind is of two kinds: first, the *saṃcita-citta* (accumulating mind), because it is the locus where immeasurable seeds accumulate;

second, the *vicitra-citta* (variegated mind), because it evolves with distinctions in its objects and modes of activity (*ākāra*). In states such as the cessation samādhi, the second kind of mind is absent; therefore, it is so named."

The state of mindlessness is like a four-legged horse; because it lacks one leg, it is also called "legless. As it is with the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), so should it be understood for the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*).
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that the mind is defiled [and so forth], because this alone is able to maintain the seeds of both the defiled and the pure.
The tenth [section] cites the defiled and pure minds; this generally subsumes the meaning of the preceding nine chapters.

Since the preceding nine do not go beyond [the processes of] saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, it first cites a sūtra as proof, and subsequently establishes the eighth consciousness as the basis of defilement and purity.

First, it provides a general clarification that taking the mind as the basis means that all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena—whether defiled or pure—take the eighth consciousness as their foundation.
It is the root; it arises from the mind and abides in dependence upon the mind. This means that it is able to maintain all seeds and serves as the basis for manifest phenomena (*pravṛtti-dharma*).
That is to say, it transforms into those [phenomena] and acts as their support.

Thus, the seven preceding manifest consciousnesses all abide in dependence upon the eighth consciousness. Regarding "that which receives their perfuming," this refers to the eighth consciousness receiving their...

Regarding the statement that the first seven consciousnesses perfume and maintain their seeds: it is the eighth consciousness that is able to maintain the seeds of the three natures—defiled and pure—of the preceding seven.
For this reason, the eighth is described as the "mind of defilement and purity. Below, the division into defilement and purity refutes the position that there is no eighth consciousness.
First, the defiled aspect is explained. Defiled phenomena are of two kinds: namely, afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*). Afflictions refer specifically to the delusions (*moha*).

Within these twelve links of dependent origination, the three branches of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) constitute the afflictions (*kleśa*). The two branches of karma—volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*)—constitute karma.

The results are suffering (*duḥkha*), which consists of the five branches beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the two branches beginning with birth (*jāti*). Through afflictions, karma is generated; through karma, results are brought about.

These three categories—affliction, karma, and suffering—differ in their types. The seeds serve as the cause for the active manifestations (*samudācāra*), and the active manifestations serve as the seeds.

As for the fruit [of this]: if there were no eighth consciousness to maintain the seeds of afflictions, then after a sentient being has traveled through the three realms and nine stages with a mind free of defilement, the afflictions would manifest without seeds and arise spontaneously.

This would be like the case of Udraka Rāmaputra, who was born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception; once his evolving consciousnesses had ceased, at the end of his life, he fell into the body of a flying fox. Above...
The forest-dwelling birds eat, and those below devour the fish in the abyss;

such manifestations of afflictions would all have to arise without cause, because apart from the eighth consciousness, other factors—such as mind, matter, and non-associated formations—lack the capacity to maintain seeds.

Since consciousness that has already ceased or not yet arisen is neither substantially existent nor possesses the capacity to maintain seeds, if the various afflictions were to arise without a cause, then even those in the stage of no-more-learning of the three vehicles—whose afflictions have long since been completely severed—would likewise arise without cause.
Since this is not the case, how could that [other consciousness] be so? If there were no such consciousness capable of maintaining [seeds], [the afflictions would arise without cause].
The seeds of karmic fruit would then result in the uninterrupted cycle of coming and going through the three realms and nine stages.

Consequently, the various karmic retributions of humans, devas, ghosts, and animals—such as those with fur and horns, those with needle-like throats, or those with distended bellies—would likewise be without cause;
for the consciousness of another cannot maintain seeds and cannot serve as their cause. This is like when Udraka Rāmaputra first practiced meditative concentration for a single thought-moment.
For this single moment of anger, one receives the retribution of becoming a flying wildcat. A single thought of anger is itself the seed of karmic fruit.
If there were no eighth consciousness to maintain this seed, this body of a flying wildcat would have to arise without cause.

Not only do the gods of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception fail to preserve themselves, but even the Buddhas and Arhats cannot preserve themselves once they enter the Nirvana without remainder.
Once the realms have ceased, the karmic fruits of the three realms ought to arise once again. Why is this? Because afflictions would likewise have to arise without a cause.

These afflictions are precisely the active defilements (*saṃmukhībhūta-kleśa*) that arise upon the fruit; they are like the birds in the forest of food mentioned above that swoop down to devour the fish in the deep waters—this refers to the "coming karma.
Furthermore, regarding the descent of consciousness conditioned by formations, one should explain it according to the twelve links of dependent origination.
This is difficult to refute. If this consciousness did not exist to sustain the seeds of karmic results, then the condition of *saṃskāra* for *vijñāna* would be impossible to establish.

*Saṃskāra* refers to the wholesome or unwholesome karma that actively induces future rebirth. *Vijñāna* refers to that which is subsumed under the seeds of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), which directly produce the future ripened fruit.
Both the seeds of the maturation-consciousness and the seeds of karma within that consciousness are termed the limb of *vijñāna*. Thus, the Sūtra speaks of the limb of *vijñāna*.
This applies to both the induced and the inducer, because both the seeds of karma and the seeds of consciousness are designated as "consciousness.

Since there is no fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), there would be no dharma capable of sustaining the seeds of karma and the seeds of consciousness; thus, the condition of formations (*saṃskāra*) for consciousness (*vijñāna*) could certainly not be established.

If this is not established, then the defiled consciousness at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhivijñāna*) also cannot be established, because the sixth consciousness cannot receive perfuming (*vāsanā*) nor sustain the seeds of karma. Since...

There are no seeds of karma. What, then, gives rise to name-and-form? Question: When the consciousness that links rebirth arises—accompanied by aversion and attachment—is it not the case that this volitional formation (*saṃskāra*) serves as its condition?

Answer: The consciousness that links rebirth is projected [by past karma], but it is not produced by the volitional formations of the present life. Since there is no consciousness that maintains the seeds, there is no consciousness possessing seeds. [Objection:
Even if it were the case that it is produced by the volitional formations, what fault would there be? Answer: If that were so, it could not be called "name-and-form conditioned by consciousness."

Regarding "form" (*rūpa*): it should be explained as being conditioned by the formations (*saṃskāra*). This is because name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the formations are separated by a temporal interval, and thus lack the sense of being directly conditioned [by one another].
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: Question: For what reason are the various links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, taught in this specific sequence?
Answer: Those who are deluded must first be deluded regarding the objects that ought to be known; immediately thereafter, they...
He initiates wrong conduct; because of wrong conduct, the mind becomes inverted; because the mind is inverted, there is the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*);
because of the linking of rebirth, the sense faculties become complete; because the sense faculties are complete, there is the enjoyment of objects;
because of the enjoyment of objects, there is either attachment or seeking; and because of seeking, afflictions arise at the time of searching for [objects] in various directions.
It grows. Because afflictions grow, one initiates karma that leads to future existence, whether pleasant or unpleasant.

By the power of the growth of the karma thus initiated, the fruit of suffering arises within the cycle of birth and death across the five destinies. Once the fruit of suffering has arisen, there is the suffering of old age, death, and so forth;
that is to say, the suffering of old age and death induced by the transformation of the internal body, as well as [the suffering] induced by the transformation of external objects.

It draws forth the sufferings of sorrow, lamentation, fever, and affliction. For this reason, the Blessed One taught the twelve links in this specific sequence. Since *saṃskāra* (volitional formations) and *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form) do not follow in immediate succession and are separated by vast intervals of time, they cannot function as conditions for one another; thus, the conditionality of *saṃskāra* upon *vijñāna* (consciousness) would not be established. Consequently, the subsequent links of existence (*bhava*) could also not be established. [Regarding] the various pure phenomena (*viśuddhadharma*), below... [The text continues: Next, [the Blessed One] taught the sequence of the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*). First, he taught the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) through the precepts of restraint. Second, he taught the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) through the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). Third, he taught the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) through the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, he taught the sequence of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). First, he taught the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*) because it is coarse and easily perceived. Second, he taught the foundation of mindfulness of feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) because they arise in dependence upon the body. Third, he taught the foundation of mindfulness of the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*) because the mind is the basis for the arising of feelings. Fourth, he taught the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) because it is the basis for the arising of all mental objects. Furthermore, he taught the sequence of the four right endeavors (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*). First, he taught the right endeavor to prevent unarisen unwholesome states from arising. Second, he taught the right endeavor to abandon arisen unwholesome states. Third, he taught the right endeavor to produce unarisen wholesome states. Fourth, he taught the right endeavor to increase arisen wholesome states. Furthermore, he taught the sequence of the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*). First, he taught the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi-ṛddhipāda*). Second, he taught the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of effort (*vīrya-samādhi-ṛddhipāda*). Third, he taught the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind (*citta-samādhi-ṛddhipāda*). Fourth, he taught the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-samādhi-ṛddhipāda*). Furthermore, he taught the sequence of the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*). First, he taught the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). Second, he taught the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*). Third, he taught the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). Fourth, he taught the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*). Fifth, he taught the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). Furthermore, he taught the sequence of the five powers (*pañca balāni*). First, he taught the power of faith (*śraddhābala*). Second, he taught the power of vigor (*vīryabala*). Third, he taught the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*). Fourth, he taught the power of concentration (*samādhibala*). Fifth, he taught the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*). Furthermore, he taught the sequence of the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*). First, he taught the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-sambodhyaṅga*). Second, he taught the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya-sambodhyaṅga*). Third, he taught the factor of enlightenment of vigor (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*). Fourth, he taught the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-sambodhyaṅga*). Fifth, he taught the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-sambodhyaṅga*). Sixth, he taught the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-sambodhyaṅga*). Seventh, he taught the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-sambodhyaṅga*). Furthermore, he taught the sequence of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). First, he taught right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Second, he taught right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*). Third, he taught right speech (*samyagvāc*). Fourth, he taught right action (*samyakkarmānta*). Fifth, he taught right livelihood (*samyagājīva*). Sixth, he taught right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*). Seventh, he taught right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*). Eighth, he taught right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). Furthermore, he taught the sequence of the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*). First, he taught the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*). Second, he taught the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*). Third, he taught the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*). Furthermore, he taught the sequence of the nine successive stages of meditative attainment (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ*). First, he taught the first dhyāna. Second, he taught the second dhyāna. Third, he taught the third dhyāna. Fourth, he taught the fourth dhyāna. Fifth, he taught the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Sixth, he taught the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). Seventh, he taught the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Eighth, he taught the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Ninth, he taught the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Furthermore, he taught the sequence of the ten totalities (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*). First, he taught the totality of earth (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana*). Second, he taught the totality of water (*ap-kṛtsnāyatana*). Third, he taught the totality of fire (*tejas-kṛtsnāyatana*). Fourth, he taught the totality of air (*vāyu-kṛtsnāyatana*). Fifth, he taught the totality of blue (*nīla-kṛtsnāyatana*). Sixth, he taught the totality of yellow (*pīta-kṛtsnāyatana*). Seventh, he taught the totality of red (*lohita-kṛtsnāyatana*). Eighth, he taught the totality of white (*avadāta-kṛtsnāyatana*). Ninth, he taught the totality of space (*ākāśa-kṛtsnāyatana*). Tenth, he taught the totality of consciousness (*vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana*). Furthermore, he taught the sequence of the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa dhātavaḥ*). First, he taught the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*). Second, he taught the form element (*rūpadhātu*). Third, he taught the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*). Fourth, he taught the ear element (*śrotradhātu*). Fifth, he taught the sound element (*śabdadhātu*). Sixth, he taught the ear-consciousness element (*śrotravijñānadhātu*). Seventh, he taught the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*). Eighth, he taught the odor element (*gandhadhātu*). Ninth, he taught the nose-consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*). Tenth, he taught the tongue element (*jihvādhātu*). Eleventh, he taught the taste element (*rasadhātu*). Twelfth, he taught the tongue-consciousness element (*jihvāvijñā

Explanation of Purity. There are three kinds of pure dharmas: the mundane path of purity, the supramundane path of purity, and the fruit of abandonment through the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

That which is prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is called mundane; that which is on the stages and above is called supramundane. "Heterogeneous class" refers to the class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

"Pure dharmas" refers to the dharmas cultivated and realized by those of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kauśalya*) and the ten stages of holiness (*daśa-ārya*). This class of ordinary beings first gives rise to faith and initiates the mundane and supramundane...

Because the two kinds of pure dharmas in the world serve as the subsequent conditions for the mind, if there were no eighth consciousness to maintain the seeds of these two purities, then when those two pure paths arise, they would be without a cause;
this is because the theory that other dharmas maintain the seeds has already been refuted. Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"For one who has not yet abandoned the greed associated with the desire realm and has not yet attained a mind associated with the form realm, it is precisely by means of a wholesome mind associated with the desire realm that [one attains] detachment."
Because of the desire for the attachment to sensual pleasures (*kāma-avacara-rāga*), one diligently cultivates the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

This mind of the preparatory application belonging to the realm of desire does not arise and perish simultaneously with a mind belonging to the realm of form (*rūpa-avacara-citta*); therefore, it cannot be perfumed by that [form-realm mind] to serve as its seed. This is logically untenable.

Furthermore, since the past mind belonging to the realm of form has been separated from the present meditative mind by many lifetimes and other intervening states of consciousness, it cannot serve as the seed for this present concentrated mind. Only the [unmanifested]...
Because it exists, the mind in meditative concentration bound to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) is thus established.

The maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) containing all seeds, which has been transmitted through successive succession, serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the present moment; the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This should be understood accordingly for all stages of detachment from desire (*vairāgya-bhūmi*). Such is worldly purity (*laukika-viśuddhi*). However, if one is separated from all seeds...
The theory that the son’s *vipāka-vijñāna* (maturation-consciousness) [arises] is logically untenable.
If those two pure paths were to arise without a cause, then after one has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*), those two pure paths would have to arise again.

Why? Because their support (*āśraya*) would likewise have to arise without a cause. There are, briefly, eight kinds of supports for the contaminated (*sāsrava*): first, the support of designation (*prajñapti-āśraya*); second, the support of inclusion...
1. The basis of sensation; 2. The basis of maintenance; 3. The basis of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); 4. The basis of obstruction; 5. The basis of affliction; 6.

The basis of gratification; 7. The basis of the final limit, which is the stage of *nirvāṇa with remainder*, taking the entirety of the last-mentioned basis while excluding the six bases of gathering (*saṃgraha-vastu*), the basis of cyclic existence, and the basis of obstruction; 8. *Nirvāṇa without remainder*.
In this stage, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) remaining supports (*upadhi*) are relinquished; even the conditioned uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states of the two vehicles are relinquished.

Although the Tathāgata possesses conditioned uncontaminated states, he lacks all contaminated remaining supports; therefore, it is also called the "stage of no remaining support" (*nirupadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*).
Thus, according to the gate of establishing [stages] by way of specific states, there is the state of mindless sleep and the state of mindless fainting.

The stage of the ultimate state (*atyanta-avasthā*), the stage of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the stage of birth in the realm of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva-upapatti*), the stage of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and the stage of the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*) are all designated as the "mindless ground" (*acittikā bhūmi*).

However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), it is only within the realm of nirvana without remainder that all minds are extinguished, and thus it alone is called the mindless ground; in the other stages, although there is no activity of the evolving [minds], they are not yet devoid of mind.
