These two meanings apply specifically to the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, which are uninterrupted in themselves and do not depend on other consciousnesses to induce their arising, but rather rely solely on their own kind.

It serves as the *āśraya* (basis) for opening and guiding [the mind]; this interpretation is correct. According to another interpretation, the passage below—"The previous explanation has not yet thoroughly investigated the principle"—is Anahbuddhi’s critique of Nanda.

His first objection states: "If you claim that the first five [consciousnesses] do not continue from themselves or others, and that only the sixth is used as the *āśraya* for opening and guiding, this may be as you say in the case of ordinary beings who have not attained mastery. However, if..."

In the state of mastery (*vaśitā*), when the six sense faculties function interchangeably (*indriya-saṃcāra*), they operate spontaneously and with certainty, without depending on discursive thought or seeking.
How could those five bodies of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) not then be continuous? The second objection states:

"If it is argued that there is no continuity when encountering an object suddenly (*ābhoga*), then how can the five consciousnesses of the outflow (*nisyanda*) not be continuous? For when perceiving an object, there are five types of mind. First:

First, the mind of sudden encounter (*sateri-citta*); second, the mind of seeking (*anveṣaṇa-citta*); third, the mind of determination (*niścaya-citta*); fourth, the defiled or pure mind (*kliṣṭa-śubha-citta*); and fifth, the mind of uniform outflow (*nisyanda-citta*).
For example, when the auditory consciousness hears the pronunciation of various syllables, there are the two minds of sudden encounter and seeking;

however, because one has not yet definitively ascertained which [meaning] those syllables belong to, there is no mind of determination. Subsequently, when the syllable *ga* (行) is pronounced, understanding arises through the connection with prior habitual impressions (*vāsanā*).
When [the word] "saṃskāra" (conditioned phenomena) arises, three moments of mind occur: namely, the sudden encounter (*ābhoga*), the seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*), and the determination (*niścaya*).

Because one determines that all the phonemes belong to the category of conditioned phenomena, although one knows their intrinsic nature upon hearing the phoneme for "conditioned phenomena," one does not yet know their meaning.

To cause that meaning to be known, the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is further spoken; in this case, there are only two moments of mind, namely, the sudden encounter and the seeking, as the determination has not yet occurred.
Because it is not yet definitively known to which category the character "wu" (無) belongs, the subsequent character "chang" (常) is uttered.

Through the power of the preceding character, there is a successive perfuming (*vāsanā*) that causes the subsequent characters to arise in succession, giving rise to five moments of consciousness (*citta*). In this manner, when the four characters are completed at a later time, one is finally able to understand the meaning.

Regarding these five moments of consciousness: the first and last pertain to all six consciousnesses, while the middle three belong exclusively to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Furthermore, the first three [of those middle three] belong exclusively to...

The first [moment] is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); the latter two may be either wholesome or unwholesome. Furthermore, following the five sense-consciousnesses of sudden encounter (*ābhāsagata*), there must necessarily be a mind of seeking (*paryeṣaka*).

Following the mind of seeking, it may be either distracted or undistracted. If distracted, it again gives rise to a consciousness of sudden encounter; if undistracted, it gives rise to the third [moment], the consciousness of determination (*niścaya*), and so on up to the consciousness of natural outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "That which is induced by the power of mental attention (*manasikāra*) arises through four [factors]."
The causes are as follows: first, by the power of desire; if the mind has attachment toward a certain object, the mind will frequently give rise to mental attention toward it.
Second, by the power of mindfulness; if one has already properly grasped its signs and formed a thorough mental representation of it.
The mind then frequently gives rise to mental attention toward that object. Third, by the power of the objective field:
if that objective field is either extremely vast or extremely agreeable and is present before one, the mind then frequently gives rise to mental attention toward it.
Fourth, by the power of repeated practice: if one has already become thoroughly habituated to and fully familiar with that objective field, the mind then—

In that case, many acts of attention (*manasikāra*) would arise simultaneously; otherwise, it would follow that with respect to a single object of focus, only one act of attention could arise at all times.

Furthermore, there is no occurrence of two moments of the fivefold body of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) arising together in succession, nor do they arise alternately without interval from one another. Moreover, once a moment of the fivefold body of consciousness has arisen, from—
Immediately following this, there must arise a second moment of determinate mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Because of these two moments of mental consciousness—namely, the seeking and the determination—it discriminates objects as being either wholesome, defiled, or otherwise. Now, since the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) that follow as a natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) are induced by the power of determinate attention (*manasikāra*) toward the defiled or the pure, these five sense-consciousnesses as a natural outflow are then focused intently.
Regarding the objects of focus—whether wholesome or unwholesome—one is never separated from them for even a moment.

How, then, could one not admit a continuity of many moments? Below, the proof is cited for the first five consciousnesses; the sixth is not cited as being productive [of such continuity]. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"By means of the arising of visual consciousness, three types of mind are obtainable, in their respective order: the sudden (*ābhoga*), the seeking (*paryeṣaka*), and the determining (*niścita*). The first is visual consciousness; the second..."

After the mind has reached a state of determination (*niścaya*), there subsequently arise states of defilement or purity. Following this, the subsequent eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) proceeds as either wholesome or unwholesome through its outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Yet that outflowing eye-consciousness does not function by its own power of discrimination; it functions entirely through the force of the prior determination of defilement or purity.
At the same time, it shares the same object as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and does not pursue any other object. This is because...
Because it is certain that for such a duration, the two consciousnesses of the eye and the mind proceed in a continuous stream, whether virtuous or defiled.

As with the case of the eye mentioned below, this applies analogously to all other consciousnesses. Regarding the passage "that mind" (tad-manaḥ) below, the author of the treatise explains the *Yogācāra* position by stating:
"It definitively demonstrates that for such a duration, both the visual consciousness and the mental consciousness proceed in a continuous stream. Since...

It is said that they proceed in mutual succession, certainly without any sequence of before or after. Thus, at the time of visual consciousness, it is not the case that mental consciousness is absent;
yet it is not the case that the former five consciousnesses are induced by mental consciousness, nor is it the case that the sixth consciousness is induced by the former five.
Consequently, your position regarding the principle of the mutual succession of consciousnesses fails in both respects. The third objection states: "If there is no superior object..."
Regarding continuity: if an object is particularly intense, how could it not be continuous? What is meant by an "intense object"? It is said:

such as the Hell of Intense Heat (*tapana*). What is meant by "continuity"? It is said: fierce fires blaze forth, oppressing and seizing body and mind, burning and boiling without ceasing for an eon (*kalpa*) and so forth.
This group of five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) must necessarily be continuous. As for the *krīḍā-pramoṣaka* devas, they belong to the increase of the wholesome realms.

This refers to the state of intense proliferation. Regarding the second, the state of intense proliferation: when the five sense-faculties are occupied with their objects so that one can hardly keep up, how could there be any interruption or lack of continuity?
Furthermore, the following passage cites evidence that the first five consciousnesses do not induce the sixth; thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"If this preceding moment of the six consciousnesses ceases, the mental faculty (*manas*) acts as the equal-and-immediate condition for those subsequent moments of the six consciousnesses."

As for the condition (*pratyaya*): it is simply designated that the immediately preceding ceased mind serves as the "opening and guiding support" (*āśraya*). It does not mean that they mutually induce one another.

If you maintain that there must invariably be a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) serving as the opening and guiding support for the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) in their preceding and succeeding moments, then that treatise should have stated:
"If this sixth consciousness of the preceding moment acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for those six consciousnesses of the succeeding moment."

If you maintain that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) co-arising with the five [sensory] consciousnesses also takes those five as its "opening-and-leading" support (*āśraya*), then that treatise should have stated:
"If this preceding moment of any of the six consciousnesses acts as the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for that subsequent moment of the sixth consciousness.
Since the treatise does not state this, we know that each of the five consciousnesses possesses its own continuity.
This does not mean that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) acts as the "opening and guiding support" (āśraya) for the five sensory consciousnesses.

The mental consciousness co-arising with the five [sensory consciousnesses] also continues its own stream; it is not the case that the five sensory consciousnesses induce its arising to serve as its opening and guiding support.

Therefore, one should know that when the five sensory consciousnesses arise, there must necessarily be a preceding moment of the mental consciousness co-arising with the five, which is capable of inducing the subsequent moment of mental consciousness to arise. Why, then, rely on the five sensory consciousnesses?
Thus it provides guidance. The above refutes the prior six [consciousnesses] not serving as mutual guides. Next, the sixth [consciousness] is challenged:

"In states such as the mindless absorptions, when the sixth consciousness has been severed and subsequently arises again, if the continuity of activity is taken as the guide, then since the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] are constantly continuous, why not use them as the guiding basis for the sixth? Why rely on the preceding [six]?"
5. If that sixth consciousness does not employ the seventh or eighth, but employs its own kind—that is, the five consciousnesses as its own kind—why do you not grant this?
Why then do you insist that the sixth consciousness acts as the "opening and guiding" [consciousness]? Having refuted the sixth, he refutes the seventh, saying:

"If it is claimed that when the manas associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) first undergoes transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), it must necessarily depend upon the sixth [consciousness]."
The contemplation of the two emptinesses of persons guides that wisdom so as to cause it to manifest.

If this is the case, then the seventh consciousness should likewise take the sixth consciousness as its leading support (*āśraya*). Why is this not permitted? It is difficult to explain regarding the eighth [consciousness]:

"The pure eighth consciousness, which is conjoined with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, must necessarily be produced through the skillful means of the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses]" (this refers to the stage of fruition). Furthermore, it differs [from the previous argument].

The matured mind (this refers to the stage of the cause) relies either on the afflicted manas (the seventh consciousness) or on a wholesome mind associated with compassion and vows (the sixth consciousness).

Since it is also induced by the defiled and pure states of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, one must admit that the eighth consciousness likewise takes the sixth and seventh as its leading conditions (*āśraya*).

Why do you again refuse to accept this? If one were to base it on the sixth consciousness such that the five consciousnesses could induce it as a "conducive condition" (*āśraya*), then the aforementioned faults would ensue;
therefore, it is said that [your position] has not thoroughly investigated the principle. Having thus refuted the former view, he states his own position:
"One should explain that among the six consciousnesses prior to the five consciousnesses, whichever consciousness is employed as the 'conducive support' (*āśraya-pravartaka*) is [the basis]. Thus...
It should be understood that the first five consciousnesses have six levels of supporting conditions (*āśraya*).

As for the sixth consciousness, it takes its own preceding class, or the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, as its "opening and guiding" support (*kai-dō-e*); thus, it is clear that the sixth consciousness has three levels of supporting conditions.
The seventh manas-consciousness takes its own preceding class, or the sixth consciousness, as its "opening and guiding" support; thus, the seventh has two levels. [The eighth] ālayavijñāna...

That consciousness takes its own preceding class as well as the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] as its *āśraya* (supporting condition for the opening of the path). Thus, there are three layers within the eighth [consciousness].
One interpretation holds that this explanation is also illogical; therefore, relying on its own preceding class accords more deeply with both scripture and reason.

Nanda maintains that the first five [consciousnesses] mutually serve as the opening and guiding conditions (*ābhāsana-pravartaka*), while the sixth, seventh, and eighth continue in their own respective categories (*sva-jātīya-saṃtāna*).

Sthiramati reverses this position, asserting that the first five possess continuity within their own categories, while the sixth, seventh, and eighth mutually serve as the opening and guiding conditions.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla synthesized the preceding explanations to establish the correct meaning. First, he refuted [the opposing views]; second, he established his own doctrine; and third, he guided those who rely [on the teaching].

There are three meanings: first, existence (*sattā*); second, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); and third, being the primary [condition] (*pradhāna*), acting as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Why are these three meanings established? It is said: because each serves to exclude [certain possibilities]. The term "existence" excludes that which is non-existent.

Regarding "associated activity" (*samyukta-pravṛtti*): because that [activity] lacks intrinsic substance, it is distinguished by the word "having" (*sa-*) [in *savijñānaka*]. The word "conditioning" (*ālambana*) distinguishes it from matter (*rūpa*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), as they are not capable of being conditions.
The purpose of this distinction is that only that which possesses an object (*sālambana*) and possesses efficacy (*samartha*) can induce [a result], and thus acts as the primary factor.
The two characters for "primary" (*pradhāna*) distinguish it from mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), as they are not the primary factor. It must be...
Only its own master and those possessing power can serve as a basis. Since they are capable of acting as an immediate condition (*ānantarya-pratyaya*), what is being excluded? It is said:
one excludes the consciousnesses of a different category from the two aforementioned masters to serve as the basis for one's own consciousness;

furthermore, one excludes a consciousness of the same category belonging to a subsequent moment from serving as the basis for a preceding moment of one's own consciousness. Thus, the immediate condition consists solely of [consciousnesses] of the same category and [the same continuum].

This refers to the preceding moment of thought. Question: Is this "immediately antecedent condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) as defined here identical to the "immediately antecedent condition" among the four conditions?
Answer: They are distinct. While that which serves as an "opening and guiding support" (*āvajjana-nissaya*) is necessarily an immediately antecedent condition, the converse is not always true.

There are such things as equal-and-immediate conditions (samanantara-pratyaya) that are not the "opening and guiding" support (āśraya). Because the former is broad and the latter is narrow, they are said to be distinct.
What kind of phenomena are equal-and-immediate conditions but not the opening and guiding support? They are the mental factors (caitta) of their own class that have ceased in the preceding moment.
This [consciousness] perishes first and arises later; it merely serves as a guide through its equality [with the preceding moment]. Because it lacks sovereignty, it is not the support (āśraya).
Why exclude matter (rūpa) and the non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra)? It is said: because they both lack power. Why exclude the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)? It is said:

because it lacks priority and posteriority. On this point, Prajñākaragupta raises an objection: "Since at the time of visual consciousness, mental consciousness is not absent, [visual consciousness] is therefore not..."

Since two consciousnesses arise in mutual succession, [the text] first grants a concession and subsequently refutes it, saying: "If a consciousness of this type arises, it does not allow a consciousness of that type to arise simultaneously;

thus one may say that this consciousness possesses the power of 'opening and guiding' (kai-dō-ri) for that consciousness, and it would still be acceptable to take a different type as its opening-and-guiding support (*āśraya*).
However, since the eight consciousnesses within a single body are already permitted to arise simultaneously, then this..."
It lacks the power of guidance; how could it provide guidance for something of a different category? The intent of this objection is as follows:

when the eight consciousnesses are compared with one another, the place where another arises does not obstruct my path; why, then, would another consciousness be needed to provide guidance for the self?
Furthermore, the objection states: if it were admitted that different categories mutually provide guidance, then within a single body, the eight consciousnesses should [arise simultaneously].

They do not arise simultaneously. The former master asks: "What is the fault in their not arising simultaneously? He answers: "It would be identical to the Hīnayāna view that minds do not arise concurrently.
This is because the Sautrāntikas maintain that all material phenomena (*rūpa*) and mental states (*citta*) arise in a continuous succession of preceding and succeeding moments.
Furthermore, within a single body, various consciousnesses may arise together—whether two, three, four, or even up to seven or eight—their number being indeterminate.
If there were no distinction made between different categories, then whichever consciousness among the various types were used as the introductory guide,

it would follow that heterogeneous factors such as form (*rūpa*) could all mutually serve as equivalent immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*). This would contradict the teaching of the Noble Ones,

which states that equivalent immediate conditions apply only to mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), and that form and other such factors cannot be established as equivalent immediate conditions because they are not equal.
Because it arises [from a cause]. He cites a proof, saying: "Does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* not state that matter (*rūpa*) can also possess the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
Dharmapāla explains: "This is merely a statement employing the methods of concession and refutation. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says:

"Regarding the sequence of matter and mind," this refers to the Sautrāntika masters who hold such a tenet: namely, that all instances of matter and mind arise in a continuous succession of preceding and succeeding moments.

These conditioned phenomena possess the nature of being productive causes. That is to say, they maintain that a subsequent moment of form arises immediately after a preceding moment of form, and a subsequent moment of mind, along with its associated mental factors, arises immediately after a preceding moment of mind.
Since the principle of cause and effect is thus established herein, what need is there to further postulate the *ālaya-vijñāna*?
Consciousness is the cause of all phenomena. To refute this attachment, it is provisionally conceded:

"If that were so, when one passes away from the formless realm and is born in the realm of form, the principle that the seeds of prior form can produce the present form would be untenable, because they have been severed and extinguished for a long time.

Furthermore, when the mental consciousness arises after passing away from the state of non-conception, or when the mind arises upon emerging from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), [the seeds of] the prior mind..."
The notion that seeds can produce subsequent moments of mind is entirely unreasonable, because [the seeds] have long since been severed and ceased.

Furthermore, if one disregards the principle of the concomitant arising and ceasing (*sahabhū-samprayukta*) by which seeds are grasped, and instead maintains that only the preceding moment of mind acts as the seed to project the immediately following moment of mind, then the final moment of mind of an Arhat would be impossible. It would not...
One ought to be able to enter the sublime realm of nirvana without remainder;

however, because the final mind can act as the seed and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) to give rise to further minds, there would thus be no such thing as the sublime realm of nirvana without remainder.

Therefore, form and mind arise sequentially from one another; there can only be the condition of immediate antecedence (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), but no causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). All of the above serves to refute the existence of a causal condition.

Even if one were to concede that an immediate antecedent condition might exist between them, the term "equal" (*sama*) implies that their functional efficacy (*vīrya-kāritra*) must be identical; yet the functional efficacy of form and mental factors [is not equal].
They are not equal; they do not possess this nature of being conditions. Therefore, it is said that the statement "not so" would otherwise be rendered useless.
It does not negate quantity; rather, as previously stated, quantity is indeterminate. That quantity is indeterminate means that their functional power is unequal.

If you claim that the word "etc. (ādi) does not exclude [the capacity for] power and function, but merely excludes those of a different category, this would further contradict your own tenet that consciousnesses of different categories act as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Therefore, the eight consciousnesses each serve as the opening and guiding support (*kṣaṇika-avakāśa-pratisthā*) only for their own kind in succession, because it is impossible for members of the same kind to arise simultaneously.
As for the statement that mental factors (*caitta*) should be explained as having this same support in accordance with the consciousnesses—[it refers to] consciousness.

Since that [preceding mind] also acts as an inducer at the time of induction, an objection is raised: "If it is not admitted that this consciousness and that consciousness—which are of different types—arise simultaneously as an inducing support (*āśraya*), then how can it be admitted that the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*), which are likewise of different types arising simultaneously, stand in the relationship of sovereign (*rāja*) and subordinate (*prajā*) as an inducing support?
The Master of the Treatise replies: "Although the mind and mental factors are of different types and arise simultaneously," [they do so in a manner that allows for such a relationship].

They correspond with one another, being harmoniously integrated as if they were one (sharing the same object of cognition, the same basis, arising and ceasing at the same time, and being subsumed under the same nature).

They necessarily arise and cease together (when the mind-king arises, the mental factors also arise; when the mind-king ceases, the mental factors also cease). Their activities are necessarily identical (they share the same substantial entity, the same objective field, and the same functional operation).

When one acts as the precursor, the others likewise act as precursors (when the preceding moment of the mind-king acts as a precursor, all subsequent minds and mental factors arise; therefore it is said that the others likewise act as precursors). Possessing these [characteristics]...

There are five criteria. Therefore, between the mind (*citta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*), and between mental factors and the mind, they may each serve as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for one another.
Since the various consciousnesses do not possess these five criteria, they should not be cited as an analogy. This explains the difficulty regarding the association of the various consciousnesses.
Furthermore, an external objection is raised: "If the sovereign [mind] and its [mental] factors, being of different categories, can still act as a precursor and guide for one another, then..."
It should also be explained that those of a different category from the king (the mind) likewise serve as *āvedhaka* (inducing conditions).

The Master of the Treatise replies: "However, the mental factors (*caitta*) are not *āvedhaka-adhiṣṭhāna* (inducing bases). Why? Because they are produced by the leading of that king of mind (*cittarāja*), and thus lack the nature of being sovereign.

A base is defined by the nature of sovereignty; since mental factors lack this, they are not bases. Furthermore, a base is defined by the sense of being a support (*ālambana*); mental factors are likewise so. This is the explanation.
This is the difficulty regarding the basis established by the mental factors (*caitta*). A certain person known as a śramaṇa came and raised an objection, saying:

"According to my view, when a single preceding dharma induces a single subsequent [dharma] of its own kind, it is called 'equal' (*sama*). But how can your 'single preceding dharma' inducing a 'subsequent aggregate' (*kalāpa*) be called equal?
The master of the treatise replied: "If the mind and mental factors are equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), each is only its own..."

Likewise, when the seventh and eighth consciousnesses first undergo the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the associated mental factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) lack this object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

[Question: How is it that this [condition] is lacking? [Answer: Because the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, being contaminated (*sāsrava*), do not possess mental factors such as faith; and as for uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) faith and so forth, who would serve as this object-condition for them? Even if this condition were lacking, what harm would there be to the principle? The treatise answers:

This would contradict the holy teaching that all minds and mental factors arise from four conditions. Why? Because if this one condition were missing, they would exist by only two conditions. Since the seventh and eighth consciousnesses lack mental factors such as faith while still in the causal state (*hetu-bhūmi*), when they undergo transformation...
Regarding the stages: when mental factors such as faith arise, there would be no [preceding] factor of their own kind to serve as the *āśraya* (support) for their opening and guidance;

thus, among the four conditions, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) would be missing, which contradicts the sacred teachings. This interpretation should be considered a refutation regarding each being a condition. Furthermore, an external objection states:

"If, at the time of the initial transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, the associated mental factors such as faith are induced by depending upon them," [then...]

In the states of mindlessness (*acittaka*), since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has already ceased, one might ask whether the seventh and eighth consciousnesses should serve as its "opening and guiding" (*āvedhaka*) support. The Master answers:
Although the mental consciousness is severed during the five states of mindlessness, when it arises again, its opening and guiding support is simply its own preceding class (*svajātīya*);
it does not depend on the seventh or eighth consciousnesses. Question: Since the mind has long been extinguished, how can it serve as a support? The Master answers:
Because there is no intervening mind of a different category within that interval, it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*). Why, then, can it not serve as [the support]? Question:

For what reason are the seventh and eighth consciousnesses not used as the support? The Master of the Treatise answers: When that sixth consciousness is about to cease, it has already acted as the "opening and guiding" (*kai-dao*) condition for the present consciousness.
Why, then, trouble to have a mind of a different category act as the opening and guiding support? The intent of the argument is that [the sixth consciousness itself fulfills this function].
When the preceding moment of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is about to cease, it possesses a functional efficacy capable of inducing the subsequent moment to arise.
Having performed this function, it ceases; thus, the single present moment possesses the capacity to induce the subsequent [moment], which constitutes its essential nature (*dharmatā*).
It does not take a past dharma that has already ceased and lacks substance as its basis. This explains the difficulty raised regarding the subsequent arising being dependent on another.
Furthermore, a former master raised this objection: "If that is so, why do the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises all state that the various consciousnesses mutually induce one another?
Or why is it said that the seventh consciousness arises depending on the sixth, or that the eighth consciousness arises depending on the sixth and seventh?
The Master replied: "However, within the sacred teachings, it is stated that the first six consciousnesses mutually induce one another; as for the seventh and eighth..."

The arising based on the sixth and seventh consciousnesses is explained in all cases by way of a preeminent dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), not by way of an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);

therefore, there is no contradiction. Question: Why does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* state that "if this consciousness is followed immediately by that consciousness, the latter necessarily arises," and so forth?
Answer: The phrasing is general, but the intended meaning is specific. Although the words "this" and "that" are used as general terms, their respective meanings are distinct. First:

Go and observe this: just as the six consciousnesses of different categories serve as mutually opening-and-guiding supports (*āśraya*), if one examines it closely, these two terms "this" and "that" refer to the preceding moment of this very consciousness’s own category acting as the opening-and-guiding support for the succeeding moment of that same consciousness’s own category.
This explains away the difficulty regarding the contradictions between various teachings. Since there is no longer any contradiction, the correct principle is concluded: therefore...

The basis of its own kind (*svajāti-āśraya*). It is profoundly consistent with the principles of the teachings. Question: How is the name "opening and guiding basis" (*kai-tao-yi*) to be explained? Answer: The character *yi* (basis) is general (*sāmānya*), as it applies to all three types of bases.

The two characters *kai-tao* (opening and guiding) are specific (*viśeṣa*), applying only to this one particular basis. By using the specific to distinguish the general, "opening and guiding" distinguishes this from the other two bases.
This is a case of both the general and the specific being dependent compounds (*tatpuruṣa*). Furthermore, "opening and guiding" is a collective term that generally encompasses all [three].

The "so" (place/locus) where the king resides also acts as an opening and guiding factor (*āvarjana-nayanakāraka*), yet it is not the basis (*āśraya*). The term "basis" (*āśraya*) is distinct; it applies exclusively to the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*).

As a *tatpuruṣa* compound—whether taken in its general or specific sense—it is the basis for that which opens and guides. This serves to exclude from among those things that open and guide those that are not bases, namely the mental factors (*caitta*).

If "opening" (*āva*) means to clear the way and "guiding" (*naya*) means to lead forward, both are functions (*kāritra*), while the "basis" (*āśraya*) is of the same substance (*ekadravya*). It is also...

"Opening and guiding" (*ābhāsana-pravartana*) share the same basis; this is a *dharmadhāraya* (appositional compound). Furthermore, upon the substance (*svabhāva*) there exists the function (*vṛtti*) of opening and guiding;
because the function is subsumed within the substance, "opening and guiding" is itself the basis. This is a *dharmadhāraya* of substance and function. To the objection regarding the *dharmadhāraya*:

"The two characters 'opening' and 'guiding' apply to both the primary minds (*citta-rāja*) and their mental factors (*caitta*), whereas the character 'basis' applies only to the primary mind. Now, in forming a *dharmadhāraya*, is there not a lack of justification? [Response: ...
Question: "If 'broad' [is used], it is the fault of being too inclusive. Answer: "Because it refers to a single part, there is no such fault. Question: To raise an example as an objection:

regarding the term *jñeyāvaraṇa* (obstruction to the knowable), the two characters *jñeya* (knowable) apply to all one hundred dharmas, whereas the character *āvaraṇa* (obstruction) applies only to twenty-six afflictions.
Why is this not explained by the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound? For it is indeed a single part. Answer: Regarding the two characters *jñeya*... [text fragment ends]
The one hundred dharmas are not all included; there are only seventy-four. There are no twenty-six afflictions [among them]. Why are they absent? Answer:
When the twenty-six afflictions act as obstacles, they have not yet become objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). When they become objects of knowledge, they no longer act as obstacles.
Since they do not act as obstacles at the time they are objects of knowledge, the obstacles are not objects of knowledge. [However,] when they are objects of knowledge...

At that time, it no longer acts as an obstruction; thus, the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is not an obstruction. Therefore, the two terms [obstruction and object of knowledge] do not form a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Question: In what sense does that which is an obstruction at one time not become the object of knowledge? Answer: Regarding the obstruction to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it obstructs the arising of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Since wisdom does not arise, who is there to know? Thus, knowing itself is the obstruction; therefore, the obstruction is not the object of knowledge.
If wisdom has already arisen, even though there are obstructions regarding the objects known by that wisdom, those obstructions cannot obstruct its knowing.

Therefore it is said: "At the time of being an obstruction, one is not an object of knowledge," and so forth. Question: It has been said of old that the "object of knowledge" (jñeya) is not itself an obstruction;
rather, it is obstructed *by* an obstruction. According to this explanation, the twenty-six afflictions (kleśa) function solely as the [obstructing] agents.
[Question: It is an obstruction; it does not allow that which is known to be known. [Answer: This is the question. Why, then, do you instead say it "pervades" one hundred dharmas?
[Answer: This is said in reference to when wisdom has already arisen; it is said to pervade the hundred dharmas. When wisdom has not yet arisen, it is obstructed by this obstruction. [Objection:

If that is so, one should say that it is "obstructed by an obstruction that can know"; why do you say it is an "obstruction to that which is known"? [Answer: By obstructing the object of knowledge, it causes wisdom not to know it.
It is called an "obstruction to the knowable" (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*); in reality, it also obstructs the wisdom that is capable of knowing.

Furthermore, the interpretation that what is obstructed is the "obstruction to the knowable" does not refer to the capacity to know. Based on this explanation, there are likewise not one hundred dharmas. Why is this?

Since the twenty-six afflictions (*kleśa*) serve as the obstructor, they are clearly not the "knowable. This is because when wisdom arises, the afflictions have already perished; therefore, they are [only] the "knowable."
Regarding what [is meant by "wherein"]? Question: Why is it said in all cases that they pervade one hundred dharmas? Answer:

Although the afflictions have already perished, their names and characteristics can still be known by wisdom; therefore, it is said that the objects of knowledge pervade the one hundred dharmas. Question:
Generally speaking, you take only "opening and guiding" to explain "basis," but do not take "objects of knowledge" to explain "hindrance. What is the meaning of this?
Answer: It was originally stated that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) serves as the "opening-and-guiding support" (*āśraya*).

Among the three meanings of "opening-and-guiding," it functions as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for dharmas that possess an object; these two meanings apply to mental factors (*caitta*) as well.

Nevertheless, because mental factors do not themselves serve as the support for the category of "opening-and-guiding," it is said that one uses only the aspect of "opening-and-guiding" to explain the support. Question: For what reason [is this so] regarding the mental factors?

It is not an *āvedhaka-āśraya* (enabling support). Answer: Because it lacks sovereignty, it cannot function as a support. Question: Does it not bring forth the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) to resolve the obstruction?
Answer: It was originally stated that afflictions (*kleśa*) are the obstructing factors (*āvaraṇa-dharma*), while the objects known by wisdom (*jñāna*) are the factors obstructed (*āvṛta-dharma*).

Regarding what is now called the "obstruction to the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): it is able to obstruct the afflictions (*kleśa*). Its name is established by way of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) that is being obstructed.
Since the two characters "knowable" (*jñeya*) do not directly refer to the obstruction itself, it is said that one does not bring the "knowable" forward to explain the obstruction.
As the ancients said: "The knowable is not the obstruction; rather, being obstructed, it obstructs the knowable. This perfectly accords with the principle. Therefore...
This refers to the obstruction of knowledge. To open and guide [the mind] is precisely what constitutes the support (*āśraya*). This is what is meant.
Having concluded this digression, one should now discuss the main argument (up to the point where it says): "Or because the supporting basis for opening and guiding is easily understood."

The eighth is the co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*). It takes that very co-existent support as its object.

Furthermore, the supporting condition of causes (*hetu-pratyaya*) possesses the superior function of directly producing [the effect], while the supporting condition of dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*) possesses the superior function of inducing [the effect]; therefore, these are specifically highlighted.

Alternatively, the principle that what has previously ceased gives rise to what follows later is easily understood by people, so it need not be explicitly stated. This applies to both of the above two interpretations.

The discussion on the support (*āśraya*) is concluded. Thus, having already explained the support of this consciousness, since that [support] is already established, what fault could there be in this?

Third, the explanation of the object-condition (*ālambana*). Seven [consciousnesses] take the eighth as their object; regarding this, there are four masters with differing views. Nanda maintains that it takes the sovereign (*rāja*) as its object; Ghoṣaka... [text fragment].

The master Bhadanta [Śubhagupta] maintains that it takes both the aspect (nimitta-bhāga) and the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) as its object; the master Sthiramati maintains that it takes both the seeds and the manifest as its object;
and the master Dharmapāla alone maintains that it takes only the seeing-part as its object—this is the correct doctrine. Regarding the first interpretation, this is the position held by Nanda:

he asserts that when taking the mind-king (citta-rāja) as its object, it grasps it as "I," and when taking the mental factors (caitta) as its object, it grasps them as "mine"; thus, it is said "respectively. Regarding the second interpretation, this is...
The Fire-Orator refutes Nanda’s text, stating that the Sage has taught this consciousness takes the ālayavijñāna as its object;

nowhere has it been stated that the seven [consciousnesses] take the eighth and its five mental factors as their objects. Therefore, what he has said is logically untenable. He establishes his own position, saying:

"It should take both the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) and the *darśana-bhāga* (perceptual aspect) as its objects. When taking the *darśana-bhāga* as its object, it clings to it as a self; when taking the *nimitta-bhāga* as its object, it clings to it as..."

"Belonging to me" (mamakāra). Why? Because both the perceived object and the perceiving subject have consciousness as their essence; thus, it does not contradict the Noble One’s teaching on the meaning of the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as the objective condition.
Regarding the third point, there is an interpretation which cites the passage from Ananta’s critique of Dignāga, stating: "This, too, is not logical."

Why is this so? First, it is illogical because the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) consists of the five sense faculties and the five objects; these are subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and not the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Second, it is illogical because the sacred teachings state that the seven [consciousnesses] have only internal objects.

If they were to take the objective aspect as their object, they would be taking external things as their object; how would this differ from the five sensory consciousnesses? They should instead be like the sixth consciousness, which takes common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as its object.
Third, it is unreasonable [to claim that the self] is the object [of the notion of "mine"], because one conceives of the sense organs and the body as "mine.
For those born in the formless realm, there should be no "mine," because within the formless realm, there are no forms. This is unreasonable. Fourth.

The proponent of their own position states: It must take both seeds and manifestations as its objects; that is, it takes the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as its object, grasping it as "self," and it takes the seeds as its object, grasping them as "mine.
Question: Since the seventh consciousness does not take real objects as its domain, how can it take seeds as its object? Answer:
Because the seeds are merely a portion of that very consciousness—the functional capacity to produce consciousness—and are not substantially existent entities, they can therefore be taken as objects.
The fourth interpretation represents the correct meaning of Dharmapāla. He challenges Sthiramati, saying:

"If you maintain that the seventh [consciousness] takes seeds as its object, then the seeds of form and so forth must be substantially existent dharmas; they would not be subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness, and the seventh [consciousness] could not take them as its object.

Furthermore, to maintain that seeds are not substantially existent contradicts the treatise. If one says that seeds are merely provisional entities, they cannot be called 'causal conditions' (hetu-pratyaya)."
Because the principle of dependent origination must necessarily be true. Furthermore, a general objection is raised:

The seventh [consciousness], the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), arises spontaneously as a single category and continues in a constant succession. How could it allow for a separate grasping of "self" and "mine"?

Within a single moment of mind, there cannot be both the manifest and the seed consciousnesses, nor the two objects of annihilation and permanence. If there were two such objects, how could they be separately grasped while functioning simultaneously? If...

As for the claim that what was previously severed and what is subsequently constant cannot coexist in a continuous stream, this co-arising view has operated as a single flavor from beginningless time;
since there is no sequence of before and after, how could two distinct attachments arise in succession? To state the correct principle:

one should know that the seventh consciousness only takes the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portion) of the eighth consciousness as its object, and not its other *nimitta-bhāga* (imagined portion), seeds, or mental factors (*caitta*).

And so forth. Why is this? It is because, from beginningless time, it has been of a subtle and uniform nature; it appears to be permanent because it is uninterrupted, and it appears to be unitary because it distinguishes itself from objects.
Since those phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) are all intermittent, their seeds are likewise either suppressed or sometimes permanently severed.
By this, the notion that other consciousnesses constitute the self is excluded. Furthermore, its appearance as unitary distinguishes it from the mind (*citta*).

Because it consists of many mental factors (*caitta*). Question: Why does it not take other consciousnesses as its object? Answer: That which is called "self" possesses the characteristic of activity;
since the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) perceives objects, its characteristic of activity is manifest and resembles a self; therefore, it does not take other consciousnesses as its object.

The functions of self-realization and so forth are subtle and difficult to know. Question: Why not simply take a single sensation (*vedanā*) and so on as the self, since it is also permanent and unitary?
Answer: That which is called "self" has the meaning of sovereignty, the sense of being the master of all things, and serves as the basis for all phenomena (*dharma*).
Mental factors (*caitta*) are not like this; they cannot be the self. Only the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is the basis.

Therefore, this seventh consciousness constantly clings to [the ālayavijñāna] as an internal self, because it is not [an external object] such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; it does not cling to it as an external self.
If it were to take only consciousness as its object, it would give rise only to the notion of "I" and would lack the notion of "mine. A former master raises an objection:

"If you say that the seventh consciousness does not cling to 'mine,' why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that the seventh manas-clinging is characterized by the constant coexistence of the clinging to 'I' and 'mine'?"

It is because it is appropriate. The *Hufa hui* (Assembly for Protecting the Dharma) states: "Because it follows the momentum of the discourse. What is meant by "momentum of the discourse"? It is said:

"Because it accords with the convenience of the text" and "because the expression is smooth and easy. This is what is meant by "momentum of the discourse. For example, when one says "younger brother," one immediately says "brothers"; this is what is meant by being "smooth and easy.
When I speak of "what belongs to me" (*ātmīya*), I am not asserting that there is a "mine" distinct from and separate from the self; I am merely speaking of the "younger brother."

The eighth is "my self. The first five aggregates are the provisional entity that serves as the object of the sixth [consciousness]. The latter "self" is what is conceptualized by the seventh [consciousness];
alternatively, the former "self" refers to a preceding moment and the latter "self" refers to a succeeding moment, both of which are conceptualized by the seventh [consciousness].
Alternatively, one may conceive within a single moment that "this is it. This is exclusively what is conceived by the seventh [consciousness].

Or, the former is the substance and the latter is the cognitive function of consciousness; thus, upon the basis of a single view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), they are metaphorically described by the two terms "self" and "object."
In reality, there is only the single view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). Therefore, the objection is raised: "If this is stated, it accords well with both scripture and reasoning.

What does it mean to accord with scripture? It is said: Because many passages speak only of the existence of the view of self; this is what accords with scripture. What does it mean to accord with reasoning?

It is said: "Because the grasping at 'I' and 'mine' do not arise simultaneously; this accords with reason. Regarding the fact that many passages speak only of the "view of self" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Because of this, the final stage, the view of self, pride, and so forth are always associated together. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"Because of this mental faculty (*manas*), it is always associated with the view of self, the conceit of self (*ātma-māna*), and so forth. [The terms] "I" and "mine" [are explained as follows].
Regarding the claim that the two attachments do not arise simultaneously: because the modes of apprehension (*ākāra*) and the objects (*ālambana*) are distinct for each, they cannot coexist;

such a thing does not occur. Furthermore, "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*) are like a king and his minister. The self is like the king, and what belongs to the self is like the minister.

Once something is grasped as the self, it can certainly not be what belongs to the self. Just as one who is facing directly south cannot simultaneously face north, they therefore do not arise together.

If one has already attained the state of the transformed basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it may be so for those with wholesome minds, as they do not harbor such grasping; yet this cannot be used as an analogy [for the case at hand].

This is because the objects of the two types of grasping—of persons and of phenomena—are identical. If the antidote has not yet arisen to sever that grasping at a self, and if the basis has not yet been transformed, [the mind] takes only the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, having already transformed the basis and entered the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), it likewise takes [that same object].

Regarding *tathatā* (suchness) and all phenomena, those such as the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas of the Two Vehicles who have attained the ten kinds of equality by taking only the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness) as their object, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: first, supreme delight in all marks;

second, the dependent origination of all experiences; third, being free from distinct characteristics and non-characteristics; fourth, great compassion that extensively delivers others; fifth, being without dependence.
1. Great compassion; 2. manifesting in accordance with the inclinations of all sentient beings; 3. the teaching that "I" is the self-love of all sentient beings;
4. the world and tranquility are of one single flavor; 5. the various phenomena of the world, both suffering and pleasure, are of one single flavor.

Having reached the ultimate perfection of cultivating and planting immeasurable merit, and having realized this nature, one immediately knows the differences in the resolute intentions (*adhimukti-manas-kāra*) of sentient beings in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
One is thus able to manifest the images of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) to preach the Dharma and benefit them;
therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata manifests the Body for Others' Enjoyment, which is the object of capacity for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages. Question: If this is so, why...

Therefore, in this context, it takes only the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object. Answer: The statement that it takes only the storehouse consciousness as its object is made with reference to the state prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*);

thus, it is restrictive. This is because when there is awakening, the objects are universal; when there is delusion, the objects are restricted. When there is non-self (*anātman*), the objects are pervasive;

when there is a self (*ātman*), the objects are not pervasive. Question: How is it that this consciousness, having already arisen in dependence upon that [storehouse consciousness], nevertheless takes that very same thing as its object?

Answer: Just as a subsequent moment of consciousness arises depending on the preceding mind (manas) and further takes that preceding mind as its object, the immediately preceding, extinguished mind serves as the *samanantarapratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition).

It is possible for this [preceding mind] to also function as the *ālambanapratyaya* (object-condition) for the subsequent consciousness. As for its functioning as the *āśrayapratyaya* (support-condition), it is the *adhipatipratyaya* (dominant condition).

What fault is there in its also acting as an object-condition? Question: Why does the seventh [consciousness] take only the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] as its object, and not...

Question: Why do [the first six consciousnesses] take both internal parts as their objects? Answer: Because the functioning of the two internal parts is submerged and difficult to perceive, whereas the functioning of the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part) is manifest.

Question: Since the seventh consciousness possesses its own *nimitta-bhāga* (objective part), why does it not take that as its object, but instead takes the *darśana-bhāga* of the eighth consciousness as the self?

Answer: To say that it "takes the *darśana-bhāga* as its object" refers to a remote (indirect) objectification. Question: Even if one grants that the seventh consciousness takes [the eighth] as its object...

Regarding the "distant object-condition" (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*): First, upon what phenomena does the seventh consciousness (*manas*) give rise to grasping? Answer: It gives rise to grasping toward the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of its own consciousness. Question:
When the seventh consciousness takes the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) of the eighth consciousness as its objective essence (*bhāva*), is that real or provisional?

Answer: The seventh consciousness does not cling to the *darśana-bhāga* of the eighth; it merely apprehends the intermediate, provisional characteristic of the self-aspect (*ātma-nimitta-bhāga*), which is provisional.
It is not real. Question: Is the intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) real or provisional? Answer: The intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* does not arise from real seeds;

it arises solely from the two ends [the object and the subject]. It thus encompasses both natures (*svabhāva*). If one half arises from the fundamental essence (*mūla-vastu*), it is of an unobscured nature (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*).
If one half arises from its own perceiving seventh *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect), [it is of an obscured nature].
As for that which arises, it is of an obscured nature (*nivṛta*). It arises from two mental factors (*caitta*) as a single objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), merging closely into one place.

If this refers to the seventh [consciousness], it merely grasps at its own false arising as a pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) of an obscured, provisional objective aspect as its internal self;
it does not grasp at an unobscured (*anivṛta*) objective aspect. It is like the taste of salt in water: it merely grasps...

This is water; it does not grasp the salt. Water and the taste of salt are fundamentally inseparable. Question: Regarding the seventh [consciousness] taking the eighth as its object, what kind of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does this fall under?

Answer: It falls under the category of non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), because it does not correspond to the actual state of things. This is because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] is fundamentally not the self, yet it is falsely grasped as the self;
thus, it does not correspond to the essential nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, when directly taking the seeing-part of the eighth as its object...
The *bhāga* (aspect) does not adhere to the transforming aspect (*pariṇāma-bhāga*) as its object.

Since the aspect is fundamentally not the self, yet it is falsely grasped as the self, and furthermore, it does not correspond to the aspect, there are thus two layers of non-correspondence with the object; therefore, it is known to be an invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Thus, a verse from the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says: "The manas takes the ālayavijñāna as its object, like a magnet attracting iron; it is like a snake with two heads, each acting separately."
Its activity is as follows: the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) likewise grasps the *ālayavijñāna* and is able to perform the functions of a self;
it increases the notion of "mine" and, further, acting in conjunction with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it transforms and passes away as its cause.

It generates warmth within the body and performs various movements and activities. It experiences food, drink, clothing, and other objects according to their nature; it leaps and bounds, or engages in song and dance.
They sport in various ways, sustaining the bodies of all sentient beings solely through the power of the mind.
Like a whirling firebrand, falling hair, or a city of gandharvas, failing to realize that these are but one's own mind, they give rise to false conceptualizations.
The characteristics of the body and the vessel-like world are like the momentum of a swinging swing—lacking power and lacking solidity; conceptualization is likewise so. Conceptualization...
They have no basis; they merely operate within their own respective objects. Like reflections in a mirror, consciousness arises from the movement of seeds and is perceived.
This is a delusion for the foolish, but not for those of clear intelligence. O Lord of Men, you should know that these three are all manifestations of consciousness.
In this state of seclusion, there is the perfectly realized reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
As for the verse’s statement that "deliberation constitutes its nature and characteristic," it refers to the thorough investigation of the characteristic of selflessness (*anātman*).
The fourth section explains the two gates of essential nature (*svabhāva*) and mode of activity (*ākāra*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Reflection is the mind (*manas*); the mind is the nature.
The preceding eighth consciousness has 'discernment' as its mode of activity; since it is now called 'mind,' we know it is the seventh."
The aspect (*ākāra*) is precisely the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). Its essential nature is difficult to know; its reality is revealed through its aspect.

Discursive deliberation (*manana*) is merely the aspect, and its substance is subsumed within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Therefore, prior to the first bhūmi, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in training constantly and critically deliberate upon the mark of self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*);
this is termed the outflow-tainted *manas*. Even in the stage where the basis has been transformed (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it likewise critically deliberates.
Because it lacks the characteristic of self, it is also called *manas*. The treatise asks: As the Blessed One spoke of "transcendent *manas*," how is it established?

The answer is: there are two senses. First, the name does not necessarily correspond to the meaning; that seventh [consciousness], being untainted (*anāsrava*), is not called *manas*, as its name is merely conventional.
Second, because it is able to discern and deliberate upon the characteristic of non-self, it is also called *manas*.

That [aspect] reveals and penetrates the untainted (*anāsrava*); thus one knows that this name is not exclusively tainted. Question: Among the four parts of the seventh [consciousness], which part is called "discursive deliberation" (*vitarka*)?
Answer: There are two meanings. According to the first meaning, it is the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) that is called "discursive deliberation," and it is not named "mind" (*manas*).

The two internal divisions are called "mind" (*manas*) and not "investigation" (*manana*). This is because investigation is a function, whereas the seeing division (*darśanabhāga*) is capable of investigating self and non-self, as it is the essence.
The two internal divisions cannot investigate self and non-self. This is the second meaning.

The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) has "reflection" (*manana*) as its characteristic. "Characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the essential nature, the marks, and the appearances. The two parts [the seeing-part and the self-evident part] have reflection as their nature;

thus, both the internal and external are called "mind" (*manas*). All three parts are called "reflection," with the exception of the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), which is the object of measurement because it lacks the functional capacity of being a cognizing subject.
Question: The seeing-part takes the self-image-part as its object and reflects upon the self; can this be called...?
Question: The self-witnessing division (svasaṃvittibhāga) does not take the self-image division (ātmabhāga) as its object; how, then, can it also be called "cogitation" (manana)? Answer:
Because the self-witnessing division witnesses that the seeing division (darśanabhāga) cogitates upon the grasping of a self, it is also called "cogitation."
How many mental factors (*caitta*) are associated with this manas? [The text continues until: "Therefore, there is no contradiction between the meaning of these respective passages.
This is the fifth section, the explanation of the concomitance with defilements. First, a general question is posed: "Now, as for... and so forth. Next, a specific answer is given:

the word "now" (*tāvat*) is used because there are other mental factors; these four are the most prominent, and thus they are mentioned first. From "In this regard... onwards, the meaning of "concomitance" (*sahabhū*) is explained.

First is self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), which is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*). It refers to being deluded by the appearance of a self-image that is a transformation of one's own mind, and being confused regarding the principle of the suchness of non-self;
hence it is called self-delusion. Second is self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), which is the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).

It refers to giving rise to false conceptualization regarding the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of consciousness—which is not a self—and clinging to it as a real self; hence it is called self-view. Third...

The first is *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am"). This refers to arrogance; relying on the internal self (*ātman*) that one clings to as real, it causes the cognizing mind to become haughty and conceited.
Therefore, it is called *asmimāna*. The fourth is *ātmasneha* (self-love). This is simply self-attachment (*ātmatṛṣṇā*);

toward the object of the internal self-characteristic that one clings to as real, one develops deep fondness and firmly gives rise to defiled attachment. Therefore, it is called *ātmasneha*. [The word] "and" (*ca*)...
This indicates that *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") and *ātmasneha* (self-love) are necessarily associated with *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-identity).
Since *asmimāna* arises by relying upon *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, and *ātmasneha* likewise arises by relying upon *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, pride (*māna*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are definitely associated.
This refutes the Sarvāstivāda position that craving, pride, and views cannot arise simultaneously and thus lack the quality of association (*saṃprayoga*). For this reason...
The four kinds of afflictive dharmas disturb the internal mind, causing the six external evolving consciousnesses to lack purity and remain perpetually defiled.
Because of these, sentient beings rise and sink within saṃsāra and fail to achieve liberation;
therefore, they are called "afflictions" (*kleśa*). This seventh [consciousness], the manas, apart from the four delusions, does not associate with other mental factors.
Regarding "concomitance" (*samprayukta*): first, because it is constant; second, because it internally grasps; and third, because it arises toward a homogeneous object.
Therefore, one does not apply attention (*manasikāra*) to pursue outwardly, but rather functions spontaneously and exclusively as an internal grasping.

Question: There are ten types of afflictions (*kleśa*); why are there only four here? Answer: Because of the existence of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the other four views are all [included therein].
It arises. Why? Because there are not two wisdoms (*prajñā*) within a single moment of consciousness, and all views (*dṛṣṭi*) have wisdom as their essence.

Question: How is it that this consciousness necessarily possesses the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*)? Answer: The three types—view of a self, adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—are the conceptual grasping of self (*vikalpa-ātma-grāha*) belonging to the sixth consciousness.
Since these are suddenly and completely severed upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), [the view of self]... [is absent].
The view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is essentially innate (*sahaja*); it is only during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) that it is completely abandoned.
Therefore, it does not correspond with those three [types of afflictions]. The extreme view of "mine" (*mamakāra-antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) must arise based upon a corresponding view of self;

thus, wherever there is an extreme view, there is necessarily a view of self. However, this corresponding view of self does not depend upon the extreme view; therefore, it does not correspond with it.
It is associated with extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Question: Why is this consciousness not associated with the two afflictions of doubt (*vicikitsā*) and hatred (*dveṣa*)?
Answer: Because of the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), it is characterized by careful examination and decisive clarity; since there is no room for doubt to arise, it is not associated with doubt.
Because of self-love (*ātmasneha*), one develops deep attachment; thus, aversion (*dveṣa*) cannot arise, and therefore it is not associated with aversion.

For this reason, among the ten afflictions (*kleśa*), this consciousness is associated with only four. Furthermore, it is asked: "How can the three—view (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and self-love (*sneha*)—arise simultaneously?
The answer is: "Because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) do not conflict. Furthermore, it is asked: "Greed causes the mind to sink; pride causes the mind..."
Question: One is high and one is low; how is this not contradictory? Answer: It is said that there is the distinction between the discriminative (*vikalpita*) and the innate (*sahaja*).

Regarding greed, there is the external object and the internal object. Regarding pride, there is that which is disparaged and that which is relied upon. These three—discrimination, greed, and pride—each possess both coarse and subtle aspects.

The coarse belongs to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*), while the subtle belongs to the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*). This is the meaning of their modes of activity (*ākāra*) being non-contradictory.
Does this mental consciousness (manas-citta) consist of only four mental factors? [Up to: If one explains it in this way, it does not contradict reason or scripture.

Sixth, the explanation of the remaining associated factors. First, the question: "Is it not so? and below, the response by citing the verse. Below, there are five points of meaning. The first maintains that there are only nine:
namely, the four afflictions (*kleśa*) and the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), such as contact (*sparśa*), which are necessarily associated.
Therefore, it is asked: "Since it is associated with contact (*sparśa*) and so forth, one should say 'together with contact and so forth. Why, then, does it say 'and the rest' (*cānyaiḥ*)? Answer:

Because the five [mental factors] such as the previously mentioned resultant contact (*vipāka-sparśa*) are of an unobscured nature (*anivṛta*), there was concern that these five might be confused with the eighth [consciousness], which is also unobscured.
Therefore, the word "rest" (*anya*) is placed [there]. Furthermore, "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "collection" (*samuccaya*). As for the preceding four afflictions...

The [afflictions of] *daurmanasya* (dejection) and so forth; the latter five are universal because they are necessarily associated with [the mind]. The remaining characters are not [universal]; some characters and half of others are correct, while the other half are incorrect. Question:
For what reason is this manas not associated with the object-specific (*viṣayaviśeṣa*) mental factors? Answer: Desire (*chanda*) is the aspiration for an object that has not yet been attained.
This consciousness is always in union with the eighth consciousness, taking it as its object; thus, there is no further aspiration. Therefore, [desire is absent].
It is not associated with *adhimokṣa* (resolute conviction). Since the object of resolute conviction is not yet determined, one generates a definitive understanding, confirms it, and maintains it;

this consciousness, however, is invariably and constantly grasping the eighth [consciousness] as its internal self, without any other thoughts, and thus does not require the effort of confirmation or maintenance.
Therefore, it is not associated with *adhimokṣa*. *Smṛti* (mindfulness) merely recollects past activities that have been practiced. This...

The consciousness [in question] constantly takes the manifest objects of the eighth [storehouse consciousness] as its objective support; thus, it does not require the effort of memory and is therefore not associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*).

As for concentration (*samādhi*), this consciousness is singular in its intent, focusing on a single object; yet, because it functions spontaneously, moment by moment, taking distinct objects and being neither constant nor unified, it is not associated with concentration.
Since wisdom (*prajñā*) is itself a form of seeing (*dṛṣṭi*), it is not treated separately. These four explanations are correct.

The commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "It is not associated with the wholesome [mental factors]. Question: Why is it not associated with the eleven wholesome mental factors (*caitasika*)? Answer:

Because the wholesome is pure (*viśuddha*), whereas this consciousness is defiled (*kliṣṭa*); therefore, it is not associated with the wholesome. Question: Why is it not associated with the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)? Answer:
Secondary afflictions necessarily follow a portion of the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). [This consciousness does not associate with them because it does not arise from such roots.]

Regarding the establishment of the distinctions of states: it is said that this consciousness is associated only with the four afflictions (*kleśa*) and therefore does not correspond with the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
This statement is extremely erroneous. Question: Why is it not associated with the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*)?

Answer: Regret (*kaukṛtya*) is the remorse for actions performed in the past. This consciousness always takes the eighth [consciousness] as its object in the present; [regret] does not exist [therein].

Because of doubt and regret, it is not associated with *kaukṛtya* (remorse). Sleep depends upon external conditions, involves hardship and exertion, and results in the body being unmastered and the mind becoming extremely dull;
it manifests only occasionally. This consciousness is of a single type that internally grasps the eighth [consciousness] as the self;
since it does not depend on external conditions, it is not associated with sleep. Regarding *vitarka* and *vicāra*: *vitarka* refers to...
Vitarka (applied thought) is defined as seeking; its nature is to cause the mind to operate coarsely upon the objects of mental discourse. Vicāra (sustained thought) is defined as investigation;

its nature is to cause the mind to operate subtly upon the objects of mental discourse. This consciousness operates solely by way of the internal door, is of a single class that clings to a self, and does not depend on vitarka and vicāra;
therefore, it is not associated with them. [The author] has previously refuted other points of the former master.
This is because this consciousness is clearly identified as "obscured-neutral" (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) within this very verse;

furthermore, it lacks [the mention of] being associated with secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Since there must be branches when there is a root, these remaining words are intended to show association with secondary afflictions and do not exclude the "unobscured" (*anivṛta*).
Thus, this remains a general statement. This master bases his view on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
It is taught that there are five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that are always concomitant with all defiled states.

If one were to exclude lethargy (*akarmanyatā*), lack of tranquility (*apraśāntatā*), turbidity (*dausthulya*), indolence (*kausīdya*), and dissipation (*pramāda*), then the nature of defilement could not be established.
Since the mind is already defiled when an affliction arises, these [five] must necessarily exist within that state of defilement.
Since there are five of them, they must necessarily be associated with the five *anuvyañjanas*. Question: The single factor of restlessness (*auddhatya*) pervades all defiled minds;

why is it not included among the four primary afflictions (*kleśa*), but instead placed within the category of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)? Answer: Although it pervades all defiled minds, [it is so categorized for specific reasons].

Although craving is divided into many parts, only the part belonging to craving is mentioned here; this is because one who has great desire necessarily possesses much discursive thought (*vitarka*). This is similar to sleep (*middha*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*): although they pervade all three types of minds—those associated with greed, hatred, and delusion—they are said to be "parts of delusion" (*mohāmśika*) because they are predominant in the state of delusion. Question: Other sources state that there are six [mental factors] that accompany greed and ten that accompany all defiled minds. Why does this text speak of only five? Answer: [The text speaks of five] because it intends to include those that are common to all defiled minds. Specifically, the six that accompany greed are included within the category of "associated with greed," while the ten that accompany all defiled minds are included within the category of "associated with delusion. Thus, by mentioning these two categories, all are effectively subsumed. Furthermore, the six that accompany greed are not mentioned separately because they are already included within the "associated with greed" category, and the ten that accompany all defiled minds are not mentioned separately because they are already included within the "associated with delusion" category. Therefore, by mentioning these two, all are encompassed. Consequently, there is no contradiction with other treatises. Moreover, the reason for mentioning only the "associated with greed" and "associated with delusion" categories is that these two are the most prominent among the mental factors that accompany greed and the mental factors that accompany all defiled minds, respectively.
