they lack a simultaneous support (sahabhū-āśraya), and it is proven that the sixth [consciousness] likewise lacks one. The Mahāyāna refutes this, saying:

"If you claim that the five consciousnesses lack a simultaneous support and thus prove the same for the sixth, you may not say that the five consciousnesses and their organs arise simultaneously, like a sprout [and its seed]."

Because it is like a shadow. Just as a sprout arises depending on a seed, yet the sprout and the seed exist simultaneously, so too a shadow arises depending on a body, and the body and the shadow exist together.

Likewise, consciousness arises depending on the sense faculties (indriya), and by principle they must be simultaneous; for there is no case where a preceding momentary faculty gives rise to a subsequent momentary consciousness.
Since the five consciousnesses possess simultaneous faculties, one should prove that the sixth consciousness likewise must have a simultaneous faculty.
[Question: What else could the root be if not the seventh consciousness? [Response: The Hīnayāna school says:

"We do not allow that a preceding moment of the sense organ (indriya) gives rise to a succeeding moment of consciousness; rather, we must allow that the preceding moment can induce the succeeding moment.

Thus, the *samanantara-manas* (equal-and-immediate mind) is surely the root upon which the six consciousnesses depend. [The Mahāyāna] refutes this, saying: "The *samanantara-manas* cannot serve as the root for this consciousness."
[The mind] depends [on its support]. Since consciousness and its support must necessarily exist simultaneously, one establishes the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
"The five consciousnesses and their faculties are necessarily simultaneous, because they necessarily share the same object, just like the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

By this reasoning, it is established that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) must necessarily have an uncommon, simultaneous support (*asādhāraṇa-sahabhū-āśraya*). One establishes the formal argument as follows: "The subject (*dharmin*) is the well-established mental consciousness; it must necessarily have..."

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that [the six consciousnesses] manifest their own names according to their respective bases (*āyatana*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because they are subsumed under one or another of the six well-established consciousnesses, which are not included within the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) but serve as the basis for the arising of the predominant [consciousness]. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like the eye-consciousness and so forth, which manifest their own names according to their bases;

"manifesting their own names" means, for instance, that the consciousness depending on the eye is called "eye-consciousness," and so on. "Subsumed under one or another" means being included within one of the six [consciousnesses].

[It is] included therein. Since the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, each have their own name and location based on the five sense organs, the sixth mental consciousness must likewise possess its own unique mental organ (*asādhāraṇa-manas*) to manifest its own name and location.
Therefore, it is not included among those [factors] that are immediately antecedent conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This excludes the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) position, which does not allow the seventh consciousness to serve as the basis for the arising of the sixth;
for [in that system], the sixth arises from the immediately preceding, extinguished mind (*manas*) as its root, because it gives rise to the subsequent moment of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Regarding "the predominant basis for arising," the immediately preceding, extinguished mind is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), while the root is the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). Thus, it is established that each of the six types of consciousness follows its respective predominance.
This is because it is certainly not subsumed under the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), as it is subsumed under the five superior faculties (*indriya*).
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that "that which cogitates is called the mind" (*manas*); thus, the designation "mind" is applied metaphorically based on what has already ceased.
"Discrimination by reflection is called 'manas' (the mind). First, the scripture is cited; second, the proof is established, beginning with "If... and so forth. Next, the meaning is explained:

when it is said in the teachings that there is "discrimination by reflection," this refers precisely to the seventh consciousness. The Śrāvakas (Hīnayānists) say: "The manas as discrimination by reflection is simply the sixth consciousness in its state of immediate succession (*samanantara*);
why is it necessary to separately designate the seventh as the manas of discrimination by reflection? [Thus asks] the Master of the Treatise.

The *Pòyún* (Commentary on the Refutation) says: Furthermore, when the sixth consciousness is present, the preceding moment of the equal-and-immediate mind (*samanantarā-manas*) has already ceased and lacks substantiality.
How, then, can it possess the function of deliberation (*manana*) such that it is named "mind" (*manas*)?

Why is this so? Because, according to principle, the past and future do not exist. Since that [preceding mind] does not exist, the function of deliberation certainly cannot be established. Since it is non-existent...
Consider this: how can it be called "mind" (*manas*)? If you claim that although this mind has already ceased, it is designated as such by way of metaphor, this reasoning is also incorrect.

Since the designation "mind" is established based on correct mental deliberation (*samanvāhāra*), if there is no correct mental deliberation, upon what could the metaphorical designation be established?
If it is argued that although it belongs to the past, it is called "manas" (mind) because it was once a deliberative faculty in the present, this reasoning is also incorrect.
For when the sixth consciousness exists in the present, although it performs deliberation, it is always termed "vijñāna" (consciousness) and not "manas";
it is only by depending on its past state that it is termed "manas. Therefore, one knows that apart from the sixth [consciousness], there is a separate manas.
That which constantly and thoroughly deliberates is alone entitled to be called "manas" (mind). "Manas" has the sense of being a basis;

the immediately preceding manas relies upon this seventh consciousness and is thus metaphorically given the name "manas. This is because it possesses the function of simultaneous support and deliberation.

Furthermore, the seventh consciousness is accompanied by the four afflictions and is therefore termed "defiled. Because it constantly and thoroughly deliberates, it is named "manas," and it exists perpetually.

Because it functions with non-associated ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), it is called "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*). It is precisely of an obscured nature (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*); that is, it obscures the true meaning and veils pure, sublime wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "constantly and deliberatively cogitating": this distinguishes [this manas] from the eighth consciousness and the first six consciousnesses.
"Constantly" means uninterrupted; "deliberatively" means it definitively clings to a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*). Question: The eighth consciousness is also uninterrupted, and the sixth...

Question: Since there is definitely deliberation (*manana*), why is it not called "mind" (*manas*)? Answer: There are four possibilities (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, that which is constant but not investigative: this refers to the eighth [consciousness].

It is constant and uninterrupted, yet it does not investigate or deliberate upon a self (*ātman*) or phenomena (*dharma*); therefore, it is not called mind. Second, that which is investigative but not constant: this refers to the sixth [consciousness].
Although it investigates and deliberates, it is not constant; therefore, it is not called mind. The first five [consciousnesses] are neither, and thus are not [called mind].

The seventh [consciousness] is always and invariably associated with both [constant and investigative mentation]. Because it is both constant and investigative, it alone is named *manas*. Question: What dharma does the seventh consciousness cogitate? Answer:
It clings to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness], cogitating that there is a self and dharmas.

In the stage of the Aśaikṣa (No-more-learning) of the two vehicles, although there is no clinging to a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*), because they still cogitate the clinging to dharmas as a self, it is called *manas*. At the stage of Buddhahood, both clinging to a self and clinging to dharmas are entirely absent.
There is none. It is the constant and thorough deliberation upon the principle of selflessness. The seventh [consciousness] of the Buddha-fruit is also called *manas*. Question:
Does the seventh consciousness itself possess deliberation, or is it that the *cetanā* within the universal mental factors associated with the seventh consciousness is termed "deliberative *manas*"?

Answer: Regarding the statement that "the mind which possesses volition (*cetanā*) is what is taken [as the manas]," all eight consciousnesses possess volition; why then is it attributed solely to the seventh? Question:

If it is only that which possesses volition as its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that is taken [as the manas], then why employ the mental factor (*caitta*) of volition from among the mental concomitants?

Answer: It possesses two meanings: first, there is volition through association (*samprayukta-cetanā*); second, there is volition as its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-cetanā*). Here, we take that which possesses volition as its own intrinsic nature.

The term "measure" (pramāṇa) refers to the "mind" (manas). Question: Since the mental factors (caitta) and the mind-king (citta-rāja) are of one kind, and both constantly and attentively deliberate upon and grasp the eighth consciousness as the self, why is it not said that the mental factors are the "mind"? Answer: To speak of the "mind" (manas) carries the meaning of being a "basis" (āśraya).

Although the mental factors constantly and attentively deliberate, they are not the primary agent; they are subordinate phenomena and are not the basis [upon which the mind relies]. Therefore, they are not called the "mind."
Second, the self-substance consciousness possesses mentation (*manana*) and serves as the support for the other seven consciousnesses;

taking only the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), it is designated as "mind" (*manas*). Question: If that which possesses mentation in its own substance is called "mind," then since the seventh [consciousness] has four parts, why is it specifically termed "mentating mind"?
Answer: There are two interpretations. First, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is termed "mentating."
Regarding the *pramāṇa* (cognition): the two internal parts are not called "investigation" (*saṃtīraṇa*); they are merely called "mind" (*manas*).

The aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) is not called "mind," because it possesses the function of investigation; it investigates self and non-self. The two internal parts cannot investigate self and non-self.

It is called "mind" (*manas*) simply because it has this as its essence. The second part, the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect), is characterized by deliberation (*manana*). "Characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the essential nature, the attributes, and the specific marks.
These two internal parts possess the nature of deliberation; thus, both the internal and external [aspects] are called "mind.

All three parts involve deliberation, with the exception of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), which is the object of deliberation. Question: How is it known that there are both internal and external [parts]?

Question: "The three parts are all of the nature of deliberation (*manana*). Answer: The *Śāstra* says that deliberation constitutes their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

The two internal parts constitute the essence; they are called the nature of deliberation. The external seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is the characteristic of deliberation; it is the function. One kind is deliberation; all three parts are named "mind" (*manas*).
This means that the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is not taken as deliberation, because it lacks the function of being an objective referent (*ālambaka*). Question:
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the grasping of self and phenomena as its object; because it deliberates upon the self, it is termed "deliberation" (*manana*). [Question:
The self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) does not take the self-aspect (*sva-nimitta-bhāga*) as its object; how, then, can the self-witnessing-part also be termed "deliberation"? [Answer:
Because the self-witnessing-part witnesses that seeing-part’s deliberation regarding the grasping of the self, it is also termed "deliberation. [Question: The seeing-part deliberates upon the self.

This is not subsumed under valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Question: When the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) cognizes that the seeing part (*darśana-bhāga*) conceives of a self, is the self-cognizing part also non-valid cognition?
[Answer: The seeing part conceives of a self; because the seeing part is a false attachment, it is called non-valid cognition.

Because the self-cognizing part internally cognizes that the seeing part is a false attachment, the essence of the self-cognizing part is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, both its essence and its function are [direct perception].

Regarding "investigation" (*manana*): the two internal divisions are also called *manas* (mind) and also called *vijñāna* (consciousness). The seeing division (*darśanabhāga*) is also called *manas* and also called *vijñāna*, because it is the function of the mind.
Investigation is the function; the mind is the essence. Thus, "investigation is the mind" (*mananaṃ eva manas*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Furthermore, the sūtras speak of the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation (up to the point where it says): "Therefore, there must certainly be this distinct manas.
First, the sūtra is cited; next, the proof is established, stating: "As for those two [attainments] below. Next, the meaning is explained:
"Those two attainments extinguish the six consciousnesses along with their mental factors; they are identical in substance and number, differing only in that the afflicted manas..."
If one of the two meditative attainments possesses [the seventh consciousness] while the other lacks it, then there would be a distinction between them.
If the seventh [consciousness] were non-existent, then regarding its presence or absence within those attainments, what distinction would there be between these two types of attainment?

If you argue that the distinction lies in the preparatory effort (*prayoga*), realm (*dhātu*), stage (*bhūmi*), support (*āśraya*), and so forth, this is also logically untenable. Why is this so? Because the cause of such a distinction is due to this...

Because it exists; that is to say, because this seventh consciousness exists, when one takes the mental attention (*manasikāra*) on the perception of renunciation as the precursor, causing the non-perpetually active mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) to cease, and designates it by the name "Non-ideation" (*asaṃjñin*) primarily because ideation has ceased—this meditative absorption belongs exclusively to the fourth dhyāna.
If, however, one takes the mental attention on the perception of cessation as the precursor, causing the non-perpetually active and perpetually active defiled [factors] to cease...

It is called "cessation" because it extinguishes the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*). Although it belongs to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it is not subsumed under the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
If this [defiled] mind were absent, how could its cause exist? Therefore, [the author] concludes below. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:

"Furthermore, there would be the fault that no distinction would exist between the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). As Vasubandhu explains: "If [this mind] were established as existing..."
There exists the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*); its presence or absence follows the respective order of the continuums of ordinary beings and noble ones.

By this principle, the distinction between the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) is established. Otherwise, if there were consciousness-activity in both the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*) equally, there would be no distinction between them.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that [the afflicted manas] exists in the fourth dhyāna or in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Because of their distinction, there is the departure [from the world] and peaceful abiding; because of the distinction in desire, there is the distinction between the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

Since there is no difference in the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of these two, what difference is there when both mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are extinguished? This present determination is somewhat close to the Sautrāntika school;
for that school maintains that the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are not substantially existent (*dravyasat*). How could they [the Vaibhāṣikas] possibly [accept them]?
The two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) truly possess distinct differences. Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Furthermore, because the two attainments are distinct. Why is this so?

If it is definitively taught that there is a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), then this mind exists within the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), whereas it does not exist in the other attainment [the attainment of cessation, *nirodha-samāpatti*].
Therefore, there is a distinction. If it were otherwise, the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would not be absent in both attainments."
Because they are both meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), there should be no distinction between them. Furthermore, it is said:

"The distinction between these two attainments is that within the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) there is no afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), whereas within the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) there is an afflicted mind.

If this [afflicted mind] did not exist, such a distinction between the two attainments would not exist, which would result in a great logical error. This [afflicted mind] cannot be said to exist in the fourth dhyāna.

"Existence" (bhava) refers to the distinctions of realms, stages, supports, and so forth. Furthermore, the distinction between realms and stages is only possible because of the seventh [consciousness].
Moreover, the Sūtra states regarding the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) that "by this [reason], the noble ones (*ārya*) alike censure and loathe them."
Regarding the defilement of the five non-percipient heavens: first, the scripture is cited; next, it is established through proof—namely, "as for those below... Next, the meaning is explained.

The term "one period" (eka-kalpa) refers to the beginning and end of a single retribution. If it is argued that only the sixth [heaven] is permitted and the establishment of a seventh is not allowed...

For example, among those in the Heaven of No-Thought who have entered the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the mind and mental factors have been extinguished for five hundred kalpas.

In that heaven, the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are absent for a long duration. If there were no seventh afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*), then self-grasping would be non-existent.
Where could one find an ordinary person bound by all fetters who, throughout the course of a single lifetime, is entirely devoid of self-clinging?
When those gods in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) suppress the six consciousnesses, they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa and claim for themselves the fruit of arhatship.

Yet when their retribution is exhausted and their lives end, the six consciousnesses arise again, and innate greed manifests; thus it is said that the bodies of these so-called arhats encounter further existence. Therefore...

All noble ones alike censure and loathe it. Since that [state] has been devoid of self-grasping for a long time, it should be pure and untainted like *nirvāṇa*, and thus would not be something censured and loathed by the noble ones. The Hīnayāna proponent offers this defense:

"The six consciousnesses and their mental factors of those gods cease during the first half-aeon and arise during the second half-aeon; because they exist at the beginning and the end, they do not [possess such permanence]."

This is a fallacy. The Mahāyāna refutation states: "If the mind and mental factors were extinguished during the four hundred and ninety-nine intermediate kalpas, such that the sixth consciousness did not exist, yet the grasping of a self still arose, would this not constitute a fault? The defense claims:
"There is no such fault because the sixth consciousness exists in the past and future, and it is capable of grasping a self. The refutation states: "Since that sixth consciousness is not present..."
Since that which exists in meditative absorption is impermanent and has already ceased to possess a substantial entity, how could one possibly cling to it as a self? Would this not be a fault?
Since the fruition of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*) does not exist, the sentient beings who attain non-perception likewise do not exist.

Both the cause and fruit of non-perception, as well as their acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), are all subsumed under the category of dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Dissociated phenomena possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

This has already been refuted previously; there is no need to discuss it further. Furthermore, they argue that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the grasping for a self (*ātma-grāha*) reside within the continuity of the body, yet they fail to realize that such grasping lacks the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). How, then, could it receive perfuming (*vāsana*)?

If it does not receive perfuming, how can there be habitual tendencies? Therefore, this refutation states: since the storehouse consciousness does not exist, perfuming also does not exist. Moreover, this grasping for a self is...

It is subsumed under the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), because it is of the same nature as material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). Since there is no principle for it to receive perfuming (*vāsanā*), it is said:

"The claim that other dharmas receive perfuming has already been demonstrated to be irrational. The *Saṃgrahaṇī* states: "The manifesting mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arising at the moment of birth is not [the basis of self-grasping];

rather, it is called 'possessing self-grasping' because it is induced by the force [of past habituation] and because self-grasping has not yet been permanently severed. This is analogous to epilepsy and the like; thus it accords with correct reasoning. Regarding "I":
Because the grasping and its basis have both perished together, there is no momentum to project [a future existence]; furthermore, it would be illogical for it to rely on another basis.

It is also illogical for the habitual tendencies of the grasping at a self to persist in the continuity of the body, because it is illogical for material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) to be perfumed, and because they lack such capacity.
Therefore, there must exist something distinct—thus concluding that the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) necessarily exists in those heavens.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess wholesome and defiled [minds]... (up to)... therefore, one knows that this seventh consciousness exists separately.

Regarding the six types of ordinary beings' minds of the three natures and their defiled minds—this refers to sentient beings—at the time when they possess minds of the three natures, such as wholesome, defiled, and so forth.
The first six evolving consciousnesses operate within the external gates, performing wholesome or defiled karma; meanwhile, the internal seventh consciousness, moment by moment, clings to a self.
Because of this clinging to a self, it prevents the wholesome or defiled states arising within the six consciousnesses from losing their characteristics—for instance, in acts such as giving.
Thus, when the first six consciousnesses are of a wholesome nature, they are [accompanied] by this seventh [consciousness], which is constant and unique (asādhāraṇa).

This clarifies that because of internal clinging to a self, when the six consciousnesses and so forth perform acts of giving, they are unable to realize that the three spheres are empty in essence and are unable to eliminate signs.
This self is an external condition; its mode of activity is coarse and agitated, and it does not arise from the seventh [consciousness].

Rather, it is by virtue of the seventh that the sixth gives rise to this [clinging]; it arises entirely from the seventh, which is explained here for the sake of further clarification regarding the self-clinging within the sixth consciousness.

Its substance is characterized by interruption, as it arises in alternation with minds of the three natures. Furthermore, the seventh consciousness does not arise by taking external objects as its cognitive domain.
The following citation from the *Yogācārabhūmi* serves to prove that the afflicted manas functions as the defiled support for the sixth consciousness.

Because those defilements have not been extinguished, one clings to a self at every moment, causing the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the first six evolving consciousnesses to be bound by their objects (*nimitta-bandhana*) and unable to attain liberation.
Once the manas has ceased, the sixth consciousness is immediately liberated from this bondage to objects.
What is meant by "bondage to objects"? It refers to being unable to comprehend the various wholesome and defiled karmas performed before one's eyes.
One realizes that [phenomena] are like dreams and illusions, yet one recognizes them as being real.

Because of this, the sixth consciousness-vijñāna becomes bound by its own objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) and fails to attain unimpeded liberation and mastery; therefore, it is called "bondage by signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "Based on such [realization]," the Mahāyāna raises an objection: "If you maintain that there is a sixth [consciousness] but no seventh, then..."

When the two types of minds—wholesome and non-obscured—arise among the six consciousnesses, if the seventh [consciousness] consisting of self-grasping did not exist, those two kinds of minds would become untainted (*anāsrava*).

Why? Because the afflictions that manifest simultaneously with the six consciousnesses do not arise together with those wholesome or neutral minds within one’s own continuum; thus, they do not permeate (*vāsana*) them as tainted. [This applies to] the past... [and so forth].
Because the principle that afflictions arise from external conditions as their objects does not exist, they do not perfuse the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) [dharmas].

This is because it is not through another consciousness becoming deluded regarding the principle of selflessness that wholesome states and the like become outflow-tainted; nor is it through another consciousness understanding the principle of selflessness that wholesome states and the like become outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
This demonstrates that the manifestation of defilement and the manifestation of purity both depend upon the seventh consciousness’s grasping at a self.

One does not grasp at a self, nor does one depend on another. Furthermore, it cannot be said that there exists a separate *anuśaya* (latent tendency) distinct from the mind and mental factors, which is subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*) and arises continuously during states such as the wholesome.

It is by virtue of this that the wholesome and other states become tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena. Why is this? Because those *anuśayas* do not possess a real, substantial essence; they have already been thoroughly [refuted].
Therefore, it cannot be said that those wholesome states and so forth arise from contaminated seeds. Consequently, the wholesome states and so forth become contaminated dharmas. Why is this?
Because by being associated with the outflows (*āsrava*), they become contaminated seeds. Previously, there was no self-grasping associated with the wholesome states and so forth;
thus, those seeds would become contaminated without a cause. If one were to claim that contaminated [seeds] have existed since beginningless time...

It is not the case that seeds are established by nature (*dharmatā*) without being perfumed (*vāsana*), such that when contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) arise, they take these as their cause, and when those contaminated phenomena arise, they in turn perfume and form seeds. Why is this not so?
Because it would follow that even the uncontaminated mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) would become contaminated. Furthermore, the uncontaminated mind of one in training also arises from...
The seeds of the outflowing (sāsrava) arise; however, they do not perfuse the seeds of outflowing dharmas, because within one's own continuum they do not coexist with the outflows.
If it is argued that although wholesome states and the like do not coexist with defilement, they are nevertheless induced by the first six afflictions.
Therefore, it is claimed that giving and so forth constitute *sāsrava* (outflowing) dharmas; however, this is not the case.
Although the karma of giving and so forth is induced by afflictions (*kleśa*), at the moment the karma of giving arises, the afflictions have already ceased and do not co-arise with it.
Thus, they are not the direct cause for being *sāsrava*. Why is this? Because the term "outflowing" (*sāsrava*) signifies that which co-arises with the seeds of outflow. Only then...

Because this is the primary cause. If one were to claim that a wholesome mind associated with outflows becomes "outflowing" because it is induced by the afflictions of those six consciousnesses, then neutral karma would follow from prior karma without depending on present conditions, as it would not be induced by afflictions.
Furthermore, how do these become "with outflows" (*sāsrava*)? The following establishes the correct position:

"However, various karmas such as giving become 'with outflows' only when they arise and cease simultaneously with the manifest afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) of one's own continuum, thereby mutually reinforcing one another.
'One's own' excludes the defilements of others; 'manifest' excludes latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); and 'arising and ceasing simultaneously' [establishes the necessary temporal coincidence]."

This excludes [the outflows] of the past and future, as they would mutually augment one another. It excludes the seeds of the outflows because it is by these [seeds] being perfumed that the seeds of contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are formed;

at a later time, when they manifest, they arise from these seeds, thereby establishing the meaning of "contaminated. Just as this is the case for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), so too is it for the innate contaminated [phenomena] of those in training (*śaikṣa*).
Question: While it is certainly thus for the contaminated [phenomena] of ordinary beings and those in training, what is the case for the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)?

Furthermore, how is this so? Answer: In the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), although the contaminated (*sāsrava*) ālayavijñāna has already been abandoned and thus no longer possesses the four innate afflictions (*kleśa*), the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) has not yet been forgotten. Consequently, from within the previously existing *vipākavijñāna*, there still arises the grasping at a self and phenomena;
though [the seeds] are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they arise as if contaminated. This is not contradictory to reason, because of the presence of the manas.
Because it constantly gives rise to the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), it establishes the status of both wholesome and neutral states of mind as being *sāsrava* (with outflows).

If this manas did not exist, the quality of being *sāsrava* would not be established. Therefore, we know that there exists a distinct seventh [consciousness], the innate grasping at a self, which acts as the cause for wholesome and non-obscured states to become *sāsrava*.
There are many logical arguments proving the existence of this consciousness (up to the point where it is stated that) the types of consciousness actually number eight.
Seven points constitute the proof of this meaning; namely, the six types cited above are the intended meaning within the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

However, regarding those passages in the sūtras which state that the sixth consciousness gives rise to the grasping of a self, one should know that these are all spoken according to conventional designations;
thus such words were uttered. Alternatively, they may be spoken in accordance with the six sense faculties to designate the six consciousnesses.

When discussing the ultimate principle, the categories of consciousness are distinct and actually comprise eight types; it is not meant that the categories of consciousness are limited to only six. This concludes the brief record.
The seventh manas is explained consistently across all teachings and interpreted by the assembly of sages. For those who have newly entered the Path, this consciousness must be clearly understood;

it is the cause for the arising of both the ordinary and the holy. One should thoroughly investigate its essential nature, as it establishes the foundation for both delusion and awakening, and one may thus trace back to its very source.
To be deluded regarding it constitutes the folly of clinging to persons and phenomena; to awaken to it brings about the realization of the nature of equality.

Wisdom (*jñāna*). Among all consciousnesses, it alone receives the name "mind" (*manas*). Within the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*), it acts as the sovereign of ignorance (*avidyā*). It is uninterrupted and unceasing;

though the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) treats it, it is not eliminated. It is ever-examining and eternal. Even when one has avoided it by ascending to the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), it arises again.

Although it is obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*), it does not grasp externally but takes the internal as its object. It constantly arises as active manifestation (*samudācāra*) and is capable of obscuring [the true nature].
Though they are called "unshared" (*āveṇika*), they truly obstruct the Path; they merely produce defilement and nourish rebirth.

Therefore, if one wishes to transcend the dust and toil of worldly existence, one must know the essential shortcut. Before administering the wondrous medicine, one must first ascertain the source of the illness.

If one investigates with meticulous attention and examines with a tranquil mind, what dust will not be cleared away, and what ailment will not be dissolved? This is the gateway for severing delusions.
This is essential. This concludes the second *pariṇāma* (transformation).
Having thus explained the second *pariṇāma*, what are the characteristics of the third *pariṇāma*? Regarding the third *pariṇāma*:

first, there is the summary of the preceding section and the posing of the question; subsequently, the verse provides an explanation divided into four parts. The first is the verse explaining the distinctions.

The first [section] explains the three natures through four gates regarding their essential characteristics; the second verse explains two gates concerning the association of mental factors with feeling;
the third verse explains the detailed manifestation of the distinctions among mental factors; and the fourth verse explains the various states of their actualization.
The verse says: "Next, the third transformative consciousness... [up to] ...taking the apprehension of objects as its nature and characteristic; it is wholesome, unwholesome, or neither.
This verse by Vasubandhu explains the distinct characteristics of the entity through four gates, totaling nine gates in all.
First, the gate of differentiation: that is, the third transformative consciousness has six types of differentiation. Second, the gate of essential nature: that is, the apprehension of...
1. The gate of distinct nature (*svabhāva*): its nature is discernment (*vijñapti*). 2. The gate of the three aspects (*ākāra*): its characteristic is the act of discerning. 3.
The gate of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): it is wholesome, unwholesome, or neither. The remaining five gates follow later. Regarding the first two phrases:

the sixth consciousness necessarily shares the same objects as the preceding five—namely, coarse and manifest objects—and yet possesses contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*), which are capable of establishing future existence (*punar-bhava*). Therefore, these six factors are combined.
Regarding the first [type], the "transforming" (*pariṇāma*).

The treatise says: Following the "transforming consciousness of investigation" (*vitarka-vicāra-pariṇāma-vijñāna*) among the intermediate [categories], the meaning of the objects of perception (*ālambana-artha*) shall now be explained.

First, the explanation of the meaning of the verse is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the section on distinctions; second, the general indication; third, the detailed explanation. Third...

The transforming consciousness consists of six types combined. Although consciousness is a single entity, it is designated by six names according to the distinctions among the categories of sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*).
These are: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.

Since the eyes and so forth are the organs and consciousness is their very essence, these six names are established in accordance with the organs. This is because they possess five meanings: first, the basis (*āśraya*).
Regarding the faculties (*indriya*): [the consciousness] is (1) produced by two faculties, (2) belongs to the faculties, (3) assists the faculties, and (4) is like the faculties.

First, as for "depending on the faculties": the consciousness within the eye is called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*) because consciousness arises depending on the locus of the eye, and because consciousness exists only when the eye exists. Why is this so? Because if the eye-faculty exists, consciousness is certain to exist.
It arises because one who is not blind can even see in the dark; visual consciousness does not necessarily arise simply because color exists, for those who are blind cannot see.
That which is produced by two faculties refers to the consciousness produced by the eye.

Therefore, it is called "eye-consciousness. Because consciousness undergoes transformation through the transformation of the eye, even though the form (rūpa) remains unchanged, consciousness does undergo transformation;
for example, when the visual faculty is impaired by the disease kāmalā, one perceives blue and other colors as yellow.

That which belongs to the faculty—that is, the consciousness belonging to the eye—is therefore called "eye-consciousness. [This occurs] because the seeds of consciousness follow along with [the faculty].

Because it arises based on the faculty (*indriya*), it does not follow that the seed of form (*rūpa-bīja*) or the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*) [is the primary cause]. Fourth, regarding "the assistance to the faculty":
because it assists the consciousness of the eye, it is called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣur-vijñāna*); this is because it brings about benefit or harm to that [faculty]. Why is this so?

It is because through the union of the faculty and the consciousness, there is that which is experienced, which causes the faculty to be benefited or harmed; it is not due to the objective sphere (*viṣaya*). Fifth, "according to the faculty": as with...

The consciousness of the eye is therefore called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*), because it is subsumed under the category of sentient beings. It is not the case that those forms (*rūpa*) are necessarily insentient;

however, because the sense organs (*indriya*) possess five superior qualities, they are said to be the "basis" (*āśraya*). Just as it is with eye-consciousness, so it is with the other consciousnesses.

The first four [types of consciousness] are all *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds, whereas the consciousness produced by the organ alone is a *bahuvrīhi* (relative) compound. This is because, although the organ—
[The former] is inferior because it can give rise to the superior. Next, the objection is addressed. The difficulty is raised as follows:

"If consciousness is named according to its corresponding faculty, then since all six [consciousnesses] depend upon the mind (*manas*) for their operation, they should all be called 'mental consciousness' (*mano-vijñāna*). The response states: "Although all six groups of consciousness depend upon the mind for their operation..."

Furthermore, while the five [sensory consciousnesses] share the *manas* (mind) as their common support, although the sixth consciousness has the *manas* as its unique support, it is now designated by the name "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) in accordance with that unique support. Thus, there is no risk of confusion with the group of five consciousnesses.

Just as that which discerns various forms by relying on the eye-faculty is called "eye-consciousness," so too that which discerns all phenomena by relying on the mind-faculty is called "mental consciousness. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows:]

It is called "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) solely because it depends upon the mind (*manas*). The five [sensory consciousnesses] do not depend solely upon the mind; therefore, they are not called "mental consciousness.

The designation of these consciousnesses is established according to the six meanings of "following the faculty" (*indriya-anuvidhāna*); this does not apply to the analysis of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), so it should not be used as a precedent. Question: Regarding the six [factors], such as the faculties and the consciousnesses...

Since consciousness arises based on the faculties, by what are they defined as "faculties"? The answer is: the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that both the manifest and the seed aspects constitute the faculties of the eye and so forth.
Because at the time of original perfuming, the mind transforms into something resembling form, it receives its name from that perfuming;

it is thus the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) derived from the four great elements. Therefore, in relation to the resulting consciousness that is produced, the manifest aspect is metaphorically designated as the faculty.
Regarding function: the actual function consists solely of the capacity to manifest form. The principle of the arising of consciousness is established by both the Mahayana and Hinayana schools alike.
Question: What is the meaning of "organ" (*indriya*)? Answer: "Organ" carries the meanings of being most excellent, sovereign, authoritative, predominant, and productive.
These constitute the meaning of an organ. Among these, there are the five pure material organs (*rūpa-indriya*) and the five gross material organs (*pratibimba-indriya*).

If the five pure sense-faculties (*indriya*) are considered, their essential nature consists of pure matter (*rūpa*) that is invisible and resistant (*sapratigha*), which is capable of producing the five consciousnesses and possesses the function of illuminating objects. The *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states:
"It refers to a portion of pure matter within the eye, like clarified butter (*sarpis*). Because this nature exists, visual consciousness arises; if it were absent, it would not arise. Thus...
The body faculty (*kāyendriya*) has pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) as its nature; if it were absent, [the sense] would not arise. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the eye faculty are situated upon the pupil, arranged horizontally and covered by a transparent membrane, like a crystal lens (*sphāṭika*), such that they do not obstruct one another.
The atoms of the ear faculty are situated within the ear canal, arranged in a spiral, like the rolled-up bark of a birch tree. The nose faculty..."
The atoms of the nose faculty reside within the nasal cavity; they face upward and their backs are downward, resembling a pair of fingernails.

The atoms of the tongue faculty are distributed across the tongue, shaped like a half-moon. The atoms of the body faculty dwell throughout the entire body, corresponding to the dimensions of the physical form.
If one speaks of the "dust-like" (bu chén) five sense organs, these assist the pure organs (qīng jìng gēn) in being able to illuminate their respective objects;

the [pure organs'] own substance cannot illuminate objects by itself. This is because the dust-like organs consist of coarse, manifest form (*rūpa*), yet they do not hinder them from serving as the support for the pure organs.
Question: Regarding the six sense organs, how many meanings does each possess? Answer: There are two meanings. The first is that they are the result of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
The second is the nourished (aupacayika). For example, regarding the eye-faculty: that which is produced in this life by past karma is called the "ripened eye" (vipākaja-cakṣus).
During this present life, that which grows from small to large and is nurtured from emaciated to robust due to food, drink, and so forth, is called the "nourished eye.

The same applies to the other faculties. Alternatively, it may be termed "inferior" (hīna). Next, the names established according to their respective objects will be explained. Suppose someone were to ask:
If consciousness that relies on the eye and so forth is called "eye-consciousness," then should consciousness that takes form and so forth as its object be called "form-consciousness"?

Therefore, this commentary states: it may also be called "form-consciousness. Why? Because it conforms to the definition of consciousness. What does it mean to conform? Consciousness is that which cognizes;
when it cognizes form and so forth, it conforms to the nature of consciousness. That is to say, the discernment of the six objects is what is termed "consciousness."

Now, these are established according to their objects; thus, they accord with the meaning of "consciousness. The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, only cognize form and the other [objects];

therefore, they are called "form-consciousness" up to "touch-consciousness. The sixth [consciousness] can universally cognize all phenomena (*dharma*); therefore, it is called "phenomena-consciousness" (*dharmavijñāna*).

Alternatively, because it can cognize phenomena and alone receives the name "phenomena," while the first five cannot, they are not called "phenomena. Thus, the names of the six consciousnesses are established. There is no [other basis for the name].
The fault of confusion. Suppose someone were to ask: "Since this accords with the meaning of 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*), why not establish [the sense-faculties] based on it?

To this, the commentary replies: In the state of non-mastery, the eye faculty perceives only visible forms, so there is no confusion. However, in the state of mastery, the various faculties function interchangeably;

if a single faculty were to produce consciousness that perceives all objects, how would one designate which object that consciousness pertains to? Such a confusion would arise. Therefore, [it is not established based on consciousness].

Is it established based on the object, or is it established based solely on the sense faculty? This is done to avoid error. Why would a single sense faculty produce consciousness that takes all objects as its conditions?
For instance, the eye faculty could produce ear-consciousness to take various sounds as its objects; the production of other [consciousnesses] should be explained accordingly.
The same applies to the other faculties. As the ancients said: "The ear-base can perform the Buddha-work of the nose-base," and so forth—this refers to this very meaning. Question:
If a single sense organ were to produce consciousness by taking all objects as its conditions, then a single consciousness would have to be called "all consciousnesses.

Would this not lead to confusion and constitute a great error? Answer: It is simply according to the sense organ; there is no fault of confusion. Below, the *Vyavahāra-alaṃkāra* (The Ornament of Discourse) is cited to raise an objection:
The *Vyavahāra-alaṃkāra* states that each of the Tathāgata’s five sense organs functions in relation to all five types of objects.

What is meant by "being able to take all objects as its cognitive object"? The explanation states: The five [sensory] objects are coarse and manifest, whereas the object of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is subtle.
While the five objects are mutually of the same category (*sabhāga*), the object of phenomena is not of the same category as those five types.

It is based on these coarse and manifest objects of the same category that such a statement is made; in reality, however, a single consciousness is capable of taking all things as its cognitive object. (*Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*)

[The author] cites scripture as proof: The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) discerns the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings and manifests inconceivable transformations of the three types of action (*trikarma*), such as bestowing the four kinds of prophecy upon bodhisattvas.

Is this not because the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) universally perceive all objects? If they did not universally perceive them, these great functions would not exist. The commentary says: "Accomplishing..."

The wisdom of what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is that which is formed by the transformation of the preceding five consciousnesses. Its manifestations through the three types of action (*tri-karma*) comprise ten kinds in total.

There are three transformations of the body: first, the transformation manifesting supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); second, the transformation manifesting the taking of birth; and third, the transformation manifesting the fruits of karma. There are also three transformations of speech:

first, the transformation of speech for consolation and greeting; second, the transformation of skillful means (*upāya*); and third, the transformation of eloquent discourse (*pratibhāna*). [There is also] the transformation of the mind.
There are four types: first, transformation through the mind of discernment; second, transformation through the mind of fabrication; third, transformation through the mind of initiation;

and fourth, transformation through the mind of reception. Within transformation through reception, there are further four ways of answering: first, the categorical answer (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*), as when someone asks about heaven.

1. Answering by way of a categorical response (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*): as when someone asks about heaven, one replies, "The clear element is heaven. 2. Answering by way of analysis (*vibhajyavyākaraṇa*): as when someone asks about heaven, [one analyzes it as] "The clear element constitutes heaven.

3. Answering by way of a counter-question (*paripṛcchāvyākaraṇa*): as when someone asks about heaven, [one asks back], "What do you mean by 'heaven'? 4. Answering by remaining silent (*sthāpanīyavyākaraṇa*): as when someone asks [an improper question], one remains silent.

He did not answer. These [matters] all concern the Tathāgata’s activities, such as delivering sentient beings and preaching the Dharma. The question asks: "Regarding the first transformation, it was said that the 'object, appropriation, and cognition are unknowable';
regarding the second transformation, it was said that 'it evolves based on that and takes that as its object.

Why, then, in this present verse, is the support and object of the six evolving consciousnesses not mentioned? The answer is: It is because the supports and objects of the six evolving consciousnesses are [already established].
Because they are coarse, manifest, and universally established, the three types of transformation are not mentioned in the verse.
In the preceding four fascicles, it has already been stated that the supports of the five consciousnesses are fourfold; now, we shall speak in order of their respective objects.
Next, regarding the statement that "cognizing objects constitutes its nature and characteristic" (up to) "the other bases for cognition are as previously explained," there are two [points].

This is the section explaining the door of essential nature and the door of mental aspect (*ākāra*). By means of the single term "discrimination" (*vijñapti*), both nature and characteristic are explained together. The Sūtra states:
"Eye-consciousness depends upon the eye-faculty," and so on, up to "mind-consciousness depends upon the mind-faculty. Thus, for now, this refers to the non-common [bases].
Regarding the basis: the Sūtras state that visual consciousness discerns various forms, up to and including mental consciousness discerning various phenomena (*dharmas*).
This refers, for now, to what is discerned by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) in the stage where the basis has not yet been transformed (*aśraya-parāvṛtti*).

As previously explained, this includes what is discerned by the seeing-part when it shares a common basis with others, as well as when the basis has already been transformed. All five sensory consciousnesses depend upon the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses; the sixth depends upon the second... [text ends].
8. One faculty gives rise to consciousness that takes all objects as its conditions.
Within what nature are these six evolving consciousnesses subsumed? (Up to: Because the seeds of conceptual proliferation have been eternally extinguished and eliminated.

The third section explains the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). First, the question is posed; next, the verse is cited as the answer; finally, the explanation follows. What is called "wholesome" (*kuśala*)?

It refers to that which is both its own essence and its fruit being desirable; this is termed "wholesome. What is "unwholesome" (*akuśala*)? It may be understood by reversing the definition of the wholesome.
What is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? It is so called because it cannot be defined as having either a desirable or an undesirable fruit; hence it is named "indeterminate.

That which can bring about benefit for this life and other lives means that what was beneficial in a previous life brings benefit to the present life, and what is beneficial in the present life brings benefit to future lives.

Question: If that which is beneficial to this world and the next is called "wholesome" (*kuśala*), then why is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), which has no prior or subsequent limits, called wholesome?
Answer: Because it transcends birth and death (*saṃsāra*) in this world and the next, it is therefore called wholesome.
Question: The fruits of happiness in the realms of humans and devas are also beneficial; why then are they not considered wholesome (*kuśala*)? Answer:

Although the fruits of happiness in the realms of humans and devas can provide benefit in this life, they cannot provide benefit in future lives. Because these fruits follow the transformation of karma and karma is subject to exhaustion, they are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, they are not called wholesome. They are capable of causing harm and obstruction in both this life and future lives.
Therefore, they are called unwholesome (*akuśala*). If that were so, then the suffering fruits of the miserable realms (*apāya*) would also be unwholesome, as they too are detrimental.
This is not the case; although the suffering fruits of the miserable realms can be detrimental in this life, they are not so in other lives, and thus they are not unwholesome.
Next, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) may be understood. Next, the inclusion [of these factors] is explained: these six evolving consciousnesses are associated with the ten wholesome [factors].

That which is associated with a single mind is subsumed under the category of the wholesome; it is associated with the two medium-universal and eight great-universal [mental factors] and is subsumed under the category of the unwholesome.

It is not associated with either [of these]. It is subsumed under the category of the indeterminate. If one asks: "Regarding the three natures of the first six consciousnesses, are they simultaneous or not?
The answer is: there are two masters' interpretations. One school states that the three natures of the first six types of consciousness are not simultaneous.

[The mind] arises. Since the six consciousness-bodies, like the first five consciousnesses, function toward external objects (*bāhyamukha*), there are differences in their arising as wholesome or unwholesome;
consequently, the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) must also be mutually contradictory [in nature].

How could it possibly, in a single moment, follow the five consciousnesses while simultaneously possessing all three natures? Why is this so? Because the arising of the five consciousnesses necessarily depends on the induction of the mental consciousness.

[The Master] replies: It arises simultaneously with those five consciousnesses and becomes either wholesome or defiled. If one were to allow that the three natures arise simultaneously in the five consciousnesses, then at that time the mental consciousness would also necessarily involve all three natures.
How could there be a principle whereby the six consciousnesses simultaneously involve all three natures in a single moment?
Therefore, it is known that the three natures of the six consciousnesses certainly do not arise together. Question: If this is so, why does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* state...
[Question: It is said that the *ālayavijñāna* arises simultaneously with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), and that the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) arise together.

[Answer: That statement regarding simultaneous arising refers to multiple moments occurring in succession; therefore, it is called "simultaneous. It does not mean that the three natures arise together within a single moment of consciousness.
For example, when one speaks of "one mind," this is said in reference to many instances of arising and ceasing; it does not mean that a single instance of arising and ceasing is called "one mind."
Furthermore, since we now rely on the principle that not even a single moment can admit of simultaneous arising, there is no contradiction with the treatise. One master says:

"The three natures (tri-niṣyanda) of the six consciousnesses may arise simultaneously in a single moment, because the simultaneous manovijñāna—whether it be *saṃpātaja* [sudden] or *naiṣyandika* [flowing]—may arise together with the five consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness.
Because it arises suddenly (*saṃpātaja*), it is associated with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)."
[The five consciousnesses] are associated [with mental factors]. Because they arise as outflows (*nisyanda*), they are associated with both the wholesome and the defiled.

Since both sudden occurrence (*ābhoga*) and outflow are admitted to arise simultaneously, the three natures must necessarily coexist. However, the term "admitted" (*kṣama*) is used merely as a concession.

Therefore, it is further stated that while the five consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) definitely arise together, their qualities such as wholesomeness do not necessarily coincide. Thus, your previous premise...
The objection that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) must necessarily pertain to all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*) is ultimately rendered futile.
Below, the *Yogācārabhūmi* is cited to prove that although the mental consciousness arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses, it does not share their same nature.

For instance, when practitioners of yoga enter meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), if they encounter an object such as sound and emerge from that concentration, this is a wholesome mental consciousness associated with that meditative state.
After the remaining five consciousnesses have arisen simultaneously with the [meditative absorption], one experiences this sound and only then emerges from concentration.
It is not the case that the mental consciousness associated with that absorption alone apprehends this sound while the ear-consciousness is absent.

If there were only the mental consciousness and no ear-consciousness, the mental consciousness within concentration would be unable to hear the sound; because it would not experience this sound, [the claim] would be untenable.

[The practitioner] emerges from meditative absorption. [The opponent] asks: "If one emerges from absorption as soon as the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) perceives a sound, why must it necessarily be accompanied by a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) associated with the state of concentration before emerging? [The respondent] answers: "One does not emerge from absorption at the very moment of grasping the sound;
rather, it is only after the ear-consciousness has perceived the sound that the mental consciousness associated with the state of concentration becomes active."

[One] hopes [to emerge], and then emerges from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, when the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) hears a sound, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is still in concentration.
Consequently, two consciousnesses would have to apprehend this sound simultaneously; thus, it is known that the mental consciousness must arise together with the auditory consciousness.

However, the mental consciousness while in concentration is "concomitant wholesome" (*saṃprayukta-kuśala*), whereas the auditory consciousness in concentration, which suddenly hears a sound, is by principle certainly not wholesome.
Why is this? Because at the time when the basis has not yet been transformed (*āśraya-aparāvṛtti*), the mind that arises abruptly (*ābhoga-citta*) is necessarily indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Thus, an indeterminate ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) functions simultaneously with a wholesome mental state associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

By this clear evidence, it is evident that the mental consciousness co-arising with the five [sensory] consciousnesses (*pañca-sahaja-manovijñāna*) is definitely not of the same nature as those five consciousnesses. Next, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* (Vol. 2) explains away an objection, stating: "The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* says... and so forth.

In the state of *anāgamya* (the preparatory stage), the five sensory consciousnesses do not exist. For what reason, then, is it said that [this state] functions simultaneously with the mental consciousness associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?

There are three stages of concentration: namely, entering (*praveśa*), abiding (*sthiti*), and emerging (*niṣkramaṇa*). The middle stage, "abiding," is called *samādhi*; the two stages of entering and emerging are called *samāhita*.
Here, "equipoise" (*samāhita*) refers specifically to the moments of entering and emerging from concentration. Answer: That treatise speaks in terms of the majority of cases.
There are no five consciousnesses [in this state]. This indicates that in certain limited cases, the five consciousnesses do exist;

therefore, it was previously stated that while in meditative concentration, the five consciousnesses may suddenly hear sounds. Question: Since the mental consciousness associated with the five [sensory consciousnesses] cannot share the same moral nature as the preceding five, why did the preceding text state that the three natures of the six consciousnesses can also arise simultaneously? Answer: If, among the five consciousnesses, the three natures...

They arise simultaneously. When the fifth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), follows those five consciousnesses by focusing predominantly on a single object, at that time the mental consciousness and those five consciousnesses are necessarily of the same moral quality—whether wholesome or unwholesome. If it does not focus predominantly, it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).

Therefore, the six evolving consciousnesses may coexist with the five sensory consciousnesses in all three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral). This is stated according to the stage prior to mastery.

If one reaches the stage of mastery, they do not pertain to the three natures but are comprised solely of the wholesome nature. Question: Within the stage of mastery, there are still both form and mind;
it would be appropriate for them to pertain to the three natures. Why, then, are they comprised solely of the wholesome nature? Answer: The form of the Tathāgata...

The mind is subsumed under the Truth of the Path; it is neither suffering nor its origin. Therefore, it is not unwholesome. Because the seeds of conceptual proliferation have been eternally extinguished, it is also not indeterminate.

With how many mental factors (*caitta*) are the six consciousnesses associated? [They are associated] with the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the indeterminate factors, as well as the three feelings (*vedanā*).
These two verses explain the two gates of association and coexistence with feeling. This is divided into two parts: first, a brief indication of the six states;

second, a detailed exposition of their distinctions. Now, for the first part: this verse is Vasubandhu’s ninth verse. It has two gates; the first two lines and the third line constitute the first gate.
The fifth is the section on association with mental factors (*caitta*). The final phrase [of that section] constitutes the sixth section, on concomitance with feeling (*vedanā*).

The treatise states: "These six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are collectively associated with six stages... all of which, regarding their objects of perception (*ālambana*), simultaneously apprehend both the general and specific characteristics."

Second, the explanation of the meaning of the verse is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the six stages of mental factors (*caitta*); second, the explanation of their association with feeling (*vedanā*).
The first part is further divided into two: first, the explanation of mental factors; second, the explanation of the six stages. Regarding the first:

as for the statement that [the mind] is "generally associated with the six classes of mental factors," the words are general while the intended meaning is specific. Here, they are categorized by way of the "transforming consciousnesses" (*pariṇāma-vijñāna*), and thus the eight consciousnesses are divided into three groups.

Thus, combining the preceding six into one transformative consciousness constitutes a general statement. However, when speaking in terms of evolving cognition (*pravṛtti-jñāna*), the eight consciousnesses are divided into four;
consequently, the first five and the sixth are separated into two mental categories, which constitutes a specific distinction regarding the mind (*manas*).
This statement that [the mind] is associated with all six stages refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

If one relies on the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), the statement regarding the "defiled stage" (sāsrava) applies only to thirty-four factors; the remaining seventeen factors are not associated with it.

One must not, based on this, contradict or invalidate other meanings—namely, the explanation of the meaning of association (*samprayoga*) for the universal factors (*sarvatraga*) and so forth. Question: By what meaning is the name [of these factors] obtained?
Mental factors (*caitasika*). Answer: They are called mental factors because they arise only by depending upon the mind; because they are conjoined with the mind and do not depart from it;
and because they are bound to the mind and follow its transformations. Possessing these three meanings, they are termed mental factors.
Just as things belonging to a self are designated as "mine," so too phenomena that belong to the mind are termed mental factors. Question: The mind...

What is the difference between the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) in terms of their meaning and function? Answer: With respect to the object of perception, the mind grasps only the general outline and does not engage in specific discrimination.
For example, when it is said that the mind "takes blue as its object," it merely grasps blue in its totality without further discriminating the specific characteristics of blue.
Regarding the objects of perception, mental factors do not merely grasp them in a general way, but also apprehend their subtle details;
because they are able to comprehend what the mind-king has not yet comprehended, they receive this name. They are like an apprentice painter who, following the master’s sketch, fills in the colors.

The teacher is like the master draftsman; the student is like the apprentice. Just as when the teacher has completed the outline of a form and the student fills it with colors—the colors being applied to the draft and not departing from it—so too is it when one grasps the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). When applying the colors, one causes them to appear beautiful;

likewise, when grasping the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) grasp their objects in the same way. It is consciousness (*vijñāna*) that is able to discern.

This refers to the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena; it does not refer to the apprehension of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), because [attention] is the primary factor.

If one were to take specific characteristics, that would belong to the mental factors (*caitta*). Among all dharmas, attention alone is capable of discerning numerous specific characteristics, because its power is superior in enabling the mind and mental factors to apprehend their objects. Thus, there is this general apprehension of the specific characteristics of many dharmas. (Yogācārabhūmi)

The *Śāstra* takes attention (*manasikāra*) as the first [of the five universal mental factors] because its function is preeminent; this treatise takes contact (*sparśa*) as the first because its conjunction is preeminent.
Each is established according to a single specific meaning. Thus, by means of the five universals, one discerns their characteristics:

contact is able to discern whether the mind-king (the primary consciousness) is directed toward what is agreeable, disagreeable, or neutral; feeling is able to discern whether the mind-king experiences appropriation or non-appropriation.

The characteristic of being contrary to both [the preceding]. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to discern the characteristics that serve as the causes for verbal expression in the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), because it apprehends the delimiting characteristics of objects.

That is to say, by thinking "this is blue" or "it is not blue," one subsequently gives rise to verbal expression; therefore, the characteristic of perception serves as the cause for verbal expression.
Volition (*cetanā*) is able to discern the characteristics of the mind-king regarding false causes, correct causes, and contradictory causes; that is to say, upon the object...

The characteristics of correctness, incorrectness, and so forth are the causes of volition (*cetanā*). When it is said that mental factors such as attention (*manasikāra*) and others are all called "mental concomitants" (*caitasika-dharma*), this clearly demonstrates that these mental factors also take general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as their objects.
Other treatises also state that the five object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*) likewise discern specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*);
desire (*chanda*) is also able to discern the desirable characteristics of the primary mind (*citta-rāja*), and resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is also able to discern the primary mind.
The mental factor of resolve (*adhimokṣa*) can discern the characteristics of objects. Mindfulness (*smṛti*) can also discern the characteristics of the mind-king’s habitual tendencies.
Concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) can discern the characteristics of the mind-king’s gains and losses, or its correctness and error.

By means of these ten factors, various mental concomitants—whether wholesome, defiled, or indeterminate—arise with respect to their objects. Furthermore, these ten are also able to grasp those objects.
The universal characteristics of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) also include its specific characteristics;
although the names and meanings of the various mental factors (*caitasika*) do not differ [from those of the mind], it is by virtue of these five categories that their types are distinguished.
The second part explains the six categories. First, the general heading: "That which is pervasive," and so forth. Next, the enumeration: "All," and so forth. Then, the explanation of the meaning:
"That which can definitely be found within all minds" refers to the five universal mental factors (*pañca-sarvatraga*), because they necessarily arise regardless of the specific type of mind.
"That which arises by taking distinct objects as its conditions" refers to the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca-viṣaya-pratiniyata*). [This] exists only within wholesome minds...

Those that arise [with all minds] are the eleven wholesome factors, because they exist only with wholesome minds; their essence is fundamental, and they can give rise to various afflictions, namely the six beginning with greed.
Those whose nature is exclusively the outflow of afflictions are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Those that are indeterminate with respect to both wholesome and defiled minds are the four indeterminate factors; that is, they occur across the three natures of wholesome, defiled, and neutral.
Because the minds of all [beings] are unsettled. Question: Why are there only five stages (*avasthā*) in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, whereas here there are six? Answer:
In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the root afflictions and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are combined into one category of defilement; therefore, there are only five stages.

Regarding the differentiation of the five [categories of mental factors] by means of the "four universals" (*sarvatraga*), the explanation of these four universals has already been seen in the previous fascicle within the discussion of the universal mental factors (*sarvatragadharma*). As for the nature of the "particular objects" (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*), it is universal in one respect.
All [mental factors] are universal in their objects, but none are universal in terms of time, because the four object-specific factors arise separately with respect to each object.

There are none that are universal in both respects, because desire and the others do not pervade the mind at all times. Therefore, it is said that among the object-specific factors, only the first two are universal in their objects.
The wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate are mutually exclusive; they cannot arise simultaneously in all eleven categories. They do not exist at all times;
the two consciousnesses—the seventh and the eighth—are devoid of outflows (*āsrava*). Furthermore, they do not coexist in all cases;
therefore, it is said that the wholesome exists in all stages, while the defiled is exclusively unwholesome. As for the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this exists only in the desire realm.
There is no instance where all [mental factors] arise simultaneously. There is no time when all [eight consciousnesses] exist together;

thus, it is said that among the four types of defilement, none are present in all cases. Sleep exists only in the Desire Realm. In the First Dhyāna, there is both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought).

In the Second Dhyāna, there is vitarka alone, without vicāra. In the Third Dhyāna, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra. There is no instance where all [of these] exist simultaneously; they do not arise at the same time.

They arise at times; they do not exist at all times. They are exclusively occupied by the six consciousnesses; they do not exist simultaneously at all times. Therefore, it is said that they are "indeterminate" and "not exclusively of all natures.
These six evolving consciousnesses are easily discarded and unstable, because [even] the Buddhas have already severed the causes of sorrow and suffering.

The second section explains the gate of association with feeling (*vedanā-samprayoga*). First, it provides a general indication: "Experiencing what is favorable," and so forth. Next, it provides a detailed explanation:

"These six evolving consciousnesses are easily detached and indeterminate" means that these six consciousnesses, unlike the seventh and eighth, do not have a nature that is entirely and constantly detached or indeterminate.

"Easily detached" has the meaning of being intermittent and subject to transformation; "indeterminate" refers to the mutual arising of the mental activities of joy, sorrow, and equanimity. Therefore...
All [feelings] are permeated by the three types of sensation (*vedanā*). That which accords with the body and gladdens the mind is called pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*).

That which oppresses the body and constrains the mind is called painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*). That which is neither oppressive nor gladdening for either the body or the mind is called neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
