Following these three sensations, the distinct meanings of each are clarified; alternatively, each may be divided into two. There are two ways: first, by distinguishing between body and mind. Third... [text fragment].

The feelings associated with the five consciousnesses are called bodily feelings (*kāyikī vedanā*). The three feelings associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are called mental feelings (*caitasikī vedanā*).
One [classification] distinguishes between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*); all three feelings pertain to both the tainted and the untainted. Question:

If they are called "untainted," why are they said to be suffering? Answer: Even painful feelings arise from the untainted, just as in the case of the suffering inherent in conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

[They] practice. This is all for the sake of seeking to realize the untainted (*anāsrava*). Alternatively, it is only when cultivating the untainted that one comes to know the suffering of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Or, if each is divided into three, there are likewise three: first, these three feelings (*vedanā*) all pertain to the three types of abandonment—namely, those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and those not to be abandoned (*aheya*).
Suffering, pleasure, and equanimity are likewise so. Second, [the three are]: those of the learner (*śaikṣa*), those of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and those of neither.

The stage of neither-training-nor-beyond-training also possesses all three types of sensation. What are the dharmas of training (*śaikṣa*)? They refer to those individuals in training (*śaikṣa-pudgala*), such as stream-enterers, once-returners, or non-returners;

or they are the conditioned supramundane dharmas, or the mundane wholesome dharmas. These are called the dharmas of training. Why is this? Because by relying on these dharmas, one diligently practices and trains from time to time in the higher training in ethics, the higher training in mind, and the higher training in wisdom.

What are the dharmas beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)? They refer to the Arhats whose outflows are exhausted; or they are the conditioned supramundane dharmas, or the mundane wholesome dharmas. These are called the dharmas beyond training. What are the dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training? That is to say, excluding...

Regarding the previously mentioned dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the remaining [dharmas] from stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) up to arhats—whether they fall within the continuum of any ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or consist of all those dharmas that are predominant for them—it should be known that these are called "neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training" (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*) dharmas.

[These] are divided into four, and there are also two [ways of dividing them]. First, the general division into four: wholesome [dharmas] correspond to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*); unwholesome [dharmas] correspond to painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*).
The two types of neutral feeling—obscured and unobscured—are so designated because the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is divided into two. Regarding "each being divided into four":
this means that each of the six consciousnesses possesses all four types of feeling. Thus it is said: "Each is associated with the five [types of] consciousness.
Spontaneous afflictions (*kleśa*) and spontaneous afflictions within the realms of pure suffering—these two types of affliction do not incite unwholesome karma; they are neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Because it is recorded [in the scriptures], it is associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). That which initiates unwholesome karma is an unwholesome feeling (*akuśalavedanā*) associated with the faculty of suffering.

That which is co-arisen with wholesome states and the like, and initiates wholesome karma, is likewise a wholesome feeling associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). That which does not initiate wholesome [karma] is [associated with the faculty of equanimity].
This is an indeterminate feeling (*avyākṛta-vedanā*), associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). Therefore, each of the three feelings may be divided into four types.
In the lower section of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is cited as proof that the three feelings are associated with all consciousnesses.

If these spontaneous afflictions (*kleśa*) were to pervade all consciousness, then these afflictions would universally be associated with all consciousnesses and with the faculties of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). If this...

Spontaneous afflictions do not pervade all consciousnesses; however, those associated with the sixth mental ground (*manobhūmi*) are associated with the sixth consciousness’s faculties of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity. Regarding what is pervasive and what is non-pervasive:

innate self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) is pervasive across all seven consciousnesses, whereas innate grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is non-pervasive in the first five [consciousnesses]. (From the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, Part II).

Citing evidence: The remainder—namely, those in the desire realm who do not manifest evil, as well as the spontaneous afflictions (*anābhoga-kleśa*) of the two upper realms—are all subsumed under the category of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature.
This proof demonstrates that afflictions are subsumed within both natures. Therefore, it is known that [the other categories] below follow.

Since they are already established as being common to the two defiled natures, the wholesome and pure [natures] can be understood accordingly. Thus, the two types of feeling (*vedanā*) are each common to all four natures.
Alternatively, they may be divided into five in total: the sensations of suffering and pleasure are divided into four, while the indeterminate is combined into one. Question:
Previously, equanimity was divided into two while suffering and pleasure were not; why is it that here, suffering and pleasure are divided into two while equanimity is combined into one?

Answer: Regarding the division into suffering and pleasure: because the characteristics of that which afflicts and that which gladdens the body and mind differ respectively, that which afflicts and gladdens the body is called suffering and pleasure;
that which afflicts and gladdens the mind is called grief and joy; and that which is non-discriminative is called neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.

That which involves conceptual discrimination is termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*) and "joy" (*saumanasya*). That which is most intense is "suffering" (*duḥkha*) and "pleasure" (*sukha*); that which is subtle is sorrow and joy.

As for the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), it is neither oppressive nor gratifying; it lacks distinct characteristics within body or mind, being purely non-conceptual and devoid of intensity or subtlety.
Therefore, it is not divided into two. Below, the association [of these feelings] will be explained in detail, beginning with the feeling of satisfaction.
All agreeable feelings that are associated with the five sensory consciousnesses are always termed "pleasure" (*sukha*).

Those associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), if they occur within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or in the preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first two dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), are termed only "joy" (*saumanasya*) and not "pleasure.
This is because they gladden the mind alone and do not gladden the body. However, if they occur within the first two actual dhyānas, they are termed "pleasure."
Joy (*prīti*): because both body and mind are gladdened. Regarding the "access" (*sāmantaka*) and "fundamental" (*maula*) [dhyānas], for example, the first dhyāna of the form realm has three levels:
the Brahma-pārṣadyas, the Brahma-purohitas, and the Mahābrahmās. The former two are access, while the Mahābrahmā level is called fundamental.
The second dhyāna has three levels: the Parīttābhās, the Apramāṇābhās, and the Ābhāsvaras. The former two are access, while the Ābhāsvara...
It is the fundamental [level]. In the third dhyāna there are three heavens, namely: Parīttābha (Limited Purity), Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Purity), and Ābhāsvara (Universal Purity).

The first two are called "access" (sāmantaka), while the third is called "fundamental" (maula). It is termed "fundamental" because one attains the fundamental meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of this heaven.
It is termed "access" because it is proximate to that fundamental level, being on the verge of attaining what has not yet been attained. Now, regarding the various [heavens] of the desire realm...
That which is obtained by the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the first two dhyānas, the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Parīttābha, and Apramāṇābha realms, merely gladdens the mind;
it has not yet reached a state where both body and mind are universally gladdened. Therefore, these are called "joy" (prīti) but not "bliss" (sukha).
If one is in the Abhāsvara Heaven or higher, having already attained the fundamental dhyānas, both body and mind are universally gladdened; thus, these are termed both "bliss" and "joy."

Therefore, the first dhyāna is called the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha-bhūmi*). The second dhyāna is called the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration (*samādhija-prītisukha-bhūmi*).
If one is within the third meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), whether in the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) or the fundamental stage (*maula*), one attains sublime bliss;

therefore, it is called the stage of sublime bliss free from joy (*prīti-vigata-praśrabdhisukha-bhūmi*). Because these meditative absorptions become increasingly profound, every point of contact is nothing but the object of bliss; thus, there is no distinction [between the stages].

It is distinct. This serves as a counter-illustration to show that in the first two dhyānas, the mental bliss is subtle; therefore, there is conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*). The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"The establishment of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental [dhyānas] is as taught in the Sūtras.

That is to say, this body is moistened, thoroughly moistened, thoroughly gladdened, and thoroughly pervaded by the joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha*); this is called the first dhyāna."

Regarding the proximate stage: as the Sūtra further states, "Within this very body, there is not even a small portion that is not pervaded by the joy and bliss born of seclusion. This is called the fundamental first dhyāna.
Within this very body, it is saturated, thoroughly saturated, thoroughly gladdened, and thoroughly permeated by the joy and bliss produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is called the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna.

Within this very body, there is not even the slightest part that is not pervaded by the joy and bliss born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); this is called the fundamental state (*maula*) of the second dhyāna.
It is the state in which this very body is moistened, thoroughly moistened, and completely suffused by the bliss free from joy (*prīti-virahita-sukha*).
"Joy" and "pervasive flow" refer to the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the third dhyāna.
That within this very body there is not even a single place not fully suffused with the bliss that is free from joy refers to the fundamental stage (*maula*) of the third dhyāna.
It is called "preparatory" because the dhyāna is not yet complete; it is called "fundamental" because the dhyāna is [fully] established.
Because they are fully present. Next, regarding painful sensations (*upaghātaka-vedanā*): those painful sensations associated with the five consciousnesses are always termed "suffering" (*duḥkha*).

Regarding those associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there are two differing opinions among the masters. As for the masters who maintain that there is suffering on the level of the mind:

The sixth [consciousness] is associated with five feelings. If one follows the masters who maintain that there is no suffering on the mental level (*manobhūmi*), then the sixth is associated with only three feelings:

sorrow, joy, and equanimity; the two of suffering and pleasure are excluded. However, the masters who maintain that there is suffering on the mental level state that the sixth is associated only with the feeling of sorrow and lacks the feeling of suffering.
This is because it is a mental oppression rather than physical; thus, there is sorrow but no suffering.

The following citations provide proof. Various sacred teachings state that the mental feeling of distress (*daurmanasya*) on the level of the mind (*manobhūmi*) is termed the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*). Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"In the birth within the hells, immediately after the eighth maturation (*vipāka*), there arises a sixth maturation-born [consciousness] characterized by a continuous stream of suffering and grief.

From this, it is known that suffering belongs to the first five [senses] and grief belongs to the sixth. It further states that in the hells, there are applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and grief.
[They] are associated with one part [of each]. The same applies to the realms of hungry ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*).

It is said that the vitarka and vicāra of the hells are associated with one part of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and one part of the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*). The *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"The vitarka and vicāra of hell-beings (*naraka*) are exclusively induced by contact with unpleasant objects through a mode of dejection; they are associated with mental grief and physical suffering, just like the vitarka and vicāra of hell-beings."
They experience suffering. The same applies to all vitarka and vicāra among the hungry ghosts (preta) and the animal realm (tiryagyoni).

Therefore, it is known that even extremely heavy painful sensations within the mental level (manobhūmi) are not called "suffering" (duḥkha), but are still termed "grief" (daurmanasya); how much more so for other lighter ones, which cannot be anything but grief?
The second master maintains that the mental level possesses both the two sensations of suffering and grief, referring to those born in the two realms of humans and devas.

It is always termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*) and not termed "suffering" (*duḥkha*), because it is not exceedingly heavy. If one is born in the two realms of animals or hungry ghosts, it is termed both sorrow and suffering.
For those among animals who experience a mixture [of sensations], it is light; therefore, it is termed sorrow. For hungry ghosts who experience [suffering] purely, it is exceedingly heavy;
therefore, it is termed suffering. If one is in hell, it is termed only suffering, because it is experienced purely and is exceedingly heavy. There is no...
Because of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), pleasure reaches its limit in the third dhyāna, and suffering reaches its limit in the hells; therefore, in both cases, there is no discrimination.

In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Part II, it is cited as proof that in the sixth [consciousness] there is also the experience of painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*). Spontaneous afflictions (*kleśa*) can be associated with all three types of sensation (*vedanā*);

however, a state of distressful sensation is exclusively physical pain and is not termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*). Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that for a certain class of beings in the sixth [consciousness], [the mind] is accompanied by both [types of sensation].
The view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) that arise [in this stage] are exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, he explains himself:
"According to what is stated in the treatise, the innate sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) associated with this mental level (*manobhūmi*) is subsumed under the indeterminate;

it is certainly not the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), because the treatise states that the faculty of grief is of a defiled nature (*kliṣṭa*) and is not indeterminate. Moreover, it is said that regarding the various faculties in the hells, the remaining three necessarily manifest.

This is not established. He further explains himself, saying: "The other three meditative absorptions consist of the three faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and sorrow (*daurmanasya*).

However, when one experiences the retribution of suffering in those hells, there is only the indeterminate faculty of pain (*duḥkha*); the faculties of pleasure, joy, and sorrow certainly do not manifest."

Since that indeterminate faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is necessarily associated with the active faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), how could it not be admitted that the three faculties of pleasure, joy, and sorrow are certainly not accomplished [there]?
For pleasure, joy, and sorrow do not arise simultaneously with a state of pure suffering or equanimity.
Regarding the statement that "suffering does not exist on the mental level," a teacher raises an objection, saying: "How do we know that the treatise speaks only of..."

The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is admitted [in those realms]. One should not say that they necessarily possess the three faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and sorrow (*daurmanasya*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Why is this? Because those six types of admissible consciousness do not exist at certain times. "Six types of admissible consciousness" refers to the sixfold consciousnesses associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣāvedanā*) in those painful states.
"Because they do not exist at certain times" is a challenging objection; it means: if they do not exist...
Regarding the time of experiencing neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*), there is also the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*). The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:

"That treatise should not state that only the possibility of neutral feeling is admitted while the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) is not established. Since it states that neutral feeling is possible, it must necessarily imply the faculty of mind as well;

for both that possibility of feeling and the faculty of mind are equally of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*), and thus there is no differentiating cause [to exclude one]. If it is argued that that treatise only...

Regarding the statement that the establishment of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) as being "capable of receiving" is not certain: for what reason does that treatise further state that the seeds currently active in the hells necessarily constitute eight faculties?
When it speaks of "eight faculties," it is specifically referring to the eighth consciousness, because that too is associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Below, it refutes the claim that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya-indriya*) is sixfold rather than eightfold. If one were to say [it refers to] the five...
Because consciousness does not continue [in that state], it is certainly not the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) within the hell realm.

Since the eighth consciousness is of a single type, uninterrupted, and constantly continuous, if it were definitively the faculty of sorrow, then at the stage of extreme fainting during death and birth, when the six active consciousnesses have already ceased, from where would the sorrow of the eighth consciousness arise? Thus, one knows for certain that the faculty of sorrow does not belong to the eighth consciousness.

The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is likewise. If it is claimed that the eighth [consciousness] is the sovereign retributive totality (*vipāka-saṃgṛhīta-ādhipati*), and that the faculty of suffering in hell necessarily belongs to this eighth, then when one is experiencing suffering within hell, what exactly is designated as the eighth?
Even if one maintains that the hell-beings manifest in male or female forms and takes whichever form is present as the eighth, this is also logically untenable.
Not so. The bodies in the hells may be large or small, as they lack a fixed form;
however, the fruit produced by the eighth ripening consciousness has a fixed form. Furthermore, the body summoned by those evil karmas might even be formless.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "In the case of birth from womb, egg, or moisture, at the initial stage of receiving birth, one acquires only two ripening faculties (*vipākendriya*), namely the body and life.

In the initial stage of apparitional birth (*upapāduka*), one acquires six, seven, or eight. That is to say, one without gender initially acquires six faculties, such as those at the beginning of an eon (*kalpa*).
What are these six? They are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life. If one has a single gender, at the initial stage..."
They obtain seven faculties, as do the gods and others. If one is of both sexes (dviliṅga), they initially obtain eight faculties.
How could there be those of both sexes who undergo miraculous birth (*upapāduka*)? For it is possible for those in the evil destinies (*durgati*) to be of both sexes and yet be miraculously born.
Question: Since they have no physical form, what experiences suffering? Answer: By the power of their past unwholesome karma, [suffering] naturally arises at the gates of the five sense faculties.
They constantly experience suffering, as in the case of the sixfold mutual retributions (*ṣaḍ-vipāka*).

If it is claimed that the bodies in hell necessarily possess eyes and other sense organs, and must therefore have fixed male or female forms rather than being merely transformations, then even if such fixed forms existed, what use would they serve?
For within the Great Avīci Hell, there can be no desire for sexual intercourse or similar matters. Thus, [the Yogācāra...]
Kātyāyana said: "All sentient beings in the various hells are entirely devoid of sexual activity.

Because they have for a long time continuously endured various kinds of extremely intense suffering, for this reason, those sentient beings—whether male toward a female or female toward a male—do not give rise to desire for the opposite sex; how much less could there be mutual intercourse?"
[This is] consistent. Since the root-bodies (*indriya-kāya*) of ghosts, animals, humans, and so forth, involve a mixture of suffering and pleasure, they possess sexual desire.

By this principle, it is known that the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*) definitely constitutes seven or eight [consciousnesses], because both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are associated with the feeling of equanimity.

In the hells, the suffering faculty (*duḥkhendriya*) definitely constitutes the sixth [consciousness], because the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are both associated with the feeling of equanimity. The following examples refute [the claim that] the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) lacks [these faculties].
Regarding the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*): your claim that the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) of hell possesses the faculty of sorrow is also incorrect.

Just as the third dhyāna—the stage of ultimate bliss—lacks the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one should know by analogy that in the places of ultimate suffering in hell, there is certainly no faculty of sorrow.

Therefore, the remaining three [faculties] are mentioned. It is certain that these are sorrow, joy, and pleasure. A question is asked: "If there is only the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) within hell," [how can this be so?]

There is no pleasant sensation. Why, then, does the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* state that in the Avīci hell there is no interval of pleasure amidst the suffering, and thus it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*), whereas in other hells there arises an interval of pleasure?
Although these latter do not possess [pleasant sensation] as a result of maturation (*vipākaja*), they do possess it as a natural outflow (*naiḥṣyandika*).

Answer: As stated in the *Lishi Apitan* (Abhidharmakośa-śāstra): "When humans feed their six domestic animals food that is either hot or cold, there are intervals of coolness in the hot hells and intervals of warmth in the cold hells; this warmth and coolness are results that resemble their preceding causes."

This is a fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), which is metaphorically designated as a "result concordant with its cause" (*niṣyandaphala*); one should understand that this is a conventional method of exposition (*anuvartana-yukti*).
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* states that within the Saṃjīva hell, there are times when they are struck by cool winds and their flesh and blood are restored;
at other times, they cry out, "We are revived! and those sentient beings suddenly come back to life. It is in this way that their flesh and blood are produced.

Furthermore, the claim that it is not called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) because it is interspersed with painful sensations despite the brief arising of joy and pleasure is also a method of explanation according to the principle of conformity (*anuvartana-yukti*).

Alternatively, it may be a general statement regarding places where various sensations coexist and lack ripened pleasure (*vipākaja-sukha*); therefore, it is metaphorically said to possess "pleasure of outflow" (*naiṣyandika-sukha*).
Because the locus of mixed sensation (*miśravedanā*) is also entirely suffering. As for "mixed sensation," it refers to the mixture of cold and heat sensations. Question:

Since there is no faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) on the mental level (*manobhūmi*), why does the sacred teaching state that the dejected sensation on the mental level is called the faculty of sorrow?

Answer: This is said with reference to a limited portion; for the most part, it is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). This can be understood through a general discussion in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 52.
Furthermore, it is known that in the Yoga teachings there is a continuity of suffering born of maturation (*vipākaja*) consisting of mental distress (*daurmanasya*).
Because this suffering belongs to the same category as other forms of mental distress, it is metaphorically designated as "distress" based on that commonality; in reality, however, it is suffering.

Alternatively, because that faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) can impair both body and mind, although it is subsumed under the faculty of suffering, it is also called "distress. It is termed "suffering" specifically because it impairs the body.

It is called "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*) because it afflicts the mind. For example, just as the joy (*prīti*) of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) benefits both body and mind, it is classified as the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) yet is also termed "pleasure" (*sukha*).
It is called "joy" because it benefits the mind, and "pleasure" because it benefits the body. Question: How is it known that this [joy] is also termed "pleasure"?
Could it not be admitted that it necessarily constitutes the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)? Answer: Until the third dhyāna is reached, it certainly does not exist.
Regarding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*): it is therefore said that the first and second dhyānas possess only eleven faculties and lack the faculty of pleasure.

As for these eleven faculties, they are stated in relation to the desire realm and the first two dhyānas. The first five consciousnesses exclude pleasure but possess the other four [faculties], including suffering (*duḥkha*).

The sixth consciousness is likewise. The seventh and eighth consciousnesses each possess only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). In the hells, both body and mind together constitute the faculty of suffering.

Therefore, there are eleven [mental factors]. Since it is known that the realm of Ultimate Bliss lacks the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one should know that the realm of Ultimate Suffering lacks the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

From this point downward, the conclusion indicates that in the realm of pure suffering, there are only the faculties of mental suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and not the faculties of grief, joy, or pleasure.

According to one interpretation, from the section "The six consciousnesses" downward, the five preceding [consciousnesses] and the sixth are explained as being associated with all three natures (*trividha*).

The meaning of "both" (*ubhaya*). First, the formal explanation. "In the *Yogācārabhūmi*," etc., follows as the general response to objections. "There is another interpretation," etc., follows as the explanation of the meaning;
since the refutation of attachments herein is consistent with the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it is not explained again. This concludes the brief presentation of the six stages mentioned above.
Regarding the six categories of mental factors briefly indicated previously (up to the point of "and so forth"), what are the characteristics of the first two categories?

Part Two, the Section on Extensively Revealing the Distinctions, is divided into five sections. The first, the section on the universal and object-specific factors, is further divided into three parts. First, the conclusion of the preceding section and the posing of the question.

The verse says: First, the universal mental factors such as contact (*sparśa*), up to resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), have different objects of focus (*ālambana*).
Second, this refers to Vasubandhu’s tenth verse.

The commentary says: Among the six categories [of mental factors], the first are the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitasika*); [the meaning of] the others being non-universal shall be explained in due course.

The second part, the explanation of the verses, is divided into two sections: first, the explanation of the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*); second, the explanation of the object-specific mental factors (*viniyata*). Regarding the first:

the nature, function, and distinctions of the five factors beginning with contact (*sparśa*) have already been explained in detail in the third fascicle, under the section on the first transformation (*pariṇāma*).

Therefore, they will not be restated here. At the end of that passage, it says: "The characteristics of the universal factors shall be explained extensively later. This text appears at this point; these are the universal factors.
"How should their characteristics be understood? This is the question. "By means of scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*) as authoritative criteria," this is the answer.

What is meant by scripture? It is said: As stated in the Sūtras, when the faculty of the eye, the object of form, and consciousness arise together, at the stage of their conjunction, contact (*sparśa*) is necessarily produced.

The arising of contact is invariably accompanied by sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). Therefore, these four—contact and the others—are necessarily present whenever the mind arises.

Furthermore, it is said that when the sense faculties and their objects encounter one another, consciousness cannot arise without attention (*manasikāra*). Therefore, at the moment the mind arises, there must necessarily be attention.
Attention functions within the locus of discernment, and discernment functions within the locus of attention; thus, the mind and attention are always in constant conjunction.
From this, we know that attention is also a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*). What is the reasoning for this? It is said: without contact (*sparśa*), [consciousness does not arise].
Without contact (*sparśa*), there would be no unification of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) as they encounter the same objective field.

Without attention (*manasikāra*), there would likewise be no mind that directs itself toward an object. Without feeling (*vedanā*), there would be no capacity to experience any object and give rise to states of joy, sorrow, or equanimity.

Without perception (*saṃjñā*), one would be unable to grasp the specific characteristics of an object and apply names and conventions. Without volition (*cetanā*), [there would be no formation of karma].
Without grasping at causes such as the correct or the erroneous, one produces minds of good and evil.

Now, when the eight consciousnesses arise together, they touch objects, move toward objects, experience objects, and grasp objects; they differentiate and grasp causes such as the correct and the incorrect, producing good and non-good without a single deficiency.

(This means that when consciousness arises, there must be a "threefold conjunction. Where there is a threefold conjunction, contact is necessarily produced; for that threefold conjunction must arise by...)

Contact exists. If contact did not exist, the mind and mental factors could not combine to touch upon a single object; therefore, we know it must exist. Although contact exists, if there were no attention (*manasikāra*) to draw the mind toward its own object, the sovereign mind would encounter objects in a state of distraction, not knowing where it is directed.

Thus, contact and attention mutually produce one another: when attention is active, contact resides within that attention; when contacting an object, attention resides within that contact. When the various consciousnesses perceive objects, these two mental factors always serve as the primary function.

Drawn by these two, the mind approaches the object, and subsequently experiences the goodness or evil of that object. Toward what is good, it gives rise to compliance, thereby producing a mind of attachment; toward what is evil, it gives rise to opposition, thereby producing a mind of aversion; toward neutral objects, it feels neither aversion nor attachment.

It is neither pleasant nor unpleasant; it is simply neutral. This feeling is subsumed under one of the "one-or-the-other" [categories] within the state of mindlessness. Therefore, when the state of mindlessness arises, this "one-or-the-other" does not exist. One never observes a state of mind that possesses consciousness yet lacks the "one-or-the-other. Since feeling consists of the experiencing of the agreeable and the disagreeable, [it must be present].

Affection arises and aversion arises; subsequently, one demarcates boundaries and establishes limits regarding pleasant and unpleasant objects, determining right and wrong, and weighing worthiness and unworthiness. This perception (*saṃjñā*) is also subsumed under one of the "invariably concomitant" factors (*anivārya-eka-deśa*) within the state of mindlessness;

therefore, in the state of mindlessness, this invariably concomitant factor does not exist. One never observes a state of mind that lacks this invariably concomitant factor. Once boundaries have been established for its own object, one then apprehends the characteristics of correct causes, false causes, and so forth, within those bounded objects, and performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds.

This volition (*cetanā*) is also subsumed under one of the invariably concomitant factors within the state of mindlessness; when the state of mindlessness arises, this invariably concomitant factor does not exist. One never observes a state of mind that lacks this invariably concomitant factor. Therefore, these five are called the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*); whenever there is a state of mind, they necessarily [arise].
There are these five. The mind-king is like a sovereign, while these five universal factors are like supporting ministers.

Based on this teaching and reasoning, it is established that the five factors beginning with contact are present in all minds, in all stages, at all times, and in all natures; therefore, they are called "universal" (sarvatraga).

Next, regarding the "object-specific" (viṣaya-viśeṣa) mental factors, these refer to those ranging from desire (*chanda*) to wisdom (*prajñā*), up to concentration (*samādhi*); they are not universal (*sarvatraga*) like faith (*śraddhā*), greed (*lobha*), and so forth.
There are two explanations for the classification of object-specific factors into three parts. First, the formal explanation of the five objects:

the first line provides a general heading indicating the names and sequence of the five objects, while the subsequent lines provide the specific definitions of their meanings. As for the term "object-specific," it means that the objects perceived by these five mental factors are each distinct.
Each is distinct; they are not like the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), which share the same object. Therefore, they are called "particular" (*viniyata*). What is desire (*chanda*)?
Its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the longing and aspiration for an object that one finds pleasing. Its functional activity (*karman*) is to serve as the basis for diligence (*vīrya*).
Among worldly and world-transcending phenomena, there is none that is not accomplished through such liking and aspiration. What, then, is meant by the "object"?
Regarding the object of pleasure (*sukha-viṣaya*), there are three teachers with differing views. One teacher says: "That which is pleasant is an object of delight.
Because one has the hope of seeing or hearing such a delightful object, it is called pleasure. An objection is raised:

"Even regarding an object of aversion, when it has not yet come together [with oneself], one hopes for its non-union; and when it has already come together, one hopes for its separation. These too would then be matters of pleasure."
Is this not desire? Why must it be something desirable (*abhinandya*) for it to be considered desire? The commentary states:

"To long for that which is not yet attained" refers to the desirable essence itself at the time when one constantly seeks that which has not yet been attained. "To long for separation from that" refers to the desirable essence itself at the time when one merely seeks separation from that [object].
It does not mean that one gives rise to longing by seeking an object that is inherently loathsome (*jugupsanīya*).
How could it be called "desire"? Therefore, regarding objects that are loathsome or neutral, there is absolutely no fondness or delight.

Even when directed toward an object that is pleasing, if the mind of aspiration does not arise, there is likewise no fondness or delight. The second master says: That which is "delighted in" is the object sought;
one seeks union with an object that is pleasing and seeks separation from an object that is loathsome. Regarding...
Because there is a simultaneous aspiration toward both objects, the third master says that what is "desired" (*kāma*) refers to the object of contemplation.
One gives rise to a fondness for all objects—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or otherwise—and after examining and scrutinizing them, one then forms an aspiration;
therefore, it is called "desire" (*chanda*). If one does not fondly desire to examine and scrutinize, but rather engages with the object spontaneously, these are all [not instances of desire].
When it enters the mind, there is immediately a total absence of desire. By this principle, desire is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*).

Among the three explanations, the latter is considered superior. To distinguish it from others, one master says: "It is necessarily by the power of the object, through the longing and aspiration of pleasure and desire, that the various minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) apprehend their objects.
Therefore, when the mind arises, this [desire] must certainly be present. Thus, the Sūtra states that desire is...
Regarding the fundamental nature of all phenomena: this erroneous attachment takes *manasikāra* (attention) to be *chanda* (desire). First it is refuted and subsequently demolished as follows:
When the mind and mental factors apprehend external objects, they do so entirely through *manasikāra*; what connection does desire have? Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"If the sense faculties are unimpaired, the object is present, and *manasikāra* correctly arises, only then can consciousness be produced. It does not say that [consciousness] is produced by desire.

Regarding the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), he further refutes [the opponent] by analogy, saying: "If you claim that desire is the root of phenomena and that all minds and mental factors arise because of desire, then since the Sūtra states that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the root of all phenomena, do not all minds and mental factors likewise arise from craving? Question: Since minds and mental factors and so forth do not arise from desire, why does the Sūtra make such a statement? Answer: [The Sūtra speaks thus] with reference to the fact that they are produced by the force of craving. Furthermore, it is said: "Desire is the root of phenomena; from desire arises grasping. This means that when one desires an object, one subsequently grasps it. It is not that minds and mental factors arise directly from desire itself. Moreover, the Sūtra says: "Craving is the root of all phenomena. This refers to the fact that craving is the cause for the arising of future existence. It is not that minds and mental factors arise directly from craving. Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "Ignorance is the root of all phenomena. This means that ignorance is the cause for the arising of future existence. It is not that minds and mental factors arise directly from ignorance. Therefore, although the Sūtra speaks of desire and so forth as roots, this is merely a conventional designation based on their causal efficacy; it does not mean that minds and mental factors arise directly from them. However, when the sutras state that desire (*chanda*) is the root of all phenomena, they mean that all undertakings arise from the inclination of delight;
therefore, it is said that desire is the root. Alternatively, this desire is wholesome desire (*kuśala-chanda*), which can induce diligence (*vīrya*) and assist in accomplishing all virtuous deeds;
thus, the treatise states that its function is to serve as the basis for exertion. When the sutras state that desire is the root, they do not mean...

Desire (*chanda*) is the primary cause for the arising of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). What is resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*)? It is with respect to a determined object; that is to say, it is free from doubt.
Its essential nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the confirmation and maintenance of whatever has been determined. Its function (*karman*) is to be unshakeable.
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, "confirming and maintaining whatever has been determined" means: "This thing must be exactly so, and not otherwise."
The remaining [mental factor] is decisive conviction (*adhimokṣa*). Because of this conviction, no superior conditions can divert it;
for, by the power of clear evidence from both scripture and reasoning, one is able to examine, decide, and maintain the object with certainty.
Consequently, other conditions cannot pull it away, causing one to abandon this object and move toward another. Therefore, regarding an object of doubt, the mind is not decisive.
There is no resolve whatsoever [in that state], nor is it included among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*). This distinguishes it from the following:

one master claims that when the mind and its mental factors apprehend their respective objects, there is no place of obstruction, and thus all possess resolve (*adhimokṣa*). This is a mistaken identification of a universal factor as resolve.
First, this is refuted; subsequently, it is demolished by stating: "That which is able to be unobstructed is precisely the objective referent (*ālambana*); that which is not obstructed..."
This refers to the mind that takes [an object] as its focal point. Before a thought has even been raised, the mind and its objects are fundamentally not mutually obstructive.

At the moment a superior mind (*viśeṣa-citta*) suddenly arises, this is entirely due to the power of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and mental attention (*manasikāra*). What does it have to do with resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)?

If this superior arising were not dependent on the sense faculties and mental attention, but instead awaited resolute conviction, then this resolute conviction would be unable to function independently.

[If] birth were further dependent on something else, and if that which is resolved upon (*adhimokṣa*) were further dependent on something else, then that which is depended upon would itself have something else to depend upon;
in this way, there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)? The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
Its essence is causing the mind to clearly remember and not forget an object with which one is familiar; its function is non-distraction. [This refers to] a familiar object.

"Previously experienced" refers to that which was previously apprehended. "Non-distraction as its function" means that because mindfulness clearly remembers the object, it prevents the mind from being distracted;
therefore, mindfulness serves as the basis for concentration (*samādhi*) and acts as its function by being able to produce right concentration.
Thus, it is said here that its function is to serve as the basis for concentration. Consequently, regarding any matter never before experienced or practiced, mindfulness will certainly not arise.
That which has been previously experienced and practiced passes by like the wind over the ear; lacking a concentrated mind, it cannot be clearly remembered, and mindfulness does not arise.
Therefore, this [mental factor] is also not subsumed under the universal (sarvatraga) factors. To distinguish it from others below, one master says: "Whenever the mind arises..."

It must necessarily be accompanied by mindfulness (*smṛti*). This is because mindfulness, through its clear registration of an object so that it is not forgotten, serves as the cause for recollection at a later time.

This [position] is also erroneous, as it falsely grasps the universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*) of application (*manasikāra*) to be mindfulness; this was previously refuted. Later, it is further demolished as follows:

If one claims that because there is recollection at a later time, there must necessarily have been mindfulness beforehand acting as its cause, then it would follow that later mindfulness could possess delusion (*moha*) or faith (*śraddhā*). [This is absurd.]
And so forth. Even in the aforementioned cases where these serve as causes, it is as in the state of the seventh and eighth transformations of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*):

although there was no faith previously, faith can nevertheless arise; yet, since there was delusion prior to the seventh transformation, [faith] certainly would not have arisen. How, then, could a preceding moment be the cause of a subsequent moment?
However, the cause of the preceding mind and mental factors does not reside in the presence of mindfulness; rather, it truly arises from the present universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
The power of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) is so strong that it is sufficient to serve as the cause for recollection at a later time;
therefore, one must not maintain that mindfulness (*smṛti*) necessarily exists within the mind itself. What is meant by "concentration" (*samādhi*)? The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

"Perception is the focused application of the mind, which prevents the mind from scattering toward various objects. Wisdom is the basis of reliance, because when the mind abides in calm concentration, one knows things as they truly are. Thus, [mindfulness] is attained.
That which is desired is what one wishes to obtain, as in the contemplation of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*).

That which is loathed is what one wishes to lose, as in the contemplation of the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*). That which is neither is that which is neither obtained nor lost. Regarding the phrase "the mind is focused":
this indicates the nature of the object toward which this mind desires; it is that which enables the mind to abide in this object, rather than referring exclusively to a single [object].

This refers to the term "object" (*ālambana*). If it were to refer to a single object alone, then since the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) contemplates the eight truths across the upper and lower realms with distinct objects before and after, there would be no sustained focus;
consequently, there would be no meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, the term "sustained focus" does not refer to a single object alone.
Even if it were a single object, if the mind is not bound to it with sustained focus, concentration will not arise. Thus, it is not subsumed under the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
The following section distinguishes [this view] from others. One master says: "Although the mind is not focused intently on a single object, concentration (samādhi) nevertheless arises at that time;

it is simply that the characteristics of this concentration are subtle and hidden, such that those with coarse minds do not perceive them themselves. This is truly a universal mental factor (sarvatraga), and it is no mere idle claim.
The following refutation states: "If you claim that this concentration causes the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta) to harmonize and together move toward a single object..."
Therefore, the argument that this is a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*) is also logically untenable.
Its function is to cause the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness to harmonize and converge upon a single object; it is not a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

If you argue that this concentration is a universal factor because it prevents the mind from having divergent objects for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), this is also logically untenable, because a momentary mind is the smallest unit of time. By itself—
However, there is no change regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*). Why must it necessarily wait for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) before becoming unchanging?
If it is argued that the mind which grasps the object of focus through concentration is a pervasive factor (*sarvatraga*), this is also illogical;
for that which causes the mind to apprehend the object is attention (*manaskāra*), not the mind in concentration. Some say that this [is] concentration...

The essence [of concentration] is the concentrated mind. Why is this so? The Sūtra states that this concentration is called "training of the mind" (*citta-śikṣā*), and it is also called "one-pointedness of mind" (*citta-ekāgratā*).
Therefore, the essence of concentration is the mind itself. This reasoning is also not correct. It is by relying on concentration that the mind is gathered, which is termed "training of the mind";
it is by causing the mind to be one-pointed that it is termed "one-pointedness of mind. How could one say that concentration is identical to the mind?

Yes. Since this concentration (*samādhi*) is subsumed within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), one may formulate the following formal argument (*prayoga*):

Concentration is not identical to the mind, because it is subsumed under the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), just like mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Regarding the term "subsumed," it refers to [the inclusion of] concentration as a faculty, concentration as a power, concentration as a factor of enlightenment, and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), and so forth. As for the phrase "just like mindfulness and wisdom," since mindfulness, wisdom, and the others...
Since there exists a distinct nature [of phenomena], why is it that this alone is not so, yet you claim it is "identical to mind"? What is wisdom (*prajñā*)?
Its essential nature (*svabhāva*) consists in the discernment (*viveka*) of all phenomena regarding the objects under investigation.

Its function (*karma*) is to eliminate hesitation by attaining certainty through such discernment; that is, within objects that are either beneficial, detrimental, or neither, one employs the mind of wisdom.
Through investigation and discernment, one subsequently reaches certainty; thus, the mind is free from doubt.

Therefore, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are like the two wheels of a chariot or the two wings of a bird—neither can be dispensed with. Wisdom must arise through concentration, and certainty is attained through wisdom;
by relying on this, one forever severs all doubts regarding objects that are not to be scrutinized as well as the deluded mind.
In the middle [category], because there is no wisdom of decisive discernment (*viniścaya-jñāna*), it is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*). This distinguishes it from the lower category.

Some say that even in states of mind characterized by delusion regarding objects that are not being investigated, wisdom does arise; however, its characteristics are subtle and hidden, making it difficult to perceive, and thus it is not accepted as a "great" [universal] factor.

How can it be known that this exists? Why is it considered a "great reception" (*mahāvedanā*)? Because within the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is described as a "universal mental factor" (*mahābhūmikadharma*).
As the verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Feeling, perception, volition, contact, desire, wisdom, mindfulness, attention, resolve, and concentration—these ten are universal across all minds;
therefore, they are all called universal mental factors. [The opponent] refutes this, saying: "The various schools' Abhidharmas..."
This would result in mutual contradiction and a lack of definitive standard; how then can you maintain that these constitute a fixed authority?

For instance, the *Abhidharmakośa* names the six factors—delusion (*moha*), negligence (*pramāda*), indolence (*kausīdya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), torpor (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—as the "great afflictive ground-factors" (*kleśamahābhūmika*).

Therefore, if one compares them by way of their "grounds" (*bhūmi*), since factors such as desire (*chanda*) and contact (*sparśa*) are likewise pervasive across all grounds, desire and the others could also be termed "great ground-factors" (*mahābhūmika*). If...

When desire and the other [mental factors] are compared with contact and the others as universal factors (*sarvatraga*), they are not of equal status; how, then, could they be called "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika*)?
This is because the universal factors extend across all four categories of universality, whereas the object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyata*) extend only across two.

Furthermore, the Sūtra states that the five beginning with contact are universal; if one were to claim that ten factors are universal, it would contradict the scriptural authority of the Sūtra. Thus, it is not so.

One should hold firmly to this. Below, the refutation by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is set forth: "The five factors, such as desire and so forth, are certainly not universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), because they are not contact (*sparśa*) and the like, just like faith, greed, and so forth."
There is an interpretation that these five are necessarily mutually supportive (and so on, up to) coexist with the *ālayavijñāna*, and instances of this kind are not limited to one.
Second, there is an extensive analysis of the states in which these five manifest. Some say that these five modes of activity do not contradict one another;

they mutually benefit each other, are always present wherever [the consciousnesses] reside, and whenever any one arises, the other four must necessarily be present. Others say that these five manifest...

Their arising is indeterminate. Why is this? Because among these four "all-inclusive" categories (*sarvatraga*), the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that there is no subsequent [category] nor the two simultaneous "all-inclusive" categories.
Furthermore, it states that these five arise in relation to the four objects; since the objects are indeterminate, the subjective factors (*ālambaka*) are also indeterminate.
Therefore, one should say that these five may sometimes arise as one, sometimes as two, or sometimes as three.
At times four arise; at times five arise; and there are occasions when none of the five arise simultaneously. Therefore, they are said to be "indeterminate.
Regarding the occasion when one arises: this refers to each mental factor arising with respect to its own respective object.

Although there are two mental factors regarding the object under observation, because at times concentration arises but wisdom does not, and at other times wisdom arises but [concentration] does not, [only one arises].

Because it is characterized by concentration (*samādhi*), it also arises as a single state within a mind that is otherwise ignorant and distracted. In order to bring this restlessness to an end, one focuses on a single object;
yet, being unable to discern right from wrong or gain from loss, it possesses concentration without wisdom—a fact well known to the world.
Question: Since there is no discernment within the mind of one who is ignorant, why is it said that they take the object of observation as their cognitive support (*ālambana*)? Answer:

Upon reaching the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one possesses a slight degree of the power of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and is thus able to take an object as support;

therefore, it is said that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) takes the object of observation as its support. Alternatively, because this state occurs for the majority [of such practitioners], it is said that there is concentration but no wisdom. Among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), in the east...
In playfulness, one forgets what is behind; in distraction, one forgets what is before. Although one may concentrate on a single object, the three poisons still arise.
Is it not thus that there can be meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without wisdom (*prajñā*)? At times two [mental factors] may arise together:

namely, when regarding a desired and determinate object, desire and resolve (*adhimokṣa*) arise; or when regarding a desired and previously experienced object, desire and mindfulness (*smṛti*) arise; or regarding a desired...
Within the observation of an object, there arises desire and concentration; or desire and wisdom;
or, regarding a determined and previously familiar object, there arises resolve and mindfulness; or, regarding a determined object of observation, there arises resolve and concentration;
or resolve and wisdom; or, regarding a previously familiar object of observation, there arises mindfulness and concentration; or mindfulness and...

Regarding wisdom (*prajñā*): either concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom arise with respect to the object of observation; generally, for these two together, there are ten phrases. Or, at times, three [mental factors] arise:
namely, with respect to what is desired, determined, and previously practiced, desire (*chanda*), understanding (*adhimokṣa*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*) arise.

With respect to what is desired, determined, and being observed, desire, understanding, and concentration (*samādhi*) arise; or desire, understanding, and wisdom arise. With respect to what is desired and previously practiced...
Regarding the object of observation: one gives rise to desire, concentration, and wisdom; or, regarding the desired object of observation, one gives rise to desire, concentration, and wisdom.

Regarding the determined and previously practiced object of observation, one gives rise to understanding, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; or, regarding the determined object of observation, one gives rise to understanding, concentration, and wisdom.
Regarding the previously practiced object of observation, one gives rise to mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. In all cases, these three are likewise [applied].

There are ten phrases in total. As for "sometimes four arise," this refers to the arising of desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and concentration (*samādhi*) with respect to that which is desired, determined, previously practiced, and observed;

or the arising of desire, resolve, mindfulness, and wisdom (*prajñā*); or the arising of desire, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom with respect to that which is desired, previously practiced, and observed;
or the arising of desire, resolve, concentration, and wisdom with respect to that which is desired, determined, and observed.
Alternatively, regarding what has been previously practiced with certainty, one gives rise to understanding (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
There are four such factors, which together constitute five categories. At times, five may arise simultaneously—that is, when all four objects are present and the five mental factors arise together.

Thus, regarding these four objects giving rise to five mental factors, their simultaneous arising constitutes the general case, while their arising individually constitutes the specific case. When one [object] arises, there are five categories.
When two [objects] arise, there are ten phrases; when three arise, there are ten phrases; when four arise, there are five phrases; when five arise, there is one phrase.
Altogether, this totals thirty-one phrases. Furthermore, there are five occasions when none arise simultaneously:

for instance, they do not arise when these four objects are absent, because they arise only in relation to their respective objects; nor do they arise at the moment of the *sater-luò-xīn* (the sudden, initial mind), as it lacks...
Because it is a form of discrimination (*vikalpa*), it does not arise simultaneously with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Because it is not pervasive of the mind, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses [do not possess] these five object-specific mental states (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*). These points should be reflected upon according to reason through their various classifications.
The three consciousnesses are associated with sensation (*vedanā*). The first [consciousness] is associated with cognition (*vijñāna*); the subsequent one is associated with sensation.

Regarding the presence or absence of the first seven and the eighth consciousness according to their respective stages: in the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the seventh consciousness possesses only wisdom (*prajñā*), while the eighth consciousness is entirely absent.

In the stage where the basis has already been transformed, both consciousnesses possess all five [mental factors]. This has already been explained in detail within the section on the two types of transformative consciousness.
Next, regarding the six consciousnesses: in all their states, they are associated with the five factors, as there is no contradiction whether they have undergone transformation (*parāvṛtti*) or not.
Next, regarding the first five consciousnesses: one master says that these five are entirely non-existent; another master says that these five may exist.
This means that although these five [consciousnesses] lack predominance (*adhipatya*), they do possess a degree of feebleness; it does not mean they are entirely absent.

It is simply because they are so feeble that they appear as if they were non-existent. Regarding the passage "excluding the inferior," the question asks: since the five sensory consciousnesses are distracted and lack focused concentration, how can they be considered predominant?
How can there be meditative concentration? For one enters concentration only when the mind is drawn into equanimity. The answer states:

If we discuss this in terms of the moments of emerging from or entering into concentration, the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are indeed precluded due to their discursive movement; however, if one perceives objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) while remaining in concentration, [they are present].

It must necessarily be associated with consciousness. Therefore, while it is possible for there to be concentration (*samāhita*), the statement that the five sensory consciousnesses lack concentration merely excludes *samāpatti* (meditative attainment), not *samādhi* (concentration).
*Samāpatti* refers to the moments of emerging from and entering into meditative absorption; *samādhi* refers to the period of remaining within that absorption.

For this reason, when the sacred teachings speak of the supernormal powers of the eye and ear, they explicitly demonstrate that the first five consciousnesses also possess wisdom (*prajñā*). This wisdom...
This is because it is the wisdom associated with the two consciousnesses of eye and ear, and also because it is the wisdom associated with the consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body.
Below, the five mental factors are concluded by way of two stages: if one refers to the stage of non-mastery, these five mental factors may sometimes be dissociated;
however, at the time of attaining mastery, these five are necessarily present. One contemplates the truths of suffering, origin, path, and cessation with delight.
Because he establishes the truths of both the provisional and the non-provisional, his aspiration does not diminish.

Because he understands the infinite within the one and the one within the infinite, his resolute conviction does not diminish. Because he perceives the distant past as if it were today, his mindfulness does not diminish.

Because walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are all without exception samādhi, his concentration does not diminish. In the five consciousnesses, there is always the performance of their respective functions.

Because it is wisdom (*jñāna*), raising the eyebrows, blinking the eyes, opening the mouth, moving the tongue, looking about, or frowning—all these are nothing other than Buddha-activities (*buddhakārya*); therefore, wisdom does not diminish.
By means of these five factors, within the state of mastery (*vaśitā*), all eight consciousnesses attain association (*samprayoga*).

Next, regarding association with feeling (*vedanā*), there are two masters' explanations: the former is partial and the latter is definitive. The former explains that [wisdom] is associated with the three feelings according to one's desire.

The two mental factors of *daurmanasya* (sorrow) and *duḥkha* (pain) are excluded because their objects are not desirable. The remaining four mental factors—*vitarka* (applied thought), *vicāra* (sustained thought), *smṛti* (mindfulness), *samādhi* (concentration), and *prajñā* (wisdom)—are associated with the other four feelings (*vedanā*).

Although *duḥkha-vedanā* is excluded, this is because these five factors involve decisive judgment, clear recollection, focused attention, and discernment, which are absent in the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
Since the first five consciousnesses are subsumed under *duḥkha-vedanā*, consciousness (*vijñāna*) itself does not associate with these four mental factors.
It should be so; for even painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) is not dissociated [from them]. According to the correct principle, all five factors are associated with the five feelings (*pañcavedanā*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that regarding the unsurpassed Dharma, one feels longing, sorrow, and distress because one seeks to realize it.

When one is in a state of sorrow and distress, is this not the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)? Seeking to realize [the goal] is not something pleasant; why then do you say that the faculty of grief is not associated [with these factors]?

It is associated with desire (*kāma*). Is it not the case that one desires to be separated from painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*)? It is an established principle that there is suffering on the mental level (*manobhūmi*);

why then do you say that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is not associated with desire? The treatise states that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is associated with grief and suffering; if desire were absent, how could there be craving?
Furthermore, below the section on the faculty of suffering, it is proven that four [mental factors] are associated with the faculty of suffering. Because...
The former master said: "The five consciousnesses lack definitive discernment, clarity, and mindfulness; therefore, these [four dharmas] do not associate with the five consciousnesses.

To this, it is replied: Since the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) already associates with the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), what fault is there in the four dharmas also associating with suffering?
Furthermore, although the first five consciousnesses lack the four predominant dharmas, they do possess subtle functions such as the sealing of the object (*viṣayamudraṇa*).

4. How can it be said that they do not exist? Because of these five bases, they are necessarily associated with the five feelings (*vedanā*). Regarding these five, there are four further analytical classifications.
These five, moreover, pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), all three realms (*traidhātuka*), and to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Since these five pertain to all natures and all stages (*bhūmi*), one knows that the three natures and the three realms are all pervaded by the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Since neither transformation nor non-transformation is excluded, one should know that both the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), and so forth, must likewise exist.
Such categories may be understood by applying this analogy accordingly.
