If one harbors resentment—and so forth, as explained at length regarding various miscellaneous defiled matters—the term "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*) also includes the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), because these are of the nature of being outflows (*niṣyanda*) from those prior afflictions.
Other defiled phenomena that are of the same category as the afflictions are called only "secondary afflictions" because they are not included within the [primary] afflictions themselves;
because they are manifold; because they include the afflictions; and because they include other defilements. It is not [the case that they are not secondary afflictions].

There are only twenty. The reason why only these twenty are mentioned here is that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are not included, as they pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and because this [treatment] is intended to be concise and precise.
Furthermore, these remaining defiled phenomena are either states (*avasthā*) or outflows (*niṣyanda*), and are all subsumed under the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Regarding how they should be considered according to their respective categories, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*: "In this way... [and so forth].
All afflictions (*kleśa*) are merely specific manifestations of these four characteristics within this context; one should understand that they are subsumed according to their respective natures.
As for the four characteristics: first, that which arises in all unwholesome minds; second, that which arises in all defiled minds;
third, that which arises in each distinct unwholesome mind; and fourth, that which arises in wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate minds. Namely:

The two medium-level secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) arise throughout all unwholesome minds. To the eight great secondary afflictions, one adds wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*) and wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*);
these ten secondary afflictions arise throughout all defiled minds. The ten small secondary afflictions, such as anger (*krodha*), arise from distinct unwholesome minds;
when one arises, a second necessarily does not. The four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*) arise throughout both wholesome and unwholesome minds.
When an indeterminate mind arises, these secondary afflictions (upakleśa) operate briefly within twelve bases (āyatana) if they belong to the desire realm (kāmadhātu). That is to say:

attachment, aversion, and delusion operate by relying on the bases of engaging in misconduct; anger and so forth, up to guile (śāṭhya), operate by relying on the bases of strife, contention, and rivalry;
lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya) operate by relying on the basis of violating ethical discipline (śīla); and deceit (māyā) and so forth, up to scheming (sāṃdhāna)...

Harmfulness operates in dependence on the sphere of following and practicing what is not the dharma of virtuous persons. Deceitfulness and so forth, up to association with evil friends, operate in dependence on the sphere of wrong livelihood.
Intolerance, indulgence, and so forth, up to unequal craving and attachment, operate in dependence on the sphere of attachment to sensual desires.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of existence (*astidṛṣṭi*), and the view of non-existence (*nāstidṛṣṭi*) operate in dependence on the meaning of the Dharma as it has been heard.

The mind operates by way of reflecting with discernment upon its objects; it operates by way of the skillful means of mental tranquility (*śamatha*)—holding the mind through non-attention toward desire and so forth, based on the meaning being reflected upon;
it operates by way of looking back with affectionate attachment, based on the successive enjoyment of material wealth and the Dharma;
and [it operates] based on the lack of integrity, the lack of gentleness, and the lack of conformity to one's own kind. Based on...

They function in relation to dwelling places that are not mixed with others; from sensual thoughts (*kāma-vitarka*) up to thoughts of attachment to family life (*jāti-saṃyoga-vitarka*), they function in dependence on secluded bedding and lodgings.
Sorrow, lamentation, and so forth, function in dependence on places where manifold sufferings accumulate.

Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, there are the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), yokes (*yoga*), graspings (*upādāna*), fetters (*bandhana*), stains (*mala*), arrows (*śalya*), outflows (*āsrava*), stumps (*khila*), and floods (*ogha*).
The names [of these] are omitted here as the text would be too voluminous.
Regarding these twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the principles and scriptural citations cited therein should be understood as previously explained.

Third, there are ten classifications by way of various categories. First, the classification of the provisional and the real: the ten minor secondary afflictions refer to anger (*krodha*) and so forth; the major secondary afflictions...

Third: namely, heedlessness (*pramāda*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*). Together with the ten secondary [afflictions], these are all established based on the three equal states and so forth, and are therefore all nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*).
The four beginning with lethargy (*styāna*) are definitely substantially existent (*dravyasat*). The three beginning with restlessness (*auddhatya*) apply to both the nominal and the substantial.
All twenty [afflictions] arise through the power of either innate or discriminative afflictions; thus, they are all common to both.
Regarding the two categories of innate and discriminative: those that arise from the seventh consciousness following the innate fundamental afflictions are [the innate ones].

That which is innate arises from the sixth consciousness; that which arises following the fundamental afflictions through discrimination is discriminative, because the secondary afflictions follow the fundamental ones.
Among these twenty [secondary afflictions], the ten minor ones do not correspond with one another (up to the point that they oppose only the wholesome through torpor, restlessness, and so forth).
There are three [points]: the gate of association within their own class. Among these twenty, the ten minor [afflictions] have no sense of mutual correspondence within their own class;

this is because among these twenty, the minor [afflictions] definitely lack mutual correspondence, as they are incompatible with one another, their modes of activity (*ākāra*) being coarse and violent, each acting as a primary factor.
Since the two intermediate [unwholesome mental factors] arise together with unwholesome minds, they arise accordingly—either as minor or major, or both.
The eight major [factors] are taught in the treatises to pervade all defiled minds; thus, they are capable of arising together with both the minor and the intermediate. Question:
Since the eight major factors pervade all defiled minds and are capable of arising together, why is it stated in other places that six or five are pervasive? Answer: If [the mind is] obscured...
When lethargy (*styāna*) is predominant, restlessness (*auddhatya*) does not arise; when restlessness is predominant, lethargy does not coexist with it.

Because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are mutually contradictory, these two are said not to pervade all defiled minds (*kliṣṭa-citta*). As for the five [factors] said to be pervasive, they exclude non-discernment (*asamprajanya*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), and distraction (*vikṣepa*);
this is because lethargy, restlessness, and the like do not contradict the defiled or the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), but only contradict wholesome states (*kuśala-dharma*).

Therefore, this contradicts [the claim that it is] exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*). This is different from the contradiction with the fourth fascicle regarding [the claim that it is] exclusively wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*);

the latter is a term of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), whereas this is a term of affirmation (*paridīpana*). Since this is exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*), it does not coexist with the eighth [consciousness]. [The universal mental factors] such as contact (*sparśa*) and attention (*manaskāra*) may exist in association with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).

Fourth, regarding the gates of association with the various consciousnesses: the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) lacks all three grades—small, medium, and great. The seventh consciousness possesses the eight [great] afflictions;

some say it possesses five, while others say it possesses six, as explained in the preceding text. The sixth consciousness possesses all three grades—small, medium, and great. The five sensory consciousnesses lack the small grade;
as for those that share the medium and great grades, they arise simultaneously within their own class, unlike the small grade which does not follow its own class in this way.
All [of these] co-arise. Since the first five arise simultaneously within their own category, they may also exist [in this manner].

For this reason, the five feelings associated with the intermediate and great [mental states], up to the intermediate and great secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), are also [to be understood] according to the meaning of reality.
5. The Section on the Five Feelings (*pañca-vedanā-mukha*). Regarding the statement that those [mental factors] which are "middling" or "great" are associated with the five feelings:

this refers back to the fact that the middling and great [factors] coexist with the five consciousnesses; they too should be associated with the five feelings, because the first five consciousnesses are associated with the five feelings.

According to one interpretation, among the ten minor [afflictions], the three—sycophancy (*śāṭhya*), deception (*māyā*), and arrogance (*mada*)—are excluded. These ten factors, such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, are associated with the three feelings of joy (*saumanasya*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

It should be so. Excluding the feelings of suffering and pleasure, the three—flattery (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), and pride (*mada*)—are associated with the four feelings of sorrow (*daurmanasya*), joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), excluding only the feeling of suffering.

According to one interpretation, because the seven [mental factors] beginning with anger (*krodha*) are states of aversion (*dveṣa*), they lack pleasure and are thus associated only with the four feelings.

As for the three—flattery, deceit, and pride—they are associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); since the mental consciousness possesses the feeling of suffering, these [three] should likewise be associated with it as well. Therefore...

"Concomitant with the five feelings. This characteristic of these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) being concomitant with feeling is exactly the same as what is stated regarding the primary afflictions (*mūlakleśa*);

this is the actual meaning. In that [text], it says: "The three—greed, hatred, and delusion—whether arising simultaneously (*sahaja*) or through discrimination (*vikalpita*), are all capable of being associated with the five feelings.
These secondary afflictions are all outflows (*niṣyanda*) from specific states (*avasthā*) that are particular aspects of greed and the others.

Therefore, since those [secondary afflictions] are associated with all five [sensations], these [primary afflictions] should be understood in the same way. Although these [primary afflictions]—such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth—are associated with four [sensations], excluding pleasure (*sukha*), it is stated therein that hatred (*pratigha*) is associated with joy (*prīti*) and pleasure when encountering a favorable object. Thus, one should know that within this context, the three grades—small, medium, and great—are all associated with all five sensations;
this is the correct meaning. If one were to speak according to their coarse characteristics, the objects of the five [afflictions] such as anger are as follows:

Because the factors of hatred (*dveṣa*) lack joy and pleasure, they consist only of the three feelings of sorrow (*daurmanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and [neutral] sensation. The two factors of concealment (*mrakṣa*) and stinginess (*mātsarya*), being divisions of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*), consist only of the two feelings of joy (*saumanasya*) and equanimity.
The remaining three factors—sycophancy (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), and pride (*mada*)—are likewise divisions of greed and delusion; they should increase the feeling of pleasure (*sukha*).

Thus, according to the former master’s interpretation, the seven factors beginning with anger (*krodha*) are associated with only three feelings, while the remaining four are associated with all four feelings, excluding only [the specific exceptions mentioned].

This is the meaning of suffering (*duḥkha*). Among the two meanings—concomitance with the five feelings according to the great [elements] and according to the coarse characteristics—the latter meaning is correct, as it accords with the sense of reality (*yathārtha*).
Therefore, there is no other explanation. Of these two meanings, the latter is the definitive one.

Thus, these twenty [mental factors] and the five object-specific factors (pañca-viṣaya-niyata-bhūmikā dharmāḥ)—up to [the point where] distraction (vikṣepa) and concentration (samādhi) are associated—present no logical fault.
These twenty factors may all arise simultaneously with the five object-specific factors. Suppose someone were to ask:

Defiled mindfulness (*kliṣṭa-smṛti*) and defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭa-prajñā*) have mindfulness and wisdom as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). How, then, can they be associated (*saṃprayukta*) with anything else? Therefore, this commentary explains:

defiled mindfulness (which is actually *muṣitasmṛti*, "loss of mindfulness") and defiled wisdom (which is actually *asaṃprajanya*, "lack of clear comprehension") possess two kinds of natures: first, mindfulness and wisdom; second, ignorance (*avidyā*).
Although they do not coexist with [pure] mindfulness and wisdom, because they coexist with ignorance, they are also said to be associated. Suppose someone were to ask: mindfulness...
If anger takes the past as its object while it confronts a present object, how can they be associated? Therefore, this commentary explains:

mindfulness also takes as its object a present thing that belongs to a class previously experienced, and anger likewise can take a momentary past thing as its object; thus, they can be associated. Furthermore, if it is asked:

"Since concentration is always characterized by focused attention and is free from distraction and wandering, how can it arise simultaneously [with anger]? This commentary explains: [it is because of] defilement...

At the time of emerging from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the mind is likewise agitated; therefore, there is no fault in the association of distraction (*vikṣepa*) with concentration, as they do not contradict each other in their modes of activity (*ākāra*), since both share a portion of greed (*rāga*) and delusion (*moha*).

Among the [ten] secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), two are associated with all [three poisons], while eighty are associated with the great [afflictions]. (This continues until... because they do not contradict the modes of activity of greed and delusion.

The seven [subsidiary afflictions] associated with the primary afflictions (*anuvartaka*) consist of the two medium-associates (*madhya-anuśaya*) and the eight universal-associates (*mahābhūmika-anuśaya*); all of these are associated with the ten types of root afflictions.

Only the ten minor-associates (*parīttakleśabhūmika*) certainly do not arise together with views (*dṛṣṭi*) or doubt (*vicikitsā*), because the minor-associates are coarse and agitated, whereas views and doubt are subtle and refined.

Wrath (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) are all branches of hatred (*dveṣa*); they may be associated with pride (*māna*) and delusion (*moha*), but not with [views or doubt].

Greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) do not coexist; stinginess (*mātsarya*), being a derivative of greed, may also coexist with delusion (*moha*) and pride (*māna*), but it does not coexist with hatred, because love and hatred cannot stand together.
Arrogance (*mada*), being a derivative of greed, coexists only with delusion. Because greed is characterized by downward-looking and pride by upward-looking, they are distinct from one another.
The three—concealment (*mrakṣa*), deception (*māyā*), and guile (*śāṭhya*)—are derivatives of both greed and delusion, and thus coexist with greed, delusion, and pride. Among these three, delusion...

It is categorized as a derivative of greed (*lobha*) within the three [categories] when it coexists with greed and conceit (*māna*). Furthermore, because it also coexists with delusion (*moha*), it differs from *mada*, which is exclusively a derivative of greed and distinct from conceit.
The seven minor [afflictions] and two intermediate ones are comprised exclusively of the unwholesome; the three major and eight minor ones also pertain to the indeterminate.

These eight are associated with the three natures. As for the seven minor ones, they are: anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), avarice (*mātsarya*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*); as well as the two intermediate ones.

Only those that are exclusively unwholesome (akuśala) are the three—flattery (śāṭhya), deceit (māyā), and arrogance (mada)—as well as the eight great secondary afflictions (upakleśa). Those that are both unwholesome and obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) are common to both natures.

The seven minor [afflictions] and two middle [afflictions] are comprised solely within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). (Up to: Pride (*māna*) does not take lower realms as its object, because it is not something relied upon there.
The nine [afflictions] are associated with the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms. The seven minor and two middle [afflictions] are comprised solely within the desire realm;

that is to say, anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāśa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) are subsumed under hatred (*dveṣa*), because hatred does not exist in the higher realms. Furthermore, because those in the higher realms practice the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), they do not possess stinginess (*mātsarya*). They practice...

Because they are the ten wholesome dharmas (*daśakuśaladharma*), they are non-obscured (*anivṛta*). There are no [unwholesome] secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) among them. Deceit (*māyā*) and guile (*śāṭhya*) pertain to both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as they are subdivisions of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*).

The remaining minor secondary afflictions (*parīttakleśabhūmika*) and the eight universal secondary afflictions (*mahābhūmika*) are of the nature of outflows (*niḥṣyanda*) from the three poisons: greed, hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion.
Therefore, they pervade all three realms. First, the manifestation [of these afflictions] in the lower realms is explained.

If an affliction of a higher realm arises in a lower stage, it may give rise to the first ten [afflictions] of the higher realm, because through craving for the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the higher realm, one gives rise to pride, deceit, and flattery toward others.

If an affliction of a lower realm arises in a higher realm, the higher realm gives rise only to the latter ten; that is, the six intermediate ones and the following, because of slandering cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), as well as the lower [realms].

Because it arises precisely when moistening birth is about to occur, it is associated with wrong view; thus, it slanders cessation and the path. Because it is associated with craving, it moistens birth downward.
Therefore, it is said that "wrong view and craving may both give rise to it. The ten minor [afflictions] are merely distinctions of states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*);

they differ from the intermediate and great [afflictions], which possess the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*). Consequently, they are not the actual moistening nor the actual slandering of cessation. Next...
Explaining the objects of focus (*ālambana*): First, it clarifies how those in lower realms take higher realms as objects. Regarding "those that follow the great and follow what is below":

these refer to the associated afflictions such as greed (*rāga*) that take higher realms as their objects; because they take the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of higher realms as their objects, they are associated with the greed and other afflictions of those higher realms.

Since these ten types pervade the defiled mind, one master says that the ten minor [afflictions] of the lower realms do not take the higher realms as objects. This concerns their mode of activity (*ākāra*).

They are coarse and proximate, for they cannot reach up to grasp the dharmas of the higher meditative absorptions. One master says that the ten minor [defilements] can also take the higher realms as their objects;
even regarding the dharmas of superior stages, envy and other such states can arise. Next, it clarifies how the higher realms take the lower as their objects:

the eight major and ten minor [defilements], including flattery and deception, can also take the lower realms as their objects when one is in a higher realm, because one relies on the meditative absorption of the higher stage to feel pride toward the lower.

Because it belongs to the realm [of form], it arises in association with pride (*māna*) and other afflictions of the lower realms. Regarding the statement that Brahmā gives rise to flattery and deception toward the Śākya son:
it is as when the Great Brahmā King, within his own assembly, concealed his true state and manifested deceptive signs to mislead the bhikṣu Aśvajit, in order to avoid being questioned by him;
thus he indulged in self-conceited praise and the like. The *mada* (intoxication/arrogance) of the upper realms is not...

Regarding those that take the lower realm as their object: because the conceit of the lower realm is not something to be relied upon, all twenty are neither included within the category of those in training (*śaikṣa*) nor those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); this is because these [twenty] are exclusively defiled, whereas those [two categories] are exclusively pure.
The ten [categories of] learners and non-learners: these twenty are all not subsumed under the stage of learning (śaikṣa) or the stage beyond learning (aśaikṣa).

This is because these twenty secondary afflictions (upakleśa) are exclusively defiled, whereas the stages of learning and beyond learning consist solely of the pure. Therefore, they do not associate with defiled mental factors (cittasamprayukta).

The latter ten are exclusively abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), because envy and other such afflictions arise toward [the truths of] cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).

These eleven are what is abandoned. The "latter ten" refers to the two secondary [afflictions] among the middling and great categories; these two middling ones and the eight great ones are abandoned through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, and are not non-abandonable (*aprahātavya*).
This is because they arise in association with both innate (*sahaja*) and discriminative (*vikalpita*) afflictions.
Therefore, those that arise through discrimination (*vikalpita*) are abandoned only by insight (*darśana-heya*). Those that are innate (*sahaja*) are abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

As for those abandoned by insight, they follow the fundamental afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*) in their delusion regarding the characteristics of the Four Truths; whether deluded in a general or specific manner, they all arise simultaneously with the fundamental afflictions.

Thus, following the fundamental afflictions, they all pertain to the four categories (*catuṣkoṭi*). Regarding the intimacy or remoteness of their delusion concerning the Truths, it is as follows: [text continues]
Just like the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are therefore abandoned through both [paths]. One master says:

"The first ten minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*) are abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they take coarse, conventional worldly objects as their domain and arise spontaneously (*svarasena*) without conceptualization (*avikalpa*). Another master says:

"The ten minor ones also pertain to both types of abandonment, because they arise through the power of both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*) afflictions. They take others as their objects...

Because anger and other afflictions arise from the fundamental view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), those [afflictions] abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) take as their objects whatever is to be taken by those fundamental views—either collectively or individually—and thus they all pertain to the four noble truths. One master says:

"Anger and the others arise only from the fundamental delusions regarding the four truths; they do not directly delude the truths themselves, because their modes of activity (ākāra) are coarse and superficial."
Because they are unable to produce deep attachment [to them]. One master says: "The ten minor [afflictions] can also directly delude one regarding the Four Truths;
because they produce fear toward the Truths of Cessation and the Path, they also give rise to envy and so forth."

However, the ten [afflictions] such as anger take only existing entities as their objects (and so forth); those that take contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) as objects should be understood according to the above.

Regarding the twelve types of objects: the ten [afflictions] such as anger take only objects that possess substantial reality (*savastuka*), because they must rely upon a primary objective essence (*bhūta-vastu*) in order to arise.
Although their immediate objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are all contaminated, the primary essences upon which they depend may be either [contaminated or uncontaminated].

The untainted (*anāsrava*) and so forth are all explained according to the primary afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the objective entities (*vastu*), the objects (*viṣaya*), and the names of objects (*nāmaviṣaya*).
*Cheng weishi lun*, Scroll Six;
*Cheng weishi lun*, Scroll Seven.
The Layman of Jintan, Wang Kentang, verified the meanings.
It has already been stated that there are twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). What are the characteristics of the four indeterminate [mental factors]?
Section Five: The Indeterminate [Factors] is divided into three parts. First, concluding the previous section and posing the question.
The verse says: "The indeterminate [factors] are regret, sleep, vitarka, and vicāra; each has two.
These first two characters provide a general summary of the category. The following four types of mental factors are enumerated:
first, regret (kaukṛtya); second, sleep (middha); third, vitarka; and fourth, vicāra. Each of these two pairs...
Two or three characters explain the indeterminate meaning. Within this, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the names.

That is to say, remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) constitute one pair; investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) constitute another pair. These are the former two pairs. Remorse and sleep are two;

investigation and analysis are two; within the former two, there are again the latter two. Second, the explanation of the meanings: that is to say, remorse and sleep each possess both wholesome (*kuśala*) and defiled (*kliṣṭa*) aspects.
There are two meanings; for each of these two, there are two [further categories]. This applies even to *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought), where each likewise has two.

The treatise states: "Because regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*) occur throughout the stages of both the wholesome and the defiled, they are designated as 'indeterminate' (*aniyata*)."

The third section, the explanation of the meaning of the verse, has two parts: first, the direct explanation of the verse’s meaning; second, the detailed analysis. Regarding the first: first, the general explanation; second, the specific explanation. Now, for the first:

first, the explanation that because [the nature] is indeterminate within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it distinguishes itself from the previously mentioned wholesome and unwholesome factors such as faith, attachment, and so forth.
One interpretation holds that because [the mental factors] are not fixed across all eight consciousnesses, they exclude the five universal factors (*sarvatraga*).
Another interpretation holds that because they are not fixed across all three realms and nine stages, they exclude the five object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyata*).

*Regret* (*kaukṛtya*) refers to the mental state of remorse regarding actions that have been performed or not performed, whether wholesome or unwholesome, and whether defiled or undefiled; its essential nature is a state of dejection and retrospective distress. It functions as an obstacle to *śamatha*.

[This is explained] according to the characteristics of delusion (*moha*), and is designated as conventionally existent (*saṃvṛti-sat*). Among the individual [mental factors], there are three [categories]. First, the explanation of *regret* (*kaukṛtya*) and *drowsiness* (*middha*). Regarding *regret*: first, it is called "badly done" (*kaukṛtya*).

That is to say, with respect to wholesome or unwholesome deeds already performed or not yet performed—whether defiled or undefiled—it takes dejection and retrospective transformation as its essence, and it is able to obstruct *śamatha*.

Regarding karma: The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that it has as its essence the remorse of a mind characterized by delusion, based on whether an action was performed with pleasure or without pleasure, whether it was something that should have been done or should not have been done;
whether it is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; whether it occurred at the proper time or the improper time;
and whether it was appropriate or inappropriate. Its function is to obstruct the stability of the mind. "Performed with pleasure" means preceded by a desire for it.

Regarding the performance of wholesome and unwholesome deeds: those who do not delight in acting are compelled to act by the power of others and by the afflictions (*kleśa*), according to what is appropriate for them.
That which pertains to the category of delusion (*moha*) is subsumed under the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

As for "time," it refers to the period until one has attained liberation; "non-time" refers to the period after one has already attained liberation. "That which ought to be so" refers to this specific context.

Regarding those who say it should not be so: [The questioner asks] concerning the non-contextual [usage], the verse uses the single term *kaukṛtya* (remorse). The prose commentary attributes it by stating that *kaukṛtya* means *an-avadya-karaṇa* (bad conduct).
Is "not to regret" (*mā kaukṛtyam*) and "bad conduct" (*kaukṛtya*) one and the same dharma? Answer: Bad conduct (*kaukṛtya*) is the cause, while remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is its essence (*svabhāva*).

Because the essence is [derived from] the cause, the treatise attributes it by stating that "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*) means "bad conduct" (*kaukṛtya*). Question: What is the difference between the essence and the cause?

[The opponent] says: "They are distinct. [For] *kaukṛtya* (remorse) is the cause, while the essence of *vipratisāra* (regret) is the effect. How is this known? Because one first performs an unwholesome action and only later does one subsequently regret it.
This is the presentation of the reasoning. [The author] asks: "If this is so, then cause and effect are not identical. Why, then, are they treated as the same? [The opponent] says:

"It is because the *Śata-dharmamukha-śāstra* lists it as *kaukṛtya*, whereas the present verse uses the term *vipratisāra*. According to the commentary, these belong to the category of the mental factors (*caitta*)."
This verse refers to remorse (*kaukṛtya*), which is the "evil deed" (*akukṛta*) among the hundred dharmas; it does not mean that [the absence of action] itself constitutes a single dharma.
Question: If evil deeds previously committed that are unwholesome are called "evil deeds," can the regret for not having performed wholesome deeds in the past also be called "evil deeds"?
Answer: It is also subsumed under "evil deeds," because by not performing wholesome deeds, one has acted wrongly.
Therefore, one expresses regret, saying: "I previously did not perform such actions; it was because of my past evil deeds that I have failed to do so.
As for the hindrance of *śamatha* (calm abiding), it is the ability to still the mind; thus, it is called "stopping" (*śama*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:
"Regarding the stages of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and exertion (*pragraha*), the hindrances are the coverings of lethargy, sleep, restlessness, and remorse," as explained previously.
As it has been said: because it can induce both sinking (*laya*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*).

*Middha* (sleep)—also referred to as *svapna*—has its essence defined as the mind being withdrawn and lacking mastery over its own functioning; its function is to obstruct *vipaśyanā*. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:
Based on the causes and conditions of sleep, this belongs to the category of delusion (*moha*). Its essence is the contraction of the mind; it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
It may occur at the proper time or the improper time, and may be appropriate or inappropriate. Its function is to serve as the basis for neglecting one's duties.
As for the causes and conditions of sleep, they are said to be physical emaciation and fatigue, heaviness of the limbs, and the contemplation of dark images.

Having abandoned all activities, one has repeatedly practiced sleep at such times. It may be induced by the power of another’s incantations or supernatural abilities, or by the movement of a fan and the blowing of cool breezes.
The term "a portion of delusion" (*moha-bhāga*) is used to distinguish it from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, the mention of "wholesome" (*kuśala*) and so forth indicates that this sleep is not necessarily a portion of delusion. "Time" refers to the middle watch of the night; "non-time" refers to [other periods].
"Those remaining parts that should be so" refers to those times when it is permitted; even if it is not the proper time, it may be due to illness or for the sake of adjustment.

"Those remaining parts that should not be so" refers to other instances. Regarding "having the function of being the basis for transgressing what should be done," this refers to sleep as a nature of secondary affliction (*upakleśa*). Question: What is meant by "having the function of obstructing insight (*vipaśyanā*)"? What is its name?
"Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) means that because the object is subsumed within the mind, it is called contemplation; its essential nature is wisdom (*prajñā*).
This explains the preceding term "lack of mastery": it refers to making the body lack mastery, such as when one falls asleep while sitting, or does not even perceive it when someone else shakes it.
Therefore, this causes the mind to become extremely dull, light, and superficial.
Because its nature is unable to be clear, sharp, or discerning, and because it functions through a single door, the term *mūḍha* (dark/dull) explains the character *ma* (dark).

The term *ekamukha* (single-door) explains the character *la* (brief). This means that while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) functions through both internal and external doors during the waking state, if one is in this [dreaming] state, it functions only through the internal door.
Below, the meaning of "dark/dull" and "single-door" is further explained: the concentrated mind is focused on a single object; it is "brief" and not...

Because it is obscure, it is said that "obscure" distinguishes [sleep] from being in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Because waking involves extensive objects of perception, it cannot be called "concise";
thus, "concise" specifically differentiates it from the state of waking. The single character "to cause" (*ling*) precisely reveals that sleep has a practical function.

Among the five states of non-consciousness, that which is "deep sleep" is provisionally designated as "sleep," but it is not actual sleep. Actual sleep must necessarily be associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*).

Therefore, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established as follows: Sleep, though obscure and attenuated, is not devoid of essence and function, because it is associated with the mind, just like other hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and fetters (*paryavasthāna*).

"Hindrances" refers to the five hindrances: first, the hindrance of sensual desire; second, the hindrance of ill-will; third, the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness; fourth, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse;

and fifth, the hindrance of doubt. "Fetters" refers to the ten fetters: shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), sleep (*middha*), torpor (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).

Regret, envy, stinginess, anger, and concealment—since these hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and fetters (paryavasthāna) are associated with the mind, and sleep is likewise associated with the mind, there may be one who asks: "How can this sleep cause both body and mind to lack mastery?"
Regarding the question of how one can cause [the mind] to sleep when it is in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), the intent of the answer here is as follows:

It is called "sleep" by way of describing that which leads from the state of being with mind (*sacittaka*) to the state of being without mind; however, in reality, that which is without mind is not termed "sleep.

Why is this? Sleep is a mental factor (*caitta*) that possesses the capacity to induce a certain function; since that which is without mind lacks such a substantial entity, how could it possess the capacity to induce a function?

Therefore, they are not termed "sleep" (*middha*). Regarding the four meanings within the general category, one master says: "Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep have only delusion (*moha*) as their essence;

they possess no separate nature, because they are said to be comprised within the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and the portion of delusion. Another master says: "These two are not restricted solely to the defiled;
since they also pertain to the wholesome, they are not comprised within the secondary afflictions or the portion of delusion. Thus, it should be stated [that they have their own distinct natures]."
These two defiled factors have delusion (*moha*) as their essence, while the pure factors have non-delusion (*amoha*) as their essence. One teacher says: "Not so;
sleep (*middha*) is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and is not subsumed under either of the two natures of delusion or non-delusion.

[The opponent] should state that remorse (*kaukṛtya*) has volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence, and that sleep has vitarka and vicāra as its essence. He then refutes this by means of a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*): "[Sleep is defiled...]"

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are said to be a portion of delusion (*moha*) and are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of delusion. Just as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and so forth [are not portions of delusion], these two [remorse and sleep] are neutral (*avyākṛta*);
therefore, they are not portions of delusion. The fourth correct position refutes this, saying: "This statement is also incorrect.

It is not that the two factors of thought (*vitarka*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are bound together to form a single nature of remorse (*kaukṛtya*), nor is it that the two factors of thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) are bound together to form a single nature of sleep (*middha*)."

Regarding their nature: one should know that these two each possess a distinct substantial entity. Why is this? Because these two differ in their modes of activity (*ākāra*) from other mental factors (*caitta*).
As for the treatise stating that they exist as conventional (*saṃvṛti-sat*), this is said in accordance with the characteristics of delusion;
it does not mean that they lack a distinct substantial entity and are thus called conventionally existent.
"Vitarka" (applied thought) refers to seeking; it causes the mind to be hurried and agitated until the distinctions between its essential natures and categories cannot be apprehended.

Second, the explanation of *vitarka* and *vicāra* (sustained thought): Regarding *vitarka*, one interpretation holds that sometimes it is through volition (*cetanā*) that one engages with phenomena, and sometimes through wisdom (*prajñā*) that one investigates phenomena.
Its essence consists in wandering toward external objects, causing the mind to function in a coarse manner, and it acts as an obstacle to internal mental purity.

It is the karma [of vitarka]. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "Its essence consists of mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) that seeks [an object] based either on volition (*cetanā*) or on wisdom (*prajñā*), causing the mind to become coarse.
'Based on volition' and 'based on wisdom' refer respectively to the modes of seeking during the stages of deliberation and non-deliberation.
Regarding *vicāra*, one explanation says: it arises from the seeds of the *ālayavijñāna*.

It arises dependent upon the mind, is produced by the mind, and functions simultaneously with the mind. Its essence consists of being associated with the objects of investigation (*vitarka*) and engaging briefly with external objects, causing the mind to function subtly.
Its function is to obstruct the internal clarity of the mind. The *Abhidharma-samuccaya* states that it may also depend upon volition (*cetanā*).
Alternatively, it takes wisdom as its basis. Its essence consists of the mental verbalization that investigates and makes the mind subtle.

That which relies on volition (*cetanā*) and that which relies on wisdom function, respectively, as the investigative mode of activity and the mental verbalization of conceptual discrimination during states of deliberation and non-deliberation.

These two types have the function of being the basis for mental placement and non-placement. Because the modes of activity of vitarka and vicāra are similar to one another, they are treated as a pair.
The distinction is established by way of coarseness and subtlety: *vitarka* (applied thought) is shallow investigation, while *vicāra* (sustained thought) is deep investigation.

*Vitarka* initiates coarse speech, whereas *vicāra* initiates subtle speech. What is meant by "the object of mental discourse"? It is said: that which is apprehended by the mind and largely relies upon names and expressions is called the "object of mental discourse.
What is meant by "abiding" and "not abiding"? Their function is to serve as the basis for the various states of body and mind.
It is said: When body and mind are at ease, the two types of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) function with slowness;
when body and mind are not at ease, vitarka and vicāra function with haste. Alternatively, "thinking" (vitarka) is called "at ease" because it is slow and subtle, having the nature of cogitation;
"wisdom" (vicāra) is called "not at ease" because it is rapid and coarse, having the nature of discernment. Thus, body and mind may be at ease or not at ease in succession.

Both depend upon vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought); therefore, they are called "the basis. Question: Are vitarka and vicāra two provisional phenomena or two real entities? Answer:
Both take a portion of cetanā (volition) and prajñā (wisdom) as their essence. How is it known that they both employ these? It is said:
That which causes the mind to be settled is the portion of cetanā, because it is slow and subtle; that which causes the mind to be unsettled is the portion of prajñā, because it is rapid and coarse.

Therefore, if this were the case, when bringing [the mind] to rest one would employ volition (*cetanā*) without wisdom (*prajñā*), and when not bringing it to rest one would employ wisdom without volition.
Why, then, do you say they are employed together? It is said: Master Tongzhao explained that there is both the auxiliary and the primary. If volition is used as the primary, [wisdom is auxiliary].
When swift wisdom follows reflection, it can bring the mind to rest. If one employs wisdom correctly and reflects slowly in accordance with that wisdom, it likewise brings the mind to rest.
If explained in this way, there is no contradiction in employing both together.
Regarding the phrase "each of the two is twofold," there is a sense in which it refers to vitarka and vicāra; thus, the inclusion of these words is profoundly useful.

Third, there are three interpretations for explaining why each of the two is twofold. The first master says: "The two dharmas, vitarka and vicāra, each possess a distinction between two categories—defiled and pure;
this is called 'each of the two is twofold. A second master refutes this, saying: "It is not so. If one were to claim that vitarka and..."
Each has both defiled and pure aspects. Regret (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) should likewise be understood as pertaining to both the defiled and the pure.

One should explain these two as being like the preceding afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); thus it is said they are "two. Since each possesses the two natures of unwholesome (*akuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*), it is further said they are "each two.
Alternatively, "each two" may mean that each has both active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and seeds (*bīja*). A third master further refutes this, saying:
Nor is that the case. Because these two pairs are spoken of following the "indeterminate" (*aniyata*) group, one should say "two" to correctly manifest that there are two kinds of pairs.

First, to explain the "two": the first refers to regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*); the second refers to vitarka and vicāra. Within the first pair, there is one [type], regret, and two [types], sleep;
within the second pair, there is one [type], vitarka, and two [types], vicāra. Thus, they constitute two pairs by way of their types.
Because the categories are distinct, the two characters "one" and "two" manifest two pairs [of types]. Next, the explanation of "each being two" states:

this means that each of the two pairs possesses both a defiled and a non-defiled nature. This is not like faith and so forth, which are exclusively wholesome; nor is it like greed and so forth, which are exclusively defiled.
Alternatively, the word "two" is stated simply to exclude the defiled. This is because some might claim [that they are exclusively one way].

Regarding the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 58) states: "Vitarka, vicāra, kaukṛtya, and middha—these four secondary afflictions are associated with minds of all three moral natures.
If one engages in vitarka and vicāra for an excessively long duration, they cause physical exhaustion and loss of mindfulness, and the mind also becomes fatigued and impaired.
Therefore, vitarka and vicāra are termed secondary afflictions. For this reason, they are excluded here from the category of indeterminate factors (*aniyata*).
The meaning of this is made manifest by the two instances of the phrase "each has two or three [factors]. Therefore, it is further praised as being "profoundly useful.
This concludes the second section, the formal explanation of the meaning of the verse.
Regarding the fourth point, vitarka and vicāra are definitely nominally existent (prajñaptisat), for the treatise also states that they are conventionally existent (saṃvṛtisat).

Second, the analysis by way of various categories consists of eleven parts. First, regarding the distinction between the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the real (*dravya*): among the four [mental factors], only *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) are definitely provisionally existent.

Regarding the two factors of *kaukṛtya* (remorse) and *middha* (torpor), one school asserts they are provisional, while another asserts they are real. Question: If that is so, why does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* state that they are conventionally existent (*saṃvṛti-sat*)?
Answer: This is stated in accordance with their characteristics as perceived by others; it does not indicate that they lack intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*). It is just as [in the following analogy].
The internal seeds possess a real substantial entity, yet the treatise also describes them as conventionally existent (*saṃvṛti-sat*). How could it be that the internal seeds are also merely nominal?
One may formulate the syllogism as follows: Regret and torpor are real, because they are conventionally existent, just like the internal seeds.
Among the four [dhyānas], vitarka and vicāra are definitely not associated [with one another]; however, in the first two [dhyānas], there is also the sense of mutual association.

The two factors of vitarka and vicāra associate with their own respective classes; they do not arise simultaneously in association within a single moment, because they belong to different categories—the coarse and the subtle—and differ in their temporal sequence.
An objection is raised: if in the desire realm or the first dhyāna there is the time of vicāra, then vitarka does not manifest.
[Question]: Does this not result in the confusion of [the first dhyāna] with "no vitarka, only vicāra," leading to the fault of disarray? [Answer]:
Based on whether vitarka and vicāra are defiled or non-defiled, the distinctions between the three stages are established. There are three meanings for this basis of establishment:
first, establishment based on the sequential association [of mental states], namely, in the stage of the desire realm and the first dhyāna, the coarse mind and mental factors [arise] sequentially...
Because the mental continuum can be associated with both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), it is called the stage with vitarka and vicāra.
In the intermediate dhyāna, although the gross mind and mental factors continue in succession, there is certainly no vitarka;
because they can only be associated with vicāra, it is called the stage with vicāra and without vitarka. In all stages from the second dhyāna upward, as for the various minds and mental factors...
That which is a continuous succession of preceding and succeeding moments, determinedly not associated with vitarka and vicāra, is called the stage without vitarka and without vicāra. If,
within the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) and the first dhyāna, there are subtle minds and mental factors that do not associate with vitarka and vicāra,
as well as all material formations dissociated from mind (viprayuktasaṃskāra) and all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma), they do not [associate with them].
Because they are associated with both vitarka and vicāra, these are also all designated as the stage without vitarka and without vicāra.
First, [the stages] are established according to the state of freedom from desire; that is, the levels of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the first dhyāna.

Those provisional phenomena (dharmas) which have not yet abandoned desire for both vitarka and vicāra are called the stage with vitarka and with vicāra. As for those provisional phenomena of the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara),...

When *vitarka* (applied thought) has already been abandoned but *vicāra* (sustained thought) has not yet been abandoned, it is called the stage of "without *vitarka*, with only *vicāra*" (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ*).

In all stages from the second dhyāna upward, those dharmas belonging to persons who have provisionally [attained] them have abandoned both *vitarka* and *vicāra*; thus they are called the stage of "without *vitarka* and without *vicāra*" (*avitarko 'vicāraḥ*).
If one has already abandoned both in a lower stage as well, that too may be designated as "without *vitarka* and without *vicāra*. However, [this does not apply to the first dhyāna].
Because it depends on the presence or absence of those seeds and their actual manifestation, there is no confusion. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"In this context, it is called the stage 'without vitarka and vicāra' because of the abandonment of desire for vitarka and vicāra, not because they do not manifest. Why is this so?
Because even one who has not yet abandoned the desires of the desire realm, through the specific application of attention (*manasikāra*) based on instruction, at a certain time...
There are also instances where the mental activity (manas) proceeds without applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

Furthermore, for one who has already abandoned the desire for applied and sustained thought, there is still the manifestation of applied and sustained thought, as when emerging from that meditative absorption or being born in that stage.

According to the true meaning, these three are established solely in terms of realms and stages; namely, with respect to the contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena of the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
Because both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are found therein, it is called the First Ground.
Because the contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas of the intermediate dhyāna possess no vitarka and have only vicāra, it is called the Second Ground.
Because the contaminated and uncontaminated dharmas of all grounds from the Second Dhyāna upward possess neither vitarka nor vicāra, it is called the [Third Ground].

Regarding the three levels, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "In this context, the desire realm and the first dhyāna—whether in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) or as a birth (*upapatti*)—are called the level with vitarka and vicāra.
The intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), whether in meditative absorption or as a birth, is called the level without vitarka and with only vicāra."
The higher levels of the second dhyāna and the entirety of the form and formless realms are called the stage of "without vitarka and without vicāra.

Furthermore, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conditioned first dhyāna concentration is also called the stage of "with vitarka and with vicāra," because one enters this concentration by taking suchness as its object while relying on dharmas that serve as the basis for vitarka and vicāra;
it is not, however, due to the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). The rest is as previously stated.

If one were to establish the three stages based on association (*saṃprayoga*) and based on freedom from desire (*vairāgya*), the inclusion of phenomena would be incomplete and there would be great confusion.
Here, it is explained according to the second [method], which is established based on freedom from desire. The former two refer to remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*).
This [state] is described as "leisurely" (*yongyu*), being associated with vitarka and vicāra. At the time of regret (*kaukṛtya*), there is sleep (*middha*); at the time of sleep, there is regret.
Therefore, these two also possess the sense of mutual association.
All four [mental factors] are not concomitant with the seventh or eighth consciousnesses. (Up to: For this reason, the five sensory consciousnesses definitely lack vitarka and vicāra.
Third, regarding the statement that the eighth consciousness is associated with [mental factors] as previously explained:

this means that *kaukṛtya* (remorse) involves regretting prior karma, whereas the seventh consciousness functions spontaneously and constantly takes present objects as its domain; since it does not take prior karma as its object, it lacks remorse.

Furthermore, *middha* (sleep) necessarily depends on the heaviness and dullness of body and mind through the power of external conditions, whereas the seventh consciousness has, from beginningless time, been a single type of internal grasping that does not require [such conditions].
Because they depend on external objects, there is no sleep [in the first five consciousnesses]. Vitarka and vicāra both function by depending on the external gate;

since the seven consciousnesses are of a single type in their grasping at a self, they lack vitarka and vicāra. Furthermore, as for these four factors being of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), because they are intermittent, they are all dissociated from the eight consciousnesses.
Regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) correspond only with the sixth consciousness and not with the first five, because...

This is because the five great earth-elements (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) are not necessarily universal to all states of mind. One master asserts that the two factors of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are also associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).
Furthermore, it is taught that vitarka and vicāra are themselves the seven types of discrimination (*vikalpa*). These seven types of discrimination are:

first, spontaneous discrimination (*svarasavāhī vikalpa*), which refers to the five groups of sensory consciousness that do not differentiate from the appearance of their respective objects, occurring spontaneously within their own domains.

Because it functions [as such], there are two types of conceptualization with signs (*nimitta-vikalpa*): namely, the two types of conceptualization consisting of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa*), because they grasp the various signs of past and present objects.
Third is conceptualization without signs (*animitta-vikalpa*), which refers to the conceptualization of activity that aspires toward future objects.
All remaining conceptualizations take deliberative conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) as their intrinsic nature. Why is this so?

Because one engages in mental deliberation (*vitarka*), one at times seeks (*paryeṣaṇā*), at times examines (*pratyavekṣaṇā*), and at times engages in various conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) that are either defiled or undefiled.

The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Conceptualization of seeking" refers to the conceptualization that arises from observing and seeking among all phenomena. "Conceptualization of examination" refers to [the conceptualization] regarding what one has already sought...

[and what one has already]... *(Note: The source text appears to be truncated. The provided fragment ends with "己所," which likely refers to "己所尋" (what one has sought) or "己所證" (what one has realized).)*

Regarding the examination and investigation of the conceptualizations that arise from such establishment, what is called "deeply defiled conceptualization" refers to all conceptualizations accompanied by attachment to the past,
accompanied by longing for the future, and accompanied by clinging to the present;
whether they be conceptualizations of desire, conceptualizations of ill-will, or conceptualizations of harmfulness, or whatever else may accompany them.
First, there is conceptualization arising from afflictions and secondary afflictions; then, non-afflicted conceptualization, which is either wholesome or indeterminate.
This refers to conceptualization of renunciation, conceptualization of non-ill will, and conceptualization of non-harming;
or conceptualization associated with any one of the wholesome factors such as faith; or conceptualization pertaining to the modes of deportment, the arts and crafts, and various transformations.

The seven types of discrimination are all *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought). Since the five consciousnesses possess spontaneous discrimination (*svarasavāhin-vikalpa*), it follows that [this discrimination] is associated with the five consciousnesses.

The correct doctrine refutes this, stating: "The two factors of *vitarka* and *vicāra* are associated only with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and do not extend to the first five [consciousnesses].

This is because the treatises state that *vitarka* and *vicāra* are exclusively the unique attributes (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) of the mental consciousness. Furthermore, it states regarding *vitarka* and *vicāra*: [text continues].
It is associated only with sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and joy (*saumanasya*), for it is not stated that it is also associated with suffering (*duḥkha*) and pleasure (*sukha*).

This is because sorrow and joy belong to the sixth mental faculty (*manas*), whereas suffering and pleasure belong to the first five bodily faculties (*kāya*). An objection is raised: "In the first dhyāna, there is also pleasure within the mental sphere (*manobhūmi*)."
Because the mental stage of pure suffering (*duḥkhā-manobhūmi*) also possesses suffering, these vitarka and vicāra are associated with both suffering and pleasure;

however, this is simply not mentioned. It is like the case where equanimity (*upekṣā*) exists, yet it is also not spoken of. The commentary explains: "Because the feeling of equanimity is universal, it need not be mentioned."

Pleasure and pain are not universal. For what reason is it not said that, although there is mental pleasure in the first dhyāna, it is not separated from joy, and therefore it is collectively termed "joy" rather than "pleasure"?

And although there is mental pain in places of pure suffering, it is not separated from grief, and therefore it is collectively termed "grief" rather than "pain"? Therefore, vitarka and vicāra are associated only with grief.

Joy is associated with two feelings; it is not associated with the two feelings of suffering and pleasure. This citation of the two feelings of suffering and pleasure serves to prove that vitarka and vicāra are not associated with the five consciousnesses.
Furthermore, it is said that vitarka and vicāra take the sets of names (nāma-kāya), phrases (pada-kāya), and syllables (vyañjana-kāya) as their objects, which are the domain of inference (anumāna).
The five consciousnesses are not like this, as they are the domain of direct perception (pratyakṣa). This [is stated] because...

The realization of the object (*ālambana*) demonstrates that vitarka and vicāra do not correspond with the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). This subsequently encompasses both preceding meanings.

However, when it is said that the five consciousnesses possess vitarka and vicāra, this indicates that the groups of the five consciousnesses mostly arise by means of vitarka and vicāra, because the arising of the five consciousnesses necessarily depends upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
it does not mean that vitarka and vicāra correspond with them. [As stated in] the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:

The statement [in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] differs from that in the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*. Regarding the latter’s claim that spontaneous conceptualization (*svarasavāhin-vikalpa*) refers to the five sensory consciousnesses:
this is because the five sensory consciousnesses possess recollective conceptualization (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*) but lack deliberative conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).

As for the seven types of conceptualization taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, these refer to the *vitarka* and *vicāra* associated with the mental consciousness that operates simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses. How could these two cases be treated as identical?

Therefore, the evidence cited by him is unestablished. It is a thoroughly proven principle that vitarka and vicāra are the unique mental factors of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), while the five sensory consciousnesses do not partake in them.

There is an interpretation that *kaukṛtya* (remorse) is associated with *daurmanasya* (mental grief) and *upekṣā* (equanimity). Up to the realms of pure suffering (*ekāntaduḥkhagati*), it is associated with mental suffering because the mind is accompanied by pain.

Thus, there are four [factors] and five types of feeling (*vedanā*). Within this, there are three meanings: according to the first meaning, *vitarka* and *vicāra* are without the feelings of pleasure or pain;

according to the second meaning, *vitarka* and *vicāra* increase pleasure, while *kaukṛtya* has a dejected mode of activity and thus pervades mental grief, and being neutral (*avyākṛta*), it pervades equanimity; therefore, it is associated with two feelings. This refers to remorse (*tāpa*).

Because there is no joy or pleasure at the time of regret, there is sleep. At the time of gladness (*prīti*), there is the feeling of joy (*sukha-vedanā*); at the time of dejection, the feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya-vedanā*);

and in the state of equanimity, the feeling of indifference (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Thus, all three feelings are present. As for the absence of pain and pleasure, it is because they do not pertain to bodily sensation.

Vitarka and vicāra are associated with all four [feelings] except for pain; this is because during the first dhyāna, they are accompanied by joy and pleasure. One master says that these four are all associated with the feeling of pain.

[This is] associated [with suffering]. Because within the realm of pure suffering (*duḥkha-gati*), the mind possesses suffering. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 5, states: "In the hells (*naraka*), vitarka and vicāra are exclusively of a distressing nature.
Contacting unlovely objects, they induce suffering and are associated with mental grief (*daurmanasya*). Constantly seeking to escape suffering, the karma that afflicts the mind proceeds;
just as the vitarka and vicāra of those in hell experience nothing but suffering, so too are the vitarka and vicāra of hungry ghosts [the same]."
It is likewise for animals, humans, and powerful hungry ghosts (*preta*): their vitals and investigations (*vitarka-vicāra*) are for the most part characterized by dejection and only slightly by joy;
they mostly contact unpleasant objects and only rarely pleasant ones; and they mostly induce suffering.

To a small extent they induce pleasure; to a great extent they are associated with sorrow, and to a small extent with joy. To a great extent they seek liberation from suffering; to a small extent they seek the encounter with pleasure.

The mental activities that agitate the mind proceed thus. Regarding the vitarka and vicāra of the gods in the desire realm, to a great extent they are characterized by elation, and to a small extent by dejection.
To a great extent they contact agreeable objects; to a small extent they contact disagreeable objects. To a great extent...
It draws forth pleasure to a small degree and suffering to a large degree; it is associated with joy to a large degree and with sorrow to a small degree;
it mostly seeks the attainment of pleasure and only rarely seeks liberation from suffering.

As the karma that disturbs the mind unfolds, the vitarka and vicāra possessed by the deities of the first dhyāna stage are exclusively characterized by elation, exclusively contact with internally agreeable objects, and exclusively draw forth pleasure. One...
It is associated with joy; it seeks only not to be separated from pleasure, and its mental activity proceeds without affliction.
This proof that vitarka and vicāra pervade both painful and pleasant sensations is the correct principle.

The four [mental factors] are all compatible with the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca-viṣaya-viniyata-citta*), because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects of cognition (*ālambana*) are not mutually contradictory.
Regarding the five object-specific factors: their modes of activity are the mind-associates that act as the cognizing subjects, while their objects are the four types of cognitive domains.
Since these four types of domains are precisely the objects traversed by remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and the others, they are therefore not contradictory.
Regret (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) can coexist with all ten wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*), because they coexist with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) within the first dhyāna.

Thus, there are six wholesome factors [that coexist with them]. These two—regret and torpor—coexist with the ten wholesome factors. Torpor exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and therefore it lacks pliancy.
Vitarka and vicāra coexist entirely with the eleven [wholesome factors]; this is also the case when the fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*) is attained within the first dhyāna.
Because of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), regret (*kaukṛtya*) can only be associated with ignorance (*avidyā*). This is because it arises in all states, including sleep (*middha*) and so forth.

Regarding the seven afflictions (*kleśa*), regret is associated exclusively with delusion (*moha*), since delusion pervades all defiled minds. In the conventional sense, there is that which follows from delusion.
Because they manifest through mutual discourse, the karma produced by hatred is coarse in its mode of activity (*ākāra*). Greed and the others are mental only, and are thus subtle.

Because the coarse and the subtle are mutually contradictory, they do not correspond. Sleep, vitarka, and vicāra accompany all ten afflictions; this is because these ten factors all function as being simultaneously obscure and brief, as well as coarse and subtle.
Bad conduct (*kaukṛtya*) may accompany the secondary universal afflictions of the middle category; regret (*kaukṛtya*) is also common to the unwholesome.

Because they are associated with all defiled minds (*kliṣṭa-citta*), the ten [mental factors] such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth are not included, since those ten each function as a primary factor;

at the time of remorse (*kaukṛtya*), one does not follow another primary factor, and thus they are not associated. Sleep (*middha*), vitarka, and vicāra may arise together with the twenty afflictions, because they possess both dullness and clarity, as well as shallow and deep degrees of deliberation.

These four [mental factors] all pertain to the three natures—wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), and neutral (*avyākṛta*)—because they are unable to investigate the meaning of names and so forth.
[Regarding the third category,] the three natures refer to the three natures of wholesome and so forth; these four all pertain to them. Question:

Since remorse regarding performed actions is exclusively wholesome or defiled (*kliṣṭa*), how can it pertain to the neutral? Answer: Because one also feels regret regarding neutral actions; it is not only wholesome actions that one regrets.

This is the method of defilement (*saṃkleśa*). Since it was stated above that the roots and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala-dharma*), the following section distinguishes only between the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

"Wholesomeness acquired at birth" (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) refers to innate wholesomeness (*sahaja-kuśala*); "wholesomeness through application" (*prāyogika-kuśala*) refers to wholesomeness arising from discrimination (*vikalpa-ja-kuśala*). As the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
What is the wholesome acquired by birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*)? It refers to those very same wholesome dharmas which, due to prior habitual practice, have brought about such a retribution;

by virtue of this intrinsic nature, one spontaneously and effortlessly dwells with delight in that state without the need for reflection. What is the wholesome produced by application (*prāyogika-kuśala*)?
It refers to that which arises from relying upon and associating with virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*), hearing the true Dharma, and practicing according to the principle.
One practices the cultivation of pure wholesome dharmas through mental attention (manasikāra) and practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Because innate wholesome states possess the characteristic of being a result, they are coarse, vulgar, and obscure; thus, they are associated with remorse and torpor.

Because applied wholesome states possess the characteristic of being a cause, they involve vitarka and vicāra, and this applies to both applied wholesome states and those consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. The phrase "and so forth" refers to those consisting of reflection and cultivation.

This is established. It is correct that regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) are also preparatory virtues (*prayoga-kuśala*), because both regret and sleep exist within the stages of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*).
Sleep, vitarka, and vicāra all pertain to both the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*). Regret pertains only to the obscured-unspecified.
Furthermore, there are four types of unspecified states: first, ripening-unspecified (*vipāka-avyākṛta*); second, deportment-unspecified (*airyāpathika-avyākṛta*); third...

The *śailpasthānika* (pertaining to crafts) is neutral (*avyākṛta*). The four types of *nairmāṇika* (pertaining to transformations) are neutral. Although regret (*kaukṛtya*) is not by nature defiled, because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is coarse and intense, it does not pertain to the two [types of] neutral states—retribution (*vipāka*) and transformation; it pertains only to the two types of neutral states: deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craft.

This is because its mode of activity is coarse and intense, and it is not the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Concentration is precisely transformation, and its fruit is precisely retribution.
It is not fixed; therefore, it does not correspond with the transformational (*nairmāṇika*) mind. It is not a fruit; therefore, it does not correspond with the maturation-born (*vipākaja*) mind.
Regarding sleep, excluding the fourth [type], because it is not necessarily induced by a mind and one can also experience sleep while in that state, it corresponds with the first three types.

This is because one can also experience sleep while in a maturation-born mind. Regarding vitarka and vicāra, excluding the first, because the mental engagement and discernment of a maturation-born mind are subtle.
They are inferior because they cannot investigate the meanings of names and so forth.
Regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whereas dreams can universally take as their objects all things previously experienced.
Nine realms are bound [to specific levels]. Four [mental factors] exist in nine stages; however, only the first two stages and the seven higher sublime and tranquil stages are mutually exclusive.
Since regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) exist only in the desire realm, those born in the higher stages necessarily do not manifest them.

The two factors of vitarka and vicāra exist in the desire realm and the first dhyāna, but are absent from the seventh stage upward. Furthermore, those in the higher stages may give rise to [the factors of] the lower stages.

Regarding vitarka and vicāra: those of a lower stage can also give rise to vitarka and vicāra of a higher stage; vitarka and vicāra of a lower stage can also take a higher stage as their object, and vitarka and vicāra of a higher stage can also take a lower stage as their object.
Some say that this is because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) are coarse and proximate, yet extremely dull and abbreviated.
It is not the case that those born in a lower stage cannot take a higher stage as an object. This is also incorrect.

There are those who, having previously practiced meditative concentration (*samādhi*) while in a lower stage, later encounter afflictions due to false views and subsequently repent; is this repentance not taking the higher stage as its object? Furthermore, there are those who were once born in a higher stage;
even though they have later been born in a lower stage, they occasionally perceive the signs and conditions of their past lives within dreams—is this not sleep taking the higher stage as its object?

...regret is not [included] because it is the relinquishment of one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and free from desire; (up to: because all conditioned wholesome phenomena (*saṃskṛta-kuśala-dharma*) are [the domain of] those beyond training.

There are ten [types] for those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training. As for the three kinds: first, those in training; second, those beyond training; third, neither those in training nor those beyond training.
Those who train and seek liberation are those in training (*śaikṣa*). Those for whom training is perfected are those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Regret is not [the state of] being beyond training;
because when one leaves the desire realm and reaches the heaven of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), one abandons this regret.

The latter three [faculties] all pertain to the stages of both those in training and those beyond training, as these three types originally belong to the indeterminate category. If there is a person in training seeking liberation...

Regarding "liberated": these three belong to those in training (*śaikṣa*). If one is a person beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) whose training is perfected, these three then belong to those beyond training; therefore, they are called wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*).

Furthermore, because sleep, applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*) all possess arising and ceasing, they are called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Because they pertain to both those in training and those beyond training, they are called wholesome phenomena.

Moreover, there are the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the indeterminate phenomena of those in training, and [the indeterminate phenomena] of those beyond training.

Indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, as well as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*) dharmas. Sleep, vitarka, and vicāra each pertain to all [categories].

Regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep pertain only to what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because even within subsequently attained correct knowledge (*prsthalabdha-samyagjñāna*), there is still conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
