however, the gold and silver thus transformed are provisionally established resultant forms (*phala-rūpa*) that do not exist apart from the internal minds of the Śrāvakas and lesser Bodhisattvas.
This is because, according to the principle of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), there are no objects external to the mind. Now, Kātyāyanīputra was one who relied upon these Śrāvakas.
Because one has not yet attained superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the gold and silver that are transformed [by the mind] lack actual functional efficacy;

nevertheless, they do not exist apart from internal consciousness. There is no object external to the mind. Therefore, the ancient masters said: "Form arises from the sovereign power of the mind; thus, the mind can transform form.

This is why mountains are moved, oceans are covered, the earth is overturned, and heaven is turned upside down, or why the long river is stirred into butter and curd, and great [masses] are transformed.
The earth becomes gold; there is nothing whatsoever that is difficult to achieve. Regarding the second [point], the wisdom that turns according to observation:

Master Wu-xing (Asvabhāva) states that this refers to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who, when practicing the contemplations of suffering, emptiness, and so forth, or when performing the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, observe that within any single phenomenon there is only impermanence.
The various characteristics such as suffering, emptiness, and non-self are clearly not present within the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena;
rather, these manifold characteristics of suffering, emptiness, and so forth constitute the very essence of all phenomena.
If it is the case that the characteristic of impermanence exists upon the mind of the noble one during contemplation, then one knows that all phenomena are [ultimately] non-existent.
It exists apart from the observing mind. Third, "conforming to non-discriminative wisdom":

when the transforming wisdom—the fundamental wisdom of a bodhisattva—realizes *tathatā*, the object (*tathatā*) and the wisdom merge in profound harmony. Subject and object become one; there is no further discrimination.
Apart from this fundamental wisdom, there is no separate object; rather, the object conforms to the transformation of true wisdom. Therefore, it is said that [it is] "only" [consciousness].

O Mind, if you followers of the Hīnayāna cling to the notion that there are real objects external to the mind, then why do all objective appearances not manifest when you realize True Suchness (*tathatā*)?
Furthermore, the verse states that "the objects of the mind, intellect, and consciousness are all not separate from their own nature (*svabhāva*).

This "own nature" refers to the phenomena of one's own mind; or rather, it refers to the fundamental reality (*dharmatā*), which is the basis and primary substance upon which meanings depend—namely, the eighth [consciousness].
The mind. The seventh is the manas. The objects of the remaining six consciousnesses all have one's own mind as their sphere. The Buddha said:
"By this principle, I declare that all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are nothing but consciousness; there is no other reality whatsoever apart from the mind.
Thus one knows that whatever is seen or heard arises entirely from the mind; in truth, not a single dharma exists as an external object confronting the mind.
Yet, those things that appear to have an independent self-nature all arise from conditions and are formed in accordance with conceptualization;
thus, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are like illusions and dreams. There are many such scriptural teachings that serve as authentic proof, though I shall not cite them all here for fear of prolixity.
Because it is one of the five types of consciousness, such as the well-established visual consciousness, and so forth—there are indeed numerous such correct principles and proofs.
Regarding the two principles: there are four kinds of reasoning that explain the causes for the "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) nature and establish four logical arguments (*anumāna*).

The first argument establishes that the objective-image-part (*nimittabhāga*) of the five sensory objects, which is form (*rūpa*), is the direct object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses, thereby establishing [the doctrine of] Consciousness-Only.
The meaning of consciousness (*vijñapti*). Second, through inference, the sixth consciousness is established; furthermore, by implication, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are established.
All [these] take their own direct objective parts (*sākṣāt-nimitta-bhāga*) as objects, which are not separate from consciousness—this is the meaning of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

Third, through inference, it is established in general that all direct objective parts are not separate from the substance of the mind, thereby establishing consciousness-only. Fourth, through inference...
Regarding the first formal inference (*pramāṇa*) that establishes that all remote objects of perception (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are not separate from the mind, thus proving *vijñapti-mātratā*:
taking visual consciousness as an example, with the other four consciousnesses to be understood accordingly, the formal argument is stated as follows: The thesis (*pakṣa*) is:

"It is established that visual consciousness, which is a real entity (*dharmin*), does not directly perceive external forms (*rūpa*) that are separate from its own consciousness. The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because it is established... [and so forth].
Among the five consciousnesses, because it is subsumed under any one of them, it is as well-established as the other four consciousnesses.
To explain this measure (*pramāṇa*), the section is divided into two parts: first, explaining the name and eliminating objections; second, briefly presenting questions and answers.

Regarding the first, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is stated as "well-established" (*prasiddha*), which serves to exclude that which is not established for both schools. For instance, regarding eye-consciousness, the Mahāyāna school accepts the existence of others... [text continues].

Regarding the Buddha’s visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and the Buddha’s untainted (*anāsrava*) visual consciousness, these are not permitted by the Hīnayāna and are likewise excluded and not accepted by them.

Conversely, if within the Hīnayāna school one maintains that the Buddha possesses tainted visual consciousness or that the final-body Bodhisattva possesses defiled visual consciousness, this is not permitted by the Mahāyāna and must also be excluded. Thus, these two schools do not permit [these respective positions] of one another.

This is not a property that is universally established (*prasiddha*). Now, we only take the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) that is established as common to both schools (*ubhaya-siddha*) and then establish it as the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Therefore, the preceding statement says "universally established visual consciousness. If one does not specify "universally established" to distinguish between the two schools, then the preceding statement would incur the fault of having a part of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) not established for either oneself or the other. This also applies to the reason (*hetu*).

This commits the fallacy of the unestablished basis (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for one part of both the subject and the predicate, because the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) as the basis is not established for the proponent.
Therefore, the term "established" (*prasiddha*) is placed [before the subject] to exclude this.

As for the thesis-statement regarding the predicate—that it "definitely does not directly perceive form (*rūpa*) apart from its own consciousness"—this refers only to the objective essence (*bimba-rūpa*) that exists outside the sphere of the characteristics (*nimitta*) of the eye-consciousness.

Regarding the other four objects (*viṣaya*), those that are not separated from visual consciousness do not all serve as direct objects (*sākṣāt-ālambana*). If an opponent and a proponent debate, they debate only over the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the object.
If, within the Mahāyāna’s own school, one establishes that visual consciousness directly perceives its own *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), one might ask:

Why does one not state that it definitely and directly perceives the form that is inseparable from its own consciousness? The answer is: For fear of committing the fallacy of the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*).
Because it is a fallacy; that is to say, the Hīnayāna does not admit that form is not separate from visual consciousness.

Next, regarding the reason (*hetu*) "because it is subsumed under any one of the five well-established consciousnesses," the term "well-established" (*prasiddha*) is used to exclude those [consciousnesses] that are not well-established.

If one does not state the qualification "universally established" (*prasiddha*) and merely says that it is included within any one of the five consciousnesses, then this reason commits the fallacy of being unestablished for either oneself or the other party (*anyatarāsiddha*). Therefore, the word "universally established" is added to the reason as a qualification.
As for the example, "like the other universally established four consciousnesses," the term "universally established" in the example likewise excludes that which is not universally established. If...

The term "established for both parties" (*ubhayasiddha*) is established as necessary; otherwise, one would incur the fault of the thesis (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) not being established for both parties.

Therefore, the word "established" is included for the sake of exclusion. Since it has been established that the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of form is not separate from visual consciousness, the same principle applies to the remaining [objects]—sound, odor, taste, and tangibles—as they are all established in the same way, because they are each not separate from their respective four types of consciousness. Next, the question and answer are presented. First:

Question: A thesis (*pakṣa*) must be accepted by both parties. Now, when you state your proof, you say that [the sense consciousness] does not directly perceive a form (*rūpa*) that is separate from its own cognition.

Yet the opponent accepts that it directly perceives a substantial form (*svabhāva-rūpa*) that is separate from its own cognition. How can this be said to be "universally established" (*prasiddha*)? Answer:

Even the Hīnayāna schools accept that visual consciousness does not directly perceive the other four objects (*viṣaya*), because they are distinct from the visual consciousness itself. It is merely that you cause the opposing school to accept [this].
It is granted that there exists a form not directly perceived by its own consciousness; this is the basis of the thesis (*pakṣāśraya*) as established by both parties. Second, the question:

since the other school already grants that the eye-consciousness does not directly perceive the other four sense-objects, to subsequently combine these into a single thesis is to provide mutual support.

"How can this not constitute a dispute over one's own thesis (*siddhānta-vivāda*)? Answer: "What is disputed here is merely that the essential substance (*mūla-dravya*) of the object-field (*rūpa-ālambana*) is not directly perceived by the eye;
rather, they mutually differentiate one another, favoring oneself and opposing the other. This precisely constitutes the body of the thesis.

Since the Hīnayāna school admits that although the essential substance of form is distinct from visual consciousness, it is nonetheless directly perceived, our current claim that it is 'not directly perceived'—is this not a dispute over one's own thesis? (3)

Question: Regarding the point of contention within our school—that visual consciousness does not directly perceive the primary object (*svabhāva-rūpa*)—the supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like the other four consciousnesses.

Since the other four consciousnesses do not directly perceive their respective four objects, how can they be similar [to the case at hand]? Answer: The other four consciousnesses serve as the basis for the example (*dṛṣṭāntāśraya*).

Each of them possesses the property of not directly perceiving that which is distinct from its own consciousness; this is the actual body of the example (*dṛṣṭāntatattva*). Here, we are taking up this body of the example.
One does not take the basis of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). This is also like the thesis (*pakṣa*) that sound is impermanent, with the similar example (*sapakṣa*) being a jar.

One should not differentiate between sound and the jar as being distinct; rather, one takes as the reason (*hetu*) and so forth the similarity in their respective meanings of impermanence. Second, regarding inference (*anumāna*):

the formal argument (*prayoga*) states that "the remaining consciousnesses, which are universally established, are the subject (*dharmin*); they also do not directly perceive [objects] separate from themselves."

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is: "Consciousness is a nature. The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because it is of the nature of consciousness. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: "Like the five sense-consciousnesses, which are universally established (*prasiddha*). The commentary states:
The term "universally established" precedes the subject of the thesis (*pūrvaccheda*) and serves to exclude what is not universally established.

If one did not say "universally established," one would commit the fallacy of the non-establishment of a portion of the qualified object (*viśeṣya-aprasiddhi*) for either oneself or the other party. If one were to state the six, seven, or eight consciousnesses as the subject (*dharmin*), the opponent would not accept them.

If one were to establish both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses as the subject (*dharmin*), one would commit the fallacy of the property being unestablished for the opponent (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇa*).
If, however, one establishes only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as the subject, the reason (*hetu*) would then commit the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);

for the opponent could employ the seventh and eighth consciousnesses as a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) to demonstrate that the reason is not restricted to the subject alone. Now, by speaking generally of "the others" (*śeṣa*) while specifically intending the sixth [consciousness], [this fault is avoided].

The intention includes both the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses], which are established in their obscurity. Regarding the phrase "incorporating the seventh and eighth within other consciousnesses," the subsequent statement, "nor do they directly perceive phenomena external to their own consciousness," uses the word "also" (api) in the sense of "likewise" (tulya).

This means that, just as it was previously established that the five sensory consciousnesses do not directly perceive phenomena external to themselves, the reason given—"because they are of the nature of consciousness"—is identical to that of the five [sensory consciousnesses].

Because consciousness is of the nature of consciousness, it is like the well-established five sensory consciousnesses; that is to say, these too do not directly perceive objects separate from their own consciousness.
Thus, it is clearly known that [consciousness] directly perceives phenomena that are not separate from its own consciousness. Since this has been established:
Therefore, one should know that all objects which serve as the direct conditions (*sākṣāt-pratyaya*) for the sense-cognitions do not exist apart from the mind;

this is the meaning of "Cognition-Only" (*vijñaptimātra*). The third inference (*anumāna*) is stated as follows: **Thesis:** The direct conditions of the six consciousnesses necessarily do not exist apart from the substance of the six consciousnesses.

**Reason:** Because they are subsumed under either of the two parts—the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) or the aspect of appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*)—within each cognition. **Example:** Just like the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), which is the subjective perceiver.
The Hīnayāna schools accept that the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) is not separate from the substance of the mind; therefore, it is taken as a homologous example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

The "substance of the mind" here refers to the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying aspect). Although the *darśana-bhāga* also arises in dependence upon the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga*, only the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) is established here, because the existence of the *darśana-bhāga* is already commonly accepted by all parties.
As for the fourth inference: the sense organs, the body, and the environmental world are the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.
[This is] a division. Looking back at the first six [consciousnesses], they are called "distant objective conditions" (*viprakṛṣṭālambanapratyaya*).
Since the Hīnayāna does not admit an eighth consciousness, it speaks only of "distant objective conditions. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

**Thesis:** All objects perceived by their respective consciousnesses are phenomena that are definitely not separate from my own perceiving mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). **Reason:** Because they are phenomena that serve as objects of perception.

The similar example (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta) is like the associated dharmas (*saṃprayukta-dharma*). The commentary states: "This [proposition] asserts that the predicate (*uttara-pakṣa*) necessarily does not exist apart from the subject's (*ātman*) cognitive faculty (*ālambaka*).

This means that all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, being merely objects of cognition (*ālambana-dharma*), necessarily do not exist apart from the subject-consciousness (*ālambaka-vijñāna*) of the self.
If the predicate did not mention the subject's cognitive faculty, it would commit the fallacy of "partial mutual support" (*ekadeśa-āśraya-doṣa*).
This is an error. It is because the Hīnayāna also admits that the object of the knowledge of others' minds does not exist apart from the cognizing mind itself.
To exclude this [Hīnayāna] view and avoid the aforementioned fault, [the author] then states, "my own cognizer," which specifically excludes the cognizer of another.
As for the concordant example, "like associated dharmas," this refers to what was already established previously: that the direct image-part (*sākṣāt-bhāga*) is [the object].
...as they are all dharmas that serve as objects of perception (*ālambana*).
Therefore, one should have deep faith and acceptance regarding Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*). (Up to: In reality, there is also a pure portion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
III. Summary: By virtue of the above teachings and reasoning, it is known that the self and dharmas do not exist, yet emptiness and consciousness are not non-existent. Free from...
There is existence apart from non-existence; this correctly accords with the Middle Way. For this reason, the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya) spoke two verses on the Middle Way, stating:
"That which is called 'existence' refers to the delusive conceptualization of the three realms. This means there is the delusive conceptualizing mind of the three realms.

"That both of these are entirely non-existent" means that upon this deluded mind, there is an absolute absence of the characteristics of the dual grasping at self and phenomena—the grasper and the grasped. Upon this deluded mind...
There is nothing at all. To say that "only emptiness exists herein" means that within this deluded mind there is only *tathatā* (suchness);
this is emptiness, because it is manifested in dependence upon emptiness. To say that "this also exists therein" refers to within that emptiness.
There is also this delusive conceptualizing consciousness; it is precisely this false conceptualization that constitutes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Within this conventional truth, there is also the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

As for the statement "therefore, all phenomena are taught," this refers to the two categories of conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, which comprise all phenomena. Regarding the phrase "neither empty nor non-empty," it is not...
"Emptiness" refers to the mind of false conceptualization and its emptiness-nature; because the dependent and perfected natures exist, it is called "not empty," as both truths exist.
It is "not non-empty" because the characteristics of the dual grasping at self and phenomena—the grasper and the grasped—are empty;
this is the imagined nature. Regarding the phrase "because of existence, non-existence, and existence": "existence" refers to false conceptualization.
"Because there is something else": "non-existence" refers to the non-existence of the two graspings (dualistic grasping) and of self and phenomena;
"and because there is existence" means that within false conceptualization there is true emptiness, and within true emptiness there is also false conceptualization.
To say "this accords with the Middle Way" means it is not exclusively empty like [the view of] Bhāviveka and others, nor is it exclusively existent like the [view of the] Small Vehicle.

Because it [embraces] the vehicles and so forth, it is called the Middle Way. That is to say, it maintains that the two truths exist, which differs from Bhāviveka; it maintains that the grasping at the two—the self and phenomena—is non-existent, which differs from the Hīnayāna.
Therefore, it is called the Middle Way. Regarding the dependent nature as the basis for defilement and purity, this will be explained in a later fascicle.
If it is held that only internal consciousness arises appearing as external objects—up to the point of being like dream-objects and so forth—one should resolve this doubt.
Second is the objection regarding the contradiction with worldly affairs. This is the objection of the Sautrāntika masters, who say:

"If the Master of the Treatise says that there is only internal consciousness and no external objects apart from the mind, how is it that we currently perceive in the world things both animate and inanimate?"

There are [the following] determinations: determination of place, determination of time, non-determination of the body, and non-determination of function. Within this context, there are four objections: first, the objection regarding the determination of place;

second, the objection regarding the determination of time; third, the objection regarding the non-determination of the body; and fourth, the objection regarding the non-determination of function. Regarding the first objection, it says:
"If the Master of the Treatise asserts that all things are solely consciousness and that no external objects exist apart from the mind..."
Furthermore, for example, when ordinary people employ direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) to cognize the Southern Mountain, both that cognition and the mountain are situated in the south;
the mountain does not depart from the cognition, and thus one may say it is "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

However, should they suddenly employ direct perception to cognize the North, while the mountain remains fixed in the south, it certainly does not follow the shifting mind of the perceiver and turn toward the north. Since this is the case when cognizing...

Regarding the point that when one is focused on the Northern Mountain, the mind does not arise [with respect to] the Southern Mountain: this clearly demonstrates that there exists a real object of the Southern Mountain outside of consciousness.
How, then, does this establish the doctrine of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only)? As for the second difficulty concerning fixed objects:

if, at the very moment one is correctly focused on the Southern Mountain, consciousness arises manifesting the mountain and the mountain likewise arises in accordance with the mind, then the meaning of *vijñaptimātra* can indeed be established. However, as for when one is not so focused...
When one is at the Southern Mountain, the thought of the mountain does not arise; yet the mountain remains even as it does not perish along with the thought.

This is an object that exists apart from the mind. How, then, can this fulfill the meaning of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only)? These two objections above are both objections to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and to inference (*anumāna*).
Regarding the mind according to inference, the mountain as an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) would likewise exist in other locations.
Because it appears upon the mind. Regarding the third objection concerning the uncertainty of the bodies of sentient beings:
if one says that all things are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), then consider, for instance, many sentient beings together in one place;
among them, suppose half have eye diseases such as cataracts (*timira*). Among these, some might see empty flowers (*keśonduka*), while others might see hair-tufts. Or...
They see flies; or there are those who do not see objects at all. All such cases arise from the transformations of the consciousness of those with diseased eyes.
The perceived aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the transformed hairs, flies, and so forth, do not exist apart from the minds of those suffering from cataracts;
thus, they are indeed "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*). Furthermore, consider for instance five or ten people who do not suffer from cataracts, staying together in one place.

Regarding the point that all objects perceived are identical in their objective sphere (*ālambana*): since they are one and the same, it is clearly understood that there is no object external to the mind;

how then could [the claim that] "there are only consciousnesses" (*vijñaptimātra*) be established? The fourth objection, concerning the uncertainty of functional activity, is divided into three difficulties.
The first difficulty states: Furthermore, by what cause is it that the hair, flies, and so forth seen by a physician suffering from ophthalmia are not actually hair?
The actual functioning of flies and so forth is perceived by those who do not suffer from visual impairments such as floaters; thus, these are real and not non-existent.

Since you of the Mahāyāna admit that all things are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), it would follow that they must simultaneously possess actual functioning—otherwise, they would lack actual functioning at all times. Now, since this is clearly not the case, I do not understand which of these two is the truth.

Regarding Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*): A second objection asks, "Furthermore, for what reason is it that the food, drink, weapons, poison, clothing, and so forth obtained by sentient beings in a dream lack actual efficacy, whereas when those same things are obtained upon waking, they possess actual efficacy?
A third objection asks, "Furthermore, for what reason do [illusory cities] such as the City of Gandharvas (*gandharva-nagara*) lack actual efficacy?"

Function. Other things, such as brick and earthen walls, possess real functional activity. The Master answers the previous four objections by citing a verse from the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*:
"Place and time are fixed, as in a dream; the body is not fixed, as when ghosts collectively see a river of pus.
Just as in a dream, [illusory objects] have functional utility. If one relies on this verse, it is sufficient to answer the previous four objections. Now, first...
First, regarding the response to the objection concerning the fixity of location: the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:

"You yourself must admit that when sentient beings in a dream sometimes see villages, gardens, men, women, or other objects located in a single place—that is, fixed—yet at other times their dreaming mind perceives other locations, and they no longer see those previously seen villages, gardens, and so forth."
[The Master] said: "In dreams, the mind is not fixed [to a specific location]. Do you, for a moment, concede that this is *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)? The Sautrāntika replied:
"In our school, although the dream-object is fixed to a location while the dreaming mind is not, it does not exist apart from the dreaming mind of sentient beings;
thus, all are *vijñapti-mātra*. The Master said: "My position regarding objects of color-form (*rūpa*) during the waking state is likewise so. Although mountains and locations are constant..."
It is established that while the minds of sentient beings that take objects as their cognitive focus are not fixed, they never depart from the present mind.

Thus, based on the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: **Thesis:** The objective forms perceived during the waking state in our own school are existent;

it is determined that they are consciousness-only. **Reason:** Because the location of the object is fixed, whereas the mind is not fixed. **Example:** Just like the objects in a dream according to your own school.
This is the second response concerning "consciousness-only. Regarding the objection concerning the necessity of a fixed temporal sequence, the Master of the Treatise says:
"For instance, when sentient beings perceive objects such as villages or gardens within a dream, if that dreaming mind takes them as its object, these may indeed be consciousness-only."
"If it were not the case that [the object] is perceived at that time, it would not be mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). The Sautrāntika replies: "Regarding the objects within my dream:

if they are perceived by the dreaming mind, they are also mere consciousness; even when the dreaming mind does not perceive them, they do not exist apart from the dreaming mind and are thus also mere consciousness.
The Master says: "The objects and forms during my waking state are likewise so. Now, for me..."
At times one perceives the southern mountain; the mountain does not exist apart from the mind, which is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

At other times, when perceiving the mountain, although the mind does not arise [with respect to it], it does not exist apart from the present mind; this too is consciousness-only. A verse states: "The determination of place and time is like a dream.
This single line answers the first two objections. The third answers the objection regarding the indeterminacy of the body. The Master of the Treatise says: "You Sautrāntikas must also admit..."
A great multitude of hungry ghosts gather in one place. Among them, there are those who share the same karma within the five realms of existence;
these see the river of pus with certainty. Furthermore, there are three or five who, according to the power of their own individual karma, see things indeterminately;
that is, while gathered in the same place, some see fierce flames, some see excrement and filth, and some see people holding clubs.
[Objection: "If such hungry ghosts are in the same location, why is it that half see the object as fixed while the other half see different things?

Do you concede that these hungry ghosts are all *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)? [Response: "Although there are differences in what they see, none of it exists apart from the transformations of the hungry ghosts' own karmic consciousness;
thus, it is all *vijñapti-mātra*. The Master says: "In my school, it is *vijñapti-mātra*."
Consciousness is also like this. Although those of one class who suffer from cataracts perceive things differently, those of another class who do not suffer from cataracts perceive them identically;
yet, the consciousness-transformations of these two classes of sentient beings are inseparable, and all are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
As the verse says: "The body is not fixed, as for ghosts, they equally see rivers of pus and so forth. This...
The two lines of verse answer this objection. The *Ratnālokālaṃkāra* states: "As for the body being indeterminate like that of a hungry ghost (*preta*):
in reality, there is no external object outside of the clear river. Yet all hungry ghosts see it alike as being filled with flowing pus; it is not seen by only one.
However, in this place, not even a trace of pus or blood can actually be found. How could such a thing exist?"
It flows over the banks. Although there is no actual object, it is certain that it belongs to one [subject]; thus, the logical necessity is not established. One should understand this as follows:

although the mind perceiving form and so forth lacks an external object, its lack of determinacy does not exist within the body. By negating the non-existence of the object, that very [negation] becomes a reason for establishing the existence of the subject;
however, this reason suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since it also applies to cases where no object exists. Furthermore, in a place where there is no object...

There are cases where multiple bodies perceive the same thing together in an indeterminate manner. For example, although there is in reality no flowing pus in a river, hungry ghosts—due to their shared karma—do not perceive it otherwise;
rather, because they have been moved by this common state, they all see the flowing pus together. When the karma of stinginess ripens, they collectively experience this suffering.
Because their past shared karma has individually perfumed their own respective continua (*ātmabhāva*), these distinct maturations (*vipāka*) all manifest simultaneously.

It appears before them. Many sentient beings perceive this same thing together; yet, because there is actually no external object for the sake of recollection, according to that principle, you too are like this:
when all the latencies (vāsanā) created in common reach maturity, [the result arises].

Consequently, there would be no distinct objective aspects (nimitta-bhāga), such as form and so forth, arising from consciousness. Therefore, it is certain that consciousness does not arise by means of external objects.
Is this not an admission that [consciousness and its object] belong to the same realm of rebirth (*gati*)? Yet, it is not necessarily the case that their mental continuums share identical karma.
This is because we observe differences such as noble birth versus lowly birth, or wealth versus poverty; thus, [the claim of a common realm] is seen to be refuted.
Their colors and so forth should necessarily differ; since they perceive them as distinct from those other classes, it is known that this class is not the same as that one.
Furthermore, those [other beings] do not produce objects such as color through the power of external conditions.

Nevertheless, although all hungry ghosts belong to the same realm of rebirth (*gati*), their perceptions also differ according to the diverse characteristics of their karma; thus, what they perceive is likewise different. Or perhaps...
Some see the great hot Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) melting, boiling, and erupting; at other times, they see excrement and urine flowing crosswise.

Because these are not similar [to their own experience], even though they belong to the same human realm as those of meager merit, when a golden belt appears, they see it as iron chains or as a snake.
Therefore, one knows for certain that even within the human realm, there is no common perception. If this is so...
There is no difference in the nature of their vision; this is because they all possess karma of a similar kind.

However, due to the homogeneous karma (*sabhāga-karma*) of those classes, they are born into a common realm of rebirth (*sabhāga-gati*). Furthermore, there is distinct karma by which each sees individually.
It is through the power of this single capacity, according to its force, that it causes those beings to have both similar and differing perceptions. This same principle also answers other statements.

Some say that sentient beings in other realms, such as ghosts and animals, should not fail to see one another even when they are not in the same location, because their nature is the maturation (*vipāka*) of distinct karmic actions.
Although there are differences in the karma that establishes these realms, there is still non-differentiation in the karma by which they perceive one another;
that is, within the individual continuums (*saṃtati*) of those sentient beings, there exist specific seeds of karma that follow [them].

Suppose, for instance, that while dreaming, a sentient being occasionally experiences such things as the emission of impurities; you would admit that these have real functional efficacy.
Do you also accept that this is *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only)? He replies, "This is indeed consciousness-only. The Master answers by way of analogy:
"Since you admit that both the presence and absence of real functional efficacy within a dream are equally consciousness-only, it should be known that..."
In our school, both those afflicted by cataracts and those not so afflicted alike perceive objects within dreams; furthermore, there are both artificial cities and real cities.
These three types possess real and unreal functions, just as you maintain that the functions within dreams—whether real or unreal—are all *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
To establish this through formal reasoning (*pramāṇa*), one states: "The objective forms perceived during the waking state in our school are the subject (*dharmin*); they are certainly..."
The Yogācāra school argues: "Because there is a real functional activity, it is like the objective forms in your dream. This is not so.

The objective forms in your dream are a subject (dharmin) that must not belong to the Yogācāra school. The reason is: "Because there is both real and unreal functional activity, it is like the objective forms during your waking state.
Alternatively, one may say: "The states of having cataracts and being without cataracts, etc., are subjects [that likewise do not belong to the Yogācāra school]. There is... [the same reason].

The principle that "the useless is used" is also established as a tenet. The reason given is: "Because it is admitted that there are no real external objects, just as in the case of defilements in a dream.
This refers to what is stated in the verse: "Just as in a dream, [an object] has functional efficacy.

Furthermore, in the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there is a four-line verse that answers the four objections collectively by means of the single analogy of hell; the text is too extensive to be cited here.
"For what reason did the World-Honored One teach the twelve bases (up to the point of teaching them)?
This is the objection regarding contradiction with the scriptural authority (*āgama*) concerning external phenomena. The intent of the Hīnayāna objection is as follows:

If the Master of the Treatise asserts that all things are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) and that there are no real objects external to the mind, for what reason did the World-Honored One, within the *Āgamas*, state that [external objects] exist?

Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*): if all things were merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), the Blessed One should have spoken only of the base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), and it would not be appropriate for him to speak of the ten material bases (*rūpāyatana*).

Now that the Blessed One has indeed spoken of the twelve bases, it is clear that apart from the bases of mind and phenomena, there are separately ten material bases that exist externally to the mind. How can you say they are one?

All things are indeed consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). In the Master’s response, there are three parts: first, a provisional response; second, the formal response; and third, an analogical response.

Here, the initial provisional response is omitted, and only the formal response and the analogical response are revealed. Regarding the initial provisional response, he cites the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only), which states:
"Consciousness arises from its own seeds and evolves in the semblance of objective forms, in order to establish the internal and external."

Regarding the locus: the Buddha taught that there are ten. As for the statement that consciousness arises from its own seeds, this refers to the manifest activity of the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of the five consciousnesses, each of which arises from the respective seed of the five consciousnesses. Taking these seeds of the five consciousnesses as the five sense-faculties (*indriya*).

Regarding the statement that "it evolves as something resembling the aspect of an object": this refers to the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of the five consciousnesses, which, having arisen from its own seeds, is able to transform and manifest as two aspects (*dvaya-ākāra*).
The evolving seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) is called the "five consciousnesses," while the evolving image portion (*nimitta-bhāga*)—

That which appears as if it were external objects is designated as the "five objects" (*pañca-viṣaya*). In reality, however, all ten bases of faculties and objects are not separate from consciousness;
they are also *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). This [system] provisionally takes the seeds of the five consciousnesses as the five faculties.

[This is said] in response to the Sautrāntika masters, because the Sautrāntikas admit the existence of seeds. Question: Even if one admits the existence of seeds, would you not still be clinging to the notion that [seeds] exist apart from consciousness?
Answer: They maintain that seeds are held within the first six consciousnesses and do not exist apart from consciousness. The Master says:

the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) which they transform, appearing as the five external objects, likewise does not exist apart from consciousness; the seeds of the five transforming consciousnesses, which are the five sense faculties (*indriya*), also do not exist apart from consciousness.
Although they are divided into the ten bases of internal and external, all are indeed *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

Regarding the statement that the Buddha taught those as "ten": it was with a hidden intention (*saṃdhi*) to refute the non-Buddhists' attachment to the body as a single, unified self (*ekapiṇḍa-ātman*).
Thus, regarding the ineffable Dharma, he forcibly employed verbal distinctions to teach the ten bases (*āyatana*) of sense faculties and objects.
Because there is great benefit [in doing so], the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā* states: "By relying on this teaching, one can enter [the realization of] the person (*pudgala*)."

"No-self. The commentary explains: If there is one who possesses wisdom, they should rely on these scriptural teachings of the Buddha regarding the ten bases of the sense faculties and their objects, and then perform contemplation as follows:
"Throughout immeasurable kalpas, due to my evil discernment, seeking, ignorance, and delusion, I have falsely clung to my own and others' bodies as a unified self.
Because of this, I have been submerged and wandering in birth and death. Now, relying upon..."
One is taught to contemplate that one’s own body and those of others consist of nothing more than the ten bases (āyatana) of sense organs and objects to constitute their substance.
Within each of these bases, there is absolutely no function of a sovereign, independent, permanent, or unitary self; how, then, could there ever be a "self"?

By means of this, one is able to realize the principle of non-self and accomplish the contemplation of the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). This is precisely what the Mahāyāna provisionally employs as the five seeds.
This is a provisional response made for the sake of the five faculties, answering according to the Hīnayāna perspective. The Hīnayāna further objects:

"If that is so, then consider, for instance, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the five sense-objects (*pañcaviṣaya*), which is matter (*rūpa*). Since this is transformed by the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), it may indeed be 'consciousness-only' (*vijñaptimātra*) according to your school.

However, as for the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of those five objective spheres of matter, we do not yet understand of which consciousness they are the 'consciousness-only. Is it of the five consciousnesses, or of the sixth [mental consciousness]? Both...
The five objective spheres (*viṣaya*) do not directly perceive their own essential natures; rather, it is these very essential natures of the five spheres that [are perceived].

Are these not, then, existent apart from the mind? How, therefore, can they be established as *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only)? In response to this question, the Master provides his second formal answer:

"They exist as transformations of consciousness, and are not separate, real entities. This is the correct interpretation according to the fundamental tenets of the Mahāyāna, established from its own perspective.

Thus, the existence of the eighth consciousness is established. Since the Master of the Treatise states that the "substantial form" (*bhāva-rūpa*) of the five sense-objects is the direct objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, and since this objective aspect is not separate from the eighth consciousness, it is likewise *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Regarding the third analogy as a response:
this refers to the Master of the Treatise providing an analogy to answer the reason why the World-Honored One established the twelve bases (*āyatana*) for the sake of the Śrāvakas.

It is said that, just as one refutes the view of annihilationism, one speaks of the continuity of sentient beings. This is merely the Buddha’s intentional teaching (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) to dismantle the notion of a "unified self" (*piṇḍagrāha*) among sentient beings.
By provisionally designating the twelve bases (*āyatana*), he causes sentient beings to contemplate these twelve bases and realize that there is absolutely no self within them;
thus, they enter into the emptiness of the self (*ātmaśūnyatā*). Subsequently, relying on *vijñaptimātra*, they are able to contemplate all phenomena.

All [these] lack the function of maintaining a superior nature through a real track; once the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is eliminated, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is established.
Herein, the previous [objection] is answered. One must not fail to understand that answering one difficulty by concealing another is improper; therefore, it is set forth in full detail.
"Is this nature of consciousness-only not also empty? (up to: For this reason, the Compassionate Honored One [Maitreya] spoke the two preceding verses.
Regarding the objection that "consciousness-only alone establishes emptiness," the followers of the Hīnayāna raise the following objection based on the previous point:

"If it is said that all phenomena lack any real function such as maintaining their own nature, sustaining themselves, or possessing sovereign supremacy, thereby establishing the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena, then this very consciousness-only..."

Is its essence not likewise empty? The Master of the Treatise replies: "The essence of consciousness-only is indeed not empty. The Hinayana practitioner asks: "In what way is it not empty? The Master replies:

"Because it is not that which is grasped [as real]. My previous statement regarding emptiness was merely to empty away the functions—such as the imagined existence of a real essence or a superior nature—which the deluded mind clings to across all phenomena. It refers to the *parikalpita* (imagined) nature.
Phenomena that are false and illusory are themselves emptiness. This is not a mere void devoid of attachment, but the very substance of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Just as when fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) directly realizes suchness (*tathatā*), it is beyond words and transcends all marks. At that time, all imagined, illusory selves and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*) do not appear before it.
Within this state, there is only fundamental wisdom in profound accord with reality, undifferentiated between subject and object.

If this consciousness were also empty of essence, then conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) would not exist. Because conventional truth does not exist, ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) would also not exist.
One who lacks these two truths is said to have "misappropriated emptiness" (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*), and the Buddhas declare such a person to be incurable.
Therefore, all phenomena possess both emptiness and non-emptiness, as clearly explained in the preceding verse.

If the various sense-bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) also have consciousness as their essence (up to: "and if non-material consciousness were also absent"), then the fivefold characteristics of form would not exist;

this is difficult to accept. The objection from the Hīnayāna school is as follows: If one claims that all external forms have mind as their essence, such that the mind’s own self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) transforms into what appears as the grasper, which is called the "seeing aspect" (*darśanabhāga*), and transforms into what appears as the grasped—[then the following objection follows].
Regarding what is called the "objective aspect" (nimittabhāga): why is it that the manifested forms and appearances do manifest, while the transforming consciousness itself does not manifest?

Furthermore, if external matter has the mind as its essence, why is it that the manifested matter evolves as a continuous stream of a single type—just as external matter such as mountains, rivers, and the six earths [continues] for a thousand or ten thousand years?
A certain class [of external objects] undergoes no further change; moreover, their continuity is uninterrupted, and they endure for a long duration.
If sentient beings were able to transform the mind, there would be change and instability, and they could not endure for a long time.

Since external forms do not resemble the internal mind, it is clear that there are real external forms existing apart from the mind. Why, then, do you say that everything is merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*)?
The Master of the Treatise replies: "It arises through the power of the perfuming of names and words (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*).

This occurs solely because all sentient beings, from beginningless time, have mutually influenced one another through the false perfuming of names and words, thereby producing the conceptual understanding of external objects as being solid, enduring, and continuous.
Through this power, these appearances manifest; it is not that there truly exists a mind [that perceives them]."

Regarding external solidity, color, and so forth, the opponent asks again: "If it is said that there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), why do sentient beings necessarily transform into the semblance of external form and manifest it?
The Master replies: "If all sentient beings did not transform into the semblance of external form and manifest it, there would be no phenomena of defilement or purification.
For instance, all ordinary worldlings, due to their prior delusion regarding form and other such [objects]..."
Regarding the object: it is a perverted and false attachment. From this defilement, further defilement arises; its essence is precisely the two obstacles (*dvayāvaraṇa*).
You outsiders, if you do not admit that consciousness transforms to manifest as external forms, then sentient beings would not give rise to perversions.
If perverted and false attachments do not arise, then defiled afflictions will not be produced. Since defilement... [is thus absent]... [it follows that there would be no samsara].

[Question: From what cause do pure phenomena arise? Therefore, the verse of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: "The appearance of confusion and the substance of confusion should be admitted as the consciousness of form and the consciousness that is not form;
if one does not exist, the other likewise does not exist. Regarding this, "the appearance of confusion" refers to the objective aspect of form that is transformed [by consciousness].
"The substance of confusion" refers to the subjective essence of the mind that performs the transformation. "Should be admitted as the consciousness of form" means...
That which was previously mentioned as the "confused appearance" and that which is "non-form consciousness" refers to the very substance of the previously transformed mind.

If there were no other [object], there would also be no [subject]; that is, if there were no transformed appearance resembling external form-objects acting as the confused appearance, there would likewise be no consciousness-substance capable of transforming it.
Therefore, one knows that it must transform into an appearance resembling an external object. For this reason, all forms do not [exist independently].
Apart from the mind, everything is merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
Although external objects such as form appear clearly and are directly perceived, one must not grasp them as being real external forms.

This constitutes the objection based on contradiction with the tenet through the six types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The intent of the Hīnayāna objection is as follows: for instance, regarding the external objects of the five sensory realms, such as form, [they appear distinctly].
The direct perception of the five consciousnesses is obtained through direct cognition (*pratyakṣa*); this is universally established and accepted by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Why, then, do you deny it? To say that "all is representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) is a point of contention even within the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, which states:

"The existence or non-existence of all phenomena is determined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Among all forms of valid cognition, direct cognition is supreme. If there were no external objects..."
"Could it be that I have now realized such an object through direct perception? The intention [of this question] is as follows:

If the Master of the Treatise were to say that there are no external, real objects, how could he then state that the five consciousnesses apprehend external objects of the five sense-fields (*viṣaya*) by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

If [the apprehension of objects] were instead by means of inference (*anumāna*) or non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*), it would be something arisen from conceptual construction (*parikalpa*), something grasped by conceptualization, produced by forceful reflection and deliberation, and fashioned by mental construction.
The objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is not separate from the mind; thus, it can be established as "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*).

Now, since the five consciousnesses are apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as having external, real objects consisting of the five sense-fields (*viṣaya*), for what reason are they also said to be "all consciousness-only"? The Master of the Treatise answers:

For instance, when the five consciousnesses, through direct perception, take the five sense-fields as their objects, they apprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena without being accompanied by names or expressions, and without conceptual deliberation (*vitarka*).

The mind does not give rise to discrimination, nor does it grasp [objects] as external; rather, it is only the subsequent conceptualizing mental consciousness that falsely gives rise to discrimination and then grasps them as external, claiming there are real objects.
Question: Does the Hīnayāna also admit that within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one does not grasp [objects] as external?
Answer: It does. Question: How does this differ from the Mahāyāna? Answer: The *Weishi jing* (Mirror of Consciousness-Only) states: "If..."

This is the Mahāyāna position: namely, that both the five consciousnesses and the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and they do not grasp [their objects] as external.
As for the Hīnayāna school, it holds that only the five consciousnesses do not grasp [their objects] as external. The Master says:
"Since you of the Hīnayāna admit that the five consciousnesses perceiving their objects are direct perception and do not grasp them as external, it is clear that within direct perception..."
In all cases, there are no external objects; this is the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). An opponent asks:

"Are the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), which are the objects of the five consciousnesses and are perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), real or provisional? He answers: "They are real. The opponent challenges:

"If that is so, then there are real five sensory objects existing apart from the mind. Why, then, do you say 'consciousness-only'? The Master of the Treatise replies: "The five consciousnesses take the five..."
At the time of sensory objects, although these are indeed real, they are merely the objective-image (nimittabhāga) of one's own consciousness transformed by the five sense-consciousnesses;
being inseparable from the five sense-consciousnesses, they all constitute *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). Each of the five sense-consciousnesses possesses its own four parts (*caturbhāga*).

Among them, the five sensory objects are the immediate objective-images of the five sense-consciousnesses, appearing as objective images such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, transformed by the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the five sense-consciousnesses.
Manifestation. Furthermore, its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is not separate from its perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*); both are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).

When subsequent conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises, if one falsely clings to the notion that there are real objects external to the mind, this is non-existent, because it does not correspond to the actual nature of the object.
Question: For instance, when afflictions such as hatred arise within the five sensory consciousnesses, they do not correspond to the original substance (*bimba*). Why is this?

[Question: It is said that this is exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). [Answer: Although it does not correspond to the primary object (*svabhāva*), it nevertheless corresponds to the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*);

thus, it is also direct perception because the mind is devoid of grasping (*abhiniveśa*). If the anger associated with the sixth mental consciousness arises simultaneously with grasping, then both the image-aspect and the primary object do not correspond.
If it does not arise simultaneously with grasping, it is identical to the five sensory consciousnesses. [Question: Why?

Therefore, the five consciousnesses are without grasping (*anupādāna*). Answer: Because they do not extend to inference (*anumāna*) and are not the two other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they are without grasping.
Thus, one knows that the five consciousnesses, as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), take objects without grasping them as external; all are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).

Furthermore, because the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of objects such as form is not the underlying reality (*svabhāva*), it is said to be "not form. Because the objective aspect resembles the underlying reality, it is said to be "resembling form. Internal form is not...
External forms do not exist; therefore, they are said to be "not external. Internal forms appear as if they were external; therefore, they are said to be "resembling the external.
Just as objects in a dream are all transformations of consciousness alone, how can one cling to them as real external forms outside the mind?

If one perceives that all forms during the waking state are like dream-objects, yet because of this one has not yet realized that the objective realm of form is *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), there arises the seventh objection:
the difficulty regarding the contradiction between dreaming and waking. A follower of the Hīnayāna raises this objection based on the preceding point:

"If the objects of the waking state are also like dream-objects and do not exist apart from consciousness, for what reason is it that everyone knows dream-objects are transformations of the mind alone, while [the same is not known] of the waking state?"
Is it that one does not know objects are merely consciousness? The Master of the Treatise answers: It is like being in a dream before waking;

one does not realize it is a dream until the moment of awakening, at which point one realizes it was but the mind. One should understand that what is perceived during the waking state is no different from what is perceived in a dream.
That people do not realize these are but the mind and instead cling to them as truly existent is likewise a state of not yet having awakened from a great dream.
...it is so. Only upon reaching the stage of perfect awakening can one truly know it. How is this known?
It is known because the Tathāgata has described it as the "long night of birth and death. That is to say, the seventh [consciousness] is the very root of the long night of birth and death;

it is that which causes delusions to arise, leads to the creation of karma, and results in the saṃsāra of the three realms. Therefore, the *Yuishiki Shuyō* (Essentials of Consciousness-Only) asks: "If all..."

When consciousness arises appearing as a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*), is it entirely due to the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the discrimination of self and phenomena, or is it not?

If it were entirely due to this, then since the eight consciousnesses and the five sensory consciousnesses do not possess dualistic discrimination, their arising fruits should not appear as these two.
If it is not due to this, why is it stated here that only the habitual perfuming of self and phenomena serves as the cause? Answer:
Both types of discrimination are obtained through understanding. As for how they all arise from understanding:

because all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are associated with both types of discrimination belonging to the sixth consciousness, or because they are induced by these two types of discrimination of the sixth consciousness, when their subsequent fruits arise, they all resemble a self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*).

Regarding those who do not understand through insight: this refers to the sixth fundamental consciousness, which takes all things as its objective conditions and serves as the causal condition for the arising of the various consciousnesses so that they may undergo perfuming. When subsequent fruits arise, they manifest as the semblance of a self and dharmas;

or, though not external, they appear as if external, because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses reckon them as such and give rise to them as external semblances. It is like a dreamer who dreams of King Śreṇika; that king—
His appearance was upright and handsome. Later, he followed Kātyāyana to leave the household life and went to the mountains of the country of Āvanti to cultivate the Way.
The King of Āvanti took his palace women into the mountains for recreation. When the women saw that the king’s features were so upright and handsome, they gathered around him to gaze at him.
The King of Āvanti became enraged and whipped them until they were nearly dead; it was not until nightfall that they regained consciousness.
He said to Kātyāyana, "I wish to beg leave from my teacher to return briefly to my native country.
Once I have led my army to defeat that kingdom of Āpaṇatī and slain its king, I shall follow my teacher to practice the Way.
Kātyāyana granted his request and said, "If you wish to depart, stay for one night first. He settled him in a comfortable place and put him to sleep, intending to cause him to receive a dream.
He dreamed that his entire army marched to invade the kingdom of Aparāntaka; his own forces were defeated, and he himself was captured by the enemy.

His hands and feet were bound tightly, a red flower was placed upon his head, and as the drums were beaten for his execution, the king was seized with great terror and cried out until his voice failed.
Kātyāyana called to him to wake him and said to him: "If you had marched against them, you would certainly have been defeated and destroyed, just as in this dream."
The King said, "I pray that the Master will eliminate my poisonous thoughts. Kātyāyana then explained for him that all phenomena are like a country:
they are provisional names without reality. Apart from houses and other such things, there is no separate entity called a "country.
He spoke at length on various causes and conditions, down to a single atom, which is likewise not a substantial reality. There is neither "this" nor "that," and no enmity.
There is no external object. Having heard the Dharma, the King attained the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), and subsequently gradually attained the fruit of Arhatship.

Therefore, one should know that all phenomena are but consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). Dreaming and waking are identical as one. What is seen in the waking state is the manifesting mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
what is seen in the dream state is the dreaming mental consciousness. Since the discriminating mind is the same in both cases, how can there be any distinction in the objects perceived?
They are different. If delusion and awakening are such as this, how can one harbor doubts? If obscurity and clarity are thus, they may be thoroughly understood.
External forms are truly non-existent; they are nothing other than the objects of internal consciousness. (Up to: It is the same when perceiving the forms of others' minds and so forth.

The eighth [point] concerns the difficulty of apprehending the minds of others. If the Proponent says that external forms do not truly exist and are merely objects of internal consciousness, that may be so;
however, for instance, the mind of another person is a real entity—how could it not be an object of one's own mind?

The intention [of this] is as follows: If this person’s mind were to apprehend another person’s mind through direct contact, then apart from this person’s mind, there would be a separate mind serving as the object.
If this person’s mind does not apprehend another person’s mind through contact, then there is an object that is not being apprehended.
If it were to apprehend it through contact, it would contradict the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). If it apprehends it without contact, then how...?
"Does one attain the knowledge of others' minds? The Master of the Treatise replies: "Who says that another's mind is not an object within the range of this person?

If this person directly perceives another's mind, then [the knowledge] is not attained. However, if one takes another's mind as a substrate (ālambana) and transforms it into an internal image-part (nimittabhāga) for one's own perception, there is indeed the knowledge of others' minds.
Yet, at the moment one transforms the image-part for perception, one does not [perceive] the other person's [mind itself]."
In essence, however, because the image of another's mind appears upon one's own mind, it is called "knowing another's mind.
This means that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of another's mind is not separate from one's own mind, and is thus also *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). The intent is this:

when this person’s mind takes another person’s mind as its object, it transforms and gives rise to an objective aspect; yet this objective aspect present before the mind lacks any real causal function, unlike hands or other such physical entities.
Grasping an object is not like the sun extending its light to directly illuminate its object. When taking another's mind as an object, it is merely like a reflection in a mirror;
just as an external substance appears as an image within a mirror, there is no real functional activity. When taking another's mind as an object, it is likewise so.
It is not that there is no grasping of the essence of another's mind, which is why it is called "knowing another's mind"; it is not a direct [perception].
"One can understand it. Regarding "that which is personally understood," this refers to what is transformed by oneself. Furthermore, an ancient master asked:

"As for the knowledge of others' minds, since there is another person's mind that is known by one's own mind, this means that outside of one's own mind there exists another person's mind as the object of one's own mind.
How then can you say that there is no object and only consciousness? The answer is: It is because one takes [the appearance] as an object...
The objective forms (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the sensory faculties (*indriya*) of other bodies are likewise not directly perceived; they merely serve as the material basis (*ālambana-upādāna*).

This is just as when one’s own visual consciousness takes the forms of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*)—which are transformations of the eighth consciousness—as its object, it also merely takes them as a material basis and does not directly perceive them.

The same applies to the four consciousnesses, such as the auditory consciousness, when they take sounds and so forth—which are transformations of the fundamental consciousness—as their objects. This is because the fundamental...
The "substantial entity" (bhāva) is a transformation of the eighth consciousness. In relation to the five consciousnesses, it is therefore called the "reflected consciousness" (pratibimba-vijñāna).

Just as the five consciousnesses and others take the objects transformed by the root consciousness as their substantial entities, they do not directly apprehend them. Although they do indeed take them as objects, this constitutes only a "distantly perceived object-condition" (parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya).
If there are distinct external objects, how can they be called "consciousness-only"? (Up to: Therefore, one must certainly believe that all things are consciousness-only.
9. The objection that distinct objects are not consciousness. The Hīnayāna school takes up the preceding objection and says:

If it is said that when this person perceives another's mind, they rely upon another's mind as the substrate (*ālambana-pratibimba*) and transform their own *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) to perceive it, then the *nimitta-bhāga* is not separate [from the perceiving consciousness].

This person’s mind is *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). If one does not apprehend the objective essence (*bimba*) of another person’s mind, then there would be another person’s mind existing apart from this person’s mind;
how, then, could it be established as consciousness-only? The meaning of consciousness-only is that, apart from the mind, there is not even a single thing that exists;
only then is it called consciousness-only. Since another person’s mind is distinct from this person’s [mind], [it would follow that there is something external].
If the mind takes an object as its domain, how can it be established as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)? Furthermore, the objects of others are different from this object;
that is, there are distinct objects existing externally apart from this person’s mind. How then can it be established as consciousness-only? The Master of the Treatise rebukes him, saying:

"How strange is this stubborn adherence! You raise doubts at every turn. Does the teaching of consciousness-only merely describe the consciousness of a single individual? The Hīnayāna proponent asks: "Since..."

Regarding the statement that "the consciousness of a single person is not taught," how does the Master of the Treatise respond? First, he refutes the error of [classifying] the six dharma-realms as ordinary beings and the four dharma-realms as noble ones;
the Buddha-dharma realm as supreme and the three-vehicle realms as inferior; the bodhisattva as the cause and the Buddha-realm as the fruit;
and the Buddha as the one who teaches the nine [realms] while the nine seek from the Buddha—on the grounds that all sentient beings each possess their own consciousness. This...

Only then will the matter be established. If one were to speak of consciousness as belonging to a single person alone, how could there be distinctions such as ordinary beings and sages, the noble and the humble, or cause and effect?
If there were no Buddhas, what would sentient beings seek? If there were no ordinary beings, for whom would the Buddhas preach the Dharma?
One should know that my statement regarding "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) possesses a profound underlying intent. As for the single word "consciousness," it is not...
This consciousness of a single person generally reveals that all sentient beings each possess eight consciousnesses; each possesses fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*);
each has the two divisions of the seeing and the seen (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) resulting from transformation; each has distinctions of states;
each has twenty-four types of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*); and each has six kinds of true suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the principle of emptiness.
Unconditioned [phenomena]—how could they touch upon the consciousness of a single person? As for each having eight consciousnesses, this is because consciousness is their intrinsic nature.

Since the eight consciousnesses as mental sovereigns (*citta-rāja*) are the most preeminent, they are explained first. As for each having mental associates (*caitta*), these are because they are associated with consciousness;

compared to the preceding mental sovereigns, they are superior at first but inferior later, and thus they are explained next. Each has both the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*); these two...
Because they are transformations, these two cannot arise by themselves; they must depend on the manifestations produced by the two preceding kings.

Since the former is the agent and the latter is the object, they are explained next. Each has its own non-associated [factors], because they are states of consciousness. The twenty-four dharmas cannot arise by themselves;
they are provisionally established based on the distinctions among the three preceding stages. Since the former is real and the latter is provisional, they follow next.
To clarify: each has its own unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) aspect because it realizes the true nature (*dharmatā*). The preceding four [aspects] are conditioned; this one is unconditioned.
Because it exists first and then ceases, it is explained next. All such phenomena do not depart from consciousness; therefore, the name "consciousness" is established as a whole. Why?

To reveal that the eight consciousnesses are the very essence of consciousness itself. Why [are the six categories of mental factors established]? To reveal the six positions of mental concomitants (*caitta*).

Because it is associated with consciousness, what is manifested as the two aspects of the seeing and the seen? Because they are transformations of consciousness, what is manifested as the distinctions of states?
Because they are the states of consciousness, what is manifested as suchness? Because it is the true nature of consciousness, [what is manifested as suchness]?
Thus, all dharmas of the five aforementioned categories do not depart from consciousness; therefore, the general designation "consciousness" is established for them alone.

This single word "only" (mātra) merely negates the *parikalpita* (imagined) nature; it does not negate the *paratantra* (dependent-arising) nature. If one understands it in this way, it is called "correct knowledge.

One will then be well-prepared with the provisions [for enlightenment], swiftly enter into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), realize unsurpassed awakening, and universally deliver sentient beings.

How could those who wrongly grasp at emptiness ever accomplish such a task? Since the preceding [arguments] all refute the existence of phenomena external to the mind, they establish the [Yogācāra] position.

Because it is for the sake of understanding the meaning of consciousness (*vijñapti*), this passage merely negates the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). The first verse concludes the refutation of the objection that phenomena exist external to the mind.
If there is only consciousness and no external objects whatsoever, from what do the various kinds of conceptual discrimination arise?
This second verse explains the various difficulties regarding conceptual differentiation. It is divided into three parts. First, restating the meaning to pose the question:
The Hīnayāna school further presents a general objection, saying: "If consciousness alone exists and there are no external objects, by what cause do various states of mind arise?
If the mind is produced without being drawn by an object, then from what cause does this deluded mind arise? It has never occurred that..."
Regarding mind and objects: there has never been a mind that is devoid of an object.
The verse says: "By the power of all aspects of consciousness (up to) through their mutual influence, various conceptualizations arise."
Second, the verse provides a general response; this is Vasubandhu’s eighteenth verse. Regarding "the consciousness of all seeds" (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*): this refers to the eighth consciousness.
Because this consciousness can maintain the seeds of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), it is called the "consciousness of all seeds.

These seeds are each capable of producing their own specific fruits through their distinct functional capacities; thus it is named the "consciousness of all seeds. There are two types of such functional capacity.
First, that which is currently manifesting is called "functional capacity" (*śakti*); this refers to the capacity of seeds resembling those of rice, wheat, and so forth, to produce sprouts.
Second, the seeds within the eighth consciousness are called "functional capacity," because they possess the capacity to produce manifesting states (*pravṛtti*).

What is here termed "the consciousness of all seeds" (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*) refers exclusively to the functional capacity of the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), which is capable of producing all [phenomena] that exist.
Regarding the dharmas such as form and mind: form is the object of cognition (*ālambana*), while the mind is the cognizing subject (*ālambaka*).

Thus, form is an objective sphere that is not separate from the mind; this is *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). Furthermore, these mental states arise solely from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);
