why would they require an external object to arise? "Transforming in such and such a way" means that these eight consciousnesses arise from their respective seeds. This is precisely...
The self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses undergoes transformation to give rise to the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) and the image portion (*nimittabhāga*).
The image portion is not separate from the seeing portion; this is "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). Regarding "by the power of mutual succession":

this refers to other conditions as the power of mutual succession, since mental phenomena arise from four conditions while material phenomena arise from two. "Arising from various respective discriminations" means that it arises from those very [factors], namely the seeing and image portions.
These arise from the false attachment that there exists a real self and dharmas external to oneself, and from such conceptual discriminations.

Thus we know that the various consciousnesses arise solely from seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); they do not depend upon external, false objects to arise. Therefore, we know that all things are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
The Commentary states: "All-seed consciousness" refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), because it arises conditioned by the manifestation of pure seeds.
Third, the explanation of the meaning of the verse is divided into three parts: first, the direct explanation of the verse’s meaning.

This means that the term "all-seeds" (*sarvabīja*) reveals the specific functional capacities of the fundamental consciousness to produce its own effects; these capacities are the seeds themselves, and their "specificity" refers to their individual distinctions.

All [five fruits]. What are the self-fruits (*svaphala*)? They are the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*), the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
The fruit of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*) is excluded because it does not arise from seeds. The definitions of these five fruits are detailed in the eighth fascicle.

That fruit of disconnection is realized through the Path; therefore, it does not arise from seeds. It must be attained by bringing into manifestation the truly uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) Path that severs the fetters. This present...
The arising of the Path, although not produced from seeds, possesses a sense of indirect succession in relation to its fruit; however, this is not what is intended by the primary meaning here.
This is because it is said that [the Path] can produce the seeds of discrimination, whereas those [seeds] are untainted and pure.
"Differentiation" refers to all conditioned phenomena, such as form and mind. Question: If that is so, one should simply say "all aspects" (*sarvākāra*);
why then say "all-aspect consciousness" (*sarvākāravijñāna*)? Answer: Although these seeds possess the capacity to produce [phenomena], the seeds themselves have no intrinsic substance;
they take consciousness as their substance, and therefore the name "consciousness" is established for them. These seeds are precisely the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

The image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) takes its very substance from that upon which it relies. Since seeds have no distinct nature apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the two terms "seed" and "consciousness" serve to exclude what is not both seed and consciousness—namely, the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which are consciousness but not seeds;
and external seeds, which are seeds but not consciousness. Having thus excluded these, the term "seed-consciousness" further clarifies that [the seeds] are those held within consciousness.

[The text] does not explicitly reveal this seed as the consciousness that sustains it; this shall be explained extensively later in the section on causes and conditions (*pratyaya*). Next, the second phrase is explained:

because these seeds within this consciousness are assisted by other conditions, they immediately undergo such transformation and maturation. "Other conditions" refers to the successive power [of those conditions], which reveals the multiplicity of transformed seeds.
The term "thus" (*evam*) is repeated for emphasis. This [process] encompasses both the conventional designations (*nāma-kāya*) and the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).
Because the seeds of consciousness—both common and uncommon—are completely exhausted through the [exhaustion of] the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

Among the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), there are common-characteristic seeds and uncommon-characteristic seeds; it is only when the seeds within consciousness are fully exhausted that [this occurs]. Next, regarding the third phrase, "the power of mutual influence":

This refers to the eight types of manifesting consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), as well as the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with each consciousness, and the two divisions of the grasped aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the grasping aspect (*darśanabhāga*) that they transform.

Because these mutually assist one another, they are said to be "successive" (*pariṇāma*). The fourth line of the verse states that the eight manifesting consciousnesses and so forth are collectively termed "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is false discrimination; such is the category of discrimination.
This is not the only instance; thus, it is said "this and that. The meaning of this verse is to resolve an external objection:

although there are no external conditions, within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) there is the transformation of all seeds (*sarvabīja*) with their various distinctions, and through the successive differentiation of the manifesting consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and so forth, [cognition] can still arise.
Why, then, must one rely on false objects outside the mind for the various parts [of cognition] to be produced?

It is distinct. This refers to defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*). One should know that the arising of pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*) likewise does not depend on external conditions, but arises through the successive production of pure seeds and pure manifest activities.

Regarding the distinctions of seeds (*bīja*) and manifestations (*vṛtti*) as conditions for arising (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that have been explained, how should they be understood? These characteristics of conditioned arising consist first of four conditions.

The second section provides a detailed explanation of the meaning of "conditions" and is divided into five parts. First, the four conditions are clarified; this begins with the first two lines, which pose the question.

"There are, for now, four conditions" is the answer. It is stated that all four conditions function through their mutual, successive power (*anyonya-bala*); however, among them, the single factor of the seed is the direct [condition].
Based on what was said above:
one type of causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), because they serve as causal conditions in relation to one another.
One causal condition refers to conditioned phenomena directly producing their own results. "Conditioned phenomena" excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). If [it were] one...

Regarding all seeds of affliction, once they have been suppressed by the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*), they will never again have the function of manifesting as active states (*samudācāra*).
Although the seed is a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), because it cannot produce an active state, it cannot be said to directly accomplish its own fruit through that causal condition.

This is to distinguish it from what does not directly accomplish its fruit; for example, when one considers the seed of the mind in relation to the manifestation of form, it does not directly accomplish its own fruit.

These are not termed "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*). If the mental seed gives rise to the manifestation of mind, or the material seed gives rise to the manifestation of matter, and so forth, this constitutes the direct production of its own fruit;
this is the causal condition. This [definition] applies to both types of seeds, the new and the original. Regarding the "one seed":
it refers to the functional distinctions—such as those pertaining to the three natures, the three realms, and the nine stages—which are stored within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

It is able to induce a subsequent capacity of its own kind—this is what is meant by "a seed inducing a seed"—and it also gives rise to a simultaneous manifest fruit of its own kind—this is what is meant by "a seed producing a manifest [result].
This seed, in relation to those induced and produced fruits, is the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

As for the two types of manifesters, they refer to the seven evolving consciousnesses, including both the mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and their mental factors (*caitta*), as well as their aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) and seeing-aspects (*darśana-bhāga*).

There are two parts. Regarding nature (*dhātu*), realm (*dhātu*), stage (*bhūmi*), and so forth—excluding the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [states] of the Buddha-fruit—all others are capable of perfuming the eighth root consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to produce seeds of their own kind; this is what is meant by "the present perfuming the seed.

These seven types of manifest perfuming consciousnesses, in relation to the seeds within the perfumed eighth consciousness, constitute the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). [The following is] a detailed analysis. Question: Why?

Therefore, the seven preceding evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and their associated mental factors (*caitta*) only perfume the eighth [consciousness], but do not perfume the mental factors of the eighth.

Answer: Because the mental factors of the eighth are not objects of perfuming (*bhāvya*). Question: Why are the aspects (*nimitta*), the seeing-nature (*darśana-bhāga*), and so forth called "perfumers" (*bhāvaka*)?

Answer: Because they are not excluded from being the support (*āśraya*), yet they alone are capable of perfuming. Question: Why are the wholesome states of the Buddha-fruit and those that are inferior excluded?

[The question: Are they indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? [The answer: None of them are capable of perfuming (*vāsanā*). [Question: Why? [Answer: Because the fruit of Buddhahood is supremely perfect, whereas the indeterminate is extremely weak;

therefore, it does not perfume to form seeds. [Question: For what reason are the similar types of present manifestations and present existences considered "equal outflow" (*niṣyanda*), yet not "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*)?
[Answer: Because a subsequent manifestation is not produced by a preceding manifestation, but rather arises from its own seed. The *Zongjing* asks: "As for the seeds..."

On the drawing forth of seeds. What is called the "direct causal condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*)? Answer: When the preceding moment has already ceased and the succeeding moment has already arisen, the very essence of the preceding moment directly draws forth the succeeding moment;
therefore, it is called the direct causal condition. Question: Since the present draws forth the present, this is also a case where the preceding moment directly draws forth the succeeding moment.
Why, then, is it described as a "similar outflow" (*niṣyanda*)? Answer: Because the seed already exists. That is to say, the seed of the preceding moment...
The preceding moment of mental activity is the manifestation; its preceding seed flows on until it gives rise to the subsequent second moment of manifestation.
Therefore, one knows that the subsequent manifestation is not directly produced by the preceding moment. Question:

Why is the manifestation of a different category [of phenomenon] a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)? Answer: Because it is not produced directly. It is said:

Regarding "different categories" (*vijātīya*): for example, the manifestation of form (*rūpa-nimitta*) in relation to the manifestation of mind (*citta-nimitta*), or the manifestation of mind in relation to the manifestation of form, and so forth.
However, where it is stated that these serve as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), one should know that these are all merely expedient, conventional designations.

In some places, it is said only that the production of seeds from seeds is the causal condition, without mentioning the production of manifestations from seeds or the production of seeds from manifestations; this is because it speaks from the perspective of what is most prominent, rather than being exhaustive.

This is a discourse on principle. Why is this so? The Sage taught that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the *ālaya-vijñāna* stand in relation to one another as mutual causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

This is like a wick producing a flame, or like a flame being without burning [independently]. Therefore, the nature of cause and condition is definitively the mutual arising of seeds and manifestations;
how could one insist that it consists solely of seeds and not of manifestations?

The second, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), refers to the eight manifest consciousnesses. This is because these two differ in terms of clarity and dimness regarding their objects;

thus, they constitute the equal-and-immediate condition. "The eight manifest consciousnesses and their associated mental factors" specifies the substance of this condition. It is said that "only the seeing-part and the self-witnessing-part" constitute the substance of this condition.

These are collectively termed "manifest consciousnesses" to distinguish them from matter (*rūpa*), dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), seeds (*bīja*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

This is not the nature of that condition. The treatise states that the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is spoken of only in reference to all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), because they are embraced by the opening and guiding [of the way] by what has arisen previously. "Opening" (*kai*) has the sense of making room; it has the sense of clearing away that location.

"Guiding" (*dō*) has the sense of summoning and leading; it means going forward to clear away that location and summoning the subsequent dharma to arise. Thus, the preceding aggregate relates to the subsequent one.
This excludes the simultaneous and the subsequent [moments] acting as conditions for the preceding, because they do not constitute "opening and guiding" (*ābhāsana*).

"Of its own kind" (*svajāti*) indicates that it is not conditioned by another consciousness. "Immediately preceding" (*anantara*) indicates that although the preceding moment is immediately followed by the succeeding one, there is no intervening gap;
it must be immediate. "Equal" (*sabhāga*) means that the drawing power and the drawn power are equal—that is, one draws one aggregate (*skandha*).
One group [of conditions] responds to one; one group induces one. One responds to one group;
one group induces one group; one group responds to one group. One induces one dharma; one dharma responds to one. There are inequalities among these types, yet their power is entirely equal.

That they are "equal in opening and guiding" (等而開導) clarifies the meaning of conditionality (*pratyaya*): it causes that [result] to arise with certainty. This demonstrates that although the subsequent result may pass through...
For a long time; for example, the visual consciousness of eighty thousand kalpas ago is also a condition for that which follows, because that subsequent fruit is certain to arise.
This excludes the final moment of mind upon entering *nirupadhīśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, as no fruit is certain to arise from it and thus it is not such a condition.
Although there is the sense of "opening" [the way], it lacks the power of guidance. As the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "With the exception of the Arhat..."

At the time of parinirvāṇa, the final momentary mental states and their associated factors (citta-caitta-dharma), as well as all other previously arisen mental states and their associated factors, serve as the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).

Question: When the eight consciousnesses arise, what is the purpose of this condition? Answer: Within a single consciousness of one's own continuum, if the preceding moment does not cease, the subsequent moment cannot arise;
therefore, because the substance of the preceding moment occupies its own path, [the subsequent moment] cannot arise. Thus, [this condition is necessary for] consciousness.

At the time of arising, this condition must be employed. Question: Since the eight types of manifest consciousnesses mostly arise simultaneously with seeds of their own kind, why are those consciousnesses not the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for one another? Answer:

Because they do not correspond to one another, they are not subsumed under this condition. For this reason, although the eight consciousnesses may arise together, because they do not correspond to each other, they cannot [act as such conditions].

They function as mutual conditions for one another. One might ask: since the mind and its mental factors are not of the same kind as the eight consciousnesses—which always arise together with distinct bodies and functions—how can they arise simultaneously and serve as mutual conditions for one another in relation to subsequent moments?
Therefore, this explanation states: although the mind and its mental factors always arise in succession, they nevertheless [mutually...]
It should be so. Just as the light of many lamps, when combined, appears as one;

that which appears as one through combination shares the same object of perception, the same basis, arises at the same time, and is subsumed under the same nature, such that they cannot be separated or made distinct from one another.
When one [consciousness] opens the way, the others also open the way; therefore, they act as *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition) for one another.

This is not the case for the eight consciousnesses, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*), objects (*ālambana*), and supports (*āśraya*) are each distinct and unequal, and thus they do not serve as mutual conditions.

Furthermore, with the exception of those who have entered the state of nirvāṇa without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), all other minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are *samanantara-pratyaya*. This is because...

Their functional power is equal, as there is no interval between their own respective classes. Question: Since all eight consciousnesses possess this condition, it should also exist upon entering the state of the heart-mind without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
Why is it definitely absent? Answer: Regarding the entry into the state of the heart-mind without remainder, it is "subtle" because it is utterly feeble and transcends the path of words and thought;
it is "inferior" because it cannot produce further fruits. Since it lacks the capacity for guidance and opening [the way], [it does not exist].
Furthermore, since there is no dharma that arises [independently] without a cause, it is not this condition (*pratyaya*). How is this known to be so?

This question concerns the mutual functioning as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), rather than questioning the absence of other minds; for there is an established statement in the treatises, namely the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which says:
"If, at the moment when preceding consciousnesses and so forth cease, subsequent consciousnesses and so forth necessarily arise immediately thereafter, then this is called..."

Previously, it was stated that those [preceding moments] are the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for subsequent consciousnesses and so forth. Now, based on this meaning: if there were no other mind, such a principle would not exist;

therefore, it is not [the case that] this is the condition. Thus, following the preceding section, the eight types of consciousness are individually clarified as each possessing the function of being an equal-and-immediate condition.
First, regarding the eighth consciousness, the *ādāna-vijñāna*, its equal-and-immediate condition exists throughout all three realms and nine stages.
They function interchangeably. Why? Because death and birth in the lower and upper realms open up [the conditions] for one another equally.

That is to say, when one is born from a lower realm into an upper realm, the mind at the moment of death in the lower stage acts as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mind at the moment of birth in the upper stage.

When one descends from an upper realm to a lower realm, it is likewise. Therefore, they are said to be "equal. Furthermore, when a contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind ceases, it acts as [a condition] for the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind that is to arise.
Regarding the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*): the untainted (*anāsrava*) does not serve as a condition for the tainted (*sāsrava*).

That is to say, when the eighth [consciousness] is in its untainted state, it transforms into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), which continues uninterrupted until the end of the future.

How could there be a mind that constantly produces tainted states? The same applies to the relationship between the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Specifically, when a tainted indeterminate mind ceases—

An untainted wholesome mind (*anāsrava-kuśala-citta*) arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When this untainted wholesome mind ceases, concentration does not produce a tainted or neutral (*sāsrava-avyākṛta*) state, because the eighth [consciousness], which is tainted and non-obscured-neutral (*sāsrava-anivṛtāvyākṛta*), and the untainted are subsumed exclusively within the category of the wholesome nature.
This refers to the question: "From which realm is the untainted induced? The general answer is: "Either from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)."
This refers to those born as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). This is the detailed explanation. First, "the form realm" explains the projecting [karma] of the form realm.

Second, "the two vehicles" and below explain the projecting [karma] of the desire realm. "There is a certain interpretation" and below explain the form realm. Regarding "śrāvakas also have projecting [karma]," this refers next to the seventh consciousness.
The seventh manas-consciousness exists throughout all three realms and nine stages. Regarding "the seventh evolving consciousness," this clarifies the seventh...

The seven consciousnesses serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) because they follow the eighth consciousness wherever it is born, thereby binding the eighth and grasping it as a self.
Whether in death or birth across higher or lower realms, they mutually induce one another just as the eighth does.

This applies equally to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states, as they are capable of arising from one another. This is because this manas is a wisdom that functions within the causal state, which is unlike [the pure manas].

The eighth [consciousness] exists only at the stage of fruition; therefore, within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) can mutually induce one another.

That is to say, these two consciousnesses possess three grades of evolving wisdom (*parāvṛtti-jñāna*): in the first stage it evolves at a low grade, and in the eighth stage it evolves at a middle grade.

The *samyaksambuddha* (perfectly awakened) transforms at the superior grade, while the initial transformation occurs at the inferior grade; as it is not yet purely untainted (*anāsrava*), it mutually induces acquisition with the tainted (*sāsrava*).
The first five and the eighth [minds] transform only at the superior grade; therefore, when one attains the untainted, the tainted does not arise.
The fifth fascicle states: "Since the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the Noble Path and is utterly tranquil, this defiled..."
The mind and meditative absorption likewise do not exist [during that state], because their seeds have not yet been permanently severed.

Once one has emerged from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) by means of the Noble Path, these [seeds] manifest again until they are finally extinguished; this is precisely the case where the untainted (*anāsrava*) induces the tainted (*sāsrava*).

The contaminated (*sāsrava*) is exclusively obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), while the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*). Therefore, it is said that the relationship between the wholesome and the neutral is likewise.
Within the neutral, when the wisdom of the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā-jñāna*) occurs, it is called "non-defiled" (*akliṣṭa*); when this wisdom does not arise, it is also called "defiled.
This is because the preceding state induces the succeeding state. Thus, it is said that the relationship between the defiled and the non-defiled is also [the same].

They mutually guide one another. These outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) states mutually induce one another. This is because Bodhisattvas on the stages above the lower two realms are not born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Consequently, the six consciousnesses across various realms and levels may each act as mutual inducers of outflowing states and so forth;
since these are also wisdoms that transform within the causal state, they can mutually induce one another at the stage of generation when the initial non-outflowing state first arises.
Only after [the mind of] the form realm, and not in the desire realm, because the four types of preparatory wholesome states exist only in the form realm.

Subsequently, the five consciousnesses each have their own distinct realms and stages: the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body belong to the stage of the five destinies mixed together in the desire realm;
those of the form realm belong to the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion; and the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue belong exclusively to the desire realm.

In the "Ground of Mixed Dwelling in the Five Destinies," because the first dhyāna of the form realm lacks substantial food (*kavadīkāra-āhāra*) and lacks the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue, and because from the second dhyāna upward through the formless realm there is an absence of the first five consciousnesses, it is taught that only the lower two realms mutually serve as objects for one another.
One should know that the same applies when comparing the wholesome and other [moral] states; this is because the first five consciousnesses are common to both [realms].

Because of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the wholesome may serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the unwholesome and the indeterminate; likewise, the unwholesome and the indeterminate may serve as such conditions for the wholesome and so forth.
One master says that the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) may mutually induce one another, because they may arise alternately before one has attained Buddhahood.
This interpretation holds that within the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), [the mind] transforms into the untainted, as in the case of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.

Thereafter, they arise alternately. One master says: "The contaminated (*sāsrava*) may serve as a condition for the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), but the uncontaminated certainly does not give rise to the contaminated.
Why is this? Because the five uncontaminated consciousnesses do not exist except for a Buddha.

That is to say, it is only within the state of fruition that the first five consciousnesses can transform into wisdom; therefore, apart from a Buddha, there are no uncontaminated five consciousnesses. Regarding that:

The five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) are necessarily with-outflows (*sāsrava*). Because they are subsumed under the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), and because the retributive consciousness is with-outflows, the five faculties are with-outflows. Because the five faculties are with-outflows, the five consciousnesses are with-outflows.

Since the first five faculties are the direct objective aspects of the eighth [consciousness], and the eighth holds the seeds of out-flows within its causal state, they cannot become without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
Since the eighth consciousness, which is capable of transformation, is *sāsrava* (contaminated), the five sense organs (*indriya*) that it transforms are also *sāsrava*.

Since the five sense organs, as the supports (*āśraya*), are already *sāsrava*, the five consciousnesses that depend upon them (*āśrita*) likewise become *sāsrava*. "Non-common" refers to the non-common [specific] sense organs, such as the eye.

"Mandatory concomitance" refers to the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*). "Identical object" refers to the support of the same objective field (*tulyaviṣaya-āśraya*). Although it is said that the sense organ is the [support], [the consciousness] is not common to others.
It is illogical for a contaminated faculty to produce an uncontaminated consciousness. This is because the uncontaminated object is luminous, whereas the contaminated object is obscure;

that is to say, these two are distinct. Thus, throughout this detailed explanation, it is clarified that there is no principle for the existence of uncontaminated fivefold sensory consciousness within the causal stage.
This is because the vision of the untainted (*anāsrava*) does not function as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for that which is tainted (*sāsrava*).
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "The equal-and-immediate condition refers to being an equal-and-immediate [condition] without any intervening gap;

it is the meaning of 'equal-and-immediate condition' because it is the equal-and-immediate [condition] for the arising of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) belonging to both the same category and different categories. Regarding "being an equal-and-immediate [condition] without any intervening gap":

It is not necessary for there to be no interval within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). Even if moments are separated, provided that no other mind intervenes in the interim, it is still said to be "without interval.
Otherwise, the mind entering a mindless absorption would not be the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mind emerging from that absorption;
yet it is indeed that condition. Therefore, within a single continuum, the preceding mind—
Regarding the subsequent mind: because there is no intervening mind between them, it serves as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

Just as a mind relates to a [subsequent] mind, one should know that mental factors (*caitta*) are likewise. As for the immediate succession of minds and mental factors belonging to the same category or different categories:
this refers to when wholesome minds and mental factors are followed immediately by minds and mental factors of the same category (wholesome), or of a different category (unwholesome or neutral).

[They] serve as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*). In this same way, unwholesome and neutral minds and mental factors are also [equal-and-immediate conditions] for minds and mental factors that arise immediately thereafter, whether they belong to the same category (*sabhāga*) or a different category (*visabhāga*).

Furthermore, minds and mental factors of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) serve as equal-and-immediate conditions for minds and mental factors that arise immediately thereafter in the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*) realm. In the same way, [minds and mental factors of] the form realm...

Regarding the various mental states and mental factors of each realm—such as the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—one should understand that they arise immediately after [their respective] mental states and mental factors, as appropriate for each case. Question: Does every mental state arise immediately after every mental state?
Or is there a specific determination for each? There is indeed such a determination. Now, if one were to explain this in detail and specifically:
If one were to explain how such a mind arises immediately after such a mind, it would give rise to immeasurable discourse.
Therefore, one should establish only a brief and general characterization of the arising of the mind: namely, that the arising of all minds occurs by means of ten powers.
First, by the power of habitual practice; second, by the power of aspiration; third, by the power of skillful means; fourth, by the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*);
fifth, by the power of induction; sixth, by the power of the cause; seventh, by the power of the object; eighth, by the power of recollection;
ninth, by the power of mental attention (*manasikāra*); and tenth, by the power of continuity. Regarding the power of habitual practice, there are furthermore three kinds.

This refers to the inferior, medium, and superior grades. If one has not yet fully mastered the signs of entering, abiding in, and emerging from the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), it is the inferior grade.
Although one has already mastered them, because one has not yet become well-accustomed to them, it is the medium grade.

Since one has both mastered them and is well-accustomed to them, it is the superior grade. If one possesses the power of inferior practice, regarding the various dhyānas and the formless [attainments]...
Regarding the form-sphere concentrations (*rūpadhyāna*): those who possess only moderate power of cultivation can enter them only in successive order.
Those with superior power of cultivation can also enter them by means of skipping; however, they can skip over only a single stage (*ekāntara*) through skillful means.

Those with the highest power of cultivation may, according to their desire, either skip all stages or enter the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) in either forward or reverse order. "The power of aspiration" refers to...
One who has already attained the second dhyāna, having entered the first dhyāna, if they wish to emerge from it with a mind belonging to the level of the second dhyāna,
or wish to emerge with a wholesome or unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm, is able to manifest such a mind and emerge from meditative absorption.
This should be understood accordingly for all other stages as well, in detail, through the application of skillful means.
Regarding "power": it refers to the case where, for a beginner practitioner, a form-realm mind arises immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm;
an initial fundamental dhyāna mind arises immediately after a wholesome mind of the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration;
and a mind of the second dhyāna stage arises immediately after a wholesome mind of the initial fundamental dhyāna. This is explained in detail, extending up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Knowing it as it truly is: the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) refers to having entered a pure *samāpatti*, and at times returning to produce a pure attainment, or at times producing an afflicted one.

The power of induction (*ākṣepa*) refers to arising from meditative concentration until the manifesting mind of the state of concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*) proceeds in alternation with moments of non-concentrated mind, and so on.
Due to the manifestation of those contrary afflictions (*kleśa*), one immediately falls away.
Furthermore, this mind associated with those contrary afflictions only comes into manifestation through four powers, beginning with the power of the cause (*hetu-bala*).

The power of the cause refers to the fact that because one has previously habituated oneself to the obstacles that lead to falling away, one is certain to fall away. The power of the object (*viṣaya-bala*) refers to the increase in the force of the aspect of purity (*śubha-nimitta*).
Because superior objects appear before one, they are able to give rise to afflictions such as craving in accordance with them.
The power of recollection refers to the generation of conceptual proliferation through the recollective discrimination of past objects.

The power of attention refers to the mental contemplation of various pure and subtle appearances by means of investigative attention. As for the power of continuity, there are nine kinds of life-force (*jīvita*).
The final mind is associated with self-love (*ātmabhāvaprema*). Within the three realms, it causes the continuity of birth in each respective realm—desire, form, and formlessness.

That is to say, for one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm, the final mind at death, associated with self-love of the desire realm, effects the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*).
If one is reborn in the form or formless realms, then [the final mind associated with self-love of those respective realms effects the linking of rebirth].
The death-consciousness associated with craving for one's own individual existence (*ātmabhāva-tṛṣṇā*) in the form and formless realms brings about the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*).
Thus, for one passing away from the form and formless realms—whether being reborn in those very realms or in another place—one should know that there are six types of consciousness as appropriate.
Furthermore, this craving for one's own individual existence is exclusively innate (*sahaja*) and does not clearly comprehend its object.
It is comprised within the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) nature, and is able to differentiate the self-substance and produce distinct objective spheres.

By the power of this [consciousness], ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) cause the intermediate state (antarābhava) to continue without interruption; as do noble ones (ārya) who have not yet abandoned desire.
It is likewise. At the time of death, until one reaches the stage of unclear perception (*avyakta-saṃjñā*), this craving can still arise and manifest within that interval;

however, it is discerned and suppressed by the power of its antidote. For a noble one (*ārya*) who has already abandoned desire, because the power of the antidote is strong, although this craving has not yet been permanently severed, it no longer manifests. He...
By the power of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), the continuity of birth is produced.

The very first moment of the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is exclusively undefiled-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), because it is comprised within the category of maturation (*vipāka*). From that point onward, it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, as the case may be;
with the exception of the mind at death, for the mind at the death-moment of the intermediate state is always defiled (*kliṣṭa*). Just as...

Just as with the existence at death (*cyuti-bhava*), the moment of consciousness that links to the existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*) is also exclusively non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

However, in the case of Bodhisattvas who take rebirth through the power of their vows, it should be understood that all moments of mind, such as those at the time of death, are invariably wholesome (*kuśala*).
The third is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). This refers to those phenomena (up to) past and future [phenomena] which lack an external substance.

Regarding "the third is the object-condition; this refers to those phenomena": this means they are not the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), for that which is grasped as such has no intrinsic essence.

Because it cannot produce the consciousness that takes it as an object, it is not an "ālambana" (object-condition). That which is an *ālambana* must necessarily be something dependent on others (*paratantra*).

Now, this [condition] must be a substantial entity (*dravya*) that is a primary phenomenon (*dharmasvabhāva*) called an "ālambana. That which "bears its own aspect" (*sanimitta*) is the *nimittabhāga* (image-part); this is called the "aspect of the object" (*ālambananimitta*).

When the aspect and the substance are spoken of together, it is called the "ālambanapratyaya" (object-condition). The character "bearing" (*dai*) belongs to the mind (*citta*), while the character "own" (*ji*) belongs to the substance.

"Substantiality" (vastu) refers to the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga). This means that when the cognizing mind perceives an object, it brings forth its own objective aspect belonging to the substantial entity;
therefore, it is called "bearing its own aspect. There are two senses in which it "bears": first, transformational bearing (pariṇāma-parigraha).

First is "transformation-carrying" (*pariṇāma-ādāna*): this refers to the substantial object (*ālambana-pratibimba*) of the eight consciousnesses, which serves as the distant objective condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Because one relies upon this real entity as the substance, a semblance of that substance arises; this is called "transformation-carrying. Second is "clinging-carrying" (*upagṛhīta-ādāna*):

this refers to all direct objective conditions (*sannikṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*), namely the actual image-parts (*nimitta-bhāga*). This is because these image-parts are not separate from the cognizing mind. Its...

The cognizing mind directly grasps this object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) while perceiving it; this is termed "carrying along" (*parigraha*). Regarding the phrase "its own aspect," there are two meanings:
first, the aspect of essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*); second, the aspect of phenomenal appearance (*ākāra-lakṣaṇa*).

To take the first meaning, as explained in relation to the transformation that carries a remote objective condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*), it refers to the "own aspect" that appears as the objective reality (*bimba*); that is, the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) appearing as the original objective reality itself.

The essence (*tattva*). This is the characteristic of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*). Second, regarding that which is explained in terms of the directly apprehended object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) being "carried along" (*parigṛhīta*):

this refers to the self-characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the aspect of the object (*viṣaya-ākāra-bhāga*) which is directly carried along by the mind that acts as the cognizer. This is the characteristic of the essential nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).

It is not the same as the self-characteristic arising from that which carries the objective reality (*bimba*) of an indirect object-condition (*parokṣa-ālambana-pratyaya*). Thus it is said: "the mind."

"Or associated" (*saṃprayukta*) refers to the fruit of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Taking the object as the condition is the cause; that which arises—the mind and mental factors—is the fruit.
"Mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses, the sovereign minds (*citta-rāja*); "associated" refers to the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*).
Because they may arise or not arise, the word "or" is used. The *Biexing chao* states: "The object-condition..."
That which is the object of the mind’s deliberation is called the "object-condition" (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, because this very object draws forth the mind and causes it to arise—serving as that upon which the mind relies—it is also termed an "condition. Thus, the object-condition itself is called the "object-condition condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Question: If one says that [the cognition] directly grasps the aspect of the object (*viṣaya-nimitta*) and manifests as a transformation resembling the substance (*bimba*), [how does this differ from the preceding definition]?

Regarding the arising of characteristics and the formation of the two conditions—the immediate and the remote—it is as follows: even external material phenomena can constitute both the immediate and remote conditions.
For example, when one uses a mirror to reflect a person, the surface of the mirror is also able to directly grasp the reflected image of that person.
Because the reflection of a person does not depart from the surface of the mirror, it would follow that it constitutes a direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, the surface of the mirror, in relation to the external person’s primary substance (*mūla-bhāva*), would constitute an indirect objective condition (*asamnikṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*). Answer: To exclude such cases, we must specify what constitutes an objective condition.

For something to be an objective condition, it must be the object of a cognizing subject (*ālambaka-dharma*) toward which it is apprehended; only then is it termed an objective condition. Now, as for the mirror...

Since the face is not a phenomenon that performs the act of cognitive apprehension (*ālambana*), then the reflection of a person in a mirror and the actual substance of the person outside [the mirror] likewise cannot be termed "objects of apprehension.
Furthermore, lacking the quality of being an object of apprehension, they do not constitute an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The opponent asks again: "If that is so, then for example, when the sixth consciousness apprehends a non-existent phenomenon such as a flower in the sky (*ākāśa-puṣpa*), there is..."

Regarding the point that "the object of deliberation" (*ālambanārtha*) should necessarily constitute an objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), because it is that which can be deliberated upon by the cognizing subject:

the answer is that this is distinguished by the inclusion of the "basis of reliance" (*āśraya*). When the mind takes a non-existent dharma as its object, although there is the sense of being deliberated upon, the sense of being a basis of reliance is lacking.

Because things such as flowers in the sky lack substantial reality, they do not serve as a basis for the cognizing mind; nevertheless, they do not fail to function as objects of cognition (*ālambana*).

Consequently, they do not constitute [a full] cognitive condition (*pratyaya*). For this reason, one must employ a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*): First, there are those that are objects of concern (*cintya*) but not bases of reliance (*āśraya*).

These include the falsely imagined (*parikalpita*) attachments to a self (*ātman*) and so forth. Because they lack substantial reality, they merely serve as objects of concern and do not [function as a basis].

First, that which is both the object of entrustment and the object of deliberation; second, that which is the object of entrustment but not the object of deliberation—this refers to things such as persons reflected in a mirror or water.
These possess only the object of entrustment and lack the object of deliberation, because mirrors, water, and the like are not capable of deliberation. This constitutes the "both" category.
This refers to the portion of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all objects of cognition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). These four are all "neither.

This means, excluding that which is reflected by mirrors, water, and so forth, it is that which is not an object of cognition. Regarding the "intimate" and the "distant": "intimate" has the meaning of being closely attached; it has the meaning of being proximate.
That is to say, the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) is directly adjacent to the *darśanabhāga* (perceiving aspect), as there is no other intervening aspect between them.
"Distant" (*sū*) means "remote," because it is separated by the objective aspect. This refers to the external object (*ālambana*).

If it is not separate in essence from the perceiving subject—the *darśanabhāga*—then it is not separate in essence from the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying aspect). The meaning is that the objective aspect...

The image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is the immediate object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*); the seeing-part is the immediate object-condition for the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*).

All of these do not depart from the essence of the self-witnessing-part. This specifically excludes the remote object-condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*), namely the fundamental substance (*bimba*), because that substance is separated by eight consciousnesses from the seeing-part which acts as the cognizer.
This also excludes the image-parts transformed by others, as well as those [transformed by] oneself...
The objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by each of the eight consciousnesses of the body, when compared with one another, are all not direct.
Now, we take only the objective aspect transformed by its own consciousness as "direct," because it is inseparable in essence from the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) that transforms it;
there is nothing intervening to obstruct them, which constitutes the meaning of "direct. It is said to be that which is internally relied upon and apprehended by the subjective aspect.

"Those" refers to the equalizing [aspect], which is precisely the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) and the fourth portion, as well as the fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) taking suchness (*tathatā*) and so forth as its object.
All of these constitute direct objective conditions (*sākṣātālambanapratyaya*). There are four categories of direct objective conditions in total:

first, there are direct objective conditions that arise through transformation from both the substrate (*bimba*) and the mind; this refers to the objective images (*nimittabhāga*) taken as objects by the five consciousnesses when they perceive the five sensory realms.

There are four types: 1. There is that which is an immediate objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*) that arises solely from the transformation of mind and does not depend on a substantial object (*dravya*);

this refers to the aspectual objects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as it perceives its three objects. 2. There is that which is an immediate objective condition that does not arise from the transformation of mind, nor does it arise from a substantial object;
this refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) realized by fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). 3. There is that which is an immediate objective condition and yet... [text truncated]
The objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) consists of the mutual cognition between the two internal aspects; this is the remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*).

That which is separated from the cognizing mind is the distant phenomenon; specifically, it refers to that which is transformed by the consciousness of another, as well as that which is transformed by a distinct consciousness within one's own continuum, serving as the substantial basis (*pratibimba*).
The immediate object-condition (*sākṣālambana-pratyaya*), however, exists in every cognizing mind, excluding only that which is not internally apprehended.

This is entrusted to the aspect (*ākāra*) [of consciousness], because otherwise all minds and their concomitants would necessarily fail to function. Now, within the Mahāyāna, if there is no object, the mind does not arise.

Regarding the remote objective condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*), the dharma that serves as the apprehending subject may either exist or not exist, because it is a dharma external to the mind—just as when one clings to a real self or dharmas;
although they lack an underlying essence (*bhāva*), the mind nevertheless arises apart from those dharmas.
Because it arises [from causes]. At the end of the eighth mental complex (*citta-kalāpa*), there is a detailed analysis of the intimacy or distance between the eight consciousnesses. One master says:

"The eighth consciousness possesses only direct conditions (*sākṣāt-pratyaya*), because it can transform itself according to the power of karmic causes; it does not rely on remote conditions (*parokṣa-pratyaya*). Another master says:

"It definitely has remote conditions, for it must rely on another as a substrate (*ālambana-bimba*) before it can transform itself. This is the position of Dharmapāla, the King of Dharma. Regarding the mind of the eighth consciousness...
Regarding the object as cause or effect, the existence or non-existence of the remote objective condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*) is not fixed.

If, within the eighth consciousness as a cause, it relies upon the *bu-chen-gen* (minor sensory organs) and the environment of the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*) of others, and then transforms its own *xiang-fen* (objective aspect) to take them as objects, then there can be mutual enjoyment;

Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been perfected; therefore, one is said to be "one who possesses full knowledge" (*ājñātāvin*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

Alternatively, one who has cultivated this knowledge until it becomes their very nature is called 'one who possesses full knowledge,' meaning they have attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and thus know for themselves as it truly is."

It is because one knows that "I have fully understood suffering" and there is nothing further to be fully understood. Furthermore, it is said that this faculty (*indriya*) has a predominant function in the attainment of *nirvāṇa*.

Moreover, it is said that among the cessation of afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvyajñāsyāmīndriya*) has a predominant function;
among the cessation of afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) has a predominant function. Regarding...

The faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) possesses predominant efficacy within the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), because by means of it one is able to experience the joy and bliss of liberation.
Question: If something is established as a faculty (*indriya*) on account of its predominance, then ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like should also be established as faculties;

for ignorance and the other causes each possess their own distinct predominant efficacy with respect to their respective results, such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, [it is said:]...

The vocal organs, hands, feet, and the organs of excretion and reproduction should also be established as faculties (*indriya*), because they possess predominance (*ādhipatya*) respectively over speech, grasping, walking, and the acts of excretion and pleasure.
Answer: Such things as these should not be established as faculties, because the definition of what is accepted as a faculty possesses such characteristics.
As the verse says: "The basis of the mind, its differentiation, its maintenance, its enjoyment..."
Defilement (*saṃkleśa*). These are the provisions for purification (*viśuddhi*), and by this measure the faculties (*indriya*) are established.

That which is the basis of the mind consists of the six faculties, such as the eye; these six internal faculties are the foundation of sentient beings. Their differentiation is due to the male and female faculties.

Furthermore, by the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), there is the duration of this single lifetime. This constitutes defilement. By means of the five feeling-faculties, there are the provisions for purification. By...
The five faculties beginning with faith constitute purity through the final three faculties; it is by virtue of these that the establishment of the faculties reaches its ultimate purpose.

Therefore, one should not admit that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like, nor the vocal apparatus and so forth, are also established as faculties, because they lack the sense of "predominance" (*ādhipatya*) in this context.
Suppose it were asked: "Since the final three faculties are all termed 'incomplete' (*aparipūrṇa*), [how can they exist] in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)?"
Are the untainted (*anāsrava*) states also subsumed under these faculties? Therefore, this [text] specifies:
although there is untainted contemplation in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it is not clear or sharp, and thus does not constitute the latter three faculties.

This means that in the Peak of Existence, because the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) regarding the objects of observation is superior, once liberation from the active afflictions (*kleśa*) has been attained, those faculties are rendered untainted; however, [it is not so here].

Regarding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*): after the power of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) has been exhausted, one is born again in another place. These latter three faculties (*indriya*) are incompatible with birth at all stages;
therefore, they are not included therein. Here, it is merely stated that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the twenty-two faculties is as follows.

As for their functions, bases, realms of existence (*dhātu*), two types of training, three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and what is to be abandoned, each of these distinctions is explained in detail in the fifty-seventh fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*;
therefore, it is said: "One should know them as they are set forth in the treatise. This concludes the first section: the elucidation of the four conditions.
*Cheng weishi lun*, Scroll Seven;

Verified by the Layman of Jintan, Wang Kengtang.
Thus, these four conditions (pratyaya) are established as ten causes (hetu) based on the distinctions in meaning across fifteen bases (āśraya).

Second, the ten causes are used to explain the four conditions in detail. To state this in summary: one should know that the fifteen [bases] in their expanded form and the three bases in their abbreviated form do not transcend the four conditions.
The causes are themselves the bases; for example, the basis of speech (*vāk-āśraya*) is itself the four conditions.
This refers to the basis of speech. As for the ten causes: first, the cause of conventional designation; second, the cause of dependence; third, the cause of projection;
fourth, the cause of production; fifth, the cause of support; sixth, the cause of incitement; seventh, the cause of differentiation;
eighth, the cause of commonality; ninth, the cause of contradiction; and tenth, the cause of non-contradiction.
"How is it that this is established based on fifteen bases?
This is the question.

First, regarding the "basis of speech" (*vāg-āśraya*): it refers to the designation of phenomena (*dharma-nāma-saṃjñā*). [The text continues] until it clarifies that this cause is the basis of speech.

First, regarding the basis of speech: the designation of the "cause of conventional expression" is established because, in relation to phenomena associated with the desire realm, phenomena associated with the form and formless realms, and unconditioned phenomena, one designates them by means of three things—namely, phenomena (*dharma*), names (*nāman*), and conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*)—as the causes of speech.
As for what is called "phenomena," it refers to all phenomena; it is because these various phenomena that are expressed exist [that speech arises].
One is then able to cause sentient beings to give rise to mental conceptions within their minds.

Having first formed conceptions regarding these various phenomena that are expressed, one subsequently establishes their names. Once the names have been established within the mind, one is then able to produce speech.

Thus, the phenomenon, the name, and the conception—these three being the primary causes—are what give rise to the speech that is produced; it is based upon this point that [the system] is established.

The cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*). This refers to the following explanation of the cause of conventional designation: "speech" is that which expresses; "meaning" is that which is expressed;
"conventional designation" is the meaning itself; and "the locus of speech" is the cause. Therefore, the speech that acts as the expresser serves as the cause for the meaning that is expressed.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that this consists of name (*nāman*), conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*): "name" is the word; "conceptualization" is the grasping of signs (*nimitta*); and "view" is the adherence [to them].
When one is attached, one sees. Because one takes up signs according to names and becomes attached, one subsequently gives rise to verbal expression.

This takes attachment to names and signs as the cause for subsequent expression (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*). This clearly shows that this cause is the basis (*āśraya*) of speech. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

Because perception (saṃjñā) precedes it, conceptualization (vikalpa) arises; because conceptualization precedes it, speech (abhilāpa) arises. Through speech, one gives rise to various verbal expressions according to what has been seen, heard, sensed, and known;
yet one does not speak of "dharmas" [in their ultimate sense].
Second, the basis for experiencing (*anubhava-adhiṣṭhāna*), which refers to that which is depended upon; this is the "dependent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*).
Second, based on the basis for experiencing, one designates the dependent cause. "Experiencing" (*anu*) means to undergo (*anubhava*); "feeling" (*vedanā*) encompasses the five types of feeling.
The five types of sensation all have the nature of experiencing (*anubhava*). "Contemplation" (*apekṣā*) has the sense of facing toward an object;
"dependence" (*pratītya*) has the sense of relying upon an object. That is to say, the relationship between subject and object is established by means of these two.

Because one contemplates this, and because this serves as the cause for that, when one seeks or grasps at various things, this is called their "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*). For example, because one contemplates the hand, and because the hand serves as the cause.
There is the activity of direct possession, because it depends upon the feet and because the feet serve as its cause. There is the activity of coming and going.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Among sentient beings, those who desire the pleasures associated with the realm of desire depend upon these [resources];
they either seek to acquire them, accumulate them, or enjoy them. Those who desire the pleasures of the form..."
Regarding those bound to the pleasure of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they depend upon this; with respect to those various conditions, they either seek to acquire it or seek to enjoy it.
Regarding those who desire the pleasure that is not bound [to the realms], they depend upon this;
with respect to those various conditions, they either seek to acquire it or seek to enjoy it. Regarding those who do not desire suffering, they depend upon this; with respect to its arising...

Condition. Regarding those conditions for abandonment, whether for the sake of distancing oneself, or for the sake of seeking to attain, or for the sake of enjoyment—therefore, based on the basis of experience, the contributory cause (apekṣā-hetu) is designated.
The third is the basis for the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), namely the internal and external seeds (up to: because they are able to draw forth their own distant results).

Regarding the third, the basis for the habitual tendencies, the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) is designated; this refers to the stage of all internal and external seeds when they have not yet matured and have not yet been moistened.
This is called the basis for the habitual tendencies; it is precisely based upon these [seeds] in their un-... [matured state].
Regarding "moistening the seeds," this is established as the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*). To take internal seeds as an example: within the eighth consciousness, there are immeasurable seeds.

If these contaminated seeds have not yet been moistened by the water of craving, although they do not immediately produce their manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), these seeds nonetheless possess the capacity to project the arising of future manifest fruits.
Regarding its function: these very seeds are called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepaka-hetu*). That is to say, all seeds, in relation to their subsequent self-fruits, are termed the projecting cause.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "By means of pure and impure karma, the various formations (*saṃskāra*) of the three realms are perfumed (*vāsita*)."

Within the realms of the desirable and the undesirable, it draws forth a desirable or undesirable personal existence; furthermore, by the predominant power of this very [existence], external objects flourish or decline.
Therefore, it is based upon the locus of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of pure and impure karma within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
The "basis of the moistened seed" (*sābhisyandabīja-āśraya*) is established as the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*), because it is capable of producing its own immediate fruit.
Based on this basis of the moistened seed, the "generating cause" (*abhinirvṛttihetu*) is established; it serves as the basis for the prior latencies (*pūrvavāsanā*).
Regarding seeds: even if they have already been moistened and then depart, such that the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) does not immediately arise, they nonetheless remain moistened.
This very moistened seed can serve as the basis for the subsequent proximate manifest result.
The "basis of prior habitual tendencies" refers to internal and external seeds that have not yet been moistened; the "presently moistened basis" likewise refers to internal and external seeds.
As previously explained regarding "having been moistened," there is a basis for moistening upon which the cause of arising is established;

that is, with respect to the initial fruit of its own kind, the various seeds are termed the "cause of arising. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "By means of phenomena associated with the desire, form, and formless realms..."
Each arises from its own seed. "Craving" (tṛṣṇā) is named for its capacity to moisten; the "seed" is that which is moistened.
Because of these seeds thus moistened, the previously projected individual selfhood (ātman-bhava) shall come into manifestation. As the Sūtra says: "Karma is the cause that brings about birth;
craving is the cause that initiates birth. Therefore, based on the locus of moistened seeds, [one] practices giving.
It establishes the cause for arising.
Regarding the "basis of the five immediately preceding cessations," this refers to the mind and mental factors (up to their being fully encompassed by the six types of appropriation).

As for the "basis of the five immediately preceding cessations," it is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); that is, the mind and mental factors that have ceased in the preceding moment serve as [the basis].
Condition (*pratyaya*). A condition is a functional capacity that opens up, avoids, and guides; that is, the immediately preceding cessation serves as the condition.

It provides the basis for the subsequent moment’s collection of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Because those subsequent moments of mind and mental factors arise depending on the preceding moment as their conditional locus, it is called the "basis of immediate cessation" (*anantara-niruddha-āśraya*).
The sixth, the "basis of the objective sphere" (*viṣaya-āśraya*), refers to the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for all [mental states], because it provides the basis and locus of arising for all cognizing minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
This is because the mind does not arise in isolation; it arises only by depending upon an object. Regarding the "basis of the seven faculties":
These are the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*). That is to say, the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) together with the mental faculty (*manas*) constitute the six.
These six faculties are the locus upon which the eight consciousnesses, along with their associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*), depend.

Regarding the "locus of immediate cessation" (*anantaraniruddha-āśraya*), this takes the functional capacity (*śakti*) of the preceding moment of the eight consciousnesses as its locus, inducing the subsequent moment to arise. Now, regarding this locus of the faculties (*indriya-āśraya*), it takes the present...

Regarding the five material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and the seventh mind-faculty (*manas*), these are called the bases of the faculties (*indriyāśraya*). As for the eight bases of activity (*karmāśraya*):
Question: What is meant by the "bases of activity"? Answer: This refers generally to both the action itself (*karman*) and the instruments of action (*karaṇa*).
First, regarding the action itself: it refers to the craftsmanship and skill of sentient beings that can construct palaces or create various kinds of implements.
These are the "equal things. As for "instruments," these refer to the various worldly tools that assist in activity, such as axes, hammers, carts, boats, and other implements used for enjoyment.
One should know that all external auxiliary conditions that can accomplish various tasks are the bases for this functional activity; thus, one excludes the seeds within consciousness and—

The external phenomena-seeds, as well as the seeds producing actualities (*pravṛtti*), the actualities perfuming the seeds, the seeds inducing seeds, and those that serve as direct and auxiliary conditions for actualities, are not bases of activity. Regarding the nine bases of human effort (*puruṣakāra*):
from within the aforementioned bases of activity, one takes only the function of the agent or person; this excludes the internal and external seeds, and includes the remainder.
All that functions as a present condition is a basis for human effort (*puruṣakāra*); this cause can bring about the fruit of human effort.
Regarding the "basis for the ten true views": this refers to all untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena. Because their vision is not false, they are called "true.
They serve as the support for all other untainted conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
This is called the "basis" (*āśraya*). These six types mentioned above are collectively established as one "appropriating cause" (*parigraha-hetu*).

"Appropriating" (*parigraha*) means the sense of mutual involvement between cause and effect. Excluding only the direct causes and conditions, all other remote auxiliary causes and conditions are termed the "appropriating cause.
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Just as sunlight, water, and fertilizer [are related] to rice and wheat..."
Although sprouts and the like are produced from their own seeds, that which enhances their power is called the "appropriating cause" (*parigraha-hetu*).

As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Conditioned phenomena belonging to the realm of desire proceed by way of the appropriation of immediate cessation, the appropriation of objects, the appropriation of faculties, the appropriation of activity, and the appropriation of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), just as it is with phenomena belonging to the realm of desire."

It is so. The same applies to phenomena bound to the form and formless realms. Alternatively, through the influence of the apprehension of true vision (*tattvadarśana*), other unbound phenomena arise.

Therefore, based on the immediately preceding cessation, the object, the faculty, the activity, the human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and the basis of true vision, the cause of apprehension is established.
Eleventh, the basis of conformity (*anuloma-niśraya*): because it leads to and can induce unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Sixth, the basis of conformity is established as the cause of production (*ākṣepa-hetu*).

That is to say, all seeds and manifestations of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), etc., possess a nature that conforms to their own kind, as well as various dharmas of superior and similar categories; therefore, it is called the "basis of conformity. Thus it is said:
Regarding "conforming to its own nature": this excludes other dharmas from being able to serve as its basis or cause.
For example, within the eighth consciousness, the seeds of the three natures each serve as the basis and cause for the active manifestations of their respective three natures.

As for the phrase "superior dharmas of the same class," this refers to how, for instance, uncontaminated (anāsrava) dharmas only [serve as causes] for their own uncontaminated conditioned [dharmas] and...
Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) superior dharmas serve as causes; they do not serve as causes for inferior, lower, or tainted (sāsrava) dharmas.
Within the state of the tainted, there are likewise internal distinctions of superior and inferior that function as cause and effect. Herein, the "generating cause" (ākṣepahetu) is established:
it refers to the fruit produced by the initial seed in relation to the fruit subsequently drawn forth by later seeds, which is termed "projection" (ākṣepa).
Regarding the cause of origination: "inducing" means to bring forth, and "origination" means to produce. It is called a cause because it is capable of inducing and producing the fruit.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "By means of wholesome dharmas belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one can induce all superior wholesome dharmas belonging to the desire realm;

likewise, these wholesome dharmas of the desire realm can induce wholesome dharmas belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and those that are unconditioned (*anāpta*), because they are in conformity with them."
Just as it is with wholesome dharmas bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), so it is with wholesome dharmas bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*):

they can induce all superior wholesome dharmas bound to the realm of form, as well as wholesome dharmas bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and those that are unbound (*anāpta*). Just as it is with wholesome dharmas bound to the realm of form, so it is with wholesome dharmas bound to the formless realm:
they can induce all superior wholesome dharmas bound to the formless realm, as well as wholesome dharmas that are unbound. Just as it is with [wholesome dharmas]... [the same applies].

The wholesome dharmas bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) are likewise. Unbound wholesome dharmas can induce various superior wholesome dharmas that are unbound, and can also induce the realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, unwholesome dharmas can induce various superior unwholesome dharmas;

namely, sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) can induce anger (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind. As it is said:
Desire and greed are thus; so too are hatred, delusion, pride, views, and doubt—each should be understood according to its respective application.
In this way, neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena can induce wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral phenomena, just as the *ālayavijñāna* serves as the seed for wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral states.
Furthermore, neutral phenomena can induce superior neutral phenomena, just as edible food induces the experience of sensation.

It causes sentient beings who have been born to abide and remain secure, increasing their power by way of conformity to them. Therefore, based on the basis of conformity (*anulomika-adhiṣṭhāna*), the productive cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) is established.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) refers to similar dharmas acting as a similar-type cause for similar dharmas.
Belonging to their own category (*nikāya*) and level (*bhūmi*), they act as causes for those of their own category and level. It is not [the case] otherwise.
When compared across different levels (*bhūmi*), none possess the nature of being a cause. This applies to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

These causes are capable of producing results of similar outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), because the twelve distinct functional bases (*kāritra-āśraya*) each enable the attainment of their own respective results within their own realm (*dhātu*).
The cause of distinction and difference (*viśeṣa-hetu*) is established based on the locus of the functional capacity for differentiation.

That is to say, all phenomena—without distinguishing between their own nature (*svabhāva*) and the nature of others—each possess a correspondence between cause and effect; this is termed "functional capacity for differentiation.

For example, the wholesome karma of the five or eight precepts definitely induces the eighth [consciousness] of humans or devas, but does not induce the eighth [consciousness] of the three miserable realms (*apāya*), because they are not mutually compatible.

Because of their designation. If the ten unwholesome karmas definitely induce the eighth [consciousness] of the three miserable realms (*durgati*), they do not induce the eighth [consciousness] of humans or devas, because their natures are not congruent as causes.
If a phenomenon belongs to its own realm, it serves as a cause for that same realm.
In this way, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the three realms each possess their own distinct functional capacity as a cause, just as...
The one hundred and twenty offices of Chang’an each have their own official duties as the cause, corresponding to the specific functions they oversee.
As for those that are "pure causes," these take the seeds of the Three Vehicles themselves as the cause, with the respective conditioned and unconditioned fruits of the Three Vehicles as the result.
In this context, a distinct cause is established; "distinct" means that the cause and result are self-designated.

Meaning (*artha*). It is called "distinct" (*anya*) because it is not shared with others; for example, monks are designated by the characteristic of observing the fast and precepts, which is certainly not shared with laypeople.
Because the four types of karma are distinct, they are called "distinct. Thus, all phenomena, when compared with one another, possess causes of fixed distinction.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Due to the differences in the intrinsic functional capacities of the phenomena bound by desire..."
