Because they are distinct, they are able to produce various specific functional capacities.

As it is with phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), so it is with those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and those that are unbound (*anāpta*). Therefore, based on these bases of differentiated functional capacities, the cause of "distinct difference" (*visabhāga-hetu*) is established.
Thirteenth, the basis of concordant union (*sāmagrī-samprayukta-āśraya*): because [all factors] are identical in their arising and so forth, and in their single common activity (*eka-kāryatva*).
Eighth, based on the basis of concordant union, the cause of common purpose (*samāna-artha-hetu*) is established.

From the second aforementioned basis of experience (*anubhava-āśraya*) up to the twelfth basis of differentiated capacity (*viśeṣa-śakti-āśraya*), these collectively subsume the six causes and eleven bases mentioned previously.

This constitutes the essence of the locus of conjunction (*sāmagrī-sthāna*). That is to say, because each of the eleven aforementioned bases possesses the power of conjunction within its own respective attainment of birth, duration, completion, and acquisition of results, they are called the "locus of conjunction. Based on this locus, the cause of common purpose (*ekārtha-hetu*) is established;
likewise for the causes of dependence (*apekṣā*), up to the cause of specific determination (*pratiniyama*). Thus, these six causes collectively accomplish a single [result].
Therefore, it is said that the six causes function as "common purpose" (*samānārtha*). To distinguish them by briefly citing a single phenomenon:
for instance, when visual consciousness arises, it depends upon conditions such as space and light; this is established as the "condition of dependence" (*apekṣā-hetu*).

Because there are two types of seeds—the projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and the generative (*janaka*)—there arise, respectively, the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and the "generative cause" (*janana-hetu*). Next is the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Conditions (*pratyaya*), as well as faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), are established as the "appropriating cause" (*parigrahahetu*). In relation to the preceding [cause], that which induces the subsequent is the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepahetu*).
Because of the seeds of names and conventions (*nāma-saṃketa-bīja*), there is the "cause of specific determination" (*pratiniyamahetu*). Other dharmas are likewise so. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"The arising of dharmas bound by desire (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) necessarily occurs through the attainment of their own generative concordance (*svotpatti-sāmagrī*). As it is for dharmas bound by desire, so it is for those of the form (*rūpa*) and formless (*ārūpya*) realms."
The same applies to bound and unbound phenomena. Just as it is with the conjunction of birth, so too is it with the conjunction of the accomplishment of function.
Therefore, based on the locus of conjunction, the cause of common action (*ekakārya-hetu*) is designated.
The fourteenth is the basis of obstruction (*āvaraṇa-adhiṣṭhāna*). This refers to those factors that are contrary to the arising of things and so forth.

Based on the ninth basis of obstruction, one establishes the "contradictory cause" (*viruddha-hetu*); for example, afflictions (*kleśa*) can obstruct wisdom (*jñāna*), and light can obstruct darkness (*andhakāra*).
That is, light is established as the cause and darkness as the effect. Based on this, one establishes the "contradictory cause" (*viruddha-hetu*).

Regarding the phenomena to be produced, that which acts as an obstacle to their arising is called the contradictory cause. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Because a phenomenon bound by desire is about to arise..."

If an obstacle manifests, [the dharma] cannot arise. As it is with dharmas bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), so it is with those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and those that are unbound (*anāpta*).
As it is with arising, so it is with the accomplishment of its function (*kāritra*).
Therefore, based on the locus of such obstacles, the "contradictory cause" (*virodhahetu*) is established.
Fifteenth, the basis of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa-adhiṣṭhāna*). This refers to the fact that it does not contradict such matters as arising and so forth.
Based on the ten bases of non-obstruction, the cause of non-contradiction (*avirodha-hetu*) is established.

When this cause of obstruction is absent or departed from, it is termed the cause of non-contradiction. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "When dharmas bound by desire are about to arise, if there is no obstruction..."

When there is no obstruction to its manifestation, it arises at that time. As it is with phenomena bound by desire (*kāmadhātu*), so it is with those bound by form (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless (*ārūpyadhātu*), as well as those that are unbound (*anāpta*).
Just as it is with arising, so it is with the accomplishment of function. Therefore, based on the locus of non-obstruction, the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*) is established;
this is equivalent to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:

Regarding the characteristic of cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*): it should be understood that when, by virtue of something being prior, by virtue of something being established, and by virtue of their conjunction, various phenomena (*dharma*) either arise, or perform a function, or are established, or are accomplished, or are attained—this is said to be their cause.
Question: By what is it preceded? By what is it established? By the conjunction of what? What...
Regarding the arising of phenomena: what acts as the cause, what constitutes their formation, and what is attained? Answer:
Preceded by their own seeds—excluding the seeds of the support—their establishment is based upon the remaining supports, whether material or immaterial, as well as karma.
Due to the conjunction of their associates and objective referents, as appropriate, phenomena bound to the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, or those that are unbound arise;
they do so preceded by their own seeds, with those very preceding moments serving as their basis for establishment.
Because those conditions for arising act as a harmony, the karma performed by oneself is accomplished through one's own activity.
Regarding the karma performed by oneself, just as the eye has the activity of seeing, so too should it be understood that the remaining sense faculties each perform their respective activities.
Furthermore, just as the earth can support, water can moisten, fire can burn, and wind can dry, so it is in this way.

Such categories are called the distinct activities of external phenomena. Preceded by the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and desire for the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), and established by means of propositions (*pakṣa*), reasons (*hetu*), and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), the intended thesis (*sādhya-artha*) is finally established through the harmony of a non-contentious assembly and the interlocutor.
Preceded by technical expertise (*śilpa-jñāna*), one exerts effort accordingly.
Exertion (*vīrya*) serves as the establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*), for it brings about the accomplishment of various crafts and occupations through the combination of their necessary implements.

Furthermore, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) comes first; by means of the four nutriments (*āhāra*), those who dwell [in existence] are established through their support, and thus born sentient beings are nourished and able to persist. This is due to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Tathāgatas... [text truncated].
Preceded by the lineage (*gotra*), with internal causal power as the foundation and external causal power as the contributing condition, one realizes nirvāṇa,
which is the dissociation from afflictions (*kleśa-visaṃyoga*).

Thus, these ten causes are subsumed under two [primary] causes (up to the point where it is said): "The remaining auxiliary means are to be understood according to the above. Third, regarding the inclusion of characteristics:

the first [characteristic] subsumes two causes, which subsume the aforementioned causes; namely, the first is the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), which is precisely the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The second is the causal condition of skillful means (*upāya-hetu*), which is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Although the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) are both included within the category of grasping causes (*parigraha-hetu*), they are also subsumed under the causal condition of skillful means. As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*—specifically in the thirty-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi*:
"It should be known that herein, the seeds of attraction (*ākṣepa-bīja*) and the seeds of production (*abhinirvṛtti-bīja*) are called the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*); the remainder..."
The various causes are called the "causes of application" (*upāya-hetu*). As stated in the *Savitarkādibhūmi*, these correspond to the five types of yoga.
It says: "The establishment of causes has five characteristics: first, the productive cause; second, the cause of application;

third, the co-existent cause; fourth, the immediately preceding cause; and fifth, the long-past cause. The productive cause refers to the cause of origination (*utpatti-hetu*); the cause of application...

"Those" refers to the remaining causes. The co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) refers to one portion of the supporting cause (*parigraha-hetu*), such as the eye [being the cause] for visual consciousness;
likewise, the ear and so forth are [the causes] for the remaining consciousnesses. The immediately preceding ceased cause (*anantara-niruddha-hetu*) refers to the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).
The long-ago ceased cause (*dūra-niruddha-hetu*) refers to the drawing-forth cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*). Herein, the hidden meaning of that treatise is explained; first, the term "bodhi" is interpreted.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-śāstra* states: "This refers to the seeds of attraction (*ākṣepa*) and the seeds of production (*abhinirvṛtti*).
It does not mean that these are the two causes—attraction and production themselves; rather, it refers to the seeds of the various causal conditions among the six causes:

attraction, production, leading (*āvāhaka*), determination (*pratiniyama*), commonality (*sahabhū*), and non-obstruction (*avirodha*). When these are in an unripened state, they are termed 'seeds of attraction. Regarding...

The stage of having already matured is called the "arising of seeds. This is because among those six causes, the various seeds of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) do not exist outside of these two stages:

the already matured and the not yet matured. Question: Since it is granted that the four [causes], such as the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepaka*), are capable of producing, why are they not mentioned in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*?
Answer: Although the four causes, such as the projecting cause, do produce their own seeds, they also...
The manifest state is a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), yet because it is frequently interrupted, it is omitted and not mentioned here. Question:

Since it is frequently interrupted, why is it also called a "seed" (*bīja*)? Answer: It is because both the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and the productive cause are capable of directly accomplishing their own respective fruits;

therefore, they are also designated by the name "seed. This is as when one speaks of currently functioning rice or wheat as being "seeds," which is also based on their direct capacity [to produce fruit].

Because it accomplishes the fruit of actual manifestation, it is explained specifically [as such]. As for the remaining causes—namely, the first, the cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*); the second, the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*);

the fifth, the cause of appropriation (*parigraha-hetu*); and the ninth, the cause of contradiction (*virodha-hetu*)—these four causes, along with those factors among the aforementioned six causes that are not *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions), are all collectively categorized as being subsumed under the "cause of expedient means" (*upāya-hetu*), because they exist outside of the seeds of the causal conditions for arising and maturation. Regarding this:
This is further clarified by stating: it is not that these two seeds—of projection (*ākṣepa*) and production (*abhinirvṛtti*)—belong exclusively to the two causes of projection and production.

Since the seeds of the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition) are also present among the other four causes, such as the cause of development (*āvāhaka*), they are all likewise subsumed under the category of productive causes (*janaka-hetu*).
It is not merely those eight causes that are termed "remaining causes" (*avaśeṣa-hetu*); rather, [the seeds] are also included within the categories of projection and production.
Furthermore, because there are seeds that are not *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions) even among the two types of causes, these are all subsumed under the category of *upāya-hetu* (expedient causes).
Next, regarding the explanation of the "Stage with Vitarka" (*savitarkā bhūmiḥ*), the meaning of this passage is as follows:

Among the six kinds of causes, those seeds that manifest as active states (*pravṛtti*) and function as *hetu-pratyaya* are all termed "generative causes" (*janaka-hetu*), because they can directly produce their own results. This does not refer exclusively to [the seeds].
The fourth is the single cause. Excluding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), all non-causal conditions are termed "expedient causes" (*upāya-hetu*).
Within these "causes of origination," there are those that are not causal conditions, which are also called "remaining causes.
This does not refer exclusively to the nine remaining causes other than the cause of origination. To further clarify this, it is stated: "These do not directly produce their own kind of fruit."
It belongs exclusively to the productive cause (*janana-hetu*), because among the other five causes there also exist the seeds of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
It is not that only those nine are called the "remaining causes," for within those productive causes there are also factors that are not causal conditions.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explains: "Alternatively, it is said that the two seeds are themselves those two causes; the remaining causes are..."

As for the other eight [causes], there is likewise no inconsistency. Although among the two causes that draw forth [rebirth] there is the instrumental cause (*upāya-hetu*), the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is predominant.
Although among the other eight causes there is the generative cause (*janaka-hetu*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is most frequent.

It is precisely because they are "predominant" and "most frequent" that they are made manifest; this is why they are specifically mentioned. Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the stages with vitarka and so forth (*savitarkādi-bhūmi*), it says: "Or it is said..."
Arising itself is the cause of arising. As for the remaining causes, they are those nine causes; there is no inconsistency here.

Although among the seeds that constitute arising there are those that are not *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions), because they are proximate to the fruit, the sense that they directly produce the manifest state is evident; therefore, they are specifically designated as the "generative cause" (*janaka-hetu*).
Although among the seeds that constitute the projecting [cause] there are also *hetu-pratyaya* seeds, because they are distant from the fruit, [they are not so designated].
Because the meaning of "arising from one's own parents" is obscure in its manifestation, it is not described as a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).
As for the remaining [causes] that are not seed-conditions (*bīja-pratyaya*), they are all subsumed under the category of instrumental causes (*upāya-hetu*); this has already been stated above.

Regarding the four conditions (*pratyaya*) that have been explained, upon what basis are they established? (Up to: The first [condition], "capacity to produce" (*janana-samartha*), includes both progress and regression as previously described.

Fourth, the four conditions clarify their bases and their inclusion within the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). Question: Regarding the aforementioned four conditions, in relation to the fifteen locations...

How are they established? Through ten causes and two conditions. How are they subsumed? The answer is: as stated in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, they correspond to the five [conditions] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
That text says: "Furthermore, based on the objective basis of the seed-condition, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is designated;

based on the objective basis of the immediately preceding cessation-condition, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is designated; and based on the objective basis of the object-condition, the objective-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is designated."
Regarding conditions (*pratyaya*): based on the remaining bases of conditions, the sovereign condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) is established.

As for the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) being established in reliance upon seeds, these are the aforementioned seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the seeds that moisten birth (*janman*).

As for the sovereign condition being established in reliance upon the remaining [bases], these are the eleven bases of reliance (*āśraya*). The Master of the Treatise explains: "In this context, 'seeds' refers not only to the third type, the seeds of habitual tendencies..."
The basis for the child; the fourth, the basis for moistening the seeds; these also include the eleventh, the basis of conformity;
the twelfth, the basis of differentiation; the thirteenth, the basis of conjunction; and the fifteenth, the basis of non-obstruction.

Within the six aforementioned bases (*āśraya*), those that possess the sense of causal conditions are all termed "seeds" (*bīja*). If so, why does the *Yogācārabhūmi* not mention those four bases, but speak only of "seeds"?
It is said: although [the seeds] exist within the four bases such as conformity (*anuloma*) and so forth, [they are specifically designated as seeds because they function as the primary cause].
There are indeed causes and conditions for this, yet because they are frequently interrupted, they are omitted from this brief exposition on the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

Regarding the four bases of reliance (*pratisaraṇa*), because they can directly accomplish their own results, they alone receive the name "seed" (*bīja*). Alternatively, in the commentary on the "Stage with Vitarka" (*savitarkādi-bhūmi*), it is held that only the fourth [base] has the meaning of "seed.
The principles of what is taken as proximate or remote, and what is accepted or rejected, are as previously explained in the section on the "Stage with Vitarka."

This is explained in the *Vibhaṅga*. As for what is called "the immediately preceding cessation as the object-condition" (*anantara-niruddha-ālambana-pratyaya*), it does not refer exclusively to the fifth and sixth bases;

for the meaning of these two conditions—immediately preceding and object—also exists within other bases. Therefore, one should understand that this statement is intended to indicate both bases in general.
Alternatively, although the meaning of these two conditions exists in other places, they are there few and obscure.
Therefore, it is not mentioned [in that context]. Thus, it would also not be incorrect to say that there are only five or six [conditions]. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (38) states:
"If it is a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), it is called the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). If it is a contributory cause (*upāya-hetu*), it is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

The immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are spoken of only with reference to all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), because they are all..."

Furthermore, because mental factors (*caitasika*) are preceded by the opening and guiding influence of their predecessors, and because they are sustained by their objective spheres (*ālambana*), they arise and evolve.
Therefore, one should know that these are subsumed under the conditions of immediate contiguity (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Based on this, the causal factor of skillful means (*upāya-hetu*) is exclusively the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Moreover, there is the sustaining [condition] and the capacity for production.
Thus, there would be three [types of causes]. However, the treatise states that all causes are subsumed within two types of causes and does not mention three.

How is this to be reconciled? Therefore, this commentary explains: "In reality, the three conditions—dominant (adhipati), immediate (anantara), and object (ālambana)—are all subsumed under the 'expedient cause' (upāyahetu).
Yet, because the dominant condition is predominant among these expedient causes, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of them specifically."

How could other causes lack the two conditions of immediate succession (*samanantara*) and object (*ālambana*), yet they are not included within this [classification] and are thus mentioned specifically?

If they are subsumed under productive causes (*janaka-hetu*), they may either advance toward their own fruit through attraction and so forth, or recede from it by being distant and remote through attraction and so forth; these have already been fully explained above.
The causes and conditions that are taught must necessarily have their fruits (up to: ten causes and four conditions are all applicable).
Fifth, an extensive explanation of how causes and conditions produce fruits: Now, when a single mind is established, it already possesses causes and conditions;
what is induced by causes and conditions must necessarily have its fruit. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Such a cause, such a condition, such a..."
"Result. "Such is the retribution. "How many kinds of results are there? From what respective bases are they obtained?"—this is the question. The answer is:
if discussed generally for both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*), there are briefly five kinds. First is the ripened result (*vipākaphala*).

This refers to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) states produced by maturation within one's own continuum, which are summoned by contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome and unwholesome dharmas. "Contaminated wholesome" [is used] to exclude...
Regarding "untainted wholesome [states] within one's own continuum": this excludes those belonging to other bodies as well as insentient things.

If one were to speak merely of "maturation" (*vipāka*), it would refer only to the retribution among the six consciousnesses and would not encompass true maturation. Now, in order to include all such cases collectively, the term "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) is used.

However, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is also termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*), because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). This state lasts somewhat longer, until the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*), at which point one suddenly attains the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) in any of the three vehicles.
Therein, there are two types: first, the truly matured (*bhūtavi-pāka*), which is the eighth consciousness; second, that born of maturation (*vipākaja*).

This refers to the aforementioned six consciousnesses. They are called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) because they constitute the resultant consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*), and because they arise from their own seeds of maturation.
Furthermore, since the six consciousnesses arise from the true maturation-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), they are also termed "born of maturation.
These are a portion of mind and mental factors that are dull and weak in apprehending objects; they are not clear or sharp, and they do not perfume the mind of understanding.
Because it is of this kind, it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). There are four types of maturation (*vipāka*): First, maturation at a different time.
"Different" (*vi*) means distinct; it refers to the cause. "Maturation" (*pāka*) means ripening; it refers to the fruit. The cause resides in the past, while the matured fruit is in the present;

therefore, it is called "maturation. Second, maturation as a different nature. This refers to having cultivated a different cause in the past, such as the five precepts, the ten precepts, and so forth.

The maturation fruits of the general and specific retributions summoned by karma—whether the general and specific maturation fruits of the three miserable realms summoned by the ten unwholesome evil karmas, which are collectively of an indeterminate nature;

or the maturation of different classes, wherein one performs karma of a different class and undergoes birth in a different class, with the five destinies each being distinct; or the maturation that is distinct from the noble ones—namely: [The text continues: ...the maturation that is distinct from the noble ones, namely: [the four types of fruition]. (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a technical Buddhist commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* or a similar treatise concerning the classification of karmic results (*vipāka-phala*). The translation reflects the technical terminology of these texts.)
The maturation fruit (vipākaphala) functions upon the seeds of the two obstructions (āvaraṇa) by means of differentiating the various destinies and births;

therefore, it no longer exists for noble ones (ārya). Among the eight consciousnesses, only the eighth possesses these three characteristics. First, "pervasive" (sarvatraga), which excludes the first five consciousnesses.
"Two continuities" excludes the sixth [link]. "Invoked by the three karmas" excludes the seventh. Second is the "result of outflow" (*niṣyanda-phala*).

"Equal" means equality; "outflow" means a similar flow. There are two types of outflow: one real and one nominal. That which is here called "the same kind induced by the cultivation of wholesome [dharmas] and so forth" is the real outflow.
That which is called "or a subsequent result that follows the preceding karma, being similar to it" is [the nominal outflow].

Regarding "provisional outflow" (*nisyanda*) and "true outflow": those that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate are called "outflow fruits" (*niṣyandaphala*) because they are similar-type effects (*sabhāga-phala*) induced by causes of the three natures.
For example, within the eighth consciousness, seeds of the three natures each produce manifest effects of the three natures;
since the nature of the effect is identical to that of the cause, it is a case where mental seeds produce mental manifest states. As for form...
Seeds give rise to the manifestation of form. Impure seeds give rise to impure manifestations, and pure seeds give rise to pure manifestations;
this is because they share the same category of flow. Regarding "outflow" (niṣyanda) as a conventional designation: for example, one who commits killing receives the retribution of a short life.
Because in a previous life they caused the lives of others to be shortened, in the present life their own life is likewise short; thus, it is similar to that prior act of killing.

Because it resembles its fruit, the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which serves as the basis for the total retribution (*vipākaphala*) it attracts, has varying durations of life; this is termed a "concordant outflow" (*niṣyandaphala*) by convention.

In reality, however, it is an "overlord fruit" (*adhipatiphala*). This is because one takes the act of killing another to shorten their lifespan and, as a result, one's own lifespan in this present life is likewise shortened.
Because there is a sense of similarity, it is conventionally designated as "outflow" (*niṣyanda*). In reality, it is wholesome or unwholesome karma that brings about an indeterminate fruit.

Because the fruit resembles its preceding cause, it is called "outflow" (just as length resembles length). Because it is of the same category as that [cause], it is called "outflow" (as taking the life of another diminishes one's own lifespan).

Because their natures are different, it is called "conventional" (the six types of unwholesome karma from the previous stage shorten the eighth, indeterminate, lifespan). Third is the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*), which consists of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The essence of action (*kriyā*) is its substance (*svabhāva*), which is untainted (*anāsrava*). It is that which is realized through the path capable of severing [afflictions].

Because one realizes this fruit by being freed from the bonds of obstructive defilements, it is called the "fruit of dissociation" (*visamyoga-phala*). Fourth is the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*):
this refers to the various activities accomplished by an agent, such as other implements and so forth; this is called the fruit of human effort. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

A certain class [of phenomena] relies upon and follows all bases of crafts and occupations within the present life to give rise to human effort—namely, such activities as government service, agriculture, commerce, writing, calculation, and divination.
Because of this human effort, the accomplishment of various results such as crops and wealth is termed the "result of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*). This, then, is the function of human effort.
It receives the name "human result" (*puruṣakāra-phala*). This is the human activity of this person.

If a phenomenon is a human result, it takes that phenomenon as its agent and that phenomenon as its instrument, just like the activity of a man; thus, it is designated by way of analogy. Fifth is the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*).
It is called "dominant" because it is superior, excellent, and preeminent. Excluding the other four results, all other results that are obtained are [the dominant result].
This is subsumed under the fruit of the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). This predominant fruit is the most extensive;

just as the predominant condition is among the four conditions, and false view is among the five views, whatever fruit is obtained—without distinction between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), or the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—and which is not included within the previous four fruits, is all subsumed under the predominant fruit. This [fruit] exists.

There are two kinds: first, that which provides power as a sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*), such as the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) because it serves as a favorable condition for experience;
second, that which does not provide power as a sovereign fruit, such as the gold, silks, wives, and children of others.

Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, the concordant, such as the visual consciousness obtaining the condition of light; second, the discordant, such as encountering darkness and so forth. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Book 5) states: "Furthermore..."
Next, based on the basis of conditions that accord with habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the fruition of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the fruition of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*) are designated.
Based on the basis of conditions consisting of the vision of reality, the fruition of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*) is designated.

Based on the basis of conditions consisting of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), the fruition of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) is designated. Based on the remaining bases of conditions, the sovereign fruition (*adhipatiphala*) is designated. — Treatise.

The Master’s commentary states: The term "locus of habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā-sthāna*) indicates all functional capacities within each respective locus that bring about the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*);

it does not refer exclusively to the third locus. The term "locus of conformity" (*anuvṛtti-sthāna*) indicates all functional capacities within each respective locus that project the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*);
it does not refer exclusively to the eleventh locus. As for the term "locus of true vision" (*tattva-darśana-sthāna*)...
The term "all functional capacities" (*sarva-śakti*) indicates that within each respective basis (*āśraya*), there is the capacity to realize the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*);

it does not refer exclusively to the tenth basis. The term "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) indicates that within each respective basis, there is the capacity to produce the fruit of human effort;
it does not refer exclusively to the ninth basis. The term "the remaining fruits" indicates that within each respective basis, there is the attainment of the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
"All functional capacities" does not exclusively refer to the remaining eleven bases. Otherwise, the first four fruits would be too narrow and the final fruit would be too broad.
Furthermore, if one were not to mention one to encompass all, but instead take only one, it would be too narrow;
if one were to take all of them, it would be too broad. Nevertheless, each individual base contains [all of them].
The capacity to bring about the five fruits is emphasized according to what is most prominent;

thus, it is said that *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies) belongs exclusively to the third [basis], *anuvartin* (conformity) exclusively to the eleventh, *tattvadarśana* (true vision) exclusively to the tenth, and *puruṣakāra* (human effort) exclusively to the ninth.
As for the remainder, they belong to the other eleven bases—this too is not untenable. Thus, it is as follows:

Among these five fruits, the middle and lower ones are explained by correlating the ten causes and four conditions with the five fruits. First, it is clarified that five causes and one condition produce the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*);

here, the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) is primary, while the remaining causes act as auxiliaries. Next, it is clarified that seven causes and two conditions produce the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*);
here, the productive cause (*abhinirvartaka-hetu*) is primary, while the remaining causes act as auxiliaries. Regarding the phrase "the first and the last," the "first" refers to...

The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) subsequently becomes the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Furthermore, regarding the explanation that five causes and one condition obtain the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*), it is held that the "appropriating" [cause] is primary, while the remaining causes are auxiliary.
Although the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is explained through two distinct meanings, both take "contingency" (*apekṣā*) as primary;
however, they differ in the degree to which they serve as auxiliary causes and conditions. If one examines this from the perspective of the basis for human effort, then...
Excluding the seed, one cannot employ the three causes—projecting, arising, and inducing—nor the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
It should be understood that, according to the former principle, it is correct to employ only the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

As for the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), since there is no distinction between primary and auxiliary causes, and no increase or decrease regarding conditions, it is said that all ten causes and four conditions may be obtained. Thus, the *Zongjing* [Lu] states:
Question: Among the eight consciousnesses, how does each individual consciousness possess all four fruits? Answer: Take the visual consciousness as an example:
its arising from seeds is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*); its having the eye-faculty as its support is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

The mental attention (*manasikāra*) that arouses the mind for visual consciousness is called a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). Alternatively, the fact that visual consciousness is able to take real forms and so forth as its objects is also a fruit of human effort.

The eye-faculty is the eighth [consciousness's] direct objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*), and it is a fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). This applies similarly to the four consciousnesses of the ear and so forth.
All other cases are to be understood by this same principle. If the sixth [consciousness] arises from seeds as a manifest state, it is a fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because the preceding moment of the mental faculty (*manas*) acts as the inducer, or because it induces the first five consciousnesses, it is a dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

Furthermore, because it can take objects of the three times and internal or external realms as its conditions, it is called a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). Because it can produce future retributions, both collective and individual, it is called a fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). Moreover...

It serves as the cause for maturation (*vipāka*) and is also termed the fruit of maturation. If the seeds of the seventh consciousness produce its manifest state, it is called the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda*).
The preceding moment of the seventh consciousness acts as the support for the subsequent moment; this is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

It takes the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its internal self; this is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). It can serve as the support for the true ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

The basis is called the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*). If the eighth consciousness arises from seeds, it is called the flow-on fruit (*niṣyandaphala*). Its serving as the support for the seventh consciousness is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Its ability to take three objects as its cognitive domain, as well as its maintaining of seeds and receiving of perfuming, is called the human effort fruit (*puruṣakāraphala*).
Its essence is the true maturation; it is named the "fruition of maturation" (*vipākaphala*).

These four conditions, ten causes, and five fruits encompass the paths of both ordinary beings and sages, and constitute the gateway through which the teachings are established. If these are lacking, not a single dharma is complete;

if they are obscured, one will ultimately remain an outsider (*tīrthika*). Now, regarding the four conditions: the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) functions within the gateway of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) to directly produce [the result].

The "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*) refers to the meaning of opening the way for its own fruit immediately thereafter. Through it, all phenomena arise. The "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is that which possesses the support of cognition;

it is established only when such a basis exists. These two are established in relation to their respective intimacy and distance. The "dominant condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*) possesses a superior power and does not obstruct other conditions.
As for the ten causes: the "causal factor of verbal designation" (*nirukti-hetu*) serves as the gateway that precedes all phenomena. The "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*)... [understood].
The manifestation of functional activity: it draws forth that which can produce its own fruit; it gathers and sustains all conditions;
it gives rise to that which enables the birth of myriad categories; and it induces the accomplishment of various results. As for "determinate difference," the types are each distinct;
as for "common function," their essence and characteristics are identical. "Contrariety" refers to the gateway of arising obstacles; "non-contrariety" refers to conforming conditions.

Regarding the principle of arising, there are five fruits: 1. *Vipāka* (ripening): the cause arises first and the fruit ripens later; they are accomplished at different times. 2. *Niṣyanda* (outflow):
the nature of cause and fruit is identical, such that their categories do not overlap. 3. *Adhipati* (dominant): its power and function are preeminent, enabling it to assist other conditions.

4. *Puruṣakāra* (human effort): that which is accomplished through one’s own activity, whereby one obtains wealth and profit. 5. *Visamyoga* (disconnection): the severance of hindrances and the realization of truth.
Transcending all fetters, as explained by the causes and conditions above, retribution is realized as the five fruits. Thus one knows that cause and effect recompense one another;

consciousness-only transformation is certain, like a mirror manifesting images or a shadow following a form. Whether one partakes of jade-like delicacies and brocade robes, or wears a tattered robe and eats coarse herbs, [the result follows].

Whether one dwells in a golden mansion at the gate of the carriage or possesses a thousand horses while subsisting on a single ladle of water, the conditions of cause and effect are never excessive, nor do their karmic retributions ever deviate.
Thus, the "Treatise on Talent and Fate" states: "The poor have no land even for a standing needle, yet Dao Yi’s fields exceeded ten thousand *qīng*;

the starving have no storehouse for even a *dān* or a *shí*, yet Li Heng’s trees were known as 'a thousand slaves. Furthermore, it is not merely that wealth and poverty depend on the transformations of consciousness.

It is certain that one’s lifespan is likewise so. Because of the cause of killing committed by a previous mind of loving-kindness, one now certainly receives the fruit of the subsequent retribution regarding the length of life.
If it were said that the impolite must inevitably perish, why did Jie [the tyrant] live so long?
If practicing goodness brings auspiciousness, upon what basis did he meet an early end? All wise people should believe and accept this; this applies to the two preceding cases as well.
The detailed explanation of the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*) is concluded. Below, the three [sections] provide the formal explanation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Having finished the incidental discussion, one should now address the main treatise.
The preceding incidental discussion is concluded; the subsequent analysis of dependent arising (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is initiated to answer the various questions previously raised.
[The] mind.
Within the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), [these seeds] can function as three conditions—as extensively analyzed in other treatises.
This verse reiterates that, through the power of mutual interaction, various conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) arise. First, the seeds are explained.

The present [dharmas] act as successive conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for one another. The seeds held within the eighth consciousness are capable of producing manifest activities (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*);

these may be analyzed as functioning through three conditions, with the sole exception of the condition of immediate antecedence (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This is because that condition excludes seeds, and seeds do not possess the nature of that condition.
Because they directly produce their own effects, they are called the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Because they [provide support] to the faculties...
Because the body, the vessel-world, and the realm are all objects of perception for the eight consciousnesses, they are termed "object-conditions" (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Because the seeds of the perceived objects provide auxiliary assistance to the perceiving consciousnesses, or do not obstruct them, they constitute "dominant conditions" (*adhipati-pratyaya*). This is true for defiled phenomena;
it is likewise so for pure phenomena. Next, the mutual functioning of active manifestations as conditions is explained. If a manifestation induces another manifestation, the preceding...

When later moments are viewed in relation to earlier ones, they possess the sense of "opening and guiding," which constitutes the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Subsequently, a thought-moment manifests;
however, it is not directly produced by the preceding manifesting thought-moment, and thus it is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Furthermore, it may function as three of the conditions.

If one's own eight consciousnesses are viewed in relation to the eight consciousnesses of another, there are only the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); the first two conditions (the causal and equal-and-immediate conditions) do not exist. Regarding [the relationship] within oneself:

When the eight consciousnesses are considered in relation to one another, they possess the sense of mutual assistance; therefore, they definitely function as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Because there is no principle of a preceding moment ceasing for a subsequent one to arise, they necessarily lack the status of equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it may or may not exist;

this is because the first seven consciousnesses must invariably rely upon the eighth as their objective essence (*bhāva*). Thus, the eighth consciousness serves as the object-condition for the first seven.
Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): thus, the eight [consciousnesses] exist as object-conditions for the seven.

Because the eighth does not take the preceding seven as its objects, the preceding seven do not serve as object-conditions for the eighth; therefore, the seven do not exist as object-conditions for the eighth.

Regarding the meaning of the object-condition for the first six types of consciousness, the seventh consciousness lacks it in five cases and possesses it in one case, because the first five consciousnesses do not internally apprehend objects. The seventh...
The six consciousnesses take the preceding seven as their roots because there is nothing they do not take as an object.

If the first six consciousnesses were not all taken as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) by the seventh consciousness, it would be because the seventh consciousness always takes the eighth consciousness as its object and does not take others;

thus, the sixth consciousness would not be the object-condition for the first five. Therefore, the six [consciousnesses] do not exist [as objects] for the five, yet the first five are instead taken as objects by the sixth.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): thus, the five [consciousnesses] exist with respect to that [eighth consciousness]. Why is this? Because the five consciousnesses rely solely upon the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as their object-condition.

Third, regarding the preceding and succeeding moments of the same category: "preceding and succeeding moments of the same category" refers to the time when each consciousness of its own category ceases before and arises after.
This is the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which takes the preceding moment as its object-condition.

Regarding conditions: the various consciousnesses assist in their formation as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*). The sixth consciousness can admit three [conditions], excluding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

As for the remaining seven types of consciousness, they apprehend present objects and do not take that which has already ceased as an object; alternatively, one may exclude the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Although the five sensory consciousnesses only take their own specific parts (*sva-svabhāga-amśa*) as objects, it is nonetheless admitted that when they arise in a subsequent moment within their own class, they take the preceding moment as their objective condition.
As for this, the first five and the seventh consciousnesses, like the sixth consciousness, also possess three conditions.

Although it is said that the seventh has no [objective condition] with respect to the eighth, the seeds of the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) and *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) of the eighth consciousness are produced by the perfuming of the first seven consciousnesses;

therefore, they too can be said to have the sense of having an objective condition. That is to say, the first five consciousnesses perfume the seeds of the *nimitta-bhāga* of the eighth, while the seventh consciousness perfumes the [seeds of the] *darśana-bhāga*.

Regarding the differentiation of seeds: the sixth [consciousness] perfumes both the seeds of the perceived (nimitta) and the perceiving (darśana). Therefore, it is said that it can perfume and form those seeds of the perceived and the perceiving.

Fourth, the clarification of being gathered together while having distinct entities: this means that because the minds gathered together have distinct entities, they do not mutually perceive one another.

The first three conditions do not exist [between them]. When viewed in relation to one another, they possess only the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "the substance upon which they rely is the same," this means that they take the same object as their common focal point.

This meaning is not yet fully exhausted; alternatively, it may be said that they do not mutually apprehend one another from the perspective of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), whereas from the perspective of the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), [they do so].

This explains the meaning of having a mutual objective basis (*ālambana*). That is to say, because the various image-aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) arise by mutually serving as the substantial basis (*bimba*), they also serve as mutual objects of cognition.
This is like the seeds held within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), which serve as the substantial basis relied upon by the image-aspects such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth.

This is so. Because contact and the like share the same object of cognition (*ālambana*) as consciousness; because contact and the like in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possess objects of cognition;

and because the direct object-condition (*sākṣād-ālambana-pratyaya*) must necessarily exist. Otherwise, since the formless realm lacks the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), the sense-faculties (*indriya*), and the body (*deha*), [contact and the like would be impossible].

Otherwise, contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] would lack an objective referent (*ālambana*). This is because in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they take only seeds as their objects and do not take transformed matter (*rūpa*) as an object.
Even if one were to grant that transformed matter serves as an object, it must nonetheless take as its object the substantial basis (*dravya*) that resembles the seed-appearance;

for there must not be a case where the aspectual part (*nimittabhāga*) differs from its original substantial basis. Therefore, contact and the others must necessarily transform into something resembling the aspectual seeds. Thus, all aspects...
The parts arise mutually as objects for one another. Within the five consciousnesses, the four parts are of the same substance (*ekadravya*).

If the same-substance image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is divided into two aspects, it serves as the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), because the image-part is able to induce that seeing-part; thus, it is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).

Since the seeing-part is precisely that which takes the image-part as its object, it is the object-condition. Regarding the image-part, the seeing-part possesses only the dominant condition, because that image-part...

Because it does not take [the seeing] as its object, there is no objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). As for the statement that "the relationship between the seeing and self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is likewise," the seeing, being conceptual, induces the production of self-cognition;
thus, it is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Self-cognition takes the seeing-aspect as its object; thus, it is the objective condition.

For self-cognition, the seeing [aspect] possesses only the status of a dominant condition, because the seeing—being accessible to non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇa*)—is unable to take self-cognition as its object.
There is no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). As for the other two [conditions] acting as both conditions through mutual interaction:

this refers to the fact that the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and the witness-of-self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga*) mutually induce one another and serve as each other's objects. In this root verse, it is said that they arise from one another through the power of mutual interaction;
this does not refer to seeds or the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), but merely states that the presently manifest objective aspects possess mutual interaction.

This refers to the meaning of "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Fifth, regarding the pure collection of the eight consciousnesses during the stage of the revolution of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*):

within this pure collection of the eight consciousnesses, the three parts mutually serve as object-conditions for one another, because uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is capable of universally taking all things as its objects.

Specifically, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and the witness-to-self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) as its object-conditions; the self-witnessing-part takes the seeing-part and the witness-to-self-witnessing-part as its [object-conditions].
The realization [of the self-witnessing] takes the witness of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object.
With the exception of the seeing-part itself, it does not take the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object, because the image-part is not a cognizing subject (*ālambaka*). An opponent asks:

"Since you admit that manifest conceptualization arises by taking seeds and actualities as its objects, seeds should likewise arise by taking actual seeds as their objects. Now, regarding the present...
Regarding the types [of seeds] and how many conditions they can produce: as for the seed acting upon a seed, how many conditions can it produce? The Master of the Treatise answers:
Within the state of being a seed, it certainly does not arise by way of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) or the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Why is this?
Because these two conditions are established based on manifest mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). If one considers manifest states in relation to the seeds they directly produce...

This constitutes the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). If it is not a direct seed but merely serves as an auxiliary factor for its accomplishment, then it is not a causal condition;
it possesses only the status of a dominant condition. The degree of intimacy or distance between seeds is likewise the same. Thus, the summary concludes:

based on these internal consciousnesses, they mutually function as conditions for one another. This does not contradict either the sacred teachings or correct reasoning. Why, then, rely upon external conditions?

Now, the discrimination [of mind] arises. Although the term "discrimination" generally indicates the minds and mental factors of the three realms, the holy teachings manifest them through many approaches according to their predominant characteristics.
Sometimes they are said to be twofold: namely, those that fall within the mind and those that do not fall within the mind.

That which is within the three realms is called "falling," while that which is outside the three realms is called "not falling. Alternatively, they are said to be threefold: mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and...

Regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*), some explain it as being fourfold, namely the four natures of wholesome and so forth; others explain it as fivefold, namely the five states of cause, fruit, suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.
These are all explained according to what is predominant. This is analyzed in detail within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The third section, the formal explanation of dependent origination, is concluded. This completes the second verse above, which resolved various difficult points regarding differentiation.
Although internal consciousness exists and external conditions do not, by what means does the continuity of birth and death for sentient beings proceed?
This third verse explains the difficulty regarding the continuity of birth and death. It is divided into three parts. First, restating the meaning and posing the question.
The verse says: "Due to the habitual tendencies of various karmas... once the previous maturation has been exhausted, one is born again into another maturation."
Second, the verse provides a general response; it is the nineteenth verse of Vasubandhu’s commentary.
The treatise states: "All karma refers to merit, non-merit, and the imperturbable (up to: because mind and mental factors constitute their nature)."

The third section, the explanation of the meaning of the verse, is divided into four parts. First, the continuity of karmic results. This first explains the "various karmas" mentioned in the opening line of the verse, namely:

meritorious karma (*puṇya-karman*), non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karman*), and immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*). Meritorious karma refers to wholesome karma that brings about maturation (*vipāka*) in the happy realms and is conducive to experiences within the five destinies;
its essence is impure wholesome volition (*cetanā*). Both its intrinsic nature and its fruit are desirable.

Because its characteristics are preeminent, it is called meritorious karma (*puṇyakarman*). Non-meritorious karma refers to unwholesome karma that brings about maturation in the miserable realms and is conducive to experience within the five destinies;
because its intrinsic nature and its fruit are undesirable and its characteristics are base, it is called non-meritorious karma.
Immovable karma refers to that which brings about maturation in the form and formless realms and is conducive to experience therein.
The wholesome karma of the [upper] realms is called "immovable karma" because its degree of intensity causes it to abide in one-pointedness of mind without wavering;
that is, the karma of the stages belonging to the two upper dhyānas, for meditative concentration (samādhi) can cause the mind to abide in one object.

Volition (*cetanā*) is defined as the nature of karma, while the remaining factors are termed its "retinue. Since they collectively induce and fulfill the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), they are all generally designated by the name "karma. Even if...
A question is raised: "Since this karma perishes immediately upon arising, how can it bring about a fruit? To this, the following explanation is given:
Although this [karma] has no past substance despite its present activity, it is capable of bringing about a truly matured fruit (vipāka-phala) in the future;

for at the very moment the active karma is being performed, it perfumes the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna) and gives rise to a functional capacity (*śakti*) for that specific karma. That is to say:
This capacity is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*). Because it is a perfumed portion, it receives the name "habitual tendency"; it is precisely the seed.
Since it arises from perfuming, it is distinguished from what has already passed; since it is a seed, it is distinguished from what is currently manifesting.
Such habitual tendencies continue in a successive series until the time of maturation, at which point they summon the fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*). This karmic habitual tendency is precisely...

The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is superior with respect to its immediate fruit, whereas it is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). This refers to the aforementioned projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), because it is capable of projecting its own distant fruit.
Next, the second phrase is explained: the latencies of the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha-vāsanā*) all pertain to the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*).

There are four [aspects]: first, grasping at signs and views; second, grasping at name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); third, grasping at the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); and fourth, grasping at the root and the branches.

"First, regarding 'perception of characteristics' (*nimitta-dṛṣṭi*): this refers to grasping that very reality of the real grasper (*grāhaka*) and the real grasped (*grāhya*); these two are called the 'two graspings' (*dvaya-graha*). "Second, regarding 'name-and-form' (*nāma-rūpa*):
'form' (*rūpa*) is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and 'name' (*nāma*) is the four [mental] aggregates. This thus has the meaning of grasping the five aggregates.

"As previously stated, within the context of 'characteristics,' it was understood to include the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its objective essence; however, here it specifically clarifies the grasping of the immediate [object]."

First, regarding the object-condition (*ālambana*): because it cannot take phenomena external to the mind as its object. Second, regarding the transformation into the shadow-like image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*):
this is also termed "included," because it is not separate from the mind and so forth. Third, regarding the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*):

all phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are not separate from these two. Fourth, regarding the root and the derivative: the eighth consciousness, the retributive (*vipāka*), is called the "root," while the six consciousnesses...
The term "ripening" (*vipāka*) is designated as "branch" (*mala*). This refers to the appropriation of the eighth consciousness as the direct fruit, because it is the root of all ripenings.

Furthermore, it is called "root" (*mūla*) because it belongs to the category of total retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*). Other consciousnesses and their ripenings belong to the category of individual retribution (*viśeṣa-vipāka*), and are thus called "branches.

This refers specifically to the appropriation of a single ripening. That "appropriation" refers to the aforementioned four types of appropriation; they are all termed "clinging to a self" (*ātma-grāha*).
To say that it is "subsumed under the two graspings" refers specifically to the grasping of the present [existence].

That which is perfumed and activated by those graspings—the capacity within the seeds to produce [their effects] upon the fundamental consciousness—is called the "habitual energy (vāsanā) of the two graspings.

This indicates the seeds of the causes and conditions for the mind of the future maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) and its associated mental factors; these are subsumed under the category of "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*), not "dominant conditions" (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the single term "together" (*saha*) refers to the mutual conjunction of the seeds of karma and the two types of grasping (*dvaya-upādāna*).

Although the seed of karma is a remote dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) while the two types of grasping are the immediate conditions (*pratyaya*), they possess the sense of assisting one another despite this difference in proximity;
therefore, they must necessarily coexist. Question: Since the seed of karma is a remote condition, why is it mentioned first in the verse?
Answer: Although the seeds of karma are subtle, the retribution they attract is indeed manifest; therefore, the verse speaks of them first. Question:

Why must all three types of conditions be present for maturation (*vipāka*) to be established? Answer: If maturation lacked the seeds of karma as its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), what would act as the drawing force to produce superior or inferior, pleasant or unpleasant results?
If it lacked the two kinds of grasping (*dvaya-graha*) as its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), what would act as...
The seeds produced by one's own parents give rise to the various consciousnesses; yet even as they arise, there are times when they are severed, and thus possess no sense of continuity.

Therefore, it is necessarily by relying upon the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)—acting as causes, conditions, and dominant factors—that the continuity of death and birth, as well as the experience of favorable or unfavorable retributions, occurs.
[The preceding section differs from the following. This explains the latter two lines of the verse. Question: Regarding the maturation (*vipāka*), the outflow (*niṣyanda*), and the dominant...

Regarding the three fruits of the higher realms: could it be that while the results of outflow (*niṣyanda*) and dominance (*adhipati*) are inexhaustible, the karmic fruit of maturation (*vipāka*) is exhaustible?
The answer is: although the seeds of the two grasps (*dvaya-grāha*) yield fruits without end, the fruits yielded by karmic habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhaustible.
Why is this so? Because the nature of the fruit of maturation is distinct and difficult to summon, whereas the fruits of outflow and dominance...

The superior nature is easily influenced because its character is similar [to that of the cause]. What is meant by "distinctive character"? It is because it differs from the nature of karma (*karmatva*) and is not concordant with it. What is meant by "difficult to summon"?

Although it is summoned by karma, the fruit does not ripen until a different lifetime has passed. The habitual tendencies of karma (*karmavāsanā*) are like the scent of musk or the odor of foul weeds;
they have the quality of withering and ceasing, and therefore they are subject to exhaustion. As for their results of uniform outflow (*niṣyandaphala*) and dominant results (*adhipatiphala*)...
Regarding the fruit: first, because its essential nature is concordant, its nature is identical; second, because it arises simultaneously, it is easily induced.
Once this cognition has been perfumed, it is immediately able to produce the fruit; thus, the seeds of the two graspings easily induce their fruit.

What constitutes the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*)? What constitutes the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*)? The outflowing fruit is narrow, while the sovereign fruit is broad. There is only the outflowing fruit.

There must necessarily be a predominance (*adhipati*). Regarding the term "outflow" (*niṣyanda*): it refers to the fact that seeds, in relation to their actual manifestations (*samudācāra*) and their own homogeneous seeds, act as co-arising homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
As for predominance, there is no separate essence; it is of the very nature of outflow. Furthermore, because it is an outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), its nature is identical;
because it is a predominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), it is easily induced. Moreover, regarding the seed in relation to the actual manifestation:
This [result] is *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruit). With respect to its own kind of seed, it is a *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruit);

however, because the seeds of karma are of a different nature from both that present [result] and its seeds, they are merely *vipāka-phala* (ripening fruits). When a previous ripening fruit has been exhausted through enjoyment, it can no longer produce further ripening fruits;
this is because the seeds of karma that induce future lives have ripened, and thus [the result] manifests in the present body.
When the enjoyment of the matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) is exhausted before midday, this is precisely the stage when this body is approaching death.
Yet, that karma which has matured is further capable of producing the arising of other fruits;
thus, at the moment the prior karma is exhausted, the seeds for subsequent fruits ripen, and the matured fruit arises once more. For this reason, birth and death are not severed. By means of this...

The fruits of karma are never severed; birth and death continue in succession, revolving without end. Why, then, would one need to rely on conditions external to the mind for birth and death to continue in succession?
The meaning of this verse, explained below, concludes by clarifying the correct principle of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra):
that the three types of habitual tendencies (vāsanās) all have the mind and mental factors as their intrinsic nature, and therefore are not separate from consciousness.

Furthermore, regarding the continuity of birth and death through various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)—up to the passage on "simultaneous" and so forth—the meaning of the remaining text is as explained previously.

Second, the detailed explanation of the three types of habitual tendencies. According to ancient exegesis, there are generally three meanings concerning the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of habitual tendencies.

As for "habitual tendency," it differs from "seed" (*bīja*) in name but is identical in substance; "habitual tendency" is discussed in terms of the time of perfuming (*vāsanā-kāla*), whereas "seed" refers to...
Regarding the designation applied to active manifestations (*samudācāra*), there are three meanings. First, seeds are called "habit-energies" (*vāsanā*).

Here, "energy" (*vāsa*) refers to a "portion of energy," and "habit" (*vāsana*) refers to perfuming (*bhāvanā*); because this portion of energy is acquired through the perfuming of those active manifestations, seeds are termed habit-energies.
Second, active manifestations are also called "habit-energies. This means that all active manifestations are produced by seeds; thus, they are the "portions of energy" belonging to the seeds.
The three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are so called because they are like incense-encased sutras that possess a lingering fragrance.

As previously stated, they perfume the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to give rise to its own functional capacities; these very capacities are termed "habitual tendencies. "Functional capacity" is the meaning of "habitual tendency," and its substance is the seed (*bīja*).
Briefly, there are three kinds of habitual tendencies: first, the habitual tendency of names and words (*nāma-vāsanā*); second, the habitual tendency of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha-vāsanā*).
Regarding the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): there are the habitual tendencies of the three links of existence and the habitual tendencies of names and expressions (*nāma-vyañjana*).

The habitual tendencies of names and expressions refer to the specific, immediate seeds of conditioned phenomena. "Specific, immediate seeds" means that because the seeds of the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—are distinct;

that is, each phenomenon of the three natures has its own specific, immediate seed. There are two types of names and expressions: first, those that express meaning, which belong exclusively to the sixth consciousness.
It can take its own name as an object and can produce its own name; all others neither take it as an object nor can they produce it.
It is simply a specific differentiation within the sound that expresses meaning, distinguished from sounds that do not express meaning, because the latter are not "names" (*nāman*).

A name is a specific differentiation of curvature within sound and is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in nature; it cannot perfume or establish seeds for form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth. However, due to...
Because of names, the mind transforms in accordance with them, appearing as the five aggregates and the dharmas of the three natures, thereby perfuming seeds of matter and mind.
However, because internal seeds arise due to external names, they are termed "name-and-word seeds" (*nāma-vāsanā-bīja*). All perfumings are produced by the mind and mental factors;
among these seeds of the mind and mental factors, some have external conditions as their cause, while others do not depend on external ones. Those that do not depend [on external ones]...
The "external" refers to the verbal expression that manifests objects. If one relies on the external, it is called the verbal expression that signifies meaning; this is divided into two types.

However, the intrinsic nature of names (*nāma*) itself cannot permeate seeds. That which is the verbal expression manifesting objects consists of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are capable of cognizing objects—namely, all the seeing-aspects (*darśana-bhāga*) of the seven consciousnesses—and not the image-aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*). [This excludes] the image-aspect mind.

This is because it cannot manifest its object. These [factors] such as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) are not actually linguistic expressions (*nāma-vyavahāra*), yet they are like linguistic names that manifest the meanings they signify.
Just as those names can express their meanings, these mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) can manifest the objects they cognize;
therefore, seeds are perfumed in accordance with both types of linguistic expression. As for the "habitual tendencies of self-grasping" (*ātma-grāha-vāsanā*), this refers to false attachment.
The seeds of "self" and "what belongs to self. Question: Since the "self" is a product of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), how can it possess seeds? Answer:
When one clings to the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as being the self, one perfumes the seeds within those aggregates; this is called the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of self-clinging.

Innate self-clinging (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) pervades the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, whereas discriminative self-clinging (*vikalpita-ātma-grāha*) belongs exclusively to the sixth consciousness. Due to this self-clinging, seeds are also perfumed within the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).

The seeds of the five aggregates refer to the seeds of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) perfumed by names and conventions; they differentiate between self and others, and for this reason they are established separately.
As for the habitual tendencies of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*), these refer to the seeds of karma that bring about maturation (*vipāka*) within the three realms.

Depending on whether they are wholesome or unwholesome, these seeds are perfumed and formed, causing the distinctions between the various wholesome and unwholesome destinies within the fruits of maturation; therefore, they are called the habitual tendencies of the links of existence.

These are precisely the two members of the twelve links of dependent origination: volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*). Because these two members belong to the path of karma, they are not mentioned as "formations" (*saṃskāra*);
rather, they are so designated because they belong to the past. This [passage] clarifies that present seeds are perfumed and bring about results. Question:

Among the four conditions, which condition do these three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) constitute? Answer: The habitual tendency of names and words (*nāma-vāsanā*) is the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). As for the habitual tendency of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha-vāsanā*)...

The existence-constituent (*bhava-aṅga*) is a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Question: While it is true that the karma of the existence-constituent can be a dominant condition, the seeds of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) directly produce the manifestation of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*);
they ought to be the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Why, then, are they also considered a dominant condition? Answer:
Because they cause self and other to be distinct, they constitute the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Question:

When one speaks generally of the scattering of the seeds of names-and-words (*nāma-kāya*) and karma, what are they like? Answer: Names-and-words are like scattered soil; the seeds of karma are like a lump of clay.
Just as water moistens scattered soil to form a lump of clay, so too does karma summon names-and-words to become the seeds of karma. While the lump of clay has not yet dispersed, the water...

It is capable of doing so. As long as the maturation (*vipāka*) has not yet withered, the power of karma remains thus. Question: Among the three types of karma—meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable—which are their respective habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)?
Answer: They are the habitual tendencies of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*). Question: The verse speaks of the "habitual tendencies of the two graspings" (*dvaya-upādāna-vāsanā*);

among these three [types of karma], which are their habitual tendencies? Answer: They are the two habitual tendencies of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) and linguistic convention (*nāma-kāya*). Question: What are called the "two graspings"? It is said:
Because they grasp at "self" and "what belongs to self," and because they are perfumed by grasping at names and conventions, all are called "grasping" (*upādāna*).
"Grasping" has the meaning of attachment. The *Zongjing* says: "Regarding the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions, for example, Nanda had the habit-energy of desire.
Because in many past lives he had served as a king and closely associated with the five desires, [he retained this tendency]. Śāriputra had the habit-energy of anger. In the past, in many..."
Birth [occurs] because one has previously received the body of a scorpion. As for Pilingavatsa having the habit of pride (*māna*), it is because in numerous past lives he was a great Brahmin;
due to his extensive learning and many talents, his pride led him to look down upon others. Even the monk Paṇḍaka had the habit of delusion (*moha*), and so forth.
Regarding the habit-energy of karma (*karmavāsanā*): for example, the monk Gomaya-jagdhi (the "Cow-Chewer") was formerly a cow in a forest.

He hurried back and forth, accidentally tearing his *kāṣāya* robe. Due to these causes and conditions, although he had attained the fruit of the Path, because his residual habits (*vāsanā*) were not yet purified, it was as when Kāśyapa heard the lute and danced, and Ānanda always delighted in singing;
