both were formerly musicians in past lives, and thus possessed the remnants of karmic habituation. For this reason, even though they had transcended birth-and-death through the Correct [Path], they still experienced "segmented" (*paricchinna*) birth-and-death.

If one possesses [outflows], one is a worldling (*pṛthagjana*). If there is birth and death through transformation (*pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa*) arising from habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), one is a follower of the Two Vehicles (*dviyānika*).
This is because, although the followers of the Two Vehicles have severed the active outflows (*paryavasthāna*), they have not severed the habitual tendencies.
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering, extending up to old age and death, as explained in detail in the treatise.
The continuity of the three types of karma and suffering is explained by correlating them with the royal path. Regarding the three habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they were briefly clarified above;

now, below this section on afflictions, they will be extensively revealed. Through afflictions, karma, and suffering, the twelve links [of dependent origination] are subsumed. Among these, the single link of ignorance (*avidyā*) is termed "the initiator of karma."

The two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are called "moistening birth. These three afflictions are collectively termed "delusion" (*moha*). Their capacity to induce the two links of formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) is termed "karma.

The five links beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) induced by karma, as well as the two links of birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), are collectively termed "suffering" (*duḥkha*).

These three—delusion, karma, and suffering—encompass the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): those of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving, and grasping; and those of consciousness, birth, and so forth.

This refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the conceptual grasping at a self (*nāma-vikalpa-ātma-grāha*). The two links of *saṃskāra* (formative forces) and *bhava* (becoming) are the habitual tendencies of karma.

As the verse says: "Craving, grasping, and ignorance are afflictions; the two [links] of formative forces and becoming are called karma; excluding these five, the remaining seven links are each called suffering."

It is so. The first two—the latencies of afflictions and karma—act as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the suffering of birth and death, because karma and afflictions can only act as auxiliary factors in bringing about that experience. The third latency is precisely the seeds of the aforementioned suffering;

it acts as the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the suffering of birth and death, because these seeds of suffering directly produce the fruit of suffering. Regarding the latency of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha-vāsanā*), previously...
The verbal designation acts as the immediate cause (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This following of karmic seeds acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Therefore, the conditions for these habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not fixed; this is what the preceding treatise refers to as the meaning of "mutual assistance. The three types of habitual tendencies in the verse correspond respectively to afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*).
Afflictions and suffering are called "appropriation" (*upādāna*); "affliction" here refers to the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), which are termed the "appropriator" (*grāhaka*). Suffering...
The fruit of suffering is called the "appropriated" (*upādāna*). Both the appropriator (*upādātṛ*) and the appropriated are termed "appropriation" because of their clinging.
Karma is not termed "appropriation" because it lacks clinging. As for the twelve links: first, ignorance; second, formations;
third, consciousness; fourth, name-and-form; fifth, the six sense bases; sixth, contact; seventh, feeling; eighth, craving; ninth, appropriation; tenth, becoming; eleventh, birth.
Birth; and twelfth, old age and death. Ignorance (*avidyā*) has delusion (*moha*) within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as its essence.

Formations have the body, speech, and mental volition as their essence. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) has the eighth consciousness as its essence. Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) has the five aggregates of sensation, perception, formations, consciousness, and form as its essence.
The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are the six internal bases, having the six faculties as their essence. The essence of contact (*sparśa*) is pervasive.

The "contact" (*sparśa*) within the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) constitutes the entirety of the eighth contact. The first six [contacts] are maturations (*vipāka*); the seventh is excluded because it is exclusively obscured (*nivṛta*).

The essence of "feeling" (*vedanā*) is precisely feeling among the universal mental factors. The essence of "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) is greed within the three realms. The essence of "clinging" (*upādāna*) is the grasping of all afflictions.

The essence of "existence" (*bhava*) consists of the seeds of the five aggregates—beginning with consciousness—and the link of formations (*saṃskāra*). Why is this so? Because, once they have been moistened by feeling and clinging...

Because it is designated as "existence" (bhava), the essence of birth manifests as the five [aggregates] such as consciousness; the essence of old age and death is the transformation and cessation of the branch of birth.
A detailed explanation is found in the ninth and tenth fascicles of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
However, the twelve links are briefly subsumed into four [categories] (up to: or they might exceed this, resulting in an infinite regress).

Next, the individual explanations clarify that the projecting and the arising causes and effects each pertain to distinct lifetimes. The twelve links of existence are roughly divided into four classes:
first, the projecting factors (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*), namely ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), which are capable of projecting the five links beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because it is the seed for the fruit [of birth], ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the "projectors" (*ākṣepaka*).
Herein, the phrase "ignorance below" indicates the essence of ignorance; the phrase "that which is produced by it below" indicates the essence of the member of volitional formations.

This is because, among the projecting of karma, there are cases where the member of ignorance can project both general and specific retributions (*vipāka*), cases where it can project only the general retribution, and also...

Regarding those actions that produce specific retributions (*pratiniyatavipāka-karman*), only the first two are initiated by the member of ignorance (*avidyā*) and are subsumed under the member of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);
the third is not subsumed under the member of volitional formations. Therefore, the treatise distinguishes them, stating: "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).

Auxiliary karma for future lives is entirely not a member of the "formations" (*saṃskāra*) link. Because formations induce [rebirth] in a future life, they are not karma to be experienced in the present life.

Because formations are the primary inducers, they are not auxiliary karma for future lives. The two factors of the "projected" link refer to the fundamental consciousness, the internal consciousness, and so forth—the five types [of consciousness].
These are able to directly give rise to the five dharmas, beginning with consciousness, which are comprised within the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) in a future life. This is...
Because it is induced by ignorance and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Within all volitional formations, one plants the seeds of the mind;

these are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and with grasping (*sopādāna*). The *Qingliang Shu* (Commentary on the Pure and Cool) explains: "This means that once volitional formations have been set in motion, they permeate the mind through those formations, enabling this fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to attract future birth, old age, and death; therefore, it is called a 'seed. If there were no permeation by volitional formations, [it would never arise]."
Because they do not constitute seeds, it is said that among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one plants the seeds of the mind;

these are the five factors, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), which are gathered by the *saṃskāras* in a single moment without temporal sequence. Insofar as they serve as the seeds for the six faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as their maturation (*vipāka*), they are designated as the limb of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatanāṅga*).
Insofar as they serve as the seeds for contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) as their maturation, they are designated as the limbs of contact and feeling. This excludes the primary [seeds].

The seeds of consciousness constitute the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*), and the seeds of these three [aggregates] along with all other seeds of the resultant aggregates (*vipākaskandha*) are called the limb of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-aṅga*);

therefore, there is no sequence of before and after. Question: Since there is no sequence of before and after, why is it that consciousness is mentioned first, followed by contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*)? Answer:

The state of the causal stage is difficult to discern; it is only by relying on the stages that are about to arise that one speaks of five distinct categories. These five are not separate from the mind, but are merely called "seeds of the mind.
Furthermore, because the other four [causes] are set aside and the discussion proceeds in terms of the present, this passage cites the intent of this treatise to explain that sūtra;
one should examine this carefully. The latter three causes—namely the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and sensation (*vedanā*)—are spoken of in terms of seeds. Therefore...

This is called the "cause. The *vijñāna* link is the seed of the eighth consciousness; because it serves as the direct causal condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for its future maturation (*vipāka*), the seed of consciousness does not include the other seeds.
Regarding the latter three causes, they follow their respective order: that is, among the latter three types, the sequence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) places form before name.
Since the seeds of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are subsumed within form, [the seeds of] contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) [are likewise included].

Regarding their inclusion within the categories of "name" (*nāman*): this refers to the sequence of names as they are called. Some say that the single aggregate of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) subsumes all five causes;

however, it is established as four distinct types only by way of emphasizing their predominant aspects. Others say that the single category of consciousness (*vijñāna*) subsumes the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*);
yet, it is established as five distinct bases only by way of emphasizing their predominant aspects. That commentary further states: "However, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*..."

[In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*,] it is stated that only the seeds of consciousness and so forth are taken as the "projected" (*ākṣipta*). However, in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, these various members (*aṅga*) are said to be common to both the "projecting" (*ākṣepaka*) and the "projected.
This is because the seed of karma is specifically taken as the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the seed of consciousness is subsumed under the member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that they are common to both the projector and the projected, for both the seed of karma and the seed of consciousness are equally termed "consciousness. Thus, the seed of consciousness is merely...
It is the basis for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), yet it is not itself name-and-form; thus, it differs from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

Below the section on "Consciousness-Only" (*vijñaptimātra*), the text reconciles this with the *Samuccaya* to demonstrate their difference; therefore, it cites the *Samuccaya*, where consciousness is established as the "projecting agent" (*ākṣepaka*).

It specifically takes up the seeds of karma as the reason for their emergence. Because the formations (saṃskāra) permeate the mind and summon the consciousness that constitutes the future fruit, they are designated as the branch of consciousness (vijñāna).

If this is so, under what category would the seeds of consciousness be subsumed? Therefore, it is called name-and-form (nāmarūpa), because "name-and-form" is a broad term. Thus it is stated in the lower section of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.

Regarding the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, there are three parts therein. First, a general enumeration. Following the mention of the "seed of karma" and the "seed of consciousness," second, the formal establishment of the position:
because karma perfumes consciousness and thereby brings about future consciousness, these two types are designated as the "consciousness link.

The seed of karma is the projector, and the seed of consciousness is the projected; together they constitute the consciousness link. Following the statement that "the seed of consciousness is merely... third, the resolution of objections.
[The author] intends to conclude the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* by stating that [the ālayavijñāna] is merely the basis (*āśraya*) and not the substance of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

It is only in dependence upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that one speaks of the other consciousnesses existing within the *kalala*. Since this is the case for the result, it is likewise so for the cause. Question:

Since the five factors beginning with consciousness are produced through the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of karma and formations within a single moment, and thus lack any sequence of priority or posteriority, how...

Therefore, there is again a distinction between preceding and succeeding. Answer: Due to the activation by karma, although they are in reality simultaneous, they are conventionally designated as preceding and succeeding based on four types of characteristics:
First, the primary and the secondary. "Primary" refers to the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*); "secondary" refers to the other four links. The primary comes first and the secondary follows;
consciousness occupies the first position. Second, the general and the specific. "General" refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); "specific" refers to the other three links. The general...

First is the sequence of prior and subsequent; name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) occupies the second position. Third is the sequence of superior and inferior: "superior" refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), while "inferior" refers to the remaining two [links];

the superior comes first and the inferior follows, thus the six sense bases are third. Fourth is the sequence of cause and effect: "cause" refers to the link of contact (*sparśa*), and "effect" refers to the link of sensation (*vedanā*);
the cause precedes the effect, thus contact is fourth and sensation is fifth. Alternatively, the sequence may be established according to the stages in which they arise in the future.

For this reason, there is said to be a sequence of before and after. Furthermore, because the five dharmas—consciousness and so forth—arise as the fruit in the future state, they are also said to be "active" (*samudācāra*).
This is because, at the time of the cause, there is absolutely no sense of them being active.

Moreover, it is said that they are simultaneous by virtue of being produced and obtained in the future state where they arise as the fruit; for the seed that produces the manifest fruit must necessarily coexist with it. If one relies on consciousness...

At the stage when karma is perfumed and activated, it cannot be said that the production [of the fruit] and the projection [of the cause] occur simultaneously; for the moments of moistening and non-moistening necessarily do not coincide.
Herein, the single link of ignorance refers only to the afflictions that activate karma, while the single link of formations refers to the karmic habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
These two links are able to project a distant fruit and are thus termed the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and the "predominant cause" (*adhipati-hetu*).

Regarding the conditions: the five branches beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) are explained in terms of the stage when the seeds have not yet matured. Based on the stage of the future fruit (*phala*), five distinct causes are established.

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle nine, asks: "How does one proceed from the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) to the middle limit (*madhyānta*), and having arisen in the middle limit, how does one further enter into cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)?
It is said that there is one who, not understanding that the prior consciousness has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its condition, [engages] in merit or non-merit..."

Meritorious, immovable, and unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind—whether performed or accumulated—cause the consciousness that accords with those actions to flow on uninterruptedly until the end of life.
This serves as the cause for the continuity of consciousness and acts as the sign of future existence.
When this consciousness is about to produce its fruit, having already relinquished life from that prior limit, it takes birth as its own individuality in the present world. Thus it is.
At that time, the karma to be experienced upon rebirth produces name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*).

By means of this maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), it proceeds in dependence upon name-and-form; because it necessarily proceeds in dependence upon this, these two supports and the continuity of consciousness are uninterrupted.
For this reason, in the present life, consciousness conditions name-and-form, and name-and-form conditions consciousness. Just as...
Like a bundle of reeds, they proceed in mutual dependence until the end of life; these are the three "generative factors," namely craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).
Why are these called "generative"? It is because these three closely give rise to birth, aging, and death in the future world.

The five "fruits" are consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*); these five extend from the initial moment of conception up until the stage of feeling.
The stages of growth are collectively termed "birth" (*jāti*); the stages of decline and transformation are termed "aging" (*jarā*);

and the disintegration of the aggregates is "death" (*maraṇa*). One does not exist apart from these five. Based on the three times, the five present fruits are themselves the past [factors of] birth, aging, and death.
The experience of objects that gives rise to craving is the link of "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*); conditioned by craving, desire is further produced.

The four types of grasping (*upādāna*) constitute the limb of grasping (*upādānāṅga*): first, grasping at sense-pleasures (*kāmopādāna*); second, grasping at views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*); third, grasping at precepts and vows (*śīlavratopādāna*); and fourth, grasping at the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*). These are called the four graspings.

When craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) combine and moisten [the seeds], they constitute the limb of existence (*bhavāṅga*), which is the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*)—namely, the seeds of the five fruits.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states: "How do the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise through dependent origination from the middle limit to the subsequent limit?
It refers to the person (*pudgala*—here translated as 'one who repeatedly takes up existence') who has already arisen in the middle limit, experiencing two kinds of results from prior karma:
namely, the experience of internal maturation results (*vipākaphala*) and the experience of dominant results (*adhipatiphala*) produced by objects. This person, having perhaps heard [the Dharma]..."
Due to the True Dharma, or due to prior habitual practice, one is deluded regarding the two fruits.
Because of being deluded about the internal fruit of maturation (*vipāka*), one does not know, as it truly is, the suffering of future existence.

Due to the predominant power of ignorance regarding the future limit (*aparānta*) concerning future existence, one performs and accumulates formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as before; by means of this newly performed karma, [future existence arises].
This consciousness is called "consciousness following karma. Specifically, within the present life, it is said that with ignorance as a condition, volitional formations arise;

with volitional formations as a condition, consciousness arises. This consciousness, within the present life, is termed "causal consciousness" (*hetu-vijñāna*), because it is capable of appropriating the resultant consciousness of future birth.
Furthermore, taken collectively, all forms of consciousness are designated as the "sixfold group of consciousnesses" (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*). Moreover, [it is] precisely...
This consciousness is followed by the seeds of future name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), up to and including the seeds of contact (*sparśa*), which are followed by the seeds of future feeling (*vedanā*).
This should be understood as the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*) for future existence within the intermediate state.
It is so called because it is able to project the body of a single lifetime, from consciousness through to feeling, due to previous differences.

The delusion regarding the ripened fruit: having projected a future existence, one further experiences the delusion regarding the fruit of sensation produced by the second [condition], the objective realm.

Consequently, craving arises conditioned by sensation toward that objective realm. Due to this craving, one either gives rise to the quest for sensory desires (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*) or the quest for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*), and either clings to the grasping of sensory desires (*kāmopādāna*), or clings to the grasping of views, precepts, and the doctrine of self (*dṛṣṭi-śīla-ātma-vādopādāna*). Through the conjunction and nourishment provided by this craving and grasping, [the process continues].
The projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) is re-designated as "existence" (*bhava*), which is subsumed under the productive cause of future birth (*upapatti-hetu*).

Immediately following this, life comes to an end; then, with consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the first and feeling (*vedanā*) as the last, these formations (*saṃskāra*) arise—either gradually or all at once.
Thus, within this present life, one experiences the feelings produced by contact conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśaja-vedanā*).
With craving as condition, grasping arises; with grasping as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
and with birth as condition, the various sufferings such as old age, sickness, and so forth arise, or they manifest sequentially within the place of birth.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the seeds persist accordingly. Thus, within the intermediate state (*madhyānta*), conditioned by ignorance there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth, up to conditioned by sensation (*vedanā*) there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Because these serve as causal conditions, the various formations arise in the future state (*aparānta*). Furthermore, tenthly, the sequence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is established based on ten kinds of conditions:
first, the condition of the internal body; second, the condition of the enjoyment of objective spheres (*viṣaya*); internally...
The condition of the body is subsumed under the first six links. The condition of the enjoyment of objects is subsumed under the latter six links.

First, one gives rise to delusions such as the grasping at a self within the internal body; because one previously failed to understand that the maturation of the results of suffering is drawn forth by various karmas, one initiates those karmas.
Once initiated, one then follows after those karmas and frequently engages in discursive thought (*vitarka*) due to karma.
Because it acts as an auxiliary companion to consciousness, it is able to bring about three kinds of results of suffering in the future:

namely, the result of suffering comprised by the initial arising of the sense faculties (*indriya*), the result of suffering comprised by the full maturation of the sense faculties, and the result of suffering comprised by the enjoyment of objects.

These are, respectively, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as previously described, contact (*sparśa*) as the final [factor], and feeling (*vedanā*) which arises in the present life based on contact as its condition.
Regarding craving, one extensively gives rise to pursuit through the condition of enjoying sense objects;

or by way of occupations, or by way of gain, or by way of ascetic rules and observances, or by way of liberation, one initiates desire and seeking. One seeks within the internal body and seeks false liberation.
When seeking in this manner, it causes that which was previously initiated—namely, the afflictions and karma—to be drawn forth.
The fruits of birth arise within the cycle of death and rebirth across the five destinies. Once birth has been attained, aging and death follow in its wake.
Regarding the passage that speaks only of "existence" (*bhava*), this reconciles differing interpretations; all [these views] originate from the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

As for the position that only the seeds of karma are termed "existence," it is because these are what can directly induce the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*). Furthermore, within the thirty-eighth [fascicle], it is stated that there are five [aspects], beginning with consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
That which is called "existence" (bhava) is so named because it directly gives rise to the five [aggregates], such as consciousness, in the future.
The initial statement that only karma is the seed intends to convey that while the cause is virtuous or non-virtuous, the fruit is indeterminate; thus, it is termed a "ripening fruit" (vipāka-phala).

Although the five types of seeds, such as consciousness, serve as the actual causes capable of producing [the fruit], they lack the power to produce the fruit directly; therefore, they cannot be designated as "existence. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks: "What..."
Therefore, why is it not stated that the self-nature (svabhāva) serves as its own condition? Answer:
Because if that self-nature were not perverted, other conditions would be unable to increase or diminish the defilements within that self-nature. This is the intended meaning [of not stating it].
Regarding the second point, the reason only five types are taken is that the intention is to take the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) while excluding the karmic seed.
Because of the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the meaning here combines these two explanations: karma-seeds constitute one, while consciousness and the others constitute five;

thus, there are six factors that are moistened, which constitute the essence of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*). Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The six links have already been moistened."

Because they are combined under the name "existence" (*bhava*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) moisten it, just as water enters a sprout. When discussing the subject and the object together, there should be eight factors;
thus, the *Qingliang shu* states: "In total there are eight members, which are collectively established under the name 'existence. These are the four members that are produced.

This refers to birth, aging, and death. Because these are produced by the immediate conditions of craving and grasping, they are distinguished from consciousness and the other factors, which are remote conditions.

Question: Since the substance of birth, aging, and death all manifests as consciousness and the other factors, on what basis are they divided into two? Answer: They are distinguished by way of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*).
Before they have decayed, they are all subsumed under the category of "birth" (*jāti*). Decay and transformation constitute "aging" (*jarā*); the end of life constitutes "death" (*maraṇa*).

As for the statement "from the intermediate state" (*antarābhava*), it means that the aggregates of the intermediate state cease and the aggregates of the subsequent existence arise. Regarding those who have not yet undergone decay and transformation, this refers to the period up to age forty.

Question: Why are aging and death not established as separate factors (*aṅga*)? Answer: Because there is no fixed [duration] for aging; it is established as a factor in conjunction with death. Question: Why is there no fixed [duration]?
Regarding the meaning of "aging" (*jarā*): [Question] Humans, animals, and other species experience premature death before reaching old age;
therefore, there is no question of aging in the heavens. [But] the five signs of decline (*pañca-vyasananimitta*)—are these not forms of aging? [Answer] There are indeed those who grow old.

[Objection] Since aging is thus not universal, why is it established as a separate factor (*aṅga*) by being attached to death, while illness (*vyādhi*), which is likewise not universal, is not so established? [Answer] Furthermore, regarding illness...

It is not universal, as it is also indeterminate. Old age, however, is universal throughout the three realms; therefore, it is established as a link. Within all destinies and realms, except for those who die prematurely, the signs of decay are present in all cases.
One should then ask: "Since name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is not universal, why is it established as a link? [The answer is:

In the form realm in its entirety, and among those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) in the desire realm, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise instantaneously. How, then, could there be name-and-form? The reply is: [as follows].

The factors [of dependent origination] are established because they are determinate. In those born from a womb, an egg, or moisture, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are not yet complete; therefore, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is necessarily present, and this factor of name-and-form is also universally present.
As for those of apparitional birth (*upapāduka*) who possess form, although they are endowed with the five faculties at the initial stage of taking birth, these faculties have no functional activity;

at that time, they are not yet designated as the factor of the six sense bases. Furthermore, in those initially born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), although the mental faculty (*manas*) is necessarily present...
Because it is not yet clearly manifest, it is not yet designated as the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*); therefore, it is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
For this reason, the treatise states that all twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) exist, at least in part, within the two upper realms. Thus, the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:
Question: How many links are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)? Answer: All of them, at least in part. Question: How should one know that aging exists there? Answer: There...

Because all conditioned phenomena possess the nature of decay and corruption, it should be understood that what pertains to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is likewise, just as that which pertains to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, a question is asked: "Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is not omnipresent; why is it established as a separate link? For craving does not exist within the miserable destinies (*apāya*). The answer is:
"Although it is not omnipresent, it is established separately because it is determinate. That is to say, it refers exclusively to those who do not seek [liberation]."
There is no craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in the higher realms, because if one is born in a happy destiny (*sugati*), there is necessarily craving.

Although a person who has attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) does not give rise to craving, they still possess the seeds of craving that moisten rebirth (*upapatti*). Furthermore, within the miserable destinies (*durgati*), there is also craving for the objects previously manifested as "self.
When the Sūtra says there is no craving, it is said in reference to the absence of longing within the midst of pure suffering; it does not mean that craving is entirely absent there.

He asked again: "For what reason are birth and old age and death established as the 'resultant members' (*abhinirvṛtti-aṅga*), while the five factors beginning with consciousness are separately established as the 'projected members' (*ākṣepa-aṅga*)?
The intention [of this question] is: future birth and death are precisely the present consciousness and so forth;

why then are five established for the present and only one for the future? The answer was: "Because the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*) are difficult to discern, [the classification] is based on what is to come."
Regarding the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), five members are established separately because the distinctions [of its characteristics] are easily understood.

Regarding the stage of cause, two members are established collectively to manifest the three types of suffering (*triduḥkhatā*). This is because when one is in the causal stage, it is difficult to know the matters that will occur in the future fruit.

Therefore, based on the future stage of fruition, five members are established separately to manifest the distinctions. At the time of the fruit stage, the characteristics of these distinctions are clear.

This is easy to understand; therefore, they are combined into two branches to manifest the three types of suffering: birth manifests the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), old age manifests the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), and death manifests the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkha*).
The *Abhidharmakośa* follows this approach, though it simply refers to them as "abbreviated results" and "abbreviated causes.
Because the five present results can be inferred from the intermediate [stages], and because two future [results] are taught, it is called "abbreviated results. As for the two present afflictions...
In the past, it was stated that there is but one ignorance; thus, it is called a "concise cause. Since the middle section has already been explained extensively, the beginning is again concise.
By analogy, the end can be understood in the same way. To speak further beyond this would be useless.

If that is so, and if the beginning and end—which are not directly perceived—are shown through the extensive explanation of cause and effect, they may be inferred from the middle. Therefore, it should be said: "It demonstrates the cause for delusion regarding the fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*)."
Combining the delusions: this clarifies the beginning and end of the delusions that arise in the present, causing them not to function.
By distinguishing their respective characteristics, it clarifies the five stages, causing one to feel revulsion toward the future fruit. These are combined as "old age and death.

The *Abhidharmakośa* explains this based on the three time periods, while the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains it based on two time periods. Although there are differences, they can mutually illuminate one another. However, as for what is produced...
This concludes the section on the results, which follows the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa*. Furthermore, a question is raised:

"For what reason is ignorance established as the general factor for initiating karma, while craving and grasping are established separately within the stage of moistening karma? This question contains two intentions: first, it asks why the designations differ.
First question: Both [ignorance and craving] are afflictions; why is ignorance established first, while craving and grasping are established later?

Second question: There is a difference between the detailed and the concise formulations; that is, ignorance is established generally, while craving and grasping are established specifically. Therefore, both questions are contained within the subsequent answer.

First, the answer addresses the difference in the establishment of names according to the gate of superiority and inferiority. Later, the passage beginning with "The essential requirement is to irrigate repeatedly" answers two questions:

the initiation of karma and the moistening of karma, because [the latter] does not heavily perfume [the seeds]. This constitutes the reason for the expansion and abbreviation [of the text]. Master Qingliang’s *Commentary* states:

"If categorized by the two periods [past and future], the first ten belong to the same period; therefore, afflictions are of two kinds: those that can initiate [karma] and those that can moisten [it]."
Although all afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of producing and moistening [karmic action], at the stage of initiating karma, the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) predominates;
in moistening karma to lead to rebirth, the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) is superior. Thus, they each receive their respective names.

Because there is no separate perfuming or initiation [of karma] by anything other than ignorance alone, which repeatedly irrigates it, craving and grasping are distinguished [from it]. This is precisely the general meaning intended here. As for the statement regarding the "eleven extraordinary matters":
The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* explains five [distinctions]: first, the excellence of the object (*ālambana*), because it universally takes both the defiled and the pure as its object;

second, the excellence of the aspect (*ākāra*), because it conceals the true and manifests the false; third, the excellence of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), because it is the root of afflictions, karma, and birth;

fourth, the excellence of the motivation (*samutthāna*), because it equally initiates, draws forth, and gives rise to the phenomena of dependent origination that are initiated, drawn forth, and produced; fifth, the excellence of transformation (*pariṇāma*).

1. Superiority in terms of association: because it functions through four modes of association—latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), concomitance (*samprayoga*), and non-commonality (*asādhāraṇa*).

2. Superiority in terms of wrong practice: because it gives rise to practices of superimposition and denial based on the truths of suffering and its origin. 3. Superiority in terms of characteristics:

because it functions as subtle specific characteristics and as pervasive common characteristics regarding both the agreeable and the disagreeable. 4. Superiority in terms of activity: because it acts as the basis for the process of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

(9) Superiority in terms of the object (*ālambana*): because it takes as its object the subtle phenomena that are difficult to perceive. (10) Superiority in terms of the activity (*karma*): because it performs the activity of obstructing the attainment of *śamatha*.

(11) Superiority in terms of obstruction (*āvaraṇa*): because it obstructs the superior dharmas. (12) Superiority in terms of conformity (*anuvartana*): because it continues to function even up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), like a revolving wheel. (13) Superiority in terms of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*):

because it is the object to be countered by two kinds of sublime knowledge (*jñāna*). For these reasons, no others are mentioned. It is also called the "limb of initiating karma" (*karmārambha-aṅga*). This is stated provisionally based on...
Regarding "beginning and end": this means that the beginning of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is called "craving," and the subsequent stage of craving is called "grasping" (*upādāna*).

Thus, within these two—craving and grasping—craving constitutes the beginning and grasping constitutes the end. In reality, there is much active manifestation of moistening [the seeds]. One might ask:

"Since grasping is divided [into four types], why say that the power of craving alone is predominant? Therefore, it is answered: although the branch of grasping subsumes all afflictions (*kleśa*), [craving remains the primary driver].

However, because craving (tṛṣṇā) is more dominant in its moistening power, it is mentioned specifically. Furthermore, this ignorance (avidyā) is taken here solely as that which can trigger karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that truly brings about future rebirths.
Therefore, while all other links depend upon their own respective levels (bhūmi), the formations (saṃskāra) alone depend on an ignorance belonging to another level.
An example of this is how ignorance of a lower level can trigger formations of a higher level; this serves as the proof. If...

If this were not permitted, then the higher meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) produced by one who has first suppressed the defilements of a lower stage would not be a constituent of the path (*pratipad-aṅga*). Why?
Because the ignorance (*avidyā*) of that [lower] stage has not yet arisen; it is the ignorance of its own stage that gives rise to the formations (*saṃskāra*) of its own stage.
This contradicts the principle; therefore, it is known that the *upādāna* (clinging) which depends upon ignorance must belong to another stage (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, a question is asked:

For one who is born from a higher stage to a lower stage, or from a lower stage to a higher stage, what stage’s feeling (*vedanā*) does that [craving] take as its object to give rise to the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*)?
The answer is: That craving also takes the feeling of the stage where one is to be born as its object. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "From this..."
The three types of sensation give rise to the three types of craving. That is to say, due to the oppression of suffering, one develops craving for pleasant sensation;
or, one develops craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) toward pleasant sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant;

or, one develops craving for the formless realm (*arūpya-tṛṣṇā*) solely toward sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant—this refers to greed of middling and inferior grades. This is explained below under the twelve links.

Regarding the three time periods (*trikāla*), the ten causes and two fruits: the "inducers" and the "induced" are combined [into one period] because the first two are inducers and the next five are induced, and they must belong to the same single lifetime.

The "producers" and the "produced" are separated [into different periods] because the producer (the inducer) and that which is induced share one period, while the produced constitutes another period. Therefore, the first ten [factors] belong to the present, and the latter two belong to the future.

Thus, the ten causes and two fruits are definitely not of the same period. Among the causes, the first seven and the three beginning with craving (*tṛṣṇā*) constitute "appropriation" (*upādāna*) once they have been moistened.

Regarding retribution upon rebirth (*upapadya-vedanīya*): retribution upon rebirth is necessarily simultaneous [with its cause]. If it has not yet been moistened [by craving], it receives subsequent retribution (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*), and subsequent retribution thus constitutes a different lifetime.

If two [factors]—birth and old age/death—belong to the future; three—craving, grasping, and becoming—belong to the present; and seven—from ignorance through feeling—belong to the present, then their names are fixed as belonging to the same lifetime.
Thus, this single layer of cause and effect is sufficient to manifest cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and is already free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. Why [then]...?
Is it that you posit two layers of cause and effect? Or, should one exceed this, would it not lead to an infinite regress?

If, being ignorant of the prior limit, you speak of two causes, there are those even more ignorant regarding the further prior limits; for them, two causes would still be too few, and you should speak of even more.
If you claim that, being ignorant of the posterior limit, you speak of two effects, there are likewise those ignorant regarding the further posterior limits.
If two fruits were still insufficient and one were to further explain more, there would be the fault of infinite regress.

This [position] thus maintains that the twelve links are complete within two lifetimes alone, and does not allow for two sets of cause and effect across three lifetimes. If that is so, how can there be "three periods"?
This means that the two present fruits of birth and death are the results of the ten causes from the prior limit (*pūrvānta*).
In the present life there are ten causes, and in the future life there will likewise be two fruits. Thus, through these two layers of cause and effect, the three periods of time are established.
Consequently, across the three periods of time, the twelve links are complete in two layers.
Regarding the specific categories (*arthamukha*) of these twelve links: [this continues] until "therefore, this can cause the continuity of birth and death.

Third, the analysis by way of various gates consists of seventeen gates, which also briefly encompass the full meaning. As for the seventeen gates: first is the gate of the distinction between the provisional and the real.
This means that among the twelve links, nine are real and three are provisional. [The one that is real is] *bhava* (existence), which is the seed of karma and...

The five factors beginning with consciousness have already moistened the six branches; because they are collectively designated as "existence" (*bhava*), [the subsequent] two—birth (*jāti*) and old age-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—are distinct from these five.

Although they lack a separate substantial entity, they are nonetheless conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*), because their characteristics differ: [birth] is growth, while [old age-and-death] consists of decline, transformation, and destruction. Thus, they are merely nominal existents.
The second is the "one is not one thing" section. Five are "one thing," namely ignorance (*avidyā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

The remainder are "not one thing," namely the seven factors beginning with volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). This is because volitional formations encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) consists of two components.

Because of the six bases and the four graspings. Third, the section on the defiled and non-defiled gates: among [the twelve links], ignorance, craving, and grasping—these three are exclusively defiled, because they are of the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Consciousness and the other five members, as well as birth and the two [other] members—these seven are exclusively non-defiled, because they are results of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) and are of an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature.
Within the states of these seven members, the arising of the wholesome or the defiled is possible; this is a figurative designation. [End of] Yoga [Śāstra].
Section Ten: Regarding the provisional classification into two types of karma, there are those that pertain to both [types], and there are those that include the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

In the fourth section, the "Gate of Distinct and Mixed Analysis," ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are purely defiled; therefore, they do not mutually intermingle with the other members [of dependent origination].

They are called "distinct characteristics" (*pṛthak-lakṣaṇa*). Because the nine members beginning with *saṃskāra* (volitional formations) are intermingled, they are called "mixed characteristics" (*miśra-lakṣaṇa*).

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks: "For what reason are *saṃskāra* and *bhava* mixed characteristics? It is because they can induce desirable and undesirable fruits, and because they can produce the differentiation of rebirth states (*gati*). [It further asks:

"For what reason do consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and a portion of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have mixed characteristics? It is because they depend upon the intermingled..."

Because it is the time of defilement; because it is based on the time of moistening; and because it is based on the time of transformation. Why is it that consciousness (*vijñāna*) possesses characteristics mixed with sensation (*vedanā*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)? It is said:
in order to specifically manifest the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*), and to manifest the distinction between the projecting [causes] and the produced [results].

Fifth, regarding the gate of the material and the non-material: the non-material is the mind (*citta*). The six factors beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*) belong exclusively to the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*). Consciousness is the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are afflictive mental factors (*kleśa-caitta*). The two links of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitta*).
The six links beginning with formations (*saṃskāra*) pertain to both matter and mind. Regarding the sixth gate, that of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*):

all twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) are contaminated, because the uncontaminated is not a link of existence. Regarding the seventh gate, that of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): the twelve links of existence... [are conditioned].

All these are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). This [nirvāṇa] is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because it does not consist of links. Eighth, the section on the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*): Ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) pertain exclusively to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) pertain exclusively to the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the unwholesome. Existence (*bhava*) pertains to the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the unobscured-unneutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

As for the remaining seven—namely, the five beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the two beginning with birth (*jāti*)—they are exclusively unobscured-unneutral, because they are results of maturation (*vipākaphala*).

They are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If, within their specific states (*avasthā*), they also give rise to wholesome or defiled [states], then they pertain to all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). Regarding the ninefold classification by way of the three realms (*dhātu-vibhāga-mukha*):

although they all pertain to the three realms, there are those that are partial and those that are complete. In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are complete; in the [upper] two realms, they are free from defilement.
Because the six sense bases are incomplete in the formless realm, there exists only name. This is the tenth gate: the relationship between the antidotes and their objects.
The factors of the higher stages can subdue those of the lower stages; that is, by means of the six types of contemplative aspects, such as "coarseness" and "suffering.

Because those who seek rebirth in the higher realms give rise to these [aspects], there are six types of contemplative aspects: first, suffering, which refers to the mental factors arising within the body that take desire as their object.

Inability to transcend [suffering] constitutes the cause of suffering. Being oppressed by various things in the retributive body of the desire realm—such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, illness, pain, swords, and staves—constitutes the fruit of suffering.
The two types of coarseness refer to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of the desire realm, which can give rise to manifold evils;
this is the cause of coarseness. This body is composed of thirty-six substances, including the foul impurities of excrement and urine; [this constitutes the fruit of coarseness].
Accomplishment. This constitutes the coarseness of the fruit. Regarding the three obstacles: the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) covers the true nature so that it cannot be manifested;
this is the obstacle of the cause. This physical body is obstructive and lacks sovereignty; this is the obstacle of the fruit. Regarding the four excellences (also called purities):
having become weary of the base suffering of craving in the desire realm, one then rejoices in the superior meditations of the first dhyāna.

The bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) constitutes the excellence of the cause. Furthermore, one grows weary of the sufferings of hunger, thirst, and so forth within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and thus rejoices in the bliss of the flavor of dhyāna in the first dhyāna;

this constitutes the excellence of the result. Regarding the five wonders: having become weary of the coarse, distracted, and restless mind that delights in the five sensory objects and sensual desires of the desire realm, one rejoices in the bliss of the meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of the first dhyāna, wherein the mind is settled and unmoving.

Movement. This is the excellence of the cause. Furthermore, one becomes weary of the foul and impure body of the desire realm as being coarse, and thus joyfully accepts the attainment of the body of the first dhyāna, which—like a reflection in a mirror—possesses form and color yet lacks substantial obstruction. This is the excellence of the fruit.
The six "exits" (also called "leavings") refer to the state where, having become weary of the afflictive obscurations of the desire realm, one joyfully seeks the mind of the first dhyāna.
This constitutes "departure by way of cause. Subsequently, one becomes weary of the physical body of the desire realm, which is characterized by obstruction and lacks mastery;

one then aspires for the body of the first dhyāna, which has attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and is characterized by mastery and non-obstruction. This is "departure by way of result.

That is to say, it is the six [mental states] arising in one who seeks rebirth in a higher realm, consisting of weariness toward the suffering, coarseness, and hindrances of the lower stage, and aspiration for the excellence, subtlety, and transcendence of the higher stage.

This is the classification of types of modes of activity (*ākāra*). Eleventh is the gate of the classification of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth. All [such actions] are exclusively neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).

Because the impure wholesome karma (*sāsrava-kuśala-karma*) produced by noble ones (*ārya*) has clear knowledge (*vidyā*) as its condition and because it opposes the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*), it is not subsumed under the factors of existence.
From this, one should know that a noble one certainly does not perform karma that brings about a future existence; they are not deluded regarding the subsequent fruit of suffering.

Because of this inquiry, someone asks: "If that is so, then the practice of the five mixed meditations of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) would not be a constituent of volitional formations (*saṃskāra-aṅga*).

If it were a constituent of volitional formations, then an Ārya would be creating karma; if it were not a constituent of volitional formations, how could it produce rebirth there as a collective retribution? Therefore, the treatise answers:
"The mixed cultivation of dhyāna serves as a support for previous karma of the lower realms, thereby producing rebirth in the Pure Abodes and so forth; this is not contrary to reason."

The meaning is as follows: It is not contradictory in principle that those who have attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) and so forth, by means of mixed cultivation (*miśra-bhāvanā*) of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states, and by relying on the fourth *dhyāna* to support the karma for rebirth in the three heavens such as Anabhraka, are born in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

This is because the karma for their total retribution (*vipāka-karma*) and the seeds of verbal designation (*nāma-vikalpa-bīja*) were already established during the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*). Furthermore, the karma for the three lower heavens of the fourth *dhyāna* belongs to a single level (*bhūmi*).

Because they are bound [by past karma], and because their subsequent births in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens arise from karma sustained by outflow-free (*anāsrava*) merit, these are not new karmas created by the Noble Ones (*ārya*).

Regarding the twelfth section, the "Distinction between the Two Types of Abandonment," there is one interpretation that ignorance (*avidyā*) is abandoned solely through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).

This is because it must be deluded regarding the principles of the Truths (*satya*) in order to initiate the performance of karma; and since the delusions regarding the principles of the Truths are abandoned through the path of seeing, the Noble Ones certainly do not create [new karma].
There are no subsequent afflictions or karma that can certainly give rise to further delusions; therefore, they are not abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned solely through cultivation, because they moisten rebirth by greedily seeking future existence (*punar-bhava*). This is because the nine types of death-moment consciousnesses are accompanied by craving.
As long as existence (*bhava*) is not yet exhausted, these must necessarily be present. The *Miśrakābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "By the power of continuity..."
There are nine types of death-consciousness associated with self-love (*ātmabhāvātṛṣṇā*), which cause the continuity of rebirth within each of the three realms—desire, form, and formlessness.

First, one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm links the continuity of rebirth by means of a death-consciousness associated with self-love for the body of the desire realm. Second, one who [passes away from the desire realm...]
Regarding death in a realm: if one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the continuity of rebirth is linked by the death-consciousness associated with craving for the self-body of the form realm.

Third, if one dies from the desire realm and is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the continuity of rebirth is linked by the death-consciousness associated with craving for the self-body of the formless realm. Thus, there are three [types of] death in the desire realm.
There are nine types [of existence]: three each for those passing away from the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, totaling nine.

The remaining nine factors, such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), are abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). According to the correct interpretation, all of them are abandoned through both paths.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states that one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) has abandoned one portion of all the links of dependent origination (*bhavāṅga*), but not all of them entirely. This is because, if it were [otherwise], regarding ignorance (*avidyā*)...

The *aṅga* [of clinging] is abandoned only by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). Since it should be entirely abandoned during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), how can it be said that a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) has not entirely abandoned it?
If the *aṅgas* of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) were abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), they should remain entirely unabandoned during the stage of the path of seeing;
how then can it be said that he has already abandoned one part of all the *aṅgas*? If it is the case that one part of each is abandoned, then the *aṅga* of ignorance (*avidyā*) would not be...

They are abandoned only by seeing [the truths], because a portion of ignorance still remains. The two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are not abandoned solely through cultivation, for a portion of them is abandoned at the time of entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that all afflictions within the three realms [are abandoned by both seeing and cultivation].
All [karmas] capable of linking rebirth and leading to the miserable destinies are produced by this [volition], which is either conceptual or singular.
It is not said that the craving and grasping that moisten rebirth are abandoned only through cultivation; rather, the karmas that induce future existence are all abandoned through insight.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is able to initiate [the process]. From this, it is known that the three links—ignorance, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—all pertain to both what is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
However, regarding the initiation of the process by ignorance and the moistening of rebirth by craving and grasping, there is both a primary factor and an auxiliary factor.
Ignorance as the primary initiator is abandoned only by insight; craving and grasping as the primary moisteners of rebirth are abandoned only by cultivation. As for their auxiliaries:
That which assists and moistens [the roots] is indeterminate; it also pertains to both what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Furthermore, regarding defiled phenomena whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) ought to be abandoned—namely, the primary afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—when untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) arises and abandons their intrinsic nature, this is called "abandonment by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), because when light appears, darkness departs.
All tainted wholesome phenomena (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) are not abandoned by intrinsic nature, as they do not contradict the Path.
Therefore, it is asked: "If that is so, why are both called 'abandonment' (*prahāṇa*)? It is answered: "They are said to be abandonment for two reasons:

first, because of being free from bondage; second, because of non-arising. This means that the impure wholesome dharmas, such as generosity, which arise within the first six consciousnesses, are seized moment by moment by the seventh consciousness through its grasping at a self. Thus, they cannot eliminate signs and are consequently bound by signs (*nimitta-bandhana*)."

Because those [afflictions] are severed, it is called "freedom from bondage. This refers to the severing of those afflictions that take [the eighth consciousness] as their object and are associated with it.

The two instances of the word "those" (*tat*) point to non-defiled phenomena; namely, the eighth consciousness of the nature of non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), as well as the contaminated wholesome (*sāsrava-kuśala*) dharmas within the first six consciousnesses.
Because these are taken as objects and grasped as a self by the seventh consciousness, they are said to be "taken as objects" (*ālambana*). These are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas.

Being permeated by defiled dharmas is called "intermingling with them. As for what is meant by "severing their basis": the basis for the evil fruits of the three miserable realms arises from conceptual discrimination.
Once one has entered the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one can ensure that the suffering fruits of the three miserable paths never arise again.

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* also speaks of two kinds of abandonment: first, the abandonment of the bondage of objects, which means that by severing only the delusions within the mind, one [is liberated] regarding...
External sensory objects do not give rise to greed or hatred; although one conditions these objects, no attachment arises. Therefore, it is called "severing the bond of conditioning.
Second is "severing non-arising," which means that when the emptiness of phenomena is realized, the bitter fruits of the three miserable realms and evil paths can be made never to arise again.
Therefore, it is called "severing non-arising. This treatise explains these two meanings, which are derived from this sūtra, based on the principle of conditioning (*pratyaya*).

Regarding the severance of bonds: it is taught that tainted wholesome and indeterminate states are severed only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because those that take them as objects or are associated with them are innate (*sahaja*).
Regarding the non-arising of cessation: it is taught that the various evil destinies, as well as the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), are severed only by insight (*darśana-heya*).

Regarding the phrase "as the basis for that," it is because [the latter] arises through conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*). As for the instruction "it should be understood as appropriate regarding the various types of abandonment mentioned previously":

if based on a specific treatise, it is as explained in the *Prakaraṇapāda*; if based on a general treatise, it is as explained in the *Dharmaskandha*. [This concludes] the section on the thirteen [types of abandonment] categorized by the three feelings (*vedanā*).

Ten of the links are associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*), with the exception of the two links of sensation (*vedanā*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
This is because sensation does not associate with itself, and because old age and death lack pleasant feeling and may contain neutral feeling.

Eleven of the links consist of painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*), with the exception of the link of sensation. Regarding the four gates of the three types of suffering (*tri-duḥkhatā*), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* refers to the twelve links of existence (*bhava*).

The [first] eleven links are called the three types of suffering. From ignorance up to the six sense bases, their characteristic of flux is manifest; thus they are called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

The two links of contact and feeling involve the confrontation with the arising of suffering; thus they are called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). The remaining [links] merely destroy happiness;

therefore, they are called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). Although aging and death lack happiness themselves, because they destroy birth, they are also called the suffering of change. Among these, the eleven...
A small portion of the twelve links is subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), with the exception of old age and death;

this is because the suffering of change is established based on pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), and since there is no pleasure in old age and death, they are not mentioned [in this context]. A small portion of the twelve links is subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), as each of the twelve links can potentially contain suffering.
The entirety of the twelve links is subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), as they are all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).

Therefore, if one establishes the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) based on the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), then old age and death are excluded, because the state of old age and death does not admit of equanimity.

Since these three types of suffering arise from the three sensations— namely, the sensation of suffering gives rise to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the sensation of pleasure gives rise to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*),

and the sensation of equanimity gives rise to the suffering of conditioned existence— it is said that both [the latter two] sufferings are "partial" (*pradeśika*) within the twelve links of dependent origination.

They possess the nature of the three types of suffering. If they possess two types of suffering, they necessarily possess the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); therefore, it is said that they possess them "in their entirety.

As for all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), because they are momentary by nature, there are those that possess the suffering of conditioned formations but do not possess the other two types of suffering.

Furthermore, since each of the two types of suffering does not subsume the other two, it is said that they possess them "partially. This means that the two types of suffering do not pervade neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*), just as when a śrāvaka emerges from the realm [of existence].

Externally, there is only the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) and not the other two types of suffering. Furthermore, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) do not mutually encompass one another, nor is there the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Therefore, each does not encompass the other two;

for within the suffering of change there is no feeling of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*), and within the suffering of suffering there is no feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*). This explains a portion of the two meanings. (15) The Section on the Four Truths (12).
The members [of dependent origination] are all subsumed under the Truth of Suffering, because their intrinsic nature consists of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).

Ignorance, formations, craving, grasping, and becoming—these five members are also subsumed under the Truth of Origination, because their intrinsic nature consists of karma and afflictions. *Yogācārabhūmi*, Chapter Ten.
Question: Of these twelve links, how many constitute the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*), how many the path of karma (*karma-mārga*), and how many the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*)?

Answer: Three are the path of afflictions (craving, grasping, and existence); two are the path of karma (ignorance and formations); the remainder are the path of suffering (the five beginning with consciousness, and birth, old age, and death). Question:
How many links are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), and which constitute suffering in the present life? Answer: Two; namely, birth and old age.
Death. Question: How many members are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*)? Answer: From consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to feeling (*vedanā*), in their nature as seeds. Question:

How many members are subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*)? Answer: The remaining members (ignorance, formations, craving, grasping, and existence). These are thus karma and afflictions that pertain to both truths.

If considered from the perspective of reverse contemplation, they are the Truths of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) and the Path (*mārgasatya*), because the cessation of discursive thought is itself the path. Ten.

The sixth section concerns the gates of conditions (*pratyaya*). It is divided into four parts according to the text: first, a general demonstration of presence and absence; second, a detailed explanation of existence and non-existence; third, a conclusion illustrating the lack of fixed direction;
and fourth, a reconciliation of the intent of the sūtras. Regarding the first, the general demonstration: this refers to [the analysis] within the context of the four conditions.
When the various members are compared with one another, the condition of predominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*) certainly exists, because the nature of predominance is broad;

therefore, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* explains only this one. As for the remaining three conditions, their presence or absence is not fixed, because those three conditions are restricted; therefore, they are omitted and not explained.
Regarding the second part, the individual explanation, there are two sections: first, the explanation of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and later, the analysis of the other two. First—

There are four types of conditions for the cause (*hetu-pratyaya*). The first is based on actual existence (*dravya-sat*). This refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in relation to grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) in relation to birth (*jāti*); these possess the meaning of being causal conditions.

This is because the intensification of craving constitutes grasping, and the intensification of becoming constitutes existence. Regarding the statement that "craving is the causal condition for grasping":

as for what is called a "causal condition," it must necessarily produce its effect directly through its own substance (*svabhāva*). Since the intensification of craving constitutes grasping, craving is [the cause] of grasping.

The seeds are able to produce the manifest grasping; therefore, they serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Regarding "consciousness increases to become existence" (*bhava*): existence has no separate essence apart from [the seeds].

Through the moistening of craving and grasping, the five [aggregates] constitute existence. Existence is precisely the seed of consciousness, while the branch of birth (*jāti*) is the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) of consciousness.

Since the seed of consciousness gives rise to the manifest, existence serves as the causal condition for this birth. Second, the basis is indeterminate; that is to say, if one speaks of consciousness...

Regarding the statement that "the *saṃskāras* are the seeds of karma": the *saṃskāras* also function as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) in relation to consciousness (*vijñāna*). This is the intended meaning of the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) when he correlates [the members of dependent origination] with the *dharmas*.

If one were to take the seeds of consciousness as the member of consciousness (*vijñānāṅga*), then the *saṃskāras* would merely be a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and not the direct cause of consciousness.

Now, because the seeds of karma are taken as the member of consciousness (and these seeds of karma are themselves the member of *saṃskāra*), the *saṃskāras* can serve as the causal condition for consciousness. This is...
Present activity serves as the causal condition for the seeds. Regarding the three fetters, the same principle applies as when other members are compared with one another;
there is no sense of them acting as causal conditions. Fourth, reconciling other treatises: first, reconciling the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, and subsequently, reconciling the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Within the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it first indicates their existence based on ignorance; subsequently, it clarifies the meaning of their existence, explaining that this is a figurative designation, meaning they exist simultaneously with ignorance.
The latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) of karma coexist with ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, the seeds of karma are metaphorically designated as "ignorance.

In reality, it is simply the seeds of formative action (*saṃskāra*) that give rise to the manifest activity of formative action. However, in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, this is termed the "establishment of the conditions for the members" (*aṅgapratyayavyavasthāna*).

As for what is meant by the "establishment of the conditions for the members," it refers to their establishment by way of: (1) latent predispositions, (2) projection, (3) volition, and (4) coexistence.

Regarding the conditions of the members (*aṅga-pratyaya*): according to their respective requirements, the conditions of the members are established based on the characteristics of the four conditions.
For instance, ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as a condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) because it consists of predispositions from previous births;

this is because the various karmas produced by that continuity of perfuming (*vāsanā*) are capable of creating future existence (*punarbhava*). Furthermore, at that time, the currently active ignorance is able to induce [the formative forces]. Thus, it acts as a condition.
1. It is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because the various formations (*saṃskāra*) flow on and arise in a continuous succession, being differentiated by that ignorance.

2. By reflecting upon it, it serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). 3. Because it takes the state of delusion as its objective domain through improper mental application (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) such as regarding it as supreme, and because it co-exists with it, it serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). By means of that...
Through the power of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it causes the associated volition (*cetanā*) to engage with its object through inversion and thereby perform karmic activity.

Fourth, in this way, all [factors] should be understood to be exhausted according to their respective applications. Thus, regarding the relationship between ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), it functions as all four conditions;
since this has been applied as a paradigm for all [links], one should know that all twelve factors possess these four conditions. *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

[The section on] "Below" correlates with the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn), which states that there are three conditions (*pratyaya*) but no cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). The [section on] "Above" cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*;

based on the "present affection" (*vartamāna-ruci*), it takes up [the discussion from] below to correlate with the meaning above. While the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says they do not exist, the [text on] "Above" fully explains that they do.

The four positions mentioned above are indeterminate and merely provisional designations; these need not be correlated. Rather, one should correlate the two positions where the cause-condition actually exists. Based on...
Regarding the statement that "present craving and grasping" constitute the sense of being a causal condition (*pratyaya*) for one another:
