Thus, while remaining profoundly still and solid, it constantly undergoes transformation along with things; though it gives rise to a profusion of activities, it does not stir from True Suchness. Therefore, a verse says:

"It is not that one does not see True Suchness, yet one is able to understand all conditioned phenomena as being like illusions and the like—though they exist, they are not real. This refers precisely to this.

This verse intends to state that the three natures are all not separate from the mind. First, a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to demonstrate that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is conventionally existent.
The argument is stated as follows: "The mind and mental factors, as well as the dependent nature manifested by them [are conventionally existent]."

This is the subject (*dharmin*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it exists as if it were existent, though it is not [ultimately] existent. The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it is produced by a multitude of conditions. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: "like illusory phenomena," and so forth.
Next, a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is established to demonstrate that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent. The formal inference states:

Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the false imaginings of fools—such as the existence, non-existence, both, or neither of a self and phenomena—are the subject; their intrinsic nature and characteristics are entirely non-existent.

This is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is stated: "Because all things are the objects of parikalpita (imaginary construction). The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like flowers in the sky and so forth.
Next, to reveal that the pariniṣpanna (perfected nature) is real: this refers to the fact that upon that *paratantra* (dependent nature), both types of parikalpita—self and phenomena—are empty.
That which is manifested by this emptiness of the two, namely the true nature (*tathatā*) of consciousness and so forth, is called the pariniṣpanna.

This is indeed so. Therefore, it is said that what arises dependently has no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). That which lacks intrinsic nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and emptiness is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Thus, these three natures are all inseparable from the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). How can one raise the objection: "If there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), why do the holy teachings speak of the three natures?"

Regarding space (*ākāśa*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—up to this point—I have provided a brief outline of the essential points for fear of wearying the reader with excessive detail.

Section Six: Analysis by Way of Various Gates, divided into ten parts. First, the gate of the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). First, the question; second, the answer; third, the explanation beginning with "The mind, etc.

These six unconditioned phenomena are the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). However, since they pervade all things, all three [natures] may be included within them. As for "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*): [text continues].

Because they are transformations of the mind, space and so forth are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). If one clings to them as being substantially existent, they are the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
To thoroughly understand their emptiness of intrinsic nature is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the gate of the contaminated and the uncontaminated:
all contaminated minds, mental factors, and their manifestations are the dependent nature. Uncontaminated minds, mental factors, and their manifestations may pertain to both [natures].
Nature. Regarding the threefold sevenfold gate of *tathatā* (suchness), as for the mental attention (*manasikāra*) to the *pravṛtti-tathatā* (the suchness of transmigration):
it refers to those bodhisattvas who have already seen the truths and, through superior practice of the Dharma, have well-cultivated this mental attention.

At the time of [contemplating] defiled and pure phenomena, they contemplate the actual nature of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) as having been in transmigration since beginningless time. Having thus contemplated, they abandon the view of causelessness and... [incompleteness in source].
The view of a cause of equality. Second, regarding the mental application to the true suchness of the real nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa-tathatā-manasikāra*): this refers to what was explained previously;
that is, up to the point of contemplating the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena within all defiled and purified dharmas.
Once one has performed this contemplation, all views of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the mental applications that conceptualize and differentiate various characteristics no longer manifest.

3. Regarding the mental attention to the suchness of representation-only (*vijñapti-tathatā-manasikāra*): This refers to the aforementioned method, wherein one contemplates that all phenomena, from those pertaining to defilement and purification, are based upon the nature of representation-only.

Having performed this contemplation, one understands in accordance with reality that it is because the mind alone is defiled that sentient beings are defiled, and because the mind alone is pure that sentient beings are pure. 4. Regarding the mental attention to the suchness of establishment (*vyavasthāna-tathatā-manasikāra*)...
"Intention" refers to what was previously explained, up to the point of contemplating the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) regarding the nature of defiled phenomena.

Having contemplated this, one explains it to sentient beings for the sake of their understanding. "Attention to the suchness of the five wrong practices" refers to what was previously explained, up to the point of contemplating the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) regarding defiled phenomena, desiring their abandonment. For the sake of... [sentient beings].

Regarding the explanation of the afflictions: what are called "wrong practices" refer to the two afflictions of greed and hatred, which give rise to wrong practice through delusion regarding objects and views.

Pride gives rise to wrong practice through delusion regarding sentient beings and views. The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) [likewise give rise to wrong practice].

Delusion regarding the objects of knowledge gives rise to wrong conduct through the views of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Delusion regarding various views gives rise to wrong conduct through doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Delusion regarding the antidotes gives rise to wrong conduct through ignorance (*avidyā*). Delusion regarding everything gives rise to wrong conduct.

Furthermore, all ten afflictions give rise to various forms of wrong conduct by being deluded regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), because they serve as the causal basis and support for them. Moreover, the ten afflictions...
All are deluded regarding the path to cessation and give rise to various wrong practices; because of this, they are able to produce that fear.
Sixth is the mental attention to the true suchness of purity, which is as previously described, up to the point of contemplating the truth of cessation within the essence of pure phenomena.
Having reflected thus, in order to bring about realization, he teaches it to sentient beings.
This is the mental attention to the suchness of the sevenfold correct practice, as previously described, up to the pure conduct; that is, he reflects upon the Truth of the Path.
Having reflected thus, in order to bring about cultivation, he teaches it to sentient beings. These seven kinds of reality are all subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Because two, three, seven, and six are all objects of perception for fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*);
and because one, four, and five are all objects of perception for subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). If categorized according to their characteristics:

the three [categories] of the suffering and origin of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) are subsumed under the two natures of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*), because they involve false attachment and are defiled. The remaining four are all...

Included within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) are the four and six categories of phenomena. The five aggregates (*skandha*) together with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are termed the "six phenomena.

Form, sensation, perception, formations, consciousness, and the unconditioned all possess the characteristics of false conceptualization (*parikalpita*), dependent origination (*paratantra*), and the ultimate principle (*pariniṣpanna*).
Thus, it is said that they all possess the three natures. Regarding the five categories of fivefold phenomena (*pañca-pañcavastuka*): [Yogācāra...]
The *Ga* (Vol. 72) states: "If one wishes to thoroughly understand the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*), one should first understand that the realms (*dhātu*) possess five factors.
What are these five factors? First, characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); second, names (*nāman*); third, discrimination (*vikalpa*); fourth, suchness (*tathatā*); and fifth, correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*)."

What is the characteristic (*nimitta*)? It refers, in brief, to all things that serve as the basis for verbal discourse. What is the designation (*nāman*)? It refers to the linguistic expressions applied to those very characteristics.
What is conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*)? It refers to all minds and mental factors within the knowledge of the three realms. What is suchness (*tathatā*)?
It is that which is manifested by the non-existence of a self in phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and is realized by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
Practice. It is not the basis for all forms of discourse. What is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)?
Briefly, there is one kind: first, supramundane right knowledge; second, mundane-supramundane right knowledge.
What is supramundane right knowledge? It is that by means of which śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas attain penetration.

Suchness. Furthermore, because of this, those bodhisattvas, through their skillful cultivation of the means regarding the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and their abiding in the wisdom of such all-pervading suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*), swiftly realize perfection and purify the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

What is mundane and supramundane right knowledge? It refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who, having realized suchness by means of the initial right knowledge, subsequently employ the mundane and supramundane right knowledge attained thereafter to cause the mind to feel revulsion toward the faults and afflictions of the three realms within the context of the established truths (vyavasthāpita-satya), while taking delight in the tranquility of the three realms. Furthermore, by means of...
For the most part, abiding in this state, one swiftly realizes perfection and purifies the afflictive obscurations.

Furthermore, because this very wisdom has never before attained its object, it is called "supramundane"; yet, because its objective condition consists of the characteristics of verbal expression, it is also called "mundane.
Therefore, it is described as both mundane and supramundane. It was with this underlying intention (*saṃdhi*) that the Blessed One spoke these words.
I teach that there is mundane wisdom (*loka-jñāna*), supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*), and both mundane and supramundane wisdom.
Wisdom comprised within conceptual discrimination is called exclusively mundane. Wisdom comprised within the first correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is called exclusively supramundane.
Wisdom comprised within the second correct knowledge is termed both mundane and supramundane. Furthermore, [there are] seventy...

Question 4: Regarding the three natures (namely, the *parikalpita* and so forth) and the five dharmas such as *nimitta*, how many of the five dharmas are subsumed within the first nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)?
Answer: None of them are subsumed. Question: How many are subsumed within the second nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?

Answer: It is subsumed under four [aspects]: characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), names (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Question: How many [aspects] subsume the third nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*)?
Answer: It is subsumed under one: suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding this, the first meaning is precisely this passage.

Below that, the author of the treatise provides an explanation, intending to say that the outflowing mind and its associates, which manifest as if they were the signified (*abhidheya*), are called "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*); those which appear as if they were the signifier (*abhidhāna*) are called... [names].

The mind and its associates that are capable of transformation are established as "discrimination" (*parikalpa*). Uncontaminated minds and their associates, being free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), are termed "correct wisdom" (*samyagjñāna*).
As for the four categories mentioned above, because they arise from conditions, they are all subsumed under the "other-dependent" (*paratantra*);

they are not subsumed under the "imagined" (*parikalpita*) among the five categories, because the imagined is false and lacks intrinsic nature. Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "The self-characteristic of the imagined nature is non-existent."
Why is this? Because it is not subsumed within the five categories; apart from these five categories, nothing else exists. Question:
If the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) lacks intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*), how can it give rise to the act of imagining?
Answer: Because names operate upon objects; that is to say, worldly fools follow those conventional designations as they flow toward their respective objects and thus cling to them.
There is a true nature that is determined by name and meaning and is commensurate with reality.

Question: How should one know that this is a false attachment? Answer: Because the two are mutually adventitious. Why is this so? Because a name is adventitious with respect to its object, as it does not correspond to the essence [of that object];
thus it is called adventitious. Likewise, an object is adventitious with respect to its name, as it has no existence [independently of the name]; thus it is called adventitious. Or...

Furthermore, there are passages stating that the tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*), along with their object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*), are called "the characterized" (*nimitta*);

the perceiving aspect (*darśanabhāga*) is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*). Both are dependently originated (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Their non-existence as falsely grasped is the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is conventionally designated by name.
Correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*), being free from the two types of inversion, constitute the "perfected nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Or again...

In some places it is said that the two parts—the apprehended (*nimitta*) and the apprehending (*darśana*)—of the tainted mind and its mental factors are collectively termed "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).

Because they are subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and are grasped as the signified (*vācya*) according to deluded attachment, they are established as "phenomena" (*nimitta*).

Because they are grasped as the signifier (*vācaka*) according to deluded attachment, they are established as "names" (*nāman*). These are subsumed under the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Furthermore, in other places it is said that this occurs during the state of being tainted (*sāsrava*).

The central mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), such as the aspects of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), become the objects of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) through the power of names;

therefore, they are called "names" (*nāman*). Belonging to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), they are horizontally conceptualized according to names, yet their substance does not truly exist.

These are provisionally established as "objects" and "names," which constitute the objects of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). This accords with the first meaning [of the three natures]. It is not accepted that the five categories (*pañca-vastu*) are subsumed under pervasive conceptualization. Pervasive conceptualization...
Although one grasps at names, the names themselves belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); it is only the meaning within the name that is the object of false attachment.

As for the other points not mentioned here, they are identical in meaning to what was stated previously. Thus, all four explanations above originate from the sacred teachings (*āgama*). Although the phrasing differs, their meanings do not contradict one another.
Nevertheless, the first meaning alone is free from confusion and should be taken as the correct one. This is explained extensively in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
It is explained in volumes seventy-two, seventy-three, and seventy-four. Regarding the section on the five characteristics (*pañca-lakṣaṇa-dvāra*): *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 81;
*Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (顯揚論), fascicle 12, provide detailed explanations of these five characteristics. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fascicle 16, states:

"Furthermore, as previously stated, there are five kinds of characteristics, namely: the characteristic of the signifier (*abhidhāna-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of the signified (*abhidheya-lakṣaṇa*). This..."
There are two [types of] characteristics: the characteristic of attachment and the characteristic of non-attachment. Furthermore, there are three characteristics, namely:

the imputed characteristic (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*), the dependent characteristic (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), and the perfected characteristic (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*). Do the five subsume the three, or do the three subsume the five?
The verse says: Based on the three natures, one should know that five kinds of characteristics are established. These [five] each have their respective five functions as appropriate.
One should know that the five characteristics are established based on the three self-natures. Why is this? Because the first and second [characteristics] are based on the three self-natures;
the third is based on the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); and the fourth is based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Regarding the characteristic of arising (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*): the fifth [characteristic] relies upon the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Below the section on "that which is expressed" (*abhidheya*), the Master of the Treatise explains that each of the first two characteristics possesses the meaning of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). First is the general response; second is the detailed explanation. Regarding "the expressed and the expresser":

as stated in the preceding chapter, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) manifest as if they were the expressed; this is designated as the "characteristic. They appear as if they were the expresser; this is established as the "name."

The transforming mind and its associates are established as "discrimination" (*vikalpa*). When it is now said that false conceptualization (*parikalpa*) belongs to the first nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), this refers to the two aspects—the signifier (*abhidhāna*) and the signified (*abhidheya*)—within deluded imagination; these belong to the first, the thoroughly imagined nature.

Furthermore, the three factors of appearance (*nimitta*), name (*nāman*), and discrimination (*vikalpa*) are, according to their respective roles as subject and object, included within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). When the appearance is the signified, the name is the signifier; when the name is the signified, the appearance is the signifier.

Regarding "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*): conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) is the signifier (*vācaka*), while True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the signified (*vācya*). Alternatively, Correct Wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) is the signifier.

Therefore, it is said that this depends on what is appropriate. An objection is raised: "How can there be a relationship of signifier and signified between True Suchness and Wisdom? To this, the following explanation is given:
Because subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) transforms into the aspect of the signifier (*vācaka-lakṣaṇa*), it is like when correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and so forth arise:
the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) arises directly grasping the essential nature and aspect of *tathatā*.

It is not subsumed under these two aspects of the signifier and the signified (*vācya-vācaka-lakṣaṇa*), because while it possesses a seeing-part, it lacks an image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). This is called subsequently attained wisdom taking *tathatā* as its object; that is, it arises through transformation.
To take the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) as an object is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) or "carrying along" (*anuvyavahāra*), which is precisely conceptualization (*savikalpa*).
Within this very [process], the single portion among the two aspects of the signifier and the signified (*vācya-vācaka*) is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

The relationship between these two aspects—the signifier and the signified—is exclusively the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because names and objects are falsely grasped as being necessarily inseparable. This aspect of being clung to is...

That which is the object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Non-attachment to its characteristics is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*); is this not indeed the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?

Regarding the "Gate of the Fourfold Sevenfold Reality," the sixth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "That reality is further of four kinds: first, worldly reality (*loka-tattva*); second, reality according to principle (*yukti-tattva*);
third, the reality that is the object of the wisdom purified of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara-tattva*)."
Fourth is the reality that is the object of the purified wisdom regarding the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Regarding "worldly reality" (*loka-satya*):

it refers to the conventional nature (*saṃvṛti*) established through common consensus by means of the cognitive views and insights acquired through habitual practice among all worldly people regarding various phenomena.
For example, with respect to earth, they perceive it as being merely earth and not fire or other elements; likewise for water, fire, wind, form, and sound.
Odors, tastes, and tangibles; food, drink, clothing, vehicles, and various ornaments, as well as household utensils;
perfumes, garlands, ointments, songs, dances, and music; the various postures and behaviors of men and women; fields, houses, and wealth;

and suffering and pleasure—regarding suffering, one perceives it as suffering and not as pleasure; regarding pleasure, one perceives it as pleasure and not as suffering. Furthermore, to speak briefly: it is said that...
"This is this and that is not that," or "That is that and not anything else"— whatever matters are the objects of the settled conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of sentient beings in the world,
which have been handed down from ancient times by all the world, whose designations are fixed, and which are held in common by oneself and others as true,
rather than being apprehended through false conceptual construction or investigation— this is called "the worldly" (*loka*).
Reality. Regarding the reality of reasoning (*yukti-tattva*): it refers to those who possess correct knowledge;
those who are wise; those who are intelligent; those who investigate; those who examine; those who abide on the stage of analytical reflection (*vitarka-bhūmi*);

those endowed with their own eloquence; those remaining in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); and those who practice according to observation, relying upon direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture.
The three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are the objects known and the sphere of activity of the wisdom that has reached a definitive determination through excellent discernment;
because they are established by means of the principle of proof through causes and conditions as they truly are, this is called the reality of reasoning (*yukti-tattva*).

Regarding the reality that is the sphere of activity of the wisdom purified of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara-tattva*): it refers to the untainted skillful wisdom (*anāsrava-upāya-jñāna*) of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, which is untainted...

The objects of activity of right knowledge, the untainted subsequently attained mundane knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-laukika-jñāna*), and so forth, are called the reality that is the object of the knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara-tattva*). Because one takes this as an object, knowledge becomes purified with respect to the afflictive obscurations.

Furthermore, one subsequently realizes and abides in the state of non-obstruction; therefore, it is called the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇaviśuddhajñānagocaratattva*).
Question: What in the world is reality? Answer: It refers to the four noble truths—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—as manifested by their names.
By means of the discernment (*pravicaya*) of these four noble truths, one attains entry into the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

Following the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), the wisdom of ultimate reality arises. Regarding "the reality that is the domain of the wisdom purified of the cognitive obscurations" (*jñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhajñānagocaratattva*):
among the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), that which obstructs wisdom is called the "cognitive obscuration.

If the true nature (*tathatā*) is the objective sphere of the wisdom that has been liberated from the cognitive obscurations, this is termed "the reality that is the domain of the wisdom purified of the cognitive obscurations."

Indeed, it should be known. What, then, is this? It refers to that which is the sphere of activity for the non-conceptual, equalizing wisdom regarding the conventional nature and the nature free from verbal expression of all phenomena;

this is for the sake of bodhisattvas who have entered into the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and those who have already attained supreme purity. That is to say, it is the most excellent, unsurpassed *tathatā*.
The ultimate nature of the knowable (*jñeya-paryanta-tā*). This nature cannot be overturned or transcended by any analytical investigation of the true dharmas;
it is called the reality that is the object of the purified wisdom regarding the obscurations of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara-tattva*).

Because it is subsumed under the three factors of characteristics, names, and conceptualization, it is included within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). It is the reality established by worldly reasoning (*loka-nyāya-siddha-tattva*), which is the object of the purified wisdom regarding the two obscurations.
The practice of reality is subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because it is comprised of both correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*).
As the *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā* states: "Worldly consensus relies on one; Rational consensus relies on two; The sphere of pure activity has two; And the perfected nature relies on one.
This refers to the "consensus reality" (*loka-prasiddha-tattva*), which briefly consists of two types: first, worldly consensus reality...
Indeed, among the three fundamental realities, this [first] is established solely based on the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Second is the reality established by ultimate reasoning (*yukti-prasiddha-tattva*), which is established based on the three fundamental realities. Third is the reality of the pure sphere of activity (*viśuddha-gocara-tattva*).
There are also two kinds: first, the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the afflictive obscurations;

second, the reality that is the object of knowledge purified of the cognitive obscurations. These two are established solely based upon the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) among the three fundamental natures.
The other two [natures] are not the objects of this pure wisdom. Regarding the second principle, the thoroughly established reality (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*):

if one clings to it, it is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); if one does not cling to it, it is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Defilement (*saṃkleśa*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), while purity (*vyavadāna*) is the perfected nature;
thus, it pervades all three natures. Within the eightfold gate of the Four Noble Truths, each of the four truths possesses all three natures. This is the general summary. Now, [to explain further...]

Regarding the "middle" within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): the sacred teachings establish the characteristics of the Truth of Suffering through four modes of contemplation—impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and non-self (*anātman*).
These four modes each possess three natures. Regarding the three aspects of impermanence: first, because it is originally non-existent by nature.

1. The impermanence of non-existence (*abhāva-anityatā*) is established; this is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). 2. Because there is arising and ceasing, the impermanence of origination and extinction (*utpāda-bhaṅga-anityatā*) is established;

this is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). 3. Because there is transformation of states (*avasthā-pariṇāma*), the impermanence of defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-anityatā*) is established;

this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). (Once defilement is purified, it is the perfectly accomplished reality. Regarding the three types of suffering: first, because of the dual grasping at the five appropriated aggregates as a self and as phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).

Because it is the basis for the arising of grasping and attachment, it is called "suffering as the object of appropriation" (*parigṛhīta-duḥkha*); this is the nature of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Second, because the aggregates, sense bases, and elements themselves constitute birth, aging, and death, they possess the three characteristics of suffering—namely, the suffering of birth, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*)—they are called "suffering as the characteristic of phenomena" (*vastu-lakṣaṇa-duḥkha*).

This is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Third, because the three characteristics are simultaneously extinguished through the convergence of the three types of suffering, the convergence of suffering is termed the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding the three aspects of emptiness: first, because it lacks a real intrinsic nature, the emptiness of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāva-śūnyatā*) is established;

this is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Second, because it is different from the self-nature falsely grasped by delusion, the emptiness of other-nature (*anyathābhāva-śūnyatā*) is established; this is the dependent [nature].
Other-nature (*parabhāva*). Third, because its intrinsic nature is that which is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, it is established as the "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*);

this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the three types of selflessness (*anātman*): first, because both the imagined person-self and the imagined phenomenon-self are devoid of characteristics, they are termed "characterless selflessness";

this is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Second, [the distinction is made] between the provisional self (*prajñapti-ātman*) taught in the holy scriptures and the self-characteristic falsely grasped [by sentient beings].
Because they are distinct, it is called the "selflessness of distinct characteristics"; this is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Third, because its intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is manifested by the absence of "mine" (*amama*), it is called the "selflessness of intrinsic characteristics"; this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the three aspects of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*):

first, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and the attachment to those habitual tendencies—conventionally designating these as such—is called the "origination of habitual tendencies."
This is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Second, by means of karma and afflictions, it is called the "arising through motivation" (*samutthāna-samudaya*);

this is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Third, by means of suchness (*tathatā*) that has not yet abandoned its obstructions, it is called the "unliberated arising" (*asaṃyukta-samudaya*);

this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). [Question: Since suchness has not yet abandoned its obstructions, why is it called "perfected"? [Answer: It is like the case of light and the eye: the fundamental faculty is unimpaired, yet it is obstructed by a cataract, causing one's vision to appear distorted. If one speaks in terms of the [distorted] vision, it may be categorized as the imagined nature; however, if one speaks in terms of the faculty itself, is it not indeed the perfected nature? Cessation (*nirodha*).
Regarding the three truths: first, because self-nature is non-arising, one establishes the extinction of self-nature; this is the parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature).

Second, because both subject and object—the dual grasping—are non-arising through analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is called the extinction of the two graspings; this is the paratantra-svabhāva (dependent nature).
Third, because True Suchness (tathatā) is inherently quiescent from the beginning and does not depend on further extinction, it is called "extinction by its own nature" (*prakṛti-nirodha*);

this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the three aspects of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*): first, because one can know that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is definitively non-existent, it is called the "path of universal knowledge";
this is the imagined nature. Second, because one can sever the defiled portion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is called the "path of perpetual abandonment. This is...

The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is called the "path of realization" because it enables the realization of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), which is the perfected nature itself.
However, the "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) also extends to the latter two natures. If one cannot know the dependent nature and the perfected nature, what would thorough knowledge consist of?

[The seven types of thorough knowledge correspond to] the three natures; that is, the four aspects of the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) correspond to the three natures, as do those of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
Each Truth (satya) has one set of three, forming seven sets of three. As with the aforementioned seven sets of three, each triad is respectively assigned to the three natures;

hence it is said they are "assigned and explained in sequence. Regarding "either provisional or real": for example, the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is conventional/provisional in the world, the *paratantra* (dependent nature) is conventional/provisional in the sacred teachings, and only the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature) is the ultimate reality.
The nine sets of three refer to the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*); the three gates of liberation are... [text ends].
These are: first, the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*); second, the liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa*); and third, the liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa*).

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that these do not transcend existence and non-existence. "Existence" possesses two aspects: first, existence as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); second, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are also considered existence. "Non-existence" refers to what is conceptualized by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Because the followers of the Two Vehicles distance themselves from such non-Buddhist views, it is called "emptiness. This constitutes the thorough comprehension of conventional truth.
Because they are false and illusory. "Wishless" and "signless" refer to the unconditioned state of *nirvāṇa*. According to principle, these three each pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*);

yet, according to their specific characteristics, each pertains to one. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, the three gates of liberation are also established by means of the three natures.
That is to say, based on the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) is established."
Gateways. Based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the gateway of the liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) is established.

Based on the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the gateway of the liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) is established. Regarding the gateway of the tenfold patience toward non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*):

as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, how is the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena established? Answer: It is established by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). That is to say, by means of the pervasive...
Because of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one establishes the patience regarding the non-arising of intrinsic nature (*prakṛty-anutpatti-kṣānti*).

Because of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one establishes the patience regarding the non-arising of spontaneity (*svayam-anutpatti-kṣānti*). Because of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one establishes the patience regarding the non-arising of afflictions, suffering, and impurities (*kleśa-duḥkha-mala-anutpatti-kṣānti*).
These three types of patience should be understood as belonging to the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). This statement refers to these three.

Regarding "objects" (*viṣaya*): this refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), as they are the objects of focus for those three types of patience (*kṣānti*). Regarding the eleventh point, the gate of the two truths (*satyadvaya*):

the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) refers to the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*), as well as all verbal expressions based on their meanings, and the meanings understood through such verbal expressions; furthermore, it includes all previously attained worldly minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*).

Regarding the meaning of the "object of their activity" as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): it refers to noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*), the object of its activity, and the mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) associated with them. How do these three encompass those two truths? This is the question.

One should know that the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) possesses all three of these types, whereas the ultimate consists solely of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). This is the general answer. [The term] *saṃvṛti*...

There are three types: first, the conventional of designation (*prajñapti-saṃvṛti*), which is the worldly convention (*loka-saṃvṛti*); such as an army or a forest, it is the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Second, the conventional of practice (*pratipatti-saṃvṛti*), which is the rational convention (*yukti-saṃvṛti*); such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), it is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Third, the conventional of manifestation (*saṃprakhyāna-saṃvṛti*), which is the conventional of establishment (*vyavasthāna-saṃvṛti*); because it establishes true thusness (*tathatā*). This is superior.

There are also three types of "ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*): First, the ultimate meaning as object (*artha-paramārtha*), which refers to *tathatā* (suchness). It is called such because it is the object of the supreme; this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Second, the ultimate meaning as attainment (*prāpti-paramārtha*), which refers to *nirvāṇa*. It is called such because it is itself the supreme; this is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

Third, the ultimate meaning as practice (*pratipatti-paramārtha*), which refers to the noble path (*āryamārga*). It is called such because its nature is the supreme; this is also a *karmadhāraya* compound. These three types of ultimate meaning are unchanging and...
[Because they are] inverted, they are all subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Regarding the twelve doors of the range of the wisdoms, the *Yogācārabhūmi* asks:
"As for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), what kind of wisdom is its range? Is it the wisdom of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) or the wisdom of the noble ones (*ārya*)? The answer is:

Neither is within the range of activity [of the two types of wisdom], because they are without marks (*animitta*). Question: Of which wisdoms is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) the range of activity?
Answer: It is the range of activity of those two wisdoms; however, it is not the range of activity of supramundane noble wisdom (*lokottara-āryajñāna*).

Question: Of which wisdom is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) the range of activity? Answer: It is exclusively the range of activity of noble wisdom. Section Thirteen: The Gate of the Conventional and the Real. The Imagined...

Having a name but no substance, established by deluded conceptualization, it may be said to be "provisional" (*prajñapti*). When discussing its actual nature (*dharmatā*), since it possesses no characteristics, it is neither provisional nor real.

It cannot be described as provisional or real in the same way as things like a rabbit's horns, for such designations must be established upon the basis of entities—whether general or specific—that possess substantial reality.
Regarding the provisional based on the earth-element, there are three types. First, the provisional of aggregation (*saṃghāta-prajñapti*), as for example...
Vases, bowls, sentient beings, and so forth are composite phenomena (*saṃghāta-dharma*), because they are formed by the simultaneous aggregation of many factors.
While the constituent factors are real, that which is constituted is merely provisional (*prajñapti*). Second, regarding the provisional nature of continuity (*saṃtati-prajñapti*):

as with the past and future time periods, there is only cause and effect, which constitute the nature of continuity. Upon these many factors over many moments, a single provisional phenomenon is established. As the Buddha said: "In the past..."

That deer king was none other than my present self. As for the five aggregates upon which [the designation] depends, although they are substantially real in their momentary destruction, a single "sentient being" is conventionally established in relation to this continuum of many dharmas; thus, it still exists until now.

Regarding the third type, the conventional [designation] based on states (avasthā), such as the dissociated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra), these are all conventional because they are of the nature of states. [This applies to] a single dharma at a single time.

It is established upon a single [entity], just as in the case of a single form (*rūpa*). It is called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*), "visible," and "resistant," and it is also called "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth;
all these are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*) applied to a single dharma. If they were real entities, there would have to be multiple substances.

Such things as anger and resentment are all subsumed under this conventionality. Mind, mental factors, and form arise from seeds produced by causes and conditions; therefore, they are said to be real. Perfect.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is exclusively truly existent, because it arises without depending on other conditions.
Regarding the twelve aspects of identity and difference: are these three [natures] different or not different? The intent of this question is as follows:

if they are said to be not different, then it would be inconsistent to state that the dependent and the perfected exist while the imagined is non-existent. If they are different, how can it be said that they are all...?
Because they are identical, the answer is that they are neither the same nor different. Why are they not different? The answer is: because there is no separate substance.

That is to say, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is without marks; the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is without arising; and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is without essence.

These three natures are thus one single nature, and this single nature is itself the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Furthermore, the perfected true suchness (*pariniṣpanna-tathatā*) has two meanings. First, it is not...

The unchanging [nature] and the following conditions. The dependent nature has two meanings: first, it appears as if existent; second, it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). The imagined nature has two meanings: first, it exists from the perspective of sentient attachment (*sattva-vidyamāna*);

second, it is non-existent from the perspective of ultimate principle (*tattva-abhāva*). Because True Suchness is unchanging, because the dependent nature lacks intrinsic nature, and because that which is grasped is non-existent in principle, the three natures are one and the same limit.
If True Suchness follows conditions, then the dependent nature appears as if existent and that which is grasped exists from the perspective of attachment.
Because these three meanings are also not different from one another, how can they not be identical? Answer: The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is the nature of false attachment;
the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the nature of dependent origination; and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the nature of suchness (*tathatā*).

Since these three natures are each distinct, they are not non-different. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the School) states: "This dharma-gate of the three natures was taught by the Buddhas with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). All consciousnesses..."
Regarding the source of arising and the fundamental basis of the net of teachings: if one grasps them by identifying with them, one falls into ordinary, mundane views;

if one abandons them by distancing oneself from them, one loses the gateway to sagely wisdom. Therefore, Master Fazang, relying on the Huayan school, explained the meaning of the similarities and differences among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
First, the perfect realization of true suchness (*tathatā*) has two aspects: first, unchanging (*avikāra*), and second, conforming to conditions (*anuparivartin*).

The two meanings of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are: first, appearing as if it exists; second, being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). The two meanings of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are:
first, existing from the perspective of emotional attachment (*sattva-vidyamāna*); second, being non-existent from the perspective of principle (*tattva-abhāva*).

Because true suchness (*tathatā*) is unchanging, the dependent nature lacks intrinsic nature, and the imagined nature is non-existent in principle—by virtue of these three meanings, the three natures are one and the same limit. Furthermore, with respect to true suchness following conditions, the dependent nature appears to exist, while the imagined nature...

The nature of attachment exists. For these three reasons, there is likewise no difference [between them]. Therefore, the True permeates the derivative delusions, and the delusive reaches the source of the True;

essence and characteristics are mutually integrated, without obstruction or hindrance. Question: Are the "dependent [nature] appearing as existent" and so forth the same as the "existence of attachment" which is the object of grasping?
Answer: They are not different for two reasons. First, because that which is grasped by the grasping...
Because that which appears as real is [merely] appearance, there is no distinct phenomenon. Second, if one is separated from what is grasped, it does not arise even as an appearance;

the same applies to the true nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) according to conditions, because there is nothing to be grasped and no following of conditions. Furthermore, each of the three natures possesses two meanings.

Because they are not mutually contradictory, there is no difference in their nature. For instance, although the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) manifests as either defiled or pure according to conditions, it never loses its own nature of purity.
Precisely because it does not lose its own nature of purity, it is able to manifest as defiled or pure according to conditions.
It is like a bright mirror that reflects both the defiled and the pure, yet never loses the nature of the mirror itself.
It is luminous and pure. It is precisely because the mirror’s luminous purity is never lost that it is able to manifest the appearances of both defilement and purity.
Through the manifestation of defilement and purity, one knows the mirror’s luminous purity; through the mirror’s luminous purity, one knows the manifestation of defilement and purity.

Therefore, these two meanings are of a single nature. Although pure phenomena appear, they do not increase the mirror’s luminosity; although defiled phenomena appear, they do not pollute the mirror’s purity.
It is not merely that it is unstained; rather, it is by means of this that the clarity and purity of a mirror are manifested. True Suchness (tathatā) is likewise:

it is not merely that its immovable nature is pure and thus constitutes defilement and purity; rather, it is precisely through the manifestation of defilement and purity that its innate purity is revealed.

It is not merely that defilement and purity do not destroy one another; rather, they clarify the purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*). Furthermore, it is precisely because of this purity of nature that defilement and purity are established.
Therefore, these two meanings encompass each other in their entirety. Since the single nature is non-dual, how could they be contradictory?

Because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it can appear as if it exists; because it appears as if it exists, it is therefore without intrinsic nature. This is precisely what is meant by "lack of intrinsic nature."

This is precisely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Dependent origination is itself the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); this is the gateway to the non-dual Dharma (*advayadharmamukha*).
Within the nature of that which is grasped, although it appears to exist as one perceives it when one clings to it, according to the principle of reality, it is ultimately non-existent.

This is because one falsely imagines existence where there is no existence, just as one might falsely imagine a ghost upon a tree stump. Since this is now seen to be a false imagination, it is clearly understood that, in principle, it does not exist.
Therefore, there is no duality; it is of a single nature. Question: Is True Suchness (tathatā) existent? Answer: No.
Because it does not change while following conditions, and because the True Suchness of Emptiness is free from deluded thoughts. Question: Is True Suchness non-existent? Answer: No.
Because it is unchanging yet follows conditions; because it is not empty; and because it is the sphere of activity for noble wisdom. Question: Is suchness both existent and non-existent? Answer:
No, because it is of a non-dual nature and free from contradiction. Question: Is suchness neither existent nor non-existent? Answer:
Because it is endowed with dharmas and free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Question: Is the dependent nature (*paratantra*) existent?

Answer: No. Because dependent origination (*paratantra*) is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); because it is eliminated through contemplation; and because it is distinct from the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).
Question: Is the dependent nature non-existent? Answer: No. Because it is dependent origination that lacks intrinsic nature; because it can manifest the unarisen (*anutpāda*);

because it is distinct from the imagined nature (*parikalpita*); and because it is the object of wisdom (*jñāna*). Question: Is the dependent nature both existent and non-existent? Answer: No. Because it is non-dual (*advaya*).
Because it is the nature [of things]. Because it is free from contradiction. Question: Is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) neither existent nor non-existent?
Answer: No. Because there are many doors of meaning; because it is free from conceptual proliferation (prapañca). Question: Is the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) existent?

Answer: No. Because it is non-existent in principle; because it lacks essential characteristics (lakṣaṇa). Question: Is the imagined nature non-existent? Answer: No. Because it exists as a conventional appearance (yathābhāsa); because it is without marks (animitta).
Because it observes objects; because it can obscure the truth. Question: Is the parikalpita (the imagined nature) both existent and non-existent?
Answer: No, because it lacks a single intrinsic nature. Question: Is the parikalpita neither existent nor non-existent? Answer: No, because the nature of what is grasped is established.
The above concludes the protection against attachment. Now, regarding the faults incurred by such attachment: if one conceives of *tathatā* (suchness) as being exclusively...
If [the nature] were existent, there would be two faults: first, it would not follow conditions; second, it would not depend on a revealing cause (*vyañjanahetu*). Question:
The teaching states that *tathatā* (suchness) is eternally immutable. Since it does not follow conditions, is this not a fault? Answer:

When the Sage says that *tathatā* is immutable, this refers to the time when it follows conditions to manifest as defilement or purity; at that time, it constantly relies upon defilement and purity without ever losing its own essence.
The essence is precisely the permanence that is non-different from impermanence; it is called "inconceivable permanence.

This does not mean that it does not perform the functions of all phenomena, as the notion of "stagnant immutability" held by ordinary sentiment suggests. Because this permanence—which is non-different from impermanence—transcends such sentiment, it is called the "permanence of True Suchness" (*tathatā*).
As the Sūtra says, "Untainted yet tainted," which clarifies that the permanent acts as the impermanent; though tainted, [it remains untainted].
It is stained. When one clarifies that it is impermanent, it does not lose its constancy; nor is it an impermanence that differs from constancy.
Therefore, True Suchness (tathatā) is said to be impermanent. A sūtra states: "The Tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering and pleasure, and arises and ceases together with its causes.
Furthermore, based on this [garbha], there are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; thus, an impermanence that does not differ from constancy can also exist. It is not different.

The permanence of impermanence: through the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is precisely because impermanent phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) that they can constitute dependent origination.
Therefore, without departing from the nature of permanence, one attains impermanence; thus it is said to be "neither arising nor ceasing. This is the meaning of impermanence.
This, moreover, is the attainment of impermanence without differing from permanence. Furthermore, all dependent origination is itself [impermanence].
Nature is not the cessation of dependent origination; it is only when one speaks of the absence of nature that this is precisely the permanence that is no different from impermanence.
As the Sūtra says: "Form is itself emptiness; it is not that form ceases for there to be emptiness. Furthermore, "sentient beings are themselves nirvāṇa; they do not undergo further extinction."
This shares two meanings with True Suchness (*tathatā*). "True" and "conventional" are mutually fused such that they are two yet non-dual. Thus, the Treatise states:
"The obstruction of knowledge is profoundly blind and dark," which refers to the separate grasping of the true and the conventional as distinct.

Furthermore, if True Suchness did not follow conditions to manifest as defilement or purity, then dharmas such as defilement and purity would have no basis. Moreover, a dharma that exists without a basis would fall into [the error of] being a self-existent entity.
This is eternalism (*śāśvata*). Furthermore, if True Suchness (*tathatā*) were something that exists, it would not conform to defilement or purity;

since all phenomena of defilement and purity would then lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and True Suchness would likewise not conform to them, no existent phenomenon could be established—this too is nihilism (*uccheda*).

Even clinging to the four positions, such as "neither existent nor non-existent," all fall into the extremes of eternalism and nihilism. If one clings to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as being existent, this is called "already existing."

Because its essence does not rely on conditions, there is no dharma that exists without conditions; this is permanence (*śāśvata*). Furthermore, because one clings to existence, it does not rely on conditions;
because it does not rely on conditions, it cannot obtain the nature of a dharma; this is annihilation (*uccheda*). Question:
If the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) has the meaning of being existent, why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that the dependent nature is taken as existence? Answer:

This is precisely existence that is not different from emptiness. Because it lacks intrinsic nature due to its dependence on conditions, and because there is no agent within each individual condition, it is only through the non-activity of conditions that dependent origination is established. Therefore, this existence which is not [inherently] existent is "existence as other-dependent."

This is precisely the unmoving true limit (bhūtakoṭi) from which all phenomena are established. If one claims that the dependent nature exists as it is expressed by words, then it would be an existence that arises through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
If there were such an inherent nature in the conditions, they would not depend upon one another; because they would not depend on one another, the dependent nature would be destroyed.

That the dependent nature is destroyed is truly due to the attachment to existence. You fear falling into emptiness and thus establish existence, yet you do not realize that you have failed to understand.
Because phenomena arising from conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they would destroy dependent origination and thus fall into nihilism.

Furthermore, if one clings to the notion that the "other-dependent" (*paratantra*) does not exist, there are two faults: namely, if the other-dependent were a non-existent thing, then there would be nothing for conditions to give rise to.

If there were no phenomena, that would be nihilism. Question: If explaining dependent origination as empty and non-existent leads to the fallacy of nihilism, why does the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* extensively explain dependent origination as ultimate emptiness? Answer:
When the Noble Ones explain dependent origination as empty, this is an emptiness that is not different from existence; it is explained without displacing dependent origination itself.
This is the Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). If you claim that what is dependently originated is empty according to words alone, then there would be no dependent origination.

Since dependent origination would not exist, the principle of emptiness would likewise not exist. That the principle of emptiness is absent is precisely due to your attachment to emptiness. Therefore, your fear of falling into existence leads you to establish emptiness;

it is not because you fail to realize that dependently originated things lack intrinsic nature, nor because you lose the emptiness of intrinsic nature, that you instead fall back into the realm of conceptual clinging.
This is the erroneous grasping of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Thus, Bhāviveka refutes existence (*bhāva*) in order to establish it, while Dharmapāla refutes emptiness in order to establish it.

Just as the mental attachment to non-existence is the fault of nihilism (*uccheda*), if one were to say that a non-existent thing is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), then a non-existent thing would not be a condition (*pratyaya*);
and that which is not a condition is eternal (*nitya*). This applies even to the attachment to that which is neither existent nor non-existent.

All [of these views] result in the two faults of eternalism and nihilism. If one conceives of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as existing within the realm of pervasive conceptualization, then that which is illuminated by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) would logically not be empty;
this is precisely eternalism. If one falsely clings to the imagined nature as being non-existent in principle, one loses the conventional existence (*sattā*) of phenomena;
thus, this is nihilism. Even the position of "neither existent nor non-existent" possesses both of the aforementioned faults.

Having already explained the protection against errors, we shall now clarify its virtues. True Suchness (*tathatā*) has the sense of existence because it is the basis for both delusion and awakening, because it is not empty, and because it is indestructible.
True Suchness has the sense of emptiness because it is dependent upon conditions and because it stands in contrast to defilement.

Suchness has the meaning of both being and non-being, because it is endowed with all virtues, because it possesses mastery over both the adverse and the favorable, and because it is a seamless fusion.
Suchness has the meaning of neither being nor non-being, because it is neither dual nor non-dual, and because it cannot be apprehended through fixed grasping.

The dependent nature has the meaning of being, because it is established through conditions despite lacking intrinsic nature. The dependent nature has the meaning of non-being, because that which is established through conditions lacks intrinsic nature. The perfected nature...
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) has the meaning of being both existent and non-existent, because it is dependently originated and because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

The dependent nature has the meaning of being neither existent nor non-existent, because neither [of those two] can be apprehended when taken individually. The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) has the meaning of existence from the perspective of conventional cognition;

it has the meaning of non-existence from the perspective of ultimate principle; and it has the meaning of being both existent and non-existent, because it is that which is grasped as an object of attachment. The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)... [text continues].
The reckoning of "neither existence nor non-existence" is based on what is grasped; thus we know that grasping constitutes the two afflictions of annihilationism and eternalism.
Non-grasping constitutes the gateway to the nature’s virtues. It is merely the removal of deluded sentiment, not the dispatching of dharmas.

Therefore, one does not speak of the True apart from existence, for one perceives the ultimate limit of existence; nor does one contemplate dharmas by maintaining non-existence, for one realizes the nature of non-existence.
The true source does not emerge from existence or non-existence, nor does it reside within existence or non-existence. Why, then, harbor thoughts of acceptance or rejection?

This severs the delusions of what is to be determined. Thus, the three natures are one nature; though they exist through phenomenal emotion (*qing*), they are identical to true emptiness. One nature is the three natures;

though it is true suchness (*tathatā*), it is able to constitute dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Day after day there is existence, yet it is not existent; existence penetrates all the way to the source of emptiness.
Throughout the day, it is empty yet not empty; emptiness encompasses the limits of existence. Spontaneously, the single mind has no place of attachment; the myriad dharmas are all at rest.
When object and wisdom correspond, and principle and practice merge as one, only then does one enter the Mirror of the School (Zongjing).
Luminously pure and without flaw, it shatters the barriers of past and present, its light swallowing the ten thousand phenomena.
*Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only*, Scroll Eight;
*Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only*, Scroll Nine.
Verified by the Layman of Jintan, Wang Kentang.
If there are the three natures, how is it that the Blessed One said that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature?
This fifth verse explains the objection regarding the absence of intrinsic nature in three parts. First, restating the meaning and posing the question.
The verse says: "Based precisely upon these three natures... because it is always as its nature is, it is the true nature of consciousness-only.
This is the answer in two verses, namely Vasubandhu’s verses twenty-three through twenty-five.
However, the intended meaning of the answer lies solely in the first eight lines of the verse; the final four lines belong to the section on the Manifestation of the Nature of Consciousness-Only.
The Commentary states: Based on the three natures previously explained [up to this point], [the latter] would be confused with the second;

therefore, it is not discussed here. Third, the explanation of the meaning of the verse: based on the three self-natures (trisvabhāva) previously explained, the three kinds of non-self-nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) subsequently explained are established:

first, the non-self-nature of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā); second, the non-self-nature of arising (utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā); and third, the non-self-nature of the ultimate (paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā).

Regarding the nature of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): when the Blessed One spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, this does not mean that their nature is entirely non-existent.

What is the intended meaning? It is the expression "lack of nature," which is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). This is because, although they possess substantiality based on the dependent and perfected natures, [they lack intrinsic nature].
Yet foolish people falsely cling to a self and phenomena, falling into the error of reification; this very clinging is called "imaginary construction" (*parikalpita*).
To eliminate this clinging, one speaks of the "absence of nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) with respect to the non-existence of the imaginary within the existence of the dependent and the perfected.
Is it not the case that even the dependent and perfected natures lack intrinsic nature? How is it that those three [natures] are established based upon this? This is the question.

The passage beginning with "That is to say, based upon this" constitutes the answer. That is to say, based upon the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the absence of nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*) is taught.
Because their essential nature and characteristics are ultimately non-existent, like flowers in the sky or a snake upon a rope, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is established as follows:

The subject (*dharmin*) is that which is grasped by the nature of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it lacks the nature of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: because its essential nature and characteristics are ultimately non-existent. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is: like flowers in the sky. Thus, a verse from the *Avataṃsaka* states: "All things are empty and lack intrinsic nature; [they lack] characteristics..."

[The nature of] the deluded mind’s conceptualization [is the *parikalpita-svabhāva*]. Next, based on the *paratantra-svabhāva*, one establishes the "lack of intrinsic nature in terms of production" (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
This is because, like a magical illusion produced in dependence upon various conditions, it lacks that spontaneous nature which has been falsely grasped as existing since beginningless time.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows: The *paratantra* is the subject (*dharmin*); its thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is conventionally designated as lacking intrinsic nature, yet this does not mean its nature is entirely non-existent; this is the reason (*hetu*).
It is said: Because they arise dependent upon various conditions, and because of beginningless false attachment to an inherent nature, they are like illusory phenomena.

Thus, a verse from the *Avataṃsaka* says: "When observed according to reality, all things lack intrinsic nature. Subsequently, based on the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the superior absence of intrinsic nature is established;
that is to say, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which is so called because it is far removed from the aforementioned pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

Because of the grasping at the nature of a self and phenomena, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is established as follows: The subject (*dharmin*) is the perfected ultimate reality (*pariniṣpanna-paramārtha*).

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is conventionally designated as being without nature and not being a nature, and is entirely non-existent. The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is free from the aforementioned nature of a self and phenomena as they are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).
It is like space. Thus, a verse from the *Avataṃsaka* says: "Whether real or unreal, whether false or non-false, all are merely provisional designations for reality.
That which is non-false is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is the wisdom that accords with the perfected nature and achieves transcendence of the world;
these are all merely conventional names. Since even the 'real' is not ultimately real, how much more so the 'unreal'? The latter two natures are both said to be provisional."

When it is said that there is "no nature," this does not mean that nature is entirely non-existent; rather, it precisely reveals that the dependent and perfected natures do exist, yet the Buddha spoke of them as non-existent with intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣa*).
Since it is called "intentional meaning," then non-existence does not obstruct existence. Thus, existence and non-existence are mutually unobstructed;

they cancel each other out, and both delusions are simultaneously transcended, such that all things are entirely sovereign. How, then, is the principle of *dharmalakṣaṇa* (the characteristics of phenomena) any different from *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena)? Now, as for the dependent...

Its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) reveals the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is like the great empty space. Although it pervades all phenomena, it is revealed by the lack of intrinsic nature of those very phenomena.
This meaning correctly reveals that the perfected nature and the dependent nature (*paratantra*) are neither different nor non-different;

both are conventionally designated as being "without intrinsic nature. Question: Since the dependent and the perfected are neither different nor non-different, for what reason is the perfected nature called "perfected"?

Ultimate non-substantiality does not apply to the dependent nature in that way. Answer: Although the dependent nature is not the true ultimate nature, it may also be described as "ultimately non-substantial" from the perspective of the provisional teaching (*anuvartana-mukha*).

However, fearing confusion with the third [of the three natures], the truly ultimate reality, this is not stated here. Therefore, although the dependent nature is not the ultimate, it can nonetheless be described as the ultimate.
It is not non-existent; however, this is not stated here for fear of confusing it with the second [type of emptiness]. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 73, states:
"Question: Based on what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) did the Bhagavān say that all phenomena are unarisen, unceasing, and primordially quiescent?"
"Intrinsic nirvāṇa. Answer: "It is spoken thus based on the naturelessness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*). Question:
"Based upon what intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*) did the Blessed One say that all phenomena are equal to space? Answer: "Also based on the naturelessness of characteristics."
He spoke these words. Question: With what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) did the Blessed One say that all phenomena are like illusions and so forth? Answer:

He spoke these words with reference to the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), and the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of ultimate reality. Question:
With what underlying intention did the Blessed One say that one should regard form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*) as impermanent? Answer: With reference to...
Regarding the nature of the lack of self-nature in characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is said as follows: "Why is this?

Because one wishes to explain that the observation of permanence does not exist, one speaks of the observation of impermanence. Question: With what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) did the Blessed One say that one should observe form (*rūpa*) through to consciousness (*vijñāna*) as all being suffering (*duḥkha*)?
Answer: It was based on the nature of the lack of self-nature in production (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the nature of lack of intrinsic existence (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is stated as follows. This concludes the preceding explanation of the characteristics of consciousness.
This nature is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena; [it ranges] from the total negation that all phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic existence.

Next, the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) is explained, which is the interpretation of the latter four lines of the verse. The phrase "this nature" refers back to the word "nature" (*svabhāva*) in the final line of the verse, which states:
"by being far removed from the previously grasped nature of self and phenomena. This is because it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of all phenomena;
it is distinguished from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Regarding the four types of conventional truth, the first is the worldly convention (*loka-saṃvṛti*), also called the nominal (*prajñapti*).

1. The conventional truth of names (*nāma-saṃvṛti-satya*): This refers to things such as jars, basins, armies, and forests, which exist merely as provisional designations (*prajñapti*) but lack substantial reality (*dravya*).

2. The conventional truth of principles (*yukti-saṃvṛti-satya*), also called the conventional truth of differentiation according to phenomena: This refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), wherein dharmas such as the aggregates are established in accordance with their respective phenomena.

3. The conventional truth of realization (*adhigama-saṃvṛti-satya*), also called the conventional truth of establishment through skillful means (*upāya-prajñapti-satya*): This refers to the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*)...

The [truths] such as the outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth are established by way of realization with respect to suffering (*duḥkha*), its origin (*samudaya*), and so on; thus, they are called the "established conventional" (*prajñapti-saṃvṛti*).

They are also termed "provisional designations" (*prajñapti*) and "non-established truths" (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*). That is to say, the principle of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) is taught as the true nature (*tathatā*) based upon those gates of emptiness.

Because that true nature is the object of internally realized wisdom (*pratyātma-jñāna-gocara*) and cannot be expressed in words, it is called the "suchness of the two emptinesses" (*dvaya-śūnyatā-tathatā*); it is merely provisional.

Because it is so taught. Regarding the four types of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*): first is the worldly ultimate (*loka-paramārtha*), also called the truth of the manifestation of essence and function.

This refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), which possess substantial reality. Because they transcend the initial conventional level, they are called "ultimate.

Because they are designated according to the distinctions of phenomena as "aggregates" and so forth, they are called "manifestation. Second is the ultimate of reasoning (*yukti-paramārtha*), also called the differentiation of cause and effect...
The distinct truths refer to the distinctions in cause and effect regarding the knowledge, abandonment, realization, and cultivation of suffering, its origin, and so forth.
