Third, the extensive explanation of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). "When the bodhisattva reaches [the stage where] conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) appears"—this is the general explanation of the verse's meaning.
That is to say, if there were a cognition that, like an external object, conformed with suchness (*tathatā*), it would still involve apprehension (*upalabdhi*) and would not be a true realization.
At this stage, the bodhisattva has no apprehension whatsoever regarding either the objective referent (*ālambana*) or the subjective cognition (*jñāna*); they do not grasp them.
Because of the various characteristics of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), at that time one is said to truly abide in the true ultimate nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra-tathatā*).
This is the realization of *tathatā*. Wisdom and *tathatā* are equal and identical. What is meant by "equal and identical"?
It means that both the realizing wisdom and the realized *tathatā* are devoid of the characteristics of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*). Furthermore, the former does not grasp...
"Free from the various characteristics of the grasper (*grāhaka*) refers to being free from the grasped (*grāhya*);
therefore, it is said that the characteristics of both grasper and grasped are equally manifestations of the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the mind that perceives existence.

Regarding the passage beginning "There is another interpretation," there are three masters' views concerning the existence or non-existence of the characteristic and the seeing aspects. The first master says: "In this wisdom, both the characteristic and the seeing aspects are non-existent."*

It is taught that there are no characteristics of the apprehended (*grāhya*) or the apprehender (*grāhaka*). The second master refutes this position and establishes that both the characteristic (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*) divisions exist. First, he refutes the absence of characteristics (*animitta*):

if, upon a cognition, there were no characteristic such as "thusness" (*tathatā*) yet it could still take thusness as its object, then a cognition of form (*rūpa*), etc., which lacks characteristics such as sound, etc., would likewise have to take sound, etc., as its object; it would then be called a "cognition of sound," etc.
Next, the view of non-perception (*nirābhāsa*) is refuted: if wisdom lacked a perceptual portion (*darśana-bhāga*), it would be unable to take an object;

how then could it take suchness (*tathatā*) as its object? If one were to claim that it can take an object despite lacking a perceptual portion, then even insentient true suchness would be a perceiving subject.

Therefore, one must admit that this [wisdom] definitely possesses a perceptual portion. Third is the correct doctrine of Dharmapāla, which establishes that the perceptual portion exists while the objective portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) does not.

Regarding "grasping at the signless" (*animitta-grāha*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga), fascicle 73, asks: "Grasping at signs is commonly established in the world; grasping at the signless is not so established.
For what cause and for what reason is it called 'grasping at the signless'? It would be unreasonable for there to be no cause and no condition. The answer is:
"Grasping that results from the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of conventional designations (*vyavahāra*) is grasping at signs. That which is common to the world..."
That which is co-arisen, which causes defilement, and which takes up the fruit through the perfuming of ultimate wisdom and vision, is the grasping of signlessness;
it is not something co-arisen. That which brings about purification is therefore distinct from these two. Thus, these two possess causes and conditions:
just as when the eye has defects such as cataracts, the appearance of signs such as floating hairs or whirling nets becomes perceptible before one, yet if those [defects] are absent...
If there were affliction, it would be unattainable; there would only be intrinsic nature, without erroneous grasping. Question:

Regarding the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*), if one grasps its signs, that is not the grasping of the signless. If there is nothing to be grasped, then the grasping of the signless cannot be established either.

If that is so, why is it called "signless grasping"? Answer: Because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of verbal expression have been abandoned. Although this grasping still grasps the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*), because it does not grasp signs, it constitutes signless grasping. Question: If there is no apprehension (*upalabdhi*), how can there be grasping? Answer: Grasping occurs by way of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Just as one might say, "I grasp this form," yet there is no actual apprehension of a self-nature (*svabhāva*) therein; so too, although one says "I grasp the signless," there is no grasping of signs. Therefore, it is established as signless grasping. Furthermore, regarding the statement "the signless is the object of the path": this refers to the fact that the signless is the object of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). It is not that the signless is the object of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its object. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not an object for the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the object of the path of cultivation, it is said to be the object of the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its object. Furthermore, the signless is the object of the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its object. As for the statement "the signless is the fruit of the path": this means that the signless is the fruit of the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the fruit of the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its fruit. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not the fruit of the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the fruit of the path of cultivation, it is said to be the fruit of the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its fruit. Furthermore, the signless is the fruit of the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its fruit. As for the statement "the signless is the domain of the path": this means that the signless is the domain of the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the domain of the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its domain. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not the domain of the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the domain of the path of cultivation, it is said to be the domain of the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its domain. Furthermore, the signless is the domain of the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its domain. As for the statement "the signless is the support of the path": this means that the signless is the support of the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the support of the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its support. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not the support of the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the support of the path of cultivation, it is said to be the support of the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its support. Furthermore, the signless is the support of the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its support. As for the statement "the signless is the cause of the path": this means that the signless is the cause of the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the cause of the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its cause. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not the cause of the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the cause of the path of cultivation, it is said to be the cause of the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its cause. Furthermore, the signless is the cause of the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its cause. As for the statement "the signless is the basis of the path": this means that the signless is the basis of the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the basis of the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its basis. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not the basis of the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the basis of the path of cultivation, it is said to be the basis of the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its basis. Furthermore, the signless is the basis of the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its basis. As for the statement "the signless is the condition of the path": this means that the signless is the condition of the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the condition of the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its condition. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not the condition of the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the condition of the path of cultivation, it is said to be the condition of the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its condition. Furthermore, the signless is the condition of the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its condition. As for the statement "the signless is the attainment of the path": this means that the signless is the attainment of the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the attainment of the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its attainment. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not the attainment of the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the attainment of the path of cultivation, it is said to be the attainment of the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its attainment. Furthermore, the signless is the attainment of the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its attainment. As for the statement "the signless is the realization of the path": this means that the signless is the realization of the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the realization of the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its realization. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not the realization of the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the realization of the path of cultivation, it is said to be the realization of the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its realization. Furthermore, the signless is the realization of the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its realization. As for the statement "the signless is the entry into the path": this means that the signless is the entry into the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the entry into the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its entry. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not the entry into the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the entry into the path of cultivation, it is said to be the entry into the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its entry. Furthermore, the signless is the entry into the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its entry. As for the statement "the signless is the progress of the path": this means that the signless is the progress of the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the progress of the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its progress. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not the progress of the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the progress of the path of cultivation, it is said to be the progress of the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its progress. Furthermore, the signless is the progress of the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its progress. As for the statement "the signless is the completion of the path": this means that the signless is the completion of the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the completion of the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing has the Four Noble Truths as its completion. Since the signless is the cessation of all signs, it is not the completion of the path of seeing. However, because the signless is the completion of the path of cultivation, it is said to be the completion of the path. This is because the path of cultivation takes the cessation of signs as its completion. Furthermore, the signless is the completion of the path because the path of cultivation takes the signless as its completion. As for the statement "the signless is the perfection of the path": this means that the signless is the perfection of the path of cultivation. It is not that the signless is the perfection of the path of seeing. Why? Because the path of seeing

How is grasping established? Answer: Although there is no actual apprehension and no conceptual augmentation of the various distinct characteristics, grasping is nonetheless established because it is characterized by the absence of signs (*animitta*).
Question: If there is neither apprehension nor conceptual augmentation, what is the nature of this grasping?
How is this to be known? Answer: Because it grasps the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and because it grasps the signless (*animitta*).

The five kinds of objective characteristics (*nimitta*) can all be manifested as its signs. Question: If it is established as "grasping" despite not being clearly distinct, why is the cessation and non-existence of all graspings not likewise reckoned as such?
Answer: Because cessation and non-existence lack the sense of purposeful cultivation (*bhāvanā*); they are not that upon which the practitioner of meditation relies.
There is nothing to be cultivated or performed in cessation. Question: If that is so, how is its characteristic realized and known? Answer:

It is realized and known by the wisdom of internal personal realization (*pratyātma-vedya-jñāna*). Question: If that is so, why is it not explained in accordance with what has been realized? Answer: [Because it is ineffable.]

This is what is realized internally; it is not a locus for the establishment of conventional designations. What is meant here by "speaking of the apprehension of the signless" is that one does not apprehend signs.
This refers to the passage in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* beginning with "Although there is the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*)... which represents the Master’s own position.

Dharmapāla clarifies that this object-condition (*ālambana*) is suchness (*tathatā*), and that while the seeing and the image (*nimitta-bhāga*) are not fixed, the image-aspect is directly realized as the essence of suchness by fundamental wisdom.

Because it does not grasp at signs (*nimitta*), and because it is in profound union with the essence of suchness (*tathatā*), it is the sign of signlessness; it is the sign of having only the essential nature as its sign.
This is the meaning of "carrying along," and it is also the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). An objection states: if there is a seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), [how can this be so?]

If there are thus characteristics of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), how can they be called "characteristics of non-conceptualization" (*nirvikalpa*)? Furthermore, it is said that there is no "apprehending subject" (*grāhaka*). The answer is:
although the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) exists, it is devoid of conceptualization; moreover, there is no apprehending subject.

Because correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, directly embracing and adhering to its essential nature, there are no further marks of phenomenal characteristics; therefore, it is said to lack the "objective part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) and to lack an "apprehending subject."
This is because one would then be falsely grasping at a real subject of cognition (*grāhaka*) through non-conceptualization.

How could there not be an internal factor, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), which acts as the cognitive faculty? Furthermore, it is objected: "If you say there is no image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* states:

'Because it arises depending on that [object] and bears its image, it is called the objective condition (*ālambana-nimitta*). Since there is no image-part, there should likewise be no object of cognition. Dharmapāla answers:

It is said: There is also the sense of an "object-condition" (ālambanapratyaya). Although there is no objective aspect (nimittabhāga), it can be said that this wisdom arises bearing the likeness of suchness (tathatā), because the cognizing wisdom does not depart from suchness.
That is to say, the seeing-portion (darśanabhāga) of the fundamental wisdom arises by directly grasping the essence and characteristics of true suchness;
this is termed the object-condition. It is like when the self-witnessing portion (svasaṃvittibhāga) takes the seeing-portion as its object, it directly bears the seeing-portion [within itself].

The portion [of consciousness] that is designated as the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya) should likewise be understood in this way. In reality, there is no sense of "transforming and carrying over" (pariṇāma-ādāna);

rather, it is only by "clamping and carrying over" (upādāna) that it is called the object-condition. Therefore, it differs from the subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna). If [the consciousness] were to take an objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) as its transformation, it would not be a direct realization;

it would be just like the subsequently attained wisdom, which possesses conceptualization (vikalpa). Since it is distinct from the subsequently attained wisdom, it is clearly known that the "seeing-part" (darśana-bhāga) exists.

This is the division of the aspectless (nirnimitta-bhāga). The Saṃmitīya school of the Hīnayāna established the doctrine of the aspect-possessor (sanimitta-vādins) and composed the *Mahāyānaparivartaśāstra* in seven hundred verses to slander the Mahāyāna.
It refutes the meaning of the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) held by the ancient Mahāyāna masters, stating:

"If you say that your own aspect is the aspect-possessor and serves as the object-condition, then consider, for instance, how in your Mahāyāna school, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) takes reality (*tattva*) as its object."

At that time, if True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not possess an objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), then with respect to the seeing aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of the cognizing wisdom, True Suchness would lack the status of being an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
If you insist that even when fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) takes True Suchness as its object, it must also possess an objective aspect, this contradicts your own school’s tenets;
how then can you reconcile this with all the sūtras and śāstras? This single objection was leveled against the ancient Mahāyāna masters.
At that time, [the opponent] offered no defense. Tripitaka Master Ci’en (Xuanzang) defended it, saying: "In our Mahāyāna school, 'bringing along' (*dai*) has two meanings:

first, 'transformative bringing along' (*bian dai*); second, 'concomitant bringing along' (*xie dai*). If it is transformative bringing along, then it means that the self-characteristic of the semblance is brought along through transformation;

this is the characteristic of the mental image (*nimitta*). Such an image ceases to exist when fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object. If it is concomitant bringing along..."
There is thus fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) which directly grasps and takes the essence and characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness) as its object;

because it does not further transform into an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), it also constitutes a condition as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Regarding the passage "Immediately following the preparatory stage" (*prayoga-anantaram*), this explains the name of the stage. Question:

Why is this stage called "penetration" (*prativedha*)? Answer: Because at the time this wisdom arises within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) following the preparatory stage, one realizes and experiences *tathatā*.

It remains as it was before. What is called "this wisdom" is none other than non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). "Essence" (*ti*) means penetration; "realization" (*hui*) means thorough understanding.
When principle transcends deluded emotions, it is termed "True" (*zhen*); when the essence of all phenomena is identical, it is designated as "Suchness" (*tathatā*).

To illuminate this principle is called "seeing"; seeing is itself the Path (*mārga*). As for the mention of "the beginning," there should be an objection here: if illuminating the principle is called "seeing," [how can there be a beginning?]
From the second bhūmi upward, do they not also illuminate the principle? Therefore, the present commentary explains: because this is the very first [instance], it receives this name;
the others follow according to their specific meanings.
Now, this path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is briefly explained as being of two kinds (up to: that which is able to exhaustively bring benefit and happiness to all beings in the future.
III. Detailed Explanation of the Path of Seeing. Now, this path of seeing is briefly of two types. [This is] the general heading. First, the True Path of Seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*).
Below, there is the specific explanation of the distinctions between the two paths of seeing. That is to say: if it is the single-moment True Path of Seeing, or the three-moment Path of Seeing...

Regarding the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*): if there is the true path of seeing consisting of three moments of mind, or the path of seeing characterized by sixteen moments of mind, what is the single-moment true path of seeing?

It refers to the arising of the wisdom of the twofold emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā-jñāna*). Within the preceding path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), it simultaneously abandons the seeds of the two obstacles of conceptualized self and phenomena (*parikalpita-ātma-dharma-āvaraṇa*).
Within the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), it simultaneously realizes that which is manifested by the twofold emptiness of conceptualized self and phenomena.

*Tathatā*. Question: Since the preparatory (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), liberation (*vimukti*), and special progress (*viśeṣa*) [moments] consist of many *kṣaṇas*, why is it said that a single mind is called the "True Path of Seeing" (*darśanamārga*)?
Answer: Although they consist of many *kṣaṇas* until the task is finally completed, they all collectively constitute a single path of seeing characterized by one aspect (*ekalakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*);
therefore, they are designated as a single mind. As for the statement that they consist of many *kṣaṇas*, this refers to this single-mind path of seeing.

Because it includes the fruit immediately preceding [the path], the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and all superior paths (*viśeṣa-mārga*), there are many moments in between (one moment of cultivation in the stage of preparation, one moment of vision in the uninterrupted path, one moment of entry in the superior path, and one moment of realization in the path of liberation; thus, there are many moments).

One master says: "In this stage, there is gradual abandonment and gradual realization. Grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is coarse and superficial, whereas grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is deep and subtle. It is necessary...
First, one severs the grasping at a self; having realized the emptiness of persons, one subsequently severs the grasping at phenomena and realizes the emptiness of phenomena.

Thus, it is known that there is gradual severance and gradual realization. One master says: "In this stage, there is sudden severance and sudden realization, because during the preparatory stage, the aspirational intention is so sublime that one necessarily desires to cut through everything all at once.
This interpretation is correct. What is meant by the three minds of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*)?

The path of seeing through characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*) refers to attaining the path of seeing by specifically taking the characteristics of all phenomena pertaining to sentient beings as one's object;

thus it is called the path of seeing through characteristics. This, in turn, is twofold. First, there is the threefold mental state that contemplates the non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
The non-established truth is suchness (*tathatā*). That is to say, by means of a wisdom-mind of three grades, one contemplates suchness and thereby attains the path of seeing.

Therefore, what are the three categories? First, the wisdom that internally dispels the conceptual object of sentient beings. "Internally" refers to one's own body; "conceptual" (or "provisional") means lacking intrinsic substance.

This refers to the wisdom capable of dispelling [delusion], which looks back upon the self-mastery grasped within one's own body and sees that it is not truly existent, but merely appears as a sentient being due to the internal mind.
This emulates the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), which severs the notion of a self.
[This refers to] grasping. Second, regarding the wisdom that internally dispels the provisional nature of all phenomena: "all phenomena" refers to the substantial dharmas of the five aggregates.
Furthermore, by means of the wisdom that can dispel them, one observes that the substantial dharmas of the five aggregates grasped within one's own body are likewise unattainable.

This simulates the severing of attachment to dharmas through the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*). Third, universally dispelling [attachment to] all sentient beings...
The wisdom that understands all phenomena as dependently originated refers to the comprehensive observation of all phenomena pertaining to sentient beings.

This follows the "seeing division" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), wherein both the dual attachments to self and phenomena are severed, and both the dual emptinesses of self and phenomena are realized.

Because these three types of wisdom sever [the obstacles] individually and realize them collectively, the two obstacles of persons and phenomena are each divided into upper and lower levels according to their coarseness.

The coarse is superior, while the subtle is inferior. Together they constitute four categories. However, as for the two coarse [levels], each is eliminated separately because wisdom is still weak and has not yet severed both simultaneously.
Only when wisdom reaches the upper grade can it sever both at once; thus, these are designated as "weak" (mṛdu) and so forth according to the level of wisdom.
"Weak" means inferior; the initial wisdom is called weak, the subsequent wisdom is called middling, and that which surpasses the former is called superior.
The inferior comes first; that which arises later is called "superior," as it is able to sever the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). This wisdom is the most supreme.

However, the first two types of wisdom have not yet attained excellence, as they specifically take the internal body as their object and eliminate the provisional designations of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-prajñapti*). At the time of the third moment of mind, that wisdom becomes of the highest grade (*adhimātra*).
They differ in three ways because they take as their objects, respectively, the internal and external, whether as the self (*ātman*) or as phenomena (*dharma*).

The first two are called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*) because they take each individual phenomenon of sentient beings as their respective object. The third is called "subsequent knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*) because it takes them collectively and in general, being similar in nature to the preceding two knowledges.
"Phenomenon" (*dharma*) has the meaning of emulation and study. Question: Within the Path of True Seeing (*darśanamārga*), are there both the aspect (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*)?
[The path of seeing] has two parts. Why, then, do you speak only of the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) of the *dharmatā-satyadarśana-mārga* (the true path of seeing reality)? Answer:

Although within the true path of seeing there are the self-witnessing aspects (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the two types of emptiness, it is the perceiving aspect that directly takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object; therefore, it is designated as "Dharma" (reality).

Furthermore, within the perceiving aspect, there are the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). According to the specific obstacles being abandoned, there are four perceiving aspects: those belonging to the uninterrupted paths.

Because the abandonment of delusions is distinct, the two views regarding persons and phenomena are divided; by distinguishing each phenomenon separately, the first two moments of mind are established.

Within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), because the realization of principle is identical, the two views regarding persons and phenomena are combined with the phenomena as a whole, and thus the third moment of mind is established.

Therefore, the treatise says: "Established through both the general and the specific, it is called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in terms of name and characteristic. Question: What is the true path of seeing (*tattva-darśana-mārga*) consisting of the three dharmas? Answer: The former three [moments].
The mind is said to be the true vision (*darśana-mārga*). Question: Based on what principle is it further said to be the true [vision]? Answer:

Because the path of vision with signs (*sanimitta-darśana-mārga*) takes the four truths as its object, whereas this [present one] does not take them as its object, it is the true vision-path. This is the same as the first meaning mentioned above; however, the treatise considers the latter meaning to be correct. Question:

What are the characteristics of the sixteen moments of the path of vision? Answer: They are the four [moments] regarding suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*).
Beneath each of the truths (satya), there are four minds; thus, they constitute sixteen. The "established truth" (vyavasthāna-satya) is precisely the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).

This, in turn, has two aspects. First, based on the distinction between the grasped object (grāhya) and the grasping subject (grāhaka), one separately establishes sixteen types of mind consisting of phenomena (dharma) and categories (prakāra).
What is called the "grasped object" is suchness (tathatā); what is called the "grasping subject" is correct wisdom (samyag-jñāna). "Phenomena" refers to present phenomena.

"Category" (*jāti*) refers to the class [of cognition]. That is to say, the Dharma-knowledge and Dharma-patience take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their object; this True Suchness is that which is apprehended by knowledge.
Category-patience and category-knowledge take the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) of that knowledge as their object; this seeing-part is the knowledge that performs the act of apprehension.

Therefore, these are called the sixteen moments of mind consisting of the apprehending and the apprehended. Question: What are the four moments? Answer: First, the Dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).

1. Receptivity to the Dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*). 2. Dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*). 3. Receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*). 4. Subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*). The remaining three truths are to be understood by analogy with this.

Regarding "receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering": "suffering" refers to the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). "Dharma" refers to the teachings that arise based upon the predominance of the truth of suffering.

"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the wisdom that takes the dharmas of suffering as its object during the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*). "Receptivity" (*kṣānti*) refers to the preliminary investigation [of those dharmas].
By the power of this superior influence, one gives rise to uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that directly realizes the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

By means of this wisdom, one permanently abandons all afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; this is the cause of knowledge (*jñāna*). This "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti*) is the patience immediately preceding knowledge;
it is able to contemplate the suchness (*tathatā*) underlying the Truth of Suffering and is able to sever the [afflictions] of the three realms to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.

The twenty-eight types of *anuśaya* (latent tendencies) to be abandoned are as follows: there are ten in the suffering of the desire realm; there are nine each in the suffering of the two upper realms, because hatred (*pratigha*) is excluded from them.
Thus, combined across the three realms, there are twenty-eight. Regarding "the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*): "dharma" refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) of suffering;
the wisdom that takes this suchness of suffering as its object is called the knowledge of the dharma of suffering. "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the fruit of "patience" (*kṣānti*). By means of...
Because of the preceding patience (*kṣānti*), this wisdom (*jñāna*) manifests. When this wisdom manifests, one contemplates *tathatā* (suchness) and realizes the aforementioned liberation.

Question: The "dharma of suffering" mentioned previously was explained as the teaching (*deśanā-dharma*); the "dharma of suffering" mentioned now is explained as the suchness of suffering (*duḥkha-tathatā*). Is there not reason for doubt? Answer:
The teaching that expresses and the suchness that is expressed are both termed "dharma" when taken together. Initially, wisdom takes the teaching as its object.
Now, since wisdom takes suchness as its object, how could there be any doubt? Regarding the "subsequent knowledge of patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*):

this refers to the arising of untainted wisdom immediately following the "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), and so forth. The intended meaning is that these three moments of mind, within a single instant, each internally realize their respective *dharma-patiences* and *dharma-knowledges*;
that is, one realizes the *dharma-patiences* by means of the subsequent patiences (*anvaya-kṣānti*), and realizes the *dharma-knowledges* by means of the subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Regarding the statement that "all subsequent noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) are of this same category," it means that subsequent noble dharmas depend upon preceding dharmas.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "Because the preceding serves as the basis for each subsequent one.

This refers to how, after the two [initial] minds, all subsequent noble dharmas up to those of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) arise by depending upon these two minds. As for the "knowledge of the categories of the four sufferings" (*duḥkha-prakāra-jñāna*), this...
Wisdom takes only the third, the *duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*, as its object. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"Because it is internally realized and confirmed within the *duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*, it is called *duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*.

Just as there are two knowledges regarding the truth of suffering, one should know that it is likewise for the remaining truths. Thus, taken together, there are sixteen knowledges, all of which sever the twenty-eight factors.
These sixteen moments of mind are distinct from the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). Of these, the first two observe suchness (*tathatā*), while the latter two observe knowledge (*jñāna*).

Specifically, the Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) and Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) observe suchness because they awaken to the grasped object (*grāhya*). The Subsequent Patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and Subsequent Knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) observe knowledge because they awaken to the grasper subject (*grāhaka*).
As it is with the one truth, so it is with all the remaining truths. Question: Are there distinctions among these sixteen moments of mind? Answer: There are two kinds:
the sixteen moments of mind consisting of the grasper and the grasped, and the sixteen moments of mind regarding the objects of the higher and lower truths.

Question: What are the sixteen moments of mind consisting of the grasper and the grasped? Answer: Dharma-knowledge and dharma-patience take True Suchness (tathatā) as their object; that which is True Suchness is wisdom itself.

The objects of apprehension (*grāhya*) consist of the receptivities (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) of the categories [of the truths], which take the wisdom-aspect (*jñānabhāga*) as their object. As for this wisdom-aspect, it is the apprehending wisdom (*grāhakajñāna*);

these are termed the sixteen moments of mind consisting of the apprehended and the apprehender. The receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, emulating the wisdom-aspect of the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) within the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and thereby abandons the afflictions of the truth of suffering. The dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) takes suchness as its object, emulating the true path of seeing.
The seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the middle path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) realizes the principle underlying the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

The "patience of subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) takes as its object the seeing aspect of the preceding simulative mind; it simulates the seeing aspect of the self-witnessing consciousness (*svasaṃvitti*) of the first mind, which is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*). Subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna*) takes as its object the preceding seeing aspect;
it simulates the seeing aspect of the self-witnessing consciousness of the second mind, which is the path of liberation. This applies likewise to the three truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path.

Follow this pattern. Question: Regarding the sixteen moments of mind of the lower and upper truths (*satya*). Answer: Dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) and Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) take the suchness (*tathatā*) of the lower realm as their object;

Subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and Subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) take the suchness of the upper realm as their object. Because entering into the vision of the lower realm is manifested, it is called "Dharma" (*dharma*);

that of the upper realm is called "Subsequent" (*anvaya*). These are the sixteen moments of mind regarding the objects of the lower and upper truths. The Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) is called "lower"; it is the realm currently manifest. The Form [Realm]...

The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is called "superior" (*ūrdhva*); it is the non-manifest realm. As for the sixteen moments of mind: this refers to the establishment of eight types—namely, the Dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*) and Dharma-knowledge (*dharmanirvedha*)—by contemplating the Four Noble Truths of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, by contemplating the Four Noble Truths of the two higher realms, eight types—the Subsequent Patience (*anvayakṣānti*) and Subsequent Knowledge (*anvayanirvedha*)—are established.
However, the treatise cites only the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) of the desire realm as the "Dharma" [for these patiences]. This is the first: Full Comprehension (*abhisamaya*).

*Kṣānti* (receptivity) is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*). The two types of knowledge of clear realization (*abhisamaya-jñāna*) are the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Regarding "the true path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) of the dharmas as appropriate":

this means that *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* takes the suchness (*tathatā*) of the desire realm as its object, emulating the seeing-portion of the path of uninterrupted transition within the true path of vision, and thereby abandons the afflictions of the desire realm.
*Duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* takes the suchness of the desire realm as its object, emulating the true path of vision.

The seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the middle path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) realizes the principle of the desire realm. The subsequent-knowledge-acceptance (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) takes the suchness (*tathatā*) of the two higher realms as its object;

imitating the seeing aspect of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), it abandons the afflictions of the higher realms. Subsequent-knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) takes the suchness of the higher realms as its object;

imitating the seeing aspect of the path of liberation, it realizes the principle of the higher realms. The remaining three truths are to be understood accordingly. This does not mention the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvedana*).

Regarding "division": this contemplation is performed after the preceding sixteen moments of mind; because the contemplation becomes progressively coarser, it is said that the wisdom of contemplation is the self-realization of phenomena (*dharma-svayaṃvedana*).
Since one does not contemplate wisdom itself, it is not included as a phenomenon. As for the number "one hundred and twelve":
there are forty [mental factors] for the Four Truths of the Desire Realm; for the Four Truths of each of the two upper realms, anger is excluded, thus reducing the number of truths by eight.
8. Thus, there are one hundred and twelve. Question: What are the three minds of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*)? Answer:

The wisdom that internally dispels the provisional designation of sentient beings (*sattva-prajñapti*) follows the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) to sever the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).

The wisdom that internally dispels the provisional designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*) follows the seeing-portion of the uninterrupted path to sever the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). These two distinct objects of focus are termed "phenomena" (*dharma*). [The wisdom] universally dispels existence...

The wisdom that cognizes all phenomena as being conventionally dependent on conditions imitates the "seeing portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the two kinds of emptiness within the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), thereby realizing the principle of the two kinds of emptiness.

This single, collective objectification is termed "categorical" (*anvaya*). Question: By what principle are these three [the Path of Seeing, the Path of Cultivation, and the Path of No-More-Learning] called "true"?

Answer: If these three were truly real, they would not be described as "imitating" the Dharma; rather, they would be fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) that individually severs and collectively realizes [the truths]. Question: What is the true seeing within a single mind?

Question: When the wisdom of the double emptiness arises, one simultaneously abandons the two obstacles within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and simultaneously realizes the two emptinesses within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Question: Both types of sixteen [aspects] belong to the Hīnayāna dharma; for what reason do Bodhisattvas also practice them? Answer:
This is explained in reference to the cultivation and practice of Bodhisattvas. It is for the sake of subduing those of the Two Vehicles that they cultivate and perfect the universal [knowledge].

Because it is known [as such], one must indeed cultivate that [path of seeing]. However, when other sources speak of nine types of mind regarding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and do not mention sixteen, this too is established based on the distinctions of the four noble truths as previously mentioned.
As for the sixteen types, there are sixteen prior to the established truths (*vyavasthāpanasatya*) and sixteen subsequent to them; thus, in these two successive sets, there are ten [instances] each.

There are six types. What are the nine types of mind? They refer to the patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) regarding both the phenomena (*dharma*) and their categories (*anvaya*) for each truth.

Since there are these four minds within each truth, there are sixteen (four times four). Now, when they are combined and explained, the patience regarding the phenomena is subsumed under the patience regarding the categories.

Furthermore, when conventional knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) is combined with subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), within each of the Four Noble Truths there is respectively only one patience (*kṣānti*) and only one knowledge (*jñāna*).

Therefore, it is said that patience and knowledge each have four contemplations (*vipaśyanā*), which constitute eight moments of mind (*citta*). Since there must be calm abiding (*śamatha*) wherever there is contemplation, these eight instances of calm abiding are collectively counted as one;

thus, there are nine types of mind. Question: In the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), calm abiding and contemplation are practiced in union (*yuganaddha*). Why, then, is there [only] contemplation...?

There are eight [aspects]. Is cessation (śamatha) only one? Answer: Although within the path of seeing (darśanamārga) both cessation and insight (vipaśyanā) operate in tandem, the primary objective of the path of seeing is the realization of the meaning [of the truths].
Since insight accords with this realization of the meaning, it is divided into eight; since cessation does not itself constitute the realization of the meaning, it is combined into one.
Below the various aspects of the path of seeing, there is a detailed analysis through various gates. First is the gate of the conventional and the real, which refers to the path of seeing by aspects.
Because it is established as a designation based upon the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). What is meant by "designation"?

It means that the path of seeing in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇadarśanamārga*) arises immediately after the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), up to the point where it is able to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of conceptualization;

yet no substantial entity exists that can act in this way. By giving rise to three types of mind regarding the non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhitasatya*), one is able to suppress the afflictions of conceptualization.

Regarding "sleep": one immediately gives rise to sixteen types of mental states within the context of the established truths (vyavasthāna-satya), examining them with precise scrutiny so that afflictions (kleśa) no longer arise.
At the stage of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) arises, which is capable of severing the latent tendencies of conceptualization (vikalpa-anuśaya).

This does not mean that the subsequent realization of the path of seeing (ākāra-darśana-mārga) only occurs after the true path of seeing (tattva-darśana-mārga). If one were to claim that it occurs after the true path of seeing...

If it is only upon the arising of the *prṣṭhalabdha-lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga* (the subsequently attained path of seeing) that one acts, is it not the case that one first suppresses the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) after having already severed them?
For the latent dispositions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-anuśaya*) have already been completely severed at the time of the *tattvadarśana-mārga* (the path of seeing reality). Question:

Since the two paths of seeing proceed together without contradiction, why does the verse state only that "there is nothing whatsoever to be obtained," without mentioning this [subsequent suppression]? Answer: The former... [text fragment]

The true path of seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*) realizes the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). Subsequently, the path of seeing with images (*sākāradarśanamārga*) realizes the characteristics of consciousness-only. Between these two paths, the former is superior;
therefore, the verse speaks of it specifically. The meaning of this verse is that for one who abides in consciousness-only, it is the nature (*svabhāva*) and not the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, this is a partial explanation. Regarding the two gates of wisdom: the true path of seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*) is fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*), which directly destroys the ignorance that deludes one regarding the principle (*dharmatā*).
The image path of seeing (*nimittadarśanamārga*) is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdhajñāna*); it lacks the power to destroy the ignorance that deludes one regarding the principle.
Furthermore, it is also able to destroy the ignorance of deluded phenomena; therefore, both [types of] the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are subsumed under two types of wisdom (*jñāna*). Question:

Do all subsequently attained wisdoms (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) possess the two aspects of the objective image (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective vision (*darśanabhāga*)? The position of the first master is that both the image and the vision are absent, because they are free from the dual grasping of subject and object (*grāhyagrāhaka*).
The position of the second master is that the vision exists while the image is absent; this is because subsequently attained wisdom possesses conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, the seeing [aspect] exists because it directly illuminates the object; the aspect [of the grasped] does not exist, yet it is not that the seeing-portion is non-existent.
As for the statement that it is "free from the two graspings," this is merely because there is no clinging. The third, the correct position, is that both portions exist.

Because the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) does not directly perceive suchness, it is said that "the true nature of suchness is not seen"; however, it constantly contemplates that which resembles suchness.
Is the contemplation of the characteristic of suchness not its seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*)? Is that which resembles the characteristic of *tathatā* not its image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*)?

Furthermore, within the holy teachings, it is said that subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) discriminates the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, observes the differences in the faculties and natures of sentient beings, and thereby preaches the Dharma.
It is also said that this wisdom manifests bodies, lands, and so forth, and preaches for the sake of sentient beings.

Because it is the True Dharma (*saddharma*). If it did not manifest as something resembling form (*rūpa*), how could it manifest the bodies and lands? If it did not manifest as something resembling sound (*śabda*), how could there be such matters as preaching the Dharma?
One might raise the objection: "In the state of the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has already been transformed;

therefore, it should not again manifest forms such as bodies and lands. To this, the commentary replies: "Just as after the basis of the aggregate of form has been transformed, [form] no longer appears..."

Regarding the matter of the body, the land, and other forms: if these were also to transform by shifting the basis of the four aggregates such that there were no longer feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, would the state of Buddhahood then be identical to an ordinary stone?

Furthermore, if this wisdom did not take as its object a transformation resembling sound and form based upon its own essential substance, then when it perceives form, it should likewise perceive sound and so forth, because it would be devoid of its own [specific] nature.

Because non-substantial phenomena (*avastu*) serve as the objects of cognition. Furthermore, if this wisdom were not to manifest an image when taking non-substantial phenomena such as a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns as its object, it would have no object of cognition;
for their substance is not real and thus lacks the functional capacity to serve as an object. As the *Zongjing* states:

Since there is no longer a mind of "self" and "other" consisting of objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*), those things belonging to other bodies and lands—which are phenomena distinct from one's own essence—would not carry an image (*pratibimba*) and thus should not be object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

This is because [the wisdom] directly perceives them without transforming into an objective aspect (*nimitta*), unlike *tathatā* (suchness), which is the very essence of wisdom itself. Question: If that were so, *tathatā* would not be an object-condition. Is this not the case?
[Objection: Because it appears as if it were an object. [Response: This is not so, because it arises bearing an aspect that resembles [the object].

Since a phenomenon that is distinct from its own essence lacks any reflected image, one cannot say that it arises bearing the aspect of that [object]. How, then, can it be said to have an objective support (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?

Since all such [distinct] phenomena are devoid of their own essence, if something were called an "objective support" merely because it arises without bearing an aspect, then when perceiving color-form (*rūpa*), one should likewise perceive sound.

...and so forth. Since the cognition that takes form (*rūpa*) and so on as its object does not carry the aspect (*nimitta*) of form and so on, and since it would follow that there could be no objective support-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for non-existent things such as [the horns of a rabbit], [we reply]: because it does not transform into a non-aspectual state in order to perceive the object-support.

Since the aspectless part directly illuminates the non-existent, and since "non-existence" has no substantial entity (*dravya*), how could the meaning of the objective support-condition be established? For this reason, one should know that the Buddha...
Furthermore, it cannot take non-existence as its direct object; this is the proof based on textual principle. Regarding the fourth section, the Gate of the Sixfold Clear Realization (*abhisamaya*):
first, the question is posed, followed by the naming of the term. As for "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*): *abhi* means "manifestly present," and *samaya* means "observation.

This refers to the fact that the ultimate truth is constantly present before one, and sublime wisdom is perpetually able to observe it without interruption, spontaneously and in accordance with reality; therefore, it is so called.

Regarding *abhisamaya* (clear realization), the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* states: "Clear realization (*abhisamaya*) refers to the direct observation of the objects of knowledge—whether inferior, middling, or superior—that are bound to the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness. That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is comprised within the truths of suffering and its origin;
that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is comprised within the truths of cessation and the path. Question: By means of what clear realization? The verse says:
Supramundane superior wisdom is able to eliminate what is to be abandoned through seeing; it is attained through non-conceptualization and relies solely upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
This wisdom of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is supramundane wisdom for the purpose of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing;

it belongs exclusively to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and not to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Question: What is its mode of activity? Answer: It is attained through non-conceptualization; that is, it is present before one.
One realizes non-conceptual conduct; it is not that one has not yet realized it directly. Question: What is its basis? Answer:

It relies solely on the dhyānas, not on the formless attainments (ārūpya). Question: Where does the clear realization (abhisamaya) occur? Answer: Clear realization does not arise within the miserable realms (apāya).

Because painful sensations are constantly accompanied by extreme distress, and because one cannot realize *samādhi*, there is no clear realization (*abhisamaya*) in the realms of form and formlessness either.
This is because [beings in those realms] are dominated by longing and agitation, and their aversion is weak and inferior.

Therefore, clear realization does not arise in the two realms or the three destinies; it arises only in the two destinies of humans and gods within the desire realm when a Buddha appears in the world.
[The Buddha] contemplates. He asks: "Who is able to realize through direct insight (*abhisamaya*)? He answers: "There are five types of persons (*pudgala*) who can enter into direct realization;
or, there may be none who enter it, because of selflessness (*anātman*). What are these five? First, those not yet free from desire;

second, those partially free from desire; third, those already free from desire; fourth, the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*); and fifth, the bodhisattvas. He asks: "To what extent should one say that [the path] is correct?"

Regarding the entry into clear realization (*abhisamaya*): The answer is that from the previously cultivated appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), supramundane right view (*lokottara-samyag-dṛṣṭi*) arises during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

By means of this right view, the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are permanently severed—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
One should know that up to this stage, one has entered into clear realization. Question: At this stage, all...
All phenomena that constitute the defilements of the miserable realms are entirely eliminated. Why, then, is it said only that the three fetters are forever severed? The answer is:
through the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one is deluded regarding the object; through the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), one is deluded regarding views;
and because of that doubt, one gives rise to confusion regarding the True Dharma taught by the Teacher, the Buddha, and the Saṅgha of those who practice correctly. This is so.
Therefore, it follows the stronger [factor]. It speaks only of the permanent abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*). Regarding "insight through reflection" (*cintā-abhisamaya*):
its essence is the wisdom (*prajñā*) produced by superior reflection. Reflection has three grades; "superior" excludes the other two, as they are inferior and thus not [this type of insight].

This belongs to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), being associated with the feeling of joy (*sukha-vedanā*) and excluding the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because this [stage] clarifies what is sharp. Its common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is impermanence (*anityatā*).

Regarding "suffering and so forth": this wisdom is able to observe the dharmas of the five aggregates as impermanent and so on. Because it arises from cultivation based upon reflection (*cintāmayī*), it belongs to the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Although it has not yet realized the principle (*tattva*), its observation of dharmas is superior to that of the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages because it employs the most intense [application].

It is specifically designated as "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*) because the "Heat" and other stages are proximate to seeing, whereas their objects are subtle and brief; furthermore, they have not yet realized the principle.

It is not a direct realization (*abhisamaya*). Second, the direct realization of faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*) has as its essence the pure faith in the Three Jewels through superior mundane and supramundane conditions;

this faith is also of a superior grade and is both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*). Direct realization is wisdom (*prajñā*), which, aided by faith, prevents one from falling back.
Second, the direct realization of ethical discipline (*śīla-abhisamaya*) has as its essence the bodily and vocal actions beloved by the Noble Ones (*ārya-kānta-karma*); this...

This refers to the precepts concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahabhū-śīla*). By the supportive power of these precepts, contemplation is made increasingly clear; if lacking the support of the precepts, it becomes merely "mad wisdom" (*unmatta-prajñā*).

Regarding the fourth, the realization of the truths through the wisdom of present observation (*abhisamaya-jñāna-satya-abhisamaya*), its essence consists of the noble wisdom that takes the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) as its object.

This refers to whichever stage one is in where one takes only the non-established (*apratiṣṭhita*) as an object; thus, both types of wisdom are included therein, which is why it is called "all aspects" (*sarvākāra*).
The *Mahāśāstra* (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya), fascicle 75, states that the three minds of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) constitute this clear realization (*abhisamaya*);

therefore, it should be understood that these are also subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Furthermore, it says: "By the power of this very mind, one establishes [the truths] regarding suffering and so forth."

Within the establishment of the truths (*satyavyavasthāna*), there is the second stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). It is pure and unimpeded, and the knowledge of suffering and so forth arises.
One should know that based on this knowledge, the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path are established.

That is to say, the three preceding moments of mind, together with the categories of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), are able to realize the extinction of the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through seeing, and are able to attain the permanent extinction of all afflictions and their objects.

Based on the mundane path, the supramundane path is called the "clear realization of the knowledge of the truths" (*abhisamayajñānasatyābhisamaya*). These two knowledges are precisely the two knowledges of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The two knowledges of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) are not included because they are not distinct from the ultimate clear realization (*niṣṭhābhisamaya*).

Regarding the fifth, the "clear realization of the knowledge of the truths at the conclusion of the [five] clear realizations," it refers to the noble one’s [knowledge] which takes the established truths (*vyavasthāpanasatya*) as its object.
Its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*). This refers to the subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that takes the ten established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*) and so forth as its object.

It encompasses all paths of seeing and meditation, whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Regarding the wisdom that takes the established truths as its object, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Chapter 71, etc.

states that the wisdom which takes the objects of the established truths as its domain is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this [subsequently attained knowledge]. Furthermore, it says: "Having arisen from the preceding clear realization (*abhisamaya*), at..."

Within the truths of the various knowledges of the upper and lower realms, two knowledges arise for each; this is called the "clear realization of the truths through knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization" (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna-satyābhisamaya*).

As for the sixth, the "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*) clear realization, its essence consists of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) that follow the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "It refers to the arising of all knowledge of exhaustion and knowledge of non-arising due to the permanent abandonment of what is to be abandoned by cultivation. Or...
It is exclusively supramundane, or it may pertain to both the mundane and the supramundane.

It is called "ultimate clear realization" because it is the certainty of the permanent abandonment of all afflictions within the present life, and the certainty of the permanent abandonment of all bases for rebirth in future lives.
Regarding the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*): it refers to the knowledge obtained through the exhaustion of causes. Regarding the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*):
it refers to the knowledge obtained through the abandonment of results. Question: What are the characteristics of the "clear realization through reflection" (*cintā-abhisamaya*)? Answer:

If one accomplishes the clear realization through reflection, one is able to correctly understand that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and that *nirvāṇa* is peace. Even while dwelling...

Regarding the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), no celestial Māras whatsoever can lead them astray or take it away. What are the characteristics of the clear realization through faith (*śraddhā-abhisamaya*)? Answer:

If there is one who has accomplished the clear realization through faith, whether they abide in the stage of an ordinary person or in a stage beyond that of an ordinary person, they will never proclaim that there is another great teacher, another well-spoken Dharma, or another Sangha of right practice, [nor will they disparage] the precepts... [the clear realization through faith].

Question: What are the characteristics of [the path of] contemplation? Answer: If one achieves the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of ethical discipline (*śīla*), then even toward animals one will never intentionally take their life, nor will one take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak words of ignorance or falsehood, or drink intoxicants that lead to heedlessness.
Question: What are the characteristics of the clear observation of the knowledge of truths (*jñāna-satya-abhisamaya*)? Answer: If one achieves this clear observation...
One who possesses the clear realization of the truths through wisdom never relies upon divergent views to initiate actions,

nor does they give rise to doubt or delusion regarding their own realization, nor do they become defiled by attachment to any place of birth. While they may acknowledge that practicing virtuous signs leads to purification,
they would never disparage the Three Vehicles, create karma for the evil realms, let alone commit such acts as harming one's parents or other such heinous deeds.
Regarding intermediate karma: what are the characteristics of the realization of the truths through the knowledge at the limit of clear observation (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna-satyābhisamaya*)? Answer:

If one who has accomplished the realization of the truths through the knowledge at the limit of clear observation is questioned or challenged by others regarding their own realization, they will never feel timid or afraid.
What are the characteristics of the ultimate realization (*niṣṭhābhisamaya*)? Answer: If one who has accomplished the ultimate realization never falls back.
Regarding the five bases of transgression, he never intentionally harms the life of a sentient being, nor does he take what is not given,
nor does he practice sexual misconduct or non-celibate conduct, nor does he speak falsehoods, nor does he accumulate wealth, nor does he indulge in various sensual desires. Furthermore,
he is never terrified by matters that cannot be definitively explained, and he never clings to the notion that suffering and pleasure are created by oneself or created by another.

Suffering and pleasure; suffering and pleasure created by oneself or by another; suffering and pleasure created neither by oneself nor by another, arising without cause—such categories as these are called the characteristics of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

Among the six types of clear realization, the fourth—the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) that takes non-conceptually established phenomena (*apratiṣṭhita*) as its object—is subsumed under the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

The subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that takes non-conceptually established phenomena as its object is subsumed under the three moments of the semblance path of seeing (*pratibimba-darśana-mārga*).

The fifth [type of] contemplation is included within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) because it contemplates the established truths (*vyavasthānasatya*) as conditions; however, because it also extends into the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is said to be "partial.

Although the second, the contemplation of faith, and the third, the contemplation of ethical discipline, arise simultaneously with these two [types of] path of seeing, they merely assist in non-retrogression and clarify the contemplation;
they are not, in reality, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of direct realization (*abhisamaya*). Therefore, they are not [included].
They are mutually inclusive. Those not included in the former [category] are so because they have already been practiced; those not included in the latter are so because they have not yet arisen.

Below this, "The Bodhisattva attains this" concludes that the stages are equal. Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), each stage has three parts: namely, entry (*praveśa*), abiding (*sthiti*), and [emergence].

This stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*) corresponds to the mind that enters the first bhūmi (*prathamā bhūmi*). Since the two minds of abiding and emerging belong to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one is already entered into the first bhūmi;

thus, one is called a Bodhisattva. Having been born into the family of the Tathāgata, one dwells in the Ground of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), skillfully penetrating the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and attaining all forms of equality.
As the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "Awakening penetrates the Tathāgata, for it exhausts the realm of the Buddhas."

Regarding "all that is equal": the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, chapter six, speaks of attaining three kinds of equality—namely, the equality of all sentient beings, the equality of all bodhisattvas, and the equality of all buddhas.

Regarding "having attained mastery over many hundreds of gates," the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Having entered this stage, one attains a hundred samādhis, beholds a hundred buddhas, and causes [the earth] to tremble."
They transform a hundred worlds and the sentient beings of a hundred lands; they enter a hundred dharma-gates and know the events of a hundred kalpas;
they manifest a hundred bodies and perceive a hundred bodhisattvas as their retinue; and they attain the definitive self-knowledge that their attainment of Buddhahood is unmistakable.
[He] will certainly bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings. Question: Why is it that the time for the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is particularly brief?
Answer: When light comes, darkness departs; when wisdom arises, delusion perishes. Since not even a single thought-moment exists, how can one be surprised that the time is brief?

Question: If there is no single thought-moment, when does [the path] enter the mind? Answer: It is said that, in terms of the characteristics of the Path of Seeing, many moments are required for the arrangement of phenomena to reach completion.
When one enters the mind—if it were the true path of seeing—how could it belong to the three temporal periods?

Next, what are the characteristics of the stage of cultivation? (Up to: Because one abandons the two types of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), one realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
The fourth is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). This question and its response in verse are the words of Vasubandhu; it constitutes the twenty-ninth verse.

It begins from the point after the two paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) upon first entering the stages (*bhūmi*), through the subsequent states of mind, up until the final moment of mind preceding the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).

This is collectively termed the "Stage of Cultivation" (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). Question: What is the meaning of the term "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*)? Answer: "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) means "to cultivate" (*bhāva*), and "cultivation" (*vāsanā*) means "to practice and study.

It is called "cultivation" because one cultivates and practices the conditioned and unconditioned dharmas of merit. Question: What are the characteristics of the distinctions within the stages of cultivation?
Answer: Broadly speaking, there are two. First, the ten stages as causes; second, the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). That is to say, the ten [stages]...

Because each stage (*bhūmi*) possesses the causes for the four paths—preparatory (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), liberation (*vimukti*), and special progress (*viśeṣa*). The fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is detailed in a later fascicle.
The treatise says: "From when the Bodhisattva has arisen from the aforementioned path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)... up to [the point where he] dwells in the Great Sage, who is named the Dharma-body."

Below this, the commentary by Dharmapāla and others on the verses is divided into four parts: first, the direct explanation of the meaning of the verses; second, an extensive discussion of the meanings of cultivation, abandonment, and realization within the stages (*bhūmi*);

third, the specific opening of the six types of positions of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); and fourth, the specific clarification of the four types of meaning of the transformation of the basis.
Herein is the first part. "From the preceding [stage] up to what is called 'inconceivable'": this explains the first phrase of the verse. As for the word "the rest" (*śeṣa*)...
Regarding "obstructions," these refer to the two innate obstructions (*sahaja-āvaraṇa*).

As for the statement in the *Avataṃsaka-bhāṣya* that one "removes all afflictive obstructions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*), this is because the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are also considered afflictions insofar as they act as obstructions.

They arise spontaneously and not through conceptual discrimination; therefore, they are called "innate. The above establishes the purpose of cultivation: it is for the sake of severing the innate delusions. From [the word] "furthermore"...

The section on "Cultivating the Lower [Levels]" consists of three parts: first, it presents the essential nature of the practice being cultivated; second, it distinguishes the virtues of cultivation by departing from both the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*);
and third, it explains the phrases "non-attainment" (*anupalabdhi*) and "inconceivable" (*acintya*) from the verses of the *Śāstra*. Regarding these, there are two interpretations:

the first holds that "non-attainment" refers to the departure from the grasped object, while "inconceivable" refers to the departure from the grasping subject. Alternatively, the latter interpretation maintains that "non-attainment" refers to the departure from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Its wondrous function is difficult to fathom; thus it is called "inconceivable. The former [explanation] interprets this solely in terms of its essence (*tattva*), while the latter clarifies it by correlating essence and function.
This is supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (*lokottara-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
To explain the second phrase of the verse—namely, that this inconceivable wondrous function is supramundane non-conceptual wisdom—the text asks: why is it called "supramundane"?

It is because it severs the world. What is meant by severing the world? It is because the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) and their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the root of the world, and this [wisdom] alone is able to sever them.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation that explains the term "supramundane" (*lokottara*), which is established based on two meanings.
First, it is of a single essence and untainted; second, it realizes *tathatā*. Only fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) possesses these two meanings;

other forms of wisdom do not. This refers to subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). This fundamental wisdom is the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) that can sever innate afflictions.
Because one cultivates this repeatedly, one arrives at [the state of] equanimity (*upekṣā*); thus it is said to be "abandonment. This explains the third line of the verse, namely, "repeatedly..."
One cultivates this non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) in order to abandon the seeds of the heavy obstructions (*dausthulya*). What constitutes these "heavy obstructions"?
They refer to the nature of the seeds of the two obstructions, which are characterized by incapacity and are contrary to that subtle and light non-conceptual wisdom;

thus, they are called "heavy obstructions. Because non-conceptual wisdom causes them to be eternally extinguished, it is said that [wisdom] "abandons" them; for it is this [wisdom] that is able to abandon them.

At the end [of the commentary], he explains the fourth line of the verse: "By abandoning the two types of *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness), one realizes the vast transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

Regarding the term "basis" (*āśraya*), it refers to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), which serves as the substratum for both defiled and pure phenomena. This nature is originally neither defiled nor pure;
