Through diligence (*vīrya*), patience becomes pure. Why? Because of the power of valor.
Therefore, dwelling for a long time in birth-and-death is not considered difficult, and one is able to endure the sufferings of sentient beings' hostility and the like.
Because of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), diligence is purified. Why? Because, accompanied by joy and bliss, one is able to diligently cultivate all wholesome dharmas without rest.
Because of possessing wisdom (*prajñā*), meditative concentration is purified. Why? If, by means of...
Through immeasurable gateways, one repeatedly contemplates all phenomena, thereby realizing inner tranquility and increasing meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, a verse from the *Gāthā* states: "There is no meditative absorption that does not depend upon wisdom. Moreover, there are the three successive gateways of the coarse and the subtle.
Generosity is coarse; ethical discipline is subtle. In comparison to patience, ethical discipline is coarse, while patience is subtle, and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that "the preceding are coarse and the succeeding are subtle. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"Furthermore, the sequential order of the pāramitās is established by way of their coarseness and subtlety. Why is this? Among all conditioned phenomena, the practice of generosity..."
Because it is the coarsest, morality is established first. Among the practices such as patience, morality is again the coarsest, and thus it is established next.
This continues down to wisdom: among all these practices, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is coarse, while wisdom is the most subtle; therefore, it is established last.
The first nine are all "prior-to-prior," ranging from ethical discipline (*śīla*) to wisdom (*prajñā*). Each is designated as "subsequent-to-subsequent" when viewed in relation to the others;

thus, the terms are repeated. The first [perfection] is exclusively prior, and the last is exclusively subsequent. Regarding the intermediate eight perfections, they alternate between being prior and subsequent.
Below, the four gates concerning ease and difficulty of cultivation also summarize and extend the three preceding points. These four gates above—
This is as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma*. Regarding the six types of cultivation, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Twelfth Chapter) states:

"What is cultivation? Briefly, there are five kinds: namely, cultivation based on sustenance (*upastambha*), cultivation based on mental attention (*manasikāra*), cultivation based on intention (*āśaya*), cultivation based on skillful means (*upāya*), and cultivation based on mastery (*vaśitā*). Furthermore, cultivation based on sustenance is further divided into..."
There are four types: first, cultivation based on the cause of reliance, which refers to the practice of the correct application of the pāramitās through the power of one’s spiritual lineage (gotra);
second, cultivation based on retribution, which refers to the practice of the correct application of the pāramitās through the power of one’s superior physical constitution;
third, cultivation based on aspiration, which refers to the practice of the pāramitās through the power of one’s original vows.

Practicing right conduct. Cultivation based on the power of discernment consists of four types; that is, practicing right conduct regarding the perfections (*pāramitā*) by means of the power of wisdom.
There are also four types of cultivation based on mental attention (*manasikāra*):

first, cultivation based on mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), which means generating superior resolute conviction toward all scriptural teachings associated with the perfections.

Second is cultivation based on the mental attention of relishing (*āsvādana-manasikāra*); that is, regarding the perfections already attained, one perceives their superior qualities and gives rise to deep relishing.
Third is cultivation based on the mental attention of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-manasikāra*); that is, regarding all worlds...
One deeply rejoices in all the practices of generosity and so forth performed by all sentient beings; this is cultivation based on the mental attention of joy (*muditā-manasikāra*).
Furthermore, there is cultivation based on the intention (*āśaya*), which consists of generating a deep aspiration for the superior perfections (*pāramitā*) of oneself and others in the future.
Moreover, there are six types [of intention]: the intention of non-contentment, the vast intention, and the joyful intention.
Because of the intention of altruistic benefit, the intention of non-attachment, and the excellent intention, one cultivates the various *pāramitās*. In this regard,
the bodhisattva’s intention of tirelessness toward the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) means that even if,
for a single sentient being, in a single moment, worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were filled—
One gives away the seven precious treasures within it as an act of generosity. Furthermore, one gives away as many lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River as an act of generosity.
One practices such giving for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.

Just as one does toward a single sentient being, so too does one do toward the entire realm of all sentient beings. When giving in this manner, one causes them all to [attain] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They quickly attain maturity in unsurpassed *samyak-saṃbodhi*. While practicing such distinguished giving, the bodhisattva’s intention is not yet satiated.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice this perfection of generosity, they expand—
The continuum proceeds without a single moment of decline or interruption, until finally sitting upon the seat of enlightenment.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s vast intention regarding the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice this perfection of generosity, regarding all that is comprised within giving...
The great joy produced by this [joy] cannot be equaled even by the joy produced when those sentient beings are embraced by that gift.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s joyful intention regarding the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice this perfection of generosity, they contemplate the gift...
They encompass all sentient beings as having rendered great kindness upon their own persons;
they do not view their own persons as being kind to those beings, because it is [the beings] who assist them in attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s intention regarding the kindness and virtue within the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*). Furthermore, all bodhisattvas...

When practicing such perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), although one generates great merit through extensive giving toward immeasurable sentient beings, one does not hope for their gratitude or for future karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s unstained intention regarding the perfection of generosity. Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice in this manner...

When practicing the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), one dedicates the maturation (*vipāka*) obtained from the vast accumulation of practiced giving to all sentient beings, rather than for oneself.
Furthermore, one dedicates this merit together with all sentient beings toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s [perfection] regarding the perfection of generosity.

The excellent intention regarding the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*). Furthermore, the insatiable intention of all bodhisattvas practicing from the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) refers to this:

even if bodhisattvas were to pass through as many lifetimes as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and in each such lifetime possessed a lifespan equal to as many great eons (*mahākalpa*) as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, throughout this long duration—
At that time, while constantly lacking all necessities of life and dwelling, standing, sitting, or lying down amidst a great trichiliocosm filled with blazing fires,
they are able to practice even for a single kṣaṇa the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā),
or even up to the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā). In this manner, they progressively cultivate all such distinctions.
From the aggregate of ethical discipline up to the aggregate of wisdom, they are brought to ultimate fulfillment. They are now able to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When these bodhisattvas practice these perfections from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom, they cultivate the aspirational intention toward this aggregate of ethical discipline up to the aggregate of wisdom, just as...
He is not satisfied. Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s insatiable intention regarding the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice these perfections from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom, they proceed in continuous succession. There is no...

In a single moment, there is both regression and abandonment; yet, until reaching the ultimate state of sitting upon the seat of enlightenment, such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s vast intention regarding the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice such a perfection of ethical discipline...
When reaching the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one gives rise to great joy toward all sentient beings included therein;
yet the joy produced by those sentient beings through being so included cannot equal it.
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s [intention] regarding the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom.
With a joyful intention toward the *pāramitās*, furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice these *śīlapāramitā* through to the *prajñāpāramitā*,
they perceive all sentient beings encompassed by these [perfections] as having rendered great kindness to themselves,
rather than seeing themselves as having rendered kindness to them; for [these beings] have assisted them in their pursuit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Because of [the attainment of] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Such an aspiration is called the bodhisattva’s aspirational intention regarding the benefits of practicing the *pāramitās*, from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice these *pāramitās*, from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom...

Although he bestows the great precepts upon immeasurable sentient beings and provides them with the basis for merit up to the basis for wisdom, he does not hope for a return of gratitude or for future maturation [of karmic results].
Such an intention is called the bodhisattva’s untainted intention regarding the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, all bodhisattvas...
When practicing these perfections, from the perfection of ethical discipline up to the perfection of wisdom,
one gives to all sentient beings the karmic maturation obtained from the vast accumulation of ethical discipline up to the accumulation of wisdom,
rather than for oneself. Furthermore, one dedicates this merit together with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The three types of awakening. Such an intention is called the virtuous intention of a bodhisattva regarding the practice of the *pāramitās*, from the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, there are three kinds of reliance upon the cultivation of skillful means (*upāya*):
namely, because one observes through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are entirely pure. Why is this so?
Why? Because by this means, all practices cultivated through mental attention are swiftly brought to fulfillment.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of cultivation based on mastery: namely, mastery over the body, mastery over conduct, and mastery over teaching.
Mastery over the body refers to the two bodies of all Tathāgatas—the *svābhāvika-kāya* (essential body) and the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body). Mastery over conduct refers to...
This refers to the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Tathāgatas.
Because they are able to manifest for all sentient beings every kind of practice in accordance with the Dharma, they are called "sovereigns" (*vaśin*).

This means they are able to proclaim all the various distinctions of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) without any obstruction. What are these distinctions? They consist of eighteen kinds of sustenances (*dhāraṇa*).
This serves to reveal the distinctions among the six *pāramitās*. What are these eighteen? They are: the sustenance of the body; the sustenance of the mind;

the sustenance of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*); the sustenance of virtue; the sustenance of awakening (*bodhi*); the sustenance of compassion (*karuṇā*); the sustenance of not abandoning sentient beings; the sustenance of relinquishing inferior states of mind;
the sustenance of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and the sustenance of skillful means regarding the roots of virtue (*kuśala-mūla-upāya*).

Sustenance: the sustenance of the perfect realization of roots of goodness; the sustenance of the inexhaustibility of roots of goodness; the sustenance of tirelessness; the sustenance of the fulfillment of all intended aims;
the sustenance of governing the activities of the assembly; the sustenance of entering the stages (*bhūmi*); the sustenance of manifesting the Buddha-nature;
and the sustenance of establishing Buddha-activities. Each of the six perfections, such as generosity and the rest, has three distinct varieties.

In their respective order, they are subsumed under three groups of three. It should be understood that the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*) can sustain the body, because it benefits the recipient’s physical basis through such necessities as food and drink.

The gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*) can sustain the mind, because it comforts the minds of others by freeing them from sorrow and fear. In this way, the remaining phrases should be contemplated according to their meaning. Inferior...
"Mind" refers to the minds of bodhisattvas that, out of weariness with the suffering of birth and death, resemble the minds of those of the two vehicles;
it is only through being sustained by the patience of accepting suffering that they eventually abandon this mind.

"Inexhaustible roots of virtue" means that until the very limit of cyclic existence, they constantly perform acts for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, even within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
It is not abandoned, because it is sustained by the diligence of benefiting sentient beings. Regarding the activity of governing a community:
this refers to relying upon internal realization to provide instruction and admonition to those beings being transformed;

causing those whose minds are not yet concentrated to attain concentration, and causing those whose minds are already concentrated to attain liberation—this is because it is sustained by the meditative absorption of benefiting sentient beings.

"Because of upholding. Regarding "entering the great stages": this means that one who has previously perfected the provisions through faith and understanding of the profound teachings is able to swiftly enter the first stage, the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), by being sustained by the wisdom that takes conventional reality as its object.

The remaining points are easy to understand and thus are not explained again. Regarding the "sevenfold inclusion": each of these eleven [factors] individually includes all the perfections (*pāramitā*).

Pāramitās. Because they accord with one another, this generally clarifies that the ten [pāramitās] mutually encompass one another. The *Qingliang shu* (Cool Breeze Commentary) quotes the *Prajñā-śāstra*, saying:
"The meaning of *dāna* (generosity) encompasses the six [pāramitās], such as material gifts, fearlessness, and the Dharma. The *Jizhi lun* (Treatise on the Wisdom Treatise) says:
"There are pāramitās that are not yet adorned, which are thus not encompassed; there are pāramitās that are already adorned, which are thus mutually..."
Regarding "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*): the *Chao* (Excerpts) states that the phrase "the gift of material goods, fearlessness, and the Dharma," etc., includes the latter half [of the verse], which says:
"Among these, one, two, and three are called the stages of cultivation. This means there are three kinds of giving: first, material goods; second, fearlessness; and third, the gift of the Dharma.
Material goods are the sustenance of life and constitute the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*); therefore, it is said, "among these, the first. Fearlessness is included [as the second].
Second: this refers to the body not afflicting others and enduring their afflictions, both of which possess the characteristic of fearlessness;

hence it is called "two. The Dharma-giving encompasses three: namely, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. These constitute the definitive, supreme path that gradually ripens the Buddha-dharma;

such is the characteristic of Dharma-giving, hence it is called "three. This is precisely the "abiding in cultivation" among the eighteen abidings. If one follows the gateway of elicitation (*ākṣepa-mukha*):

In that case, the former necessarily includes the latter, while the latter does not include the former. If one relies on the gate of "sustaining through inclusion," then the latter necessarily includes the former, while the former does not include the latter.
Regarding cultivation according to the pure and the mixed: there are those who cultivate one [factor] purely, and there are those who cultivate the others in a mixed manner.
When these are compared with one another, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established. As for the "pure" [cultivation], each is to be considered in relation to its own seed.
These are categorized into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). As for the "mixed" category, it is not restricted by type;

whether practiced sequentially or non-sequentially, there are likewise four propositions, following the same pattern as before. This is according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, fascicle 12, which employs a single methodological approach.
Second, the distinction; third, the demonstration of the distinction, which clarifies their mutual determination and elucidates them in relation to one another.
"These actually consist of ten" and below clarify the sixtyfold mutual inclusion: if the six perfections include the ten, the sixth includes the final four.

If the ten perfections subsume the six, the sixth [perfection] only subsumes a small portion of the sixth [wisdom], leaving something incomplete because it does not include the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and the preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*).
Therefore, only by including the latter four [perfections] are the two types of wisdom within the sixth fully subsumed.
Thus it is said: "When expanded into ten," the sixth [perfection] subsumes only non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), whereas the latter four are all subsequently attained wisdom.
They are subsumed by wisdom because they take the conventional as their object. Regarding the "eight [perfections] having five fruits":

among the five fruits, disconnection (*visamyoga*) is an uncontaminated fruit (*anāsrava-phala*), while maturation (*vipāka*) is a contaminated fruit (*sāsrava-phala*). Therefore, among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the contaminated exclude disconnection, and the uncontaminated exclude maturation.
However, there are places where it is said that they possess all five fruits; this is either because the two types of contaminants mutually support one another, or...
This is because they are either explained individually or combined. Anahbuddhi states: "Merit" refers to the immeasurable and boundless praised benefits based upon the five fruits;
all such things are called merit, meaning that they are able to permanently sever their respective counter-factors.
These perfections are the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*). In the present life, by means of this giving and so forth, one gathers benefit for oneself and others;
this is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). In future lives, as they arise successively in ever-increasing excellence, this is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
For the great bodhisattva, this is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*): it brings about great wealth, rebirth in the happy realms, and [the absence of]...

Being free from enmity, possessing abundant joy and happiness, being the most honored among sentient beings, having no harm to one’s body, and having a vast and noble lineage in successive order—these are the maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*) of the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity. These two [categories] are explained together.

Regarding the "three trainings" (*śikṣā-traya*): they are the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*), the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), and the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*). This is the definition.
Regarding the three trainings, first there are three types of precepts. First is the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint). As Vasubandhu explains:

it refers to the guarding and upholding [of the mind] against those unwholesome factors that give rise to negligence. Because it restrains all evil and unwholesome actions of body and speech, it is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*).
As for the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering virtuous dharmas), it enables one to realize all qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

Regarding the Buddha-dharma, that which benefits through ethical discipline (*śīla*) refers to being able to assist sentient beings by performing actions in accordance with the Dharma, distributing [benefits] equitably, and maturing sentient beings through faultless activity.

Some say that the latter two [types of discipline] are established based on the first, because by guarding oneself, one is able to cultivate roots of virtue such as making offerings to the Buddhas and benefiting all sentient beings. Therefore, Vasubandhu said:
One who abides in the vow of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) is able to establish the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

By means of this, one cultivates and accumulates all Buddha-dharmas and realizes great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). Furthermore, one is able to establish the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).

By means of this, one is able to bring sentient beings to maturity. Some say that the former two serve to accomplish the fruit of the latter one. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "If one is able to abide in the former two kinds..."

Pure ethical discipline is so called because it can attract and encompass the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings. These three categories of ethical discipline constitute the causes for the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
Why is this? The first is the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), the second is the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), and the third is the virtue of beneficence (*anuśaṃsā-guṇa*).

Since the four fearlessnesses, the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and so forth, do not transcend these three virtues, it is for this reason that it is said there are three categories of ethical discipline.
Regarding this [perfection] that is both shared and unshared with the two vehicles, and which is profound and vast, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"The excellence of the shared and unshared training rules (*śikṣāpada*) is as follows: because Bodhisattvas do not engage in any natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), they share these with the Śrāvakas;
yet because they do engage in certain similar prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*), they are unshared with them. Regarding these training rules..."
What constitutes an offense for a śrāvaka may not constitute an offense for a bodhisattva; conversely, there are offenses for which a bodhisattva may be culpable while a śrāvaka is not.
This is because a bodhisattva possesses the ethical discipline of body, speech, and mind, whereas a śrāvaka possesses only the two disciplines of body and speech.

Therefore, a bodhisattva may incur an offense through the mind, whereas this does not apply to śrāvakas. In brief, all actions of body and speech that benefit sentient beings and are free from fault [constitute the bodhisattva’s path].
Regarding mental actions, a bodhisattva should practice all of them and should train in all of them.

It should be understood that this is called the distinction between the common and the uncommon. Among these, all natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), such as taking life and so forth, are called "common. Similar prohibitory transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), such as digging the earth, are also [included].

Cutting living grass and so forth is called a "unique" (asādhāraṇa) offense. Regarding these training rules (*śikṣāpada*), there are cases where a Śrāvaka commits an offense while a Bodhisattva does not, such as when one stays overnight during the two periods of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) for the sake of observing what would benefit sentient beings.

Conversely, there are cases where a Bodhisattva commits an offense while a Śrāvaka does not, such as when one observes that it would be beneficial but intentionally does not act upon it; thus, a Bodhisattva incurs an offense even through the mind alone. This is not the case for Śrāvakas; for them, an offense is only established when they internally give rise to discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) such as desire and so forth. A Bodhisattva, however, incurs an offense [even by such mental activity].

These are not [the practices] of the śrāvakas and others. All faultless actions of body, speech, and mind that benefit sentient beings—every such action a bodhisattva should practice and cultivate—is what is meant here;

that is to say, they are capable of benefiting others and are without fault. Such threefold karma is what a bodhisattva should cultivate. Alternatively, there may be actions that benefit others but are not without fault, such as giving another person an improper object like a woman;

it is to preclude such things that the term "without fault" is stated. Regarding "vast and sublime," this is further due to four kinds of vastness: first, by way of the vastness of various immeasurable trainings (*śikṣāpada*).
First, because it is vast; second, because it encompasses immeasurable merit and is thus vast;

third, because it encompasses the intention for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings and is thus vast; fourth, because it establishes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and is thus vast.

(Regarding the vastness of the various and immeasurable training rules: this refers to the training rules practiced by bodhisattvas, which are both diverse and immeasurable. By means of these, in regard to...)

Regarding those who gather immeasurable and vast merit for the sake of maturing all sentient beings and for the sake of gathering them [into the fold]: these are the bodhisattvas, because they gather immeasurable accumulations of merit, whereas the śrāvakas do not.

Regarding those whose intention to bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings is vast: this refers to their exhorting sentient beings to cultivate virtue; whether it be the intention to benefit them, or the aspiration that by means of that very virtue, those individuals [themselves] may [attain such results].

One shall attain the supreme fruit, which is called the "intention of bliss. Regarding the establishment of the vastness of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment: this refers to all bodhisattvas, for it is by means of this ethical discipline (*śīla*) that they establish unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and not as śrāvakas.

Regarding the "profoundly sublime": it refers to how bodhisattvas, through these types of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), engage in the ten types of actions such as taking life and yet remain free from fault;
instead, they generate immeasurable merit and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that when bodhisattvas manifest the two karmas of body and speech through emanations (*nirmāṇa*), this is likewise [profoundly sublime].

This is the profound ethical discipline (*śīla*). By means of these causes and conditions, he may become a king and manifest various acts that afflict sentient beings, thereby establishing them within the *vinaya*.
Furthermore, he manifests various *jātaka* tales, appearing to oppress and harm other sentient beings while truly gathering them in. First, he causes their minds to become deeply...
They give rise to pure faith, which subsequently matures. This is called the profound and supreme ethical discipline (*śīla*) in which Bodhisattvas train.

Regarding this profundity and supremacy—referring to those Bodhisattvas who possess such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)—this passage demonstrates the functional power of such skillful means for a Bodhisattva.

That is to say, if a Bodhisattva knows that a person of such a type is about to initiate the application (*prayoga*) toward an unwholesome act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), they perceive that person’s mind through their knowledge of others’ minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). Since there is no other means capable of diverting that karma, [the Bodhisattva acts] in accordance with reality.

Knowing that by this karma they will certainly fall away from the happy realms and will certainly go to the evil destinies, and having known this, he gives rise to such a thought: "I shall perform this karma; I must fall into an evil destiny. It would be better for me to go there myself so that I may surely deliver them.

Although I inflict a small amount of suffering upon them in the present, it will cause them to experience much peace and happiness in the future. Therefore, just as a skilled physician acts with a mind of benefit, even though the Bodhisattva kills them, there is not the slightest fault, but rather much merit is generated.

Because of this great merit, he swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Such precepts as these are most profound. Furthermore, one should know that when Bodhisattvas manifest the two karmas of body and speech through emanations, these too are profound ethical discipline (*śīla*). By means of this...

This is the principle. Sometimes he acts as a king, manifesting various deeds that afflict sentient beings in order to establish them within the *vinaya* (discipline). His manifested body is called a "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*). In this regard, one should explain such matters as King Anala’s guidance of Sudhana and others.

Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of various *jātaka* (birth) stories—such as those of Viśvantara and others—in these instances, the Bodhisattva’s giving of his children to the brahmins is entirely a transformation.

He manifests the act of afflicting other sentient beings in order to truly gather in other sentient beings. This means that Bodhisattvas never actually afflict other real sentient beings; rather, they do so because they truly intend to gather in other real sentient beings.

This is also called "profoundly sublime. Regarding the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), there are four [stages] and three interpretations. Master Ying states: "The first concentration eliminates the obstacle of unwholesome states;

the second eliminates the obstacle of attachment to dhyāna; the third eliminates the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*); and the fourth eliminates the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). Master Xianshou states:

"The first is able to eliminate the obstacle of karma consisting of distracted and defiled activity; the second is able to eliminate the obstacle of attachment to the flavor of concentration and the tranquility of stillness; the third..."

It can eliminate the obstacle of fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*). Fourth, it can eliminate the obstacle to the wisdom that accomplishes purity; this is largely the same as what was explained previously.

Qingliang says: "This means that by using the wisdom that realizes the reality within phenomena (*jishi er zhen zhi*) to treat the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi, one achieves the first bhūmi and attains the 'Worthy Guardian' Samādhi (*bhadra-pālita-samādhi*).
Because of this samādhi, one is able to guard the virtuous and wholesome dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms."

The first three stages constitute the mundane; the fourth stage constitutes the supramundane. This is because, having realized that phenomena are themselves reality (*tathatā*), one is able to remain in meditative concentration even amidst distraction.

Second, by means of the wisdom of the function inherent in the essence, one counteracts the inability to initiate activity in the fourth stage, thereby enabling entry into the fifth stage to engage with the conventional world and achieve the "King of Accumulated Merit" concentration (*saṃbhāra-rāja-samādhi*). Third, by means of the wisdom of equality and signlessness (*animitta*).
Although one can conform to worldly conventions in the fifth stage as an antidote, one has not yet attained equality;

thus, through the functional power of the great light of *prajñā* of the sixth and seventh stages, one achieves the Mahāyāna Samādhi of Radiance. Fourth, by means of the wisdom of equality that is effortless (*anābhoga*).
This counteracts the effortful application of the seventh stage, causing one to enter the eighth stage and proceed up to the fruit of Buddhahood.

One attains the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, whereby all that is to be done is perfected. Since the fruit is already complete, the four causes are also cultivated universally; thus, this interpretation is correct.
Regarding these four objects of focus which serve as counteragents, capacities, inducers, and performers, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The excellence of the superior mind..."
How is "victory" (vibhūti) to be seen? Briefly, it should be understood through six types of distinctions: first, by the distinction of the object of focus;
second, by the distinction of variety; third, by the distinction of the antidote; fourth, by the distinction of capability; fifth, by the distinction of elicitation;
and sixth, by the distinction of activity. (This is for the purpose of manifesting its supremacy.)
The excellence of the training of the mind is addressed here in response. Regarding the distinction of the object of focus (*ālambana-viśeṣa*):

this refers to taking the Mahāyāna teachings as the object of focus (that is, bodhisattvas necessarily take the Mahāyāna as their object, whereas śrāvakas do not). Regarding the distinction of variety (*nānātva-viśeṣa*):
this refers to the various and immeasurable samādhis, such as the Mahāyāna-āloka, the Saṃbhāra-samudgata, the Śūraṅgama, and the Bhadrapāla. (Mahāyāna-āloka, Saṃbhāra...)

Regarding "the samādhis of King Samādhi and so forth": this reveals the various distinctions among such samādhis that exist only in the Mahāyāna, and not even a single type of which exists in the Śrāvakayāna and other vehicles. As for the distinction of their remedies (*pratipakṣa-viśeṣa*):
This refers to the wisdom that takes the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena as its object;

by means of the principle of "using a wedge to extract a wedge," it eliminates all obstacles and heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) within the *ālayavijñāna*. (The wisdom that takes general phenomena as its object abides as the antidote to all obstacles.

Just as a fine wedge is used to remove a coarse wedge, the various seeds of perfuming (*vāsanā*) of defiled phenomena residing in the fundamental consciousness are called "coarse"; because the various paths of antidote can remove them, they are termed "subtle" in meaning). Regarding the differentiation of capability, it refers to abiding...

The bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-sukha*): because one takes birth according to one's wish (due to possessing the capability to abide in the bliss of meditative concentration, wherever it may be beneficial for sentient beings).
They are reborn there immediately. Śrāvakas and others do not possess such a quality as this, namely, the non-retrogression from dhyāna.

As for the distinction of manifestation, it means being able to manifest unimpeded supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) throughout all worlds (for by manifesting these supernormal powers through this dhyāna, one encounters no obstacles in any world).
As for the distinction of activity, it means being able to shake, blaze, pervade, display, transform, go and return, contract and expand, and [perform] all [such deeds].
All forms and images enter into his body. Wherever he goes, among those of his own kind, he acts with mastery, whether manifesting or concealing himself.
He possesses the supernormal power of prostrating upon the earth; he bestows eloquence, mindfulness, and joy; and he emits great radiance.

Because he brings forth such great supernormal powers, [the distinction of activity refers to the deeds performed through the arousal of these powers]. Among these, because he can move all worlds, it is called "vibration. Because those very worlds are set ablaze, it is called "blazing. As for the term "pervading," one should know that it is precisely this.

The light shines universally. Regarding the term "manifestation": by this power, other sentient beings who were previously incapable suddenly become able to see immeasurable worlds, as well as other Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth. Regarding the term "transformation":

One should know that all lands and so forth are transformed into water and so forth. Regarding "coming and going," it means that in a single kṣaṇa, one is able to travel to and return from immeasurable worlds. Regarding "contracting and expanding," it means contracting the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions.

Entering a single atom, yet the atom does not increase; expanding a single atom to encompass infinite worlds in the ten directions, yet the worlds do not diminish. That all forms and images enter within the body means that within the body there appear infinite varieties of all manner of activities. Regarding "those of the same class as where one goes":

this refers to, for example, going to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where one’s physical appearance and speech are identical to those [of the gods], because one has gone there for the sake of transforming them. Going to all places is likewise so. "Manifest" (*prakāśana*) means to reveal; "conceal" (*antardhāna*) means to hide.

"Mastery over what is done" (*karmavaśitā*) refers to such things as transforming the Māra King into the body of a Buddha. "The supernormal power of subduing the earth" means being able to eclipse all other supernormal powers and bestowing eloquence (*pratibhāna*) upon those who inquire.

Therefore, it is called "bestowing eloquence. Because it bestows mindfulness and bestows happiness upon those who hear [the teaching], enabling them to attain meditative concentration, it is called "bestowing mindfulness and happiness. Regarding the emission of great radiance: it is for the purpose of summoning Bodhisattvas dwelling in other worlds afar;

it is to manifest such great supernormal powers as previously described. All such qualities are absent in the Śrāvakas, and are therefore superior. Furthermore, it is able to manifest and encompass the ten difficult practices (*duṣkaracaryā*), which are difficult to perform:

(1) the difficult practice of self-vow, because one vows to undertake the aspiration for unexcelled Bodhi; (2) the difficult practice of non-retrogression, [enduring] the manifold sufferings of birth and death...

1. The difficult practice of non-retrogression, because one does not fall back. 2. The difficult practice of non-opposition, because one does not abandon any sentient beings, even though they engage in perverse conduct. 3. The difficult practice of presence, because one manifests all manner of beneficial deeds toward those sentient beings who are one's enemies.

4. The difficult practice of non-attachment, because although born in the world, one is not defiled by worldly dharmas. 5. The difficult practice of resolute conviction, because although one has not yet fully realized it, one generates faith and understanding in all that is vast and profound within the Mahāyāna.

(7) The difficult practice of thorough penetration, because it possesses the capacity to thoroughly penetrate the selflessness of persons and phenomena; (8) the difficult practice of subsequent realization, because it is able to realize the profound and secret terminology spoken by all Tathāgatas;

(9) the difficult practice of non-abandonment and non-attachment, because one does not abandon *saṃsāra* yet remains unstained by it; (10) the difficult practice of application, because one is able to cultivate the abidings of all Buddhas, which transcend all obstacles, and throughout the limits of *saṃsāra*, spontaneously and without effort, constantly perform all deeds that benefit the welfare of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is able to induce the perfection of the *pāramitās*, the maturation of sentient beings, and the purification of the Buddha-fields.
Because it is the nature of the Buddhas' lands and dharmas, one should know that this is also a distinction in the activity of the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The distinctions in activity not previously mentioned are now further revealed here as the activities of the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration: namely, that by relying on *samādhi*, bodhisattvas are able to cultivate all the *pāramitās*;

furthermore, by relying on this concentration, they are able to skillfully bring all sentient beings to maturity, employing various means such as supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to lead sentient beings into the True Dharma. Moreover, through this power, they are able to skillfully purify all Buddha-lands and attain mastery over the mind, acting according to their wishes.

Because it is able to accomplish various Buddha-lands such as those of gold and silver; furthermore, by this power, one is able to correctly cultivate and accumulate all Buddha-dharmas. (This is the differentiation of the activity of *samādhi*. There are three types of the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*):
first, preparatory non-conceptual wisdom, which refers to the superior skillful means-intelligence prior to the contemplation of *tathatā*;

second, fundamental non-conceptual wisdom, which refers to the wisdom of the contemplation of *tathatā*; third, subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom, which refers to the [wisdom] following the contemplation...
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is able to give rise to various activities. The *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) states:

"The three types of wisdom refer to obtaining the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation from the signless Mahāyāna teachings, thereby entering into the emptiness of conceptual characteristics; these are collectively termed the non-conceptual preparatory prajñā (*anirvikalpa-prayoga-prajñā*).
If one enters into the three natures of non-substantiality, one obtains non-conceptual wisdom, which is termed the non-conceptual fundamental [wisdom] (*anirvikalpa-mūla*)."

Prajñā: When one attains fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and subsequently enters meditative observation, whether one contemplates for oneself or explains it to others according to what has been realized, this is called "subsequently attained non-conceptual prajñā. It is by virtue of possessing this meaning [that it is so designated].
Therefore, it is said that there are three categories of *prajñā*. These three may be considered in terms of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),

their basis (*āśraya*), their causal conditions (*pratyaya*), their objects of focus (*ālambana*), their modes of activity (*ākāra*), their support (*parigraha*), their companions (*sahāya*), their maturation (*vipāka*), their outflow (*niṣyanda*),

their renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*), their culmination (*niṣṭhāgata*), their benefits of preparatory effort, non-conceptualization, and subsequent attainment (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-pṛṣṭhalabdha-anuśaṃsa*), or their distinctions (*viśeṣa*).

If there is no post-attainment non-conceptualization through analogy, and if there is no effortless engagement in activities, and if it is profoundly deep, one should know that non-conceptual wisdom is called the excellence of higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
(The intent here is to state that non-conceptual wisdom is named higher wisdom; this further consists of three types:

first, preparatory non-conceptual wisdom, which refers to the wisdom of investigation; second, fundamental non-conceptual wisdom, which refers to the wisdom of direct realization; third, post-attainment non-conceptual wisdom, which refers to the wisdom that initiates activity. Among these, the wisdom of aspiration is the first excellence.)

Higher wisdom; wisdom of internal realization—this is the second higher wisdom; wisdom that sustains and maintains—this is the third higher wisdom. For now, we shall establish non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), because it alone permeates both cause and fruit. As for the wisdom of investigation (*vitarka-jñāna*):

This is the cause of this wisdom; the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) is its fruit. Thus, while establishing this [wisdom], it simultaneously establishes the other two. Now, within this context, the first [aspect] is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the last is its profundity (*gambhīratā*); [the text] provides an extensive explanation of this wisdom.

Herein, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) has as its intrinsic nature the departure from five types of characteristics. First, it departs from the absence of mental attention (*amanasikāra*).

Second, because it is free from the stage of having applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and its faults; third, because it is free from the tranquility of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*);
fourth, because it is free from the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*); and fifth, because it is free from conceptualizing the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*) in various ways.

One should know that being free from these five characteristics is what is called non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). (First, one should explain the non-conceptual wisdom: its essential nature (*svabhāva*), which is here termed its "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). That is to say, the non-conceptual [wisdom] of all bodhisattvas...)

A distinct cognition has as its intrinsic nature the departure from five kinds of characteristics. Regarding the departure from these five characteristics: if non-conceptual wisdom were simply the absence of mental attention (*manasikāra*), then states such as sleep, intoxication, or fainting would constitute non-conceptual wisdom.

If non-conceptual wisdom were that which transcends the stages of applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-bhūmi*), then all stages from the second dhyāna upward would constitute non-conceptual wisdom. If this were the case, worldly beings would attain non-conceptual wisdom.

If non-conceptual wisdom were the state in which the mind and mental factors do not function during the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*) and similar states, then because there is no mind in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and other such states, wisdom would fail to exist there. If non-conceptual wisdom were like the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa*), then it would be just like those various forms.

If it were dull and devoid of thought, this wisdom would likewise have to be dull and devoid of thought. Furthermore, there is another point: if it were like the nature of form (*rūpa*), wisdom could not be established as such.

If it were to function by conceptualizing the true object (*tattvārtha*) in a different way, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) would necessarily possess conceptualization—namely, the conceptualization that says, "This is the true object. When wisdom is free from these five characteristics, functions with respect to the true object, and does not conceptualize the true object in any other way, this is non-conceptual wisdom regarding the true object.

When such wisdom takes the true object as its object, it is like visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), which does not conceptualize; this is the meaning [of its being non-conceptual]. Thus, the non-conceptual wisdom described here is established.

Within the section on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), further verses are spoken. The verse on essential nature (*svabhāva*) says: "The essential nature of all Bodhisattvas is the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) that is far removed from five kinds of characteristics.
[The meaning of "true" is as explained above. Essential nature and self-substance (*ātman*) are not different in meaning, just as it is said of a ring and a bracelet.]
[This is] the essence of gold itself). The supporting verse says: "The support of all Bodhisattvas is not mind, yet it is mind;

it is non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna), which is not of the nature of mental deliberation. Regarding this described non-conceptual wisdom: does it depend upon mind, or does it depend upon what is not mind?

If one says it depends upon mind—since the term "mind" has the characteristic of deliberation (*manana*), that which functions in dependence upon mind cannot be non-conceptual; thus, this is unreasonable. If it depends upon what is not mind, then like various material forms (*rūpa*), it would not constitute wisdom; this too is unreasonable. To avoid these two faults:

Therefore, this verse is spoken: "That which is not of the nature of thought" means that the basis of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is not the mind (*citta*), because it is not of the nature of thought. Nor is it not-mind, because it is of the same category as the mind, serving as its support.

By taking the mind as its cause, through the power of repeated cultivation, it attains this state and is thus called "of the nature of the mind. This demonstrates that the mind which is the support of wisdom transcends all conceptualization and discrimination. The verse on causes and conditions says:

"The causes and conditions for all Bodhisattvas Are the hearing of the teachings (*śruta-vāsanā*) And the cultivation of correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*); This is non-conceptual wisdom."

Regarding the causal conditions for the bodhisattvas: it means that this wisdom arises because of that [condition]. "That which has words" (*sābhilāpa*) refers to the vocal sounds of others concerning the Mahāyāna; thus it is called "having words. "Hearing" (*śruta*) means listening; it refers specifically to that and nothing else.

The specific capacity induced by this is termed "perfuming" (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, regarding "proper mental attention" (*yoniśomanasikāra*): it means that the mental verbalization arising with this perfuming as its cause constitutes proper mental attention.

Non-conceptual wisdom arises based on this, and because it accords with the purification of reality, it is called "proper" (*yoniśas*). Since wisdom must necessarily have an object, the verse concerning the focal object says: The focal object of all bodhisattvas Is the ineffable dharma.

Nature (*dharmatā*) is non-conceptual wisdom. Regarding "the ineffable nature of reality (*tathatā*), which is the nature of selflessness": this means that all phenomena are ineffable by virtue of their imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

What is called "ineffability"? It refers to the *tathatā* manifested by the nature of selflessness. The person (*pudgala*) and all phenomena, being grasped through imagination, lack intrinsic nature; this is called "selflessness. The existence manifested by this very absence of nature is termed *tathatā*.

This statement is made so that one does not fall into the view of nihilism. The commentary on "absence of nature" explains: it refers to the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature in phenomena that are expressible; it is the departure from the expressible imagined nature.

Regarding the meaning of the nature of the grasped self-nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), in order to establish this meaning and make it clear, it is the suchness (*tathatā*) manifested by the non-existence of all persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*). It is the object of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is liberated from the two extremes of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*).

Since there is an object of cognition (*ālambana-dharma*), there must necessarily be a mode of activity (*ākāra*). The verse says: "The modes of activity of all Bodhisattvas, Furthermore, within the object of cognition, Are non-conceptual wisdom;
That which is known by them is signless (*animitta*). [Commentary: Within the object of cognition, they proceed in a manner that conforms to it; therefore, [they are called modes of activity].

Regarding the mode of activity (*ākāra*): non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) operates in a manner that conforms to the object of suchness (*tathatā*). Wisdom and suchness are equal and identical; it takes the "characteristic of being without characteristics" as its mode of activity.

Just as the eye perceives form and sees characteristics such as blue, yet this blue and so forth are not distinct from the form itself, so too is it here: there is no distinct mode of activity between wisdom and suchness. (There are two verses explaining these two points to resolve doubts, which are omitted here). What does non-conceptual wisdom sustain? The verse says:
The sustenance of all Bodhisattvas is this non-conceptual wisdom, followed by the subsequently attained [wisdom].

Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*): they are for the purpose of advancing and increasing [the practice] (by means of the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom, one attains the bodhisattva conduct; this conduct relies upon non-conceptual wisdom).

As for "for the purpose of advancing and increasing," it is in order to cause such bodhisattva conducts to increase; thus, non-conceptual wisdom is their support. Furthermore, what serves as the accompaniment for this wisdom?
The verse says: The companions of all Bodhisattvas are explained as being the two kinds of paths. These are of a non-conceptual nature and consist of the five perfections (pāramitās).

Regarding the two kinds of paths: first, the path of equipment (sambhāra-mārga); second, the path of reliance (niśraya-mārga). The path of equipment refers to the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence. The path of reliance refers to...

This is precisely the dhyāna-pāramitā. Through the various virtues produced by the previously mentioned pāramitās, and by relying upon the dhyāna-pāramitā, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is generated and grows. This wisdom is called the prajñā-pāramitā.
Until the fruit of Buddhahood is attained, in what location does this non-conceptual wisdom experience its maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*)?
The verse says: The maturation of all Bodhisattvas occurs within the two assemblies of the Buddhas; it is non-conceptual.

Wisdom. By means of application, one realizes [it] (within the two assemblies of the Buddha: that is, within the assembly of the *saṃbhogakāya* and the assembly of the *nirmāṇakāya*). When non-conceptual application functions, [this occurs].

One undergoes birth and receives the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) within the assembly of the *nirmāṇakāya*. If one has already realized non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one undergoes birth and receives the ripening fruit within the assembly of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
To clarify this meaning, it is further stated that "non-conceptual wisdom is realized through application" (*prayoga*). What is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of this? The verse says:

The outflow of all Bodhisattvas, In their successive future births, Is this non-conceptual wisdom, Whose essence becomes increasingly superior. [This refers to] the two assemblies of the [Buddha’s] bodies. In their preceding births, the non-conceptual wisdom...

One should know that their subsequent successive births become increasingly superior; this is precisely their *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruit). Regarding the departure (*niryāṇa*) of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), the verse says:
"The departure of all Bodhisattvas consists in attaining the correspondence with fulfillment; this is non-conceptual wisdom. One should know it pertains to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

(At the first stage, the Stage of Extreme Joy, upon entering the Path of Seeing, one perceives the principle of non-conceptuality across all stages and thus first attains departure. Subsequently, during the Path of Cultivation, one finally attains the correspondence with the fulfillment of the various stages. [Non-conceptual Wisdom]
Regarding wisdom: what constitutes its culmination? The verse says: "The culmination of all Bodhisattvas is the attainment of the three pure bodies;

this is non-conceptual wisdom that attains supreme mastery. (As for "the three pure bodies": although the three bodies are attained during the first stage (*bhūmi*), they are not yet pure. It is only upon reaching the tenth stage that they become pure and are then termed "culmination.

Therefore, it is said that at that time one attains the pure three bodies. Regarding "attaining supreme mastery": it means that at that time, non-conceptual wisdom not only attains the pure three bodies, but also attains supreme [mastery].)
Because of these ten kinds of mastery, it is called "ultimate. What are the benefits of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)? There are three types.
Regarding the benefit of being untainted (*asaṃkliṣṭa*) for such preparatory non-conceptual wisdom, what is the analogy? The verse says: Just as space is untainted, so is this non-conceptual wisdom;
by means of mere faith and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), even various extremely heavy evils [are overcome]. (Preparatory Non-conceptual Wisdom)

Distinctive wisdom (*viśeṣajñāna*). This refers to when Bodhisattvas first hear from others the principle of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*); subsequently, although they are not yet able to personally perceive this principle themselves, they give rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). Next, taking this resolute conviction as their basis, they employ skillful means to investigate and seek the principle of non-conceptuality;

this is called "preparatory non-conceptual wisdom" (*prayogika-nirvikalpajñāna*). Because it can give rise to non-conceptual wisdom, it also receives the name "non-conceptual. Regarding the three questions on wisdom in Vasubandhu’s commentary, the first question asks: how does one become unstained?

The answer is: "Like space, it is unstained. Next, the question is asked: "From what does it attain this lack of stain? The answer is: "From various kinds of extremely heavy evils. Finally, the question is asked: "By means of what does it attain this lack of stain? The answer is: "It is solely through faith and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*.

This means that it attains the state of being unstained by taking as its causes solely faith and the resolute conviction born of wisdom. Vasubandhu says: "The statement 'various kinds of extremely heavy evils' is spoken in order to demonstrate that those [evils] cannot defile it. The statement 'solely through faith and resolute conviction' is spoken in order to demonstrate the cause for their inability to defile it.

Because one gives rise to excellence by means of faith and delighting in the principle of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*), one is able to counteract the various evil destinies. This demonstrates that all evils do not defile it. In this context, the faculty (*indriya*)...
Regarding the non-conceptual wisdom that is fundamentally free from defilement and possesses supreme benefits, what is its analogy?

The verse says: "Just as space is undefiled, so is non-conceptual wisdom; It is liberated from all obstructions and attains the state of accomplishment. From what is it liberated? It is liberated from all obstructions. By means of what is it liberated?

It is by means of the attainment of accomplishment (*sādhana-yoga*). Such liberation occurs because, throughout the various stages (*bhūmi*), one takes the attainment of accomplishment as the cause. This demonstrates non-conceptual wisdom.

"Intelligence (*prajñā*) cures all hindrances. Wuxing says: "All hindrances" refers to the two hindrances of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) and the cognizable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). "Attaining the correspondence of accomplishment" means being in correspondence with attainment from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up until the stage of Buddhahood, which is the correspondence of accomplishment.
Regarding the subsequent non-conceptual wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) within this context, which possesses the excellence of being unstained—what is its analogy?
The verse says: "Just as space is unstained, so is this non-conceptual wisdom; It constantly operates within the world, yet is not stained by worldly phenomena.

By the power of this wisdom, one observes the various matters for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, and thus intentionally goes to take birth in that world. Once born, one cannot be stained by any worldly phenomena. There are eight such worldly phenomena: first, gain (*lābha*); second, loss (*alābha*).

Praise (3), disparagement (4), commendation (5), censure (6), suffering (7), and pleasure (8) arise from non-conceptual wisdom; therefore, this wisdom also receives the name "non-conceptual. Now, the distinctions between these three types of wisdom shall be clarified.
What is the difference between these three kinds of wisdom? The verse says: Like a mute person seeking to grasp an object; like a mute person actually grasping an object.

The three wisdoms are illustrated by these analogies: like a non-dumb person receiving meaning; like a fool seeking to receive meaning; and like a fool actually receiving meaning; and like a non-fool receiving meaning.
The three wisdoms are illustrated by these analogies: like the five [sense-consciousnesses] seeking to receive meaning; like the five [sense-consciousnesses] actually receiving meaning;
and like the *manas* receiving meaning. The three wisdoms are illustrated by these analogies: like one who has not yet understood a treatise seeking that treatise.

The "receiving of the meaning of the Dharma" follows a sequence that serves as a metaphor for the three types of wisdom. One should understand that the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) and so forth are taught through such metaphors to reveal the distinctions in the characteristics of these three wisdoms.

"Just as a mute person seeks to receive an object": this is like a mute person who, while seeking to perceive an object, is neither able to perceive it nor to speak of it. In the same way, the non-conceptual wisdom of the preparatory stage (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) seeks to realize *tathatā* (suchness), yet has not yet realized it;

it is quiescent and beyond verbal expression—know that it is likewise. "Just as a mute person correctly receives an object": this is like a mute person who correctly perceives an object without any verbal expression. In the same way, the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) correctly realizes *tathatā*, being free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

It should be understood that it is likewise so. Just as one who is not mute perceives objects—just as a person who is not mute perceives various objects and gives rise to verbal expressions—so too should it be understood that subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna) reflects upon *tathatā*, realizes its object through direct perception, and is able to give rise to verbal teachings;

it is just like this. By this principle, the verse concerning "the fool" is explained. Just as the five [consciousnesses] seek to perceive objects—just as the five consciousnesses seek to perceive their objects, and although they have what is sought, they are without conceptualization—so too should it be understood that preparatory non-conceptual wisdom (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is likewise.

Just as the five [consciousnesses] correctly perceive objects—just as the five consciousnesses correctly perceive their objects and are free from all conceptualization—so too should it be understood that fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is likewise. Just as the final...

Regarding the meaning of "reception" (*anubhava*): it is like the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which can both receive objects and perform discrimination; one should know that the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is likewise so.

Just as one who does not yet understand a treatise seeks it out to receive its doctrinal meaning, or just as one who does not yet understand a treatise seeks to recite it but has not yet mastered the recitation—so too should one know the preparatory non-conceptual wisdom (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) to be like this. Just as one studies a treatise and grasps its words and letters—so too should one know the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) to be like this.

Just as one who has already studied and practiced attains mastery over the doctrinal meaning—so too should one know the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom to be like this. Through these many analogies, corresponding respectively to their numerical order, the three [stages] beginning with the preparatory stage are illustrated.

[The Distinction of Wisdom]. Next, the distinctions between the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms are illustrated through analogies. The verse says: "Just as when a person closes their eyes, That is non-conceptual wisdom;
When those very same eyes are opened again, Subsequently attained wisdom is likewise so. One should know it to be like space."

This is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), in which material forms appear; subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) is likewise so. By these two verses, the distinction between the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms is revealed:

[the former] is like closing one's eyes, while [the latter] is like opening them; [the former] is like the appearance of forms in empty space. Both wisdoms are thus manifested: one is non-conceptual and the other is conceptual; one is equal and the other is unequal. As for preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*), it has not yet realized anything.

Therefore, these are not explained in detail. Furthermore, preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) is the cause of this fundamental wisdom, while subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is its fruit. Thus, for now, we shall distinguish the activities accomplished by non-conceptual wisdom (the cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom resulting in the fruit of Buddhahood).
Since there is no conceptual discrimination, how can one perform deeds that benefit sentient beings? The verse says:

Just as the wish-fulfilling gem and celestial music accomplish their own purposes without thought, so too do the various deeds of a Buddha constantly accomplish their tasks while remaining free from thought—just as they accomplish what is to be done while being free from conceptual discrimination.

In this verse, the wish-fulfilling jewel (*maṇi*) and celestial music serve as metaphors for manifestation. Just as the wish-fulfilling jewel, though devoid of conceptual discrimination, can accomplish whatever matters are desired by sentient beings according to their inclinations; and just as celestial music, though there is no one to strike or play it, [arises spontaneously].

According to the inclinations of sentient beings born in those various places, they produce diverse sounds. In this way, it should be understood that although the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is free from conceptualization, it is nevertheless capable of accomplishing various activities.
Next, the profundity of this non-conceptual wisdom shall be revealed. Does this wisdom function by taking the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its object, or does it take other objects?
If so, what is the fault? If it takes conceptualization as its object, it would not be "non-conceptual."

The nature [of the dependent origination] would not be established. If it were to take other objects as its conditions, since those other objects definitely do not exist, how could it take them as conditions?
The verse says: It is neither this nor another; It is not cognition, yet it is cognition; It is no different from the object; Thus cognition becomes non-conceptual.

[Non-conceptual wisdom does not take conceptualization as its condition, because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is itself non-conceptual. It does not become non-conceptual by taking conceptualization as its condition, nor does it take other things as its objective sphere. Rather, it takes this very [dependent nature] as its condition.]

Because it takes the conceptualization of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as its object, it cannot be definitively stated whether phenomena and their nature are identical or different. Therefore, this wisdom cannot be definitively described as having either a conceptualized object or a non-conceptualized object; the same applies to its own essence.

It cannot be said that this is definitively wisdom, such as preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) or subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), because conceptualization is absent therein. Nor can it be said that it is definitively not wisdom, because it takes preparatory wisdom as its preceding cause.

When wisdom becomes non-conceptual by being no different from its object, one cannot differentiate between "this is the knowing subject" and "this is the known object," nor between grasper and grasped, because conceptualization is absent.

This wisdom and its object possess no marks of distinction, like space and the light within space; therefore, this wisdom becomes non-conceptual. Other sūtras state that the nature of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-svabhāva*) is without differentiation.
[Answer: It is distinct. In order to demonstrate the meaning of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa*), another verse is spoken:

"One should know that all phenomena (*dharma*) Are by nature non-conceptual; Because that which is conceptualized does not exist, Non-conceptual wisdom [is established]. [Regarding "because that which is conceptualized does not exist"]:

this is because the objects of conceptualization—the meanings grasped through pervasive imagination (*parikalpita*)—are eternally non-existent. Other sūtras state that the nature of all phenomena is non-conceptual. If all phenomena are by their very nature non-conceptual from the beginning, why is it that all classes of sentient beings...

From the very beginning, they have been naturally liberated without the exertion of effort, for in them there is no non-conceptual wisdom. Because those sentient beings have not, from the outset, given rise to the true knowledge that directly realizes the non-conceptual nature of all phenomena.

For all bodhisattvas, regarding all phenomena, non-conceptual nature is the cause of their spiritual lineage; once realized wisdom has arisen through this principle, bodhisattvas are able to attain liberation, whereas other sentient beings are not.

Within this context, there are three types of preparatory non-conceptual wisdom, distinguished by the differences in their causes and conditions, their inducement, and their repeated cultivation (that is, these three distinctions of preparatory wisdom arise either through the power of the spiritual lineage, or through the power of inducement from previous lives, or through the power of repeated cultivation in the present). Or...

Regarding the power of the lineage (*gotrabala*): it arises because the lineage serves as its cause. Regarding the power of the inducement from previous lives: it arises because of the repeated practice performed during previous lives serving as its cause. Regarding the power of present repeated practice: it arises because the effort of the person (*puruṣakāra*) in the present life serves as its cause.
Fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*) also has three types, distinguished by being contented, non-erroneous, and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
Among these, one should know that "non-conceptual [wisdom] through contentment" refers to having reached the ultimate limit of hearing and reflection (*śrutacintā-niṣṭhāgata*).

Because of contentment, one no longer engages in conceptual discrimination; therefore, it is called "the non-conceptual wisdom of contentment. This means that when Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjanabhūmi) attain the culmination of the wisdom derived from hearing, reflection, and meditation, they give rise to contentment and think as follows:

Whatever has been heard and contemplated reaches its ultimate limit here. For this reason, it is called the non-conceptual wisdom of contentment. Furthermore, there is another meaning: one should know that there is also the non-conceptual wisdom of contentment in the world, namely, among all sentient beings.

Upon reaching the "summit of existence" (*bhavāgra*), they perceive it as *nirvāṇa* and give rise to contentment, thinking: "Beyond this, there is no further place to go. Therefore, this is called the non-conceptual wisdom of contentment. Regarding "non-inverted non-conceptual wisdom," this refers to the Śrāvakas and others;

one should know that they penetrate *tathatā* and attain the four non-inverted cognitions of impermanence and so forth. These four—inverted conceptualizations such as impermanence—are termed "non-inverted non-conceptual wisdom. Regarding "non-proliferated non-conceptual wisdom," this refers to the Bodhisattvas;

one should know that for Bodhisattvas, there is no proliferation regarding any phenomena up to and including *bodhi*. One should know that the *tathatā* realized by this wisdom transcends the path of names and words and surpasses the domain of worldly cognition. For this reason...
It cannot be expressed by names and words, nor can it be fully understood by any worldly knowledge. Subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom has five aspects, namely: thorough penetration.
Because of the distinctions between recollecting, establishing, synthesizing, according to intention, and deliberative discernment (these five distinctions of subsequently attained wisdom:

first, discernment of thorough penetration; second, discernment of recollection; third, discernment of establishment; fourth, discernment of synthesis; fifth, discernment according to intention). Among these, "discernment of thorough penetration" refers to the discernment at the time of penetration: "I have thoroughly penetrated."

Regarding the analytical investigation herein: "mental apprehension" refers to discernment; "discernment following recollection" means that upon emerging from this [state], one reflects and says, "I have realized the nature of non-conceptuality"; "discernment of establishment" means explaining this realization to others;

"discernment of synthesis" refers to the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its object collectively, observing them all as having a single characteristic, and by means of this wisdom, proceeding toward the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti*), or arising this wisdom again after the transformation has already occurred; and "discernment according to intention" is as previously described.

That is to say, whatever one contemplates, all is as one intends. Through this analytical discernment (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), one is able to transform earth and other elements into gold and so forth. One initiates this discernment in order to attain such mastery; therefore, it is called "discernment according to intention" (*yathāmanasikāra-cintā*).
There is further text remaining after this, which will not be cited here at length. Suppose someone were to ask:
regarding these three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) within the five stages, in what way do they exist—either as seeds or as manifest states? To this, he replies: "In the first stage, the *sambhāra*..."

Regarding the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*): if considered in terms of seeds, all three types of wisdom are present; if considered in terms of actual manifestation, there is only the wisdom of application.

This is because the two preceding stages have not yet attained the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), and thus lack both fundamental and subsequently attained wisdom. Regarding the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*):

Regarding these two types of wisdom (*prajñā*), there are two modes of manifestation (*samudācāra*) and three modes regarding their seeds (*bīja*). Because the time is brief, they lack the sense of applied effort (*prayoga*).
In the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), within the first seven grounds, both seeds and manifestations are of all three types;

this is because in the first seven grounds, the two cognitions—impure (*sāsrava*) and pure (*anāsrava*)—arise alternately, involving applied effort as one abandons afflictions and realizes the fruits. From the eighth ground onward... [the latter...]
On the third bhūmi and so forth, two kinds of three [aspects] are manifested; because they are effortless (*anābhoga*), they oppose applied effort (*prayoga*).
