that which takes three types of objects as its conditions during the causal stage is likewise so during the resultant stage. Because both the mental modes (*ākāra*) and the objects (*ālambana*) in the causal stage are subtle, they are said to be "unknowable.
It is not because they are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) that they are said to be unknowable; this wisdom likewise takes [those objects] as its condition.
Because it takes all conventional objects as its domain. It is also like the ālayavijñāna within the causal state (*hetu-bhūmi*):

because it can take the conventional as its object, when it takes the realm of *tathatā* (suchness) as its object, it is subsumed under non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); when it takes the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as its object, it is subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Question:
Question: Are the fundamental [wisdom] and the subsequently attained [wisdom] one or two? Answer: Their essence is one; they are divided into two according to their function.
When this [wisdom] takes suchness as its object, it is called fundamental [wisdom]; when it takes conventional truth as its object, it is called subsequently attained [wisdom]. Question:

Since these two wisdoms are of one essence, they arise without temporal sequence; how, then, can one be called "subsequently attained" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)? Answer: Because it realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is the "fundamental" (*mūla*) wisdom;

because it comprehends conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is the "subsequently attained" wisdom. Since the comprehension of conventionality necessarily depends upon the realization of the ultimate, the distinction of "before" and "after" is established as a mere designation;

it does not mean that the fundamental wisdom comes first and the subsequently attained wisdom follows later. The same division applies to the other two wisdoms, the "equality" (*samatā*) and the "wonderful" (*pratyavekṣaṇā*).

It consists of two [aspects]. Based on this, one should understand [the following]: Regarding the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*), there is one interpretation that it takes only the pure eight consciousnesses as its object, just as the latter seven wisdoms take the defiled eight consciousnesses as their objects.
There is another interpretation that it takes only *tathatā* (suchness) as its object, because the tenfold equality is precisely *tathatā*.

As for the Wisdom of Perfecting Purpose (*sādhu-vyavasthāna-jñāna*), it takes both the ultimate and conventional truths as its objects. To demonstrate that it takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* is cited;
to demonstrate that it takes conventional truth as its object, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* is cited. The ten types of equality have already been fully cited previously.

As for the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), it observes the self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena without obstruction; this refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is the observation of conventional truth. This is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

The wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) encompasses the unimpeded observation of the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; it is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*) and takes ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) as its object.

It is subsumed under fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*). Regarding the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), there is a view that it takes only the five present objects as its domain and does not take the past or future as its objects.
One interpretation holds that it takes all phenomena of the three periods of time as its universal object.

This is because the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that this wisdom is capable of performing the various transformative acts of the three types of karma, discerning the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings, and apprehending the meanings of the past, future, and present.
If it did not take [all things] as its universal object, how could it possess such functional capacities as described? Furthermore, this category of mind...

Because it arises from mental attention (*manasikāra*), because its occurrence is intermittent, and because the objects of focus (*ālambana*) are indeterminate as to whether they are few or many, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states that the five faculties operate toward the five objects; it does not say that this wisdom takes only the five objects as its domain.

Therefore, there is no contradiction. This wisdom necessarily depends on the power of mental attention to arise. Because it involves the deliverance of sentient beings, it takes conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) as its object.

Only when one contemplates the objects of the truths (*satya*) do the three types of transformative karma arise; therefore, this wisdom is subsumed solely under "subsequently attained" (*prṣṭhalabdha*) and does not extend to the "fundamental" (*mūla*).

Because the first three [wisdoms] rely upon the mental faculty (*manas*), both [types of] wisdom apply to them. This wisdom, however, relies only upon the physical faculties (*rūpīndriya*); thus, it is exclusively subsequently attained. Therefore it is said:
"Contemplating emptiness through transformed appearances is solely subsequently attained; even within the state of fruition (*phala*), it still does not directly express the ultimate truth."
Question: Since these four wisdoms equally and universally take both the ultimate and conventional realms as their objects, their sublime functions should likewise be indistinguishable.
Why, then, are they each divided into four? Answer: Although all are capable of universally taking all phenomena as their objects, their functions differ.
Specifically, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom manifests the self-enjoyment body and the self-enjoyment realm, and sustains the untainted [dharmas].

The category of the Great Mirror-like Wisdom is identical to the eighth consciousness within the causal stage; it manifests the Body of Enjoyment for Others and the Land of Enjoyment for Others for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.

The Wisdom of Accomplishing What is to be Done can manifest the Transformation Body and the Transformation Land. The category of the Wisdom of Equality observes the capacities of oneself and others as well as their faults, and bestows [teachings] according to the magnitude of their faculties.
The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation observes the functions and failings of both self and others, and according to the size of their faculties, bestows... [the great].
The rain of Dharma resolves all doubts and benefits sentient beings. Because there are many such categories with various distinctions, they are divided into four.
Below these four, there is a summary: these four wisdoms are all produced by and subsumed within bodhi;
this "produced attainment" is collectively termed bodhi. Furthermore, the four types of nirvāṇa mentioned previously are termed "attainment through manifestation."

Although there is a distinction between that which is produced by and that which is manifested by bodhi and nirvāṇa, both are nonetheless subsumed within the "attainment through transformation" discussed in the preceding section.
Question: Within the stage of the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti), there are generally four types.

Why, then, are only two of these attainments through transformation taken here, rather than the first three? Answer: Because the verse speaks of "realizing the attainment of the transformation of the basis," only these [two] are taken.
This refers to the two kinds of attainment (*prāpti*) acquired through transformation. Because both of these attainments are realized through this [process], it is asked:

Is this stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*) the stage of causal realization or the stage of resultant realization? The answer is: This is explained in terms of the stage of imminent realization within the cause;
it is not included within the stage of already-realized fruition. This concludes the fourth section above, the stage of cultivation.
[End. What are the characteristics of the subsequent stage of ultimate consummation? [From] "The body of blissful liberation, called the Dharma of the Great Muni" [to here].
This question and the verse response constitute the prose commentary by Vasubandhu, forming the thirtieth verse.
Having practiced from the beginning until reaching this ultimate point, it is therefore called "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*).

Within the path of liberation following the vajra-like mind, all stages extending to the end of the future are subsumed under this state. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states: "What is the ultimate path?

It refers to that which, by relying on the vajra-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), brings all heavy burdens (*dauṣṭhulya*) to permanent rest and all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) to permanent cessation."
Therefore, having eternally realized the fruit of disjunction from all [defilements], one subsequently attains, through the immediate transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), the ten qualities of those beyond training (*daśa-aśaikṣa-dharma*), and so forth.
The Commentary states: "The transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) attained during the preceding stage of cultivation... is entirely complete and purely untainted (*anāsrava*).
From this point downward, Dharmapāla and others explain the meaning of the verse in two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the specific clarification.
Within the direct explanation, the initial phrase of the verse is explained first. That which was transformed and attained in the preceding stage is precisely what is here termed "ultimate."
This refers to the state (*avasthā*). In the verse, this term reiterates the two fruits of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) from the preceding stage.

This fruit is comprised within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) of the ultimate stage. Regarding the "untainted realm," it means that the five abodes [of ignorance] are completely exhausted and the two types of death have forever ceased.
Infinite pure virtues are simultaneously and perfectly fulfilled, and because there is no longer any outflow or loss, it is called "untainted" (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the term "dhātu" (界), it carries the meaning of "to contain. This is because it can contain the great merits of the light of wisdom, dhāraṇī, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth.
It also carries the meaning of "cause," as it can produce the benefits and happiness of the five vehicles, both mundane and supramundane.
The five vehicles consist of humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas. Question: What is *nirvāṇa*?

Question: Since the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) is the pure realm (*viśuddhadhātu*) and can be exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), and since the category of bodhi-wisdom (*bodhiprajñā-skandha*) is originally composed of both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), why is it exclusively untainted?

Answer: Although the four types of wisdom-mind (*catur-jñāna-citta-varga*) pertain to both form and mind, they do not belong to the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) or its origin (*samudaya-satya*).
Because they are subsumed within the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), they are exclusively comprised of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

That is to say, all the qualities of the Buddha-ground—including the bodies, lands, dhāraṇīs, wisdoms, and supernormal powers—are produced from the untainted seeds of the four wisdoms, for one has eternally abandoned and exhausted all tainted seeds.
Question: It is certainly the case that the two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Enjoyment-body—are subsumed within the untainted Truth of the Path.
All transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) certainly possess birth and death; could they, then, also be subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*)? Answer:

Although their manifestations appear as bodies of birth and death—thus resembling the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*)—and although they seem to involve karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and so forth—thus resembling the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*)—the seeds of outflows (*āsrava*) have already been severed.
Therefore, in reality, they are untainted (*anāsrava*) and are subsumed under the Truth of the Path. Objection: The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises state that...

The fifteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth are exclusively *sāsrava* (with outflows). If the Tathāgata’s three bodies (*trikāya*) and four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) are all subsumed under the *anāsrava* (without outflows), how could it be that the Tathāgata lacks the five faculties (*indriya*), the five consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and the five external objects (*viṣaya*)?
There are two masters’ interpretations for resolving this difficulty. The first master represents the correct position of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*. He maintains that the Tathāgata’s merits...
The body and the land are profoundly deep and subtle; they are neither existent nor non-existent; they cannot be fathomed by the mind, nor can they be proclaimed by speech.

They are subsumed within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), and are not subsumed within the categories of the elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), or phenomena (*dharma*). Therefore, this does not contradict the principles of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

The second master asserts that [the Buddha-body] is produced from the Tathāgata’s sublime meditative concentration upon the faculties and their objects; it is subsumed as form (*rūpa*) within the untainted dharma-realm (*anāsrava-dharmadhātu*), because the Buddha...

This is because they are not subsumed under the category of the five impure consciousness-elements (*pañca-vijñāna-dhātu*). The impure five consciousnesses described in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* certainly do not belong to a Buddha.
Question: Since the five sense organs and the five objects necessarily depend on the transformation of consciousness, why are these organs and objects not subsumed under the five consciousnesses?
Answer: Although the faculties and objects are fixed based on the transformation of consciousness, there is a distinction between the coarse and the subtle.

This is because the five subtle, untainted (*anāsrava*) objects of the Tathāgata are not the same as the five coarse, tainted (*sāsrava*) objects; likewise, the five untainted consciousnesses are not the same as the five tainted consciousness-elements (*vijñānadhātu*).

This is because the Sūtras state that the untainted refers to the Buddha’s mind when it is in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whereas the treatises (*śāstra*) state that the tainted refers to...

Because the five consciousnesses are distracted. Question: Since the faculties and objects of the Tathāgata are not subsumed under the five consciousnesses, the wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) should likewise not be associated with the five consciousnesses.
With which consciousness is it associated? Answer: The wisdom of accomplished action is associated with the sixth [consciousness].
This is because it relies upon that [sixth consciousness] to initiate the three types of transformative karma (*nirmāṇa-karma*). Question: If that is so, then with...

What is the distinction between the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) and this [wisdom]? Answer: That wisdom of observation observes the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

This [wisdom of] accomplishing what is to be done takes the objects of phenomenal characteristics as its domain and initiates transformations through the three types of action (*trikarma*); therefore, they are not the same.
Question: Since these two have such differences, they should not arise simultaneously, because two consciousnesses of the same category do not co-arise.
How, then, can it be said that [the manas] arises in association with them? Answer: We do not admit that they arise simultaneously.

This principle is indeed appropriate. While their essence is one, their functions are distinct; what loss is there in this? Alternatively, the wisdom that accomplishes tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is not only associated with the sixth consciousness, but is also associated with the pure consciousness of the seventh [manas].
This is because the wisdom that accomplishes tasks relies upon the five material sense organs (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) and takes the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) as its domain;
it is thus a specific differentiation of the function of the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*). What, then, constitutes this differentiation?
Yes. That which manifests the marks of the *parasaṃbhogakāya* and its realm by means of the pure seventh consciousness is subsumed under the *samatājñāna* (the Wisdom of Equality).
That which manifests the *nirmāṇakāya* and its realm is subsumed under the *kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna* (the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks). Question:

If the *kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna* is associated with both the fifth and the seventh pure consciousnesses, would this wisdom not also include the five sensory consciousnesses? Answer: It is not that it transforms them.

The five consciousnesses can achieve the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*). That essence of wisdom is subsumed within those very consciousnesses, because the states of the transformation and non-transformation of consciousness and wisdom each possess their own distinct essence.

This is just as when *saṃsāra* is transformed into *nirvāṇa*, one cannot say that *nirvāṇa* is identical to *saṃsāra*; for the states of the transformation and non-transformation of *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa* are each distinct.
Because they possess substantial reality, one should not raise objections regarding this.

The third master maintains that the Tathāgata’s body and lands, as appropriate, are subsumed within the five aggregates (skandhas), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the eighteen elements (dhātus); and these three categories—
Sentient beings and Buddhas share [these realms] in common. The Tathāgata’s are untainted (*anāsrava*), while those of sentient beings are tainted (*sāsrava*); they do not overlap one another.

When the treatises state that fifteen of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are exclusively tainted, this is spoken from the perspective of the coarse and shallow objects of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and not from the perspective of the Mahāyāna;
therefore, it does not encompass everything. Why is this so? Because among the eighteen elements possessed by others, there is only the mind...

The faculties, mental consciousness, and the dharma-object are subsumed under the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). The remaining fifteen elements (*dhātu*) are called "outflowing" (*sāsrava*), and are thus described as coarse and superficial.

This does not mean that the Tathāgata is also outflowing. Although the eighteen elements accomplished by the Buddha are all outflow-free, they are not the sphere of knowledge accessible to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* excludes the final three [elements], but...
It is said that the fifteen elements (*dhātu*) are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*).

However, other passages state that the Buddha’s qualities, body, and lands are purely without-outflows (*anāsrava*), and are not subsumed under the categories of elements, bases (*āyatana*), and so forth that are with-outflows.

This meaning also implies that the Tathāgata’s elements, bases, and so forth are purely without-outflows; they are not the characteristics of elements, bases, and so forth that are known by the inferior wisdom of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Therefore...

This is incorrect. The principle ought to be thus. Why is this? Because the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) exhaustively encompass all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) things (the aggregate of the unconditioned [*asaṃskṛta*] is not known by the followers of the Two Vehicles);

because the phenomena of the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) exhaustively encompass all mundane and supramundane phenomena (the elements and bases outside of these phenomena are not known by the followers of the Two Vehicles);
and because mundane and supramundane phenomena do not transcend these three categories. If one were to depart from these three...

Regarding the statement that there are dharmas distinct from the categories: this would imply that besides the eighteen *dhātus* there are nineteen *dhātus*, besides the twelve *āyatanas* there are thirteen *āyatanas*, and that the five *skandhas* have six *skandhas*.
However, such things as nineteen *dhātus*, thirteen *āyatanas*, and six *skandhas* are like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit;
they are denied by the Buddha because he does not allow them to exist. Therefore, one should know that the Buddha...

Nor is it apart from the aggregates, bases, and elements. If you claim that because it transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is not subsumed under the elements, bases, and so forth, then would not these very things you have described—the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), bliss, goodness, permanence, and so on—be themselves conceptual proliferations?

Nor should it be said that this is not so. Furthermore, in various places it is taught that one transforms impermanent aggregates (*skandha*) to obtain permanent aggregates, and transforms impermanent elements (*dhātu*) to obtain permanent elements, and so forth.
Are these not, indeed, subsumed within the Tathāgata’s aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*āyatana*)?

Therefore, we know that the statement "the Tathāgata is not subsumed within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases" means that he is not characterized by the aggregates, bases, and elements as they are known by the inferior wisdom of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Therefore, it was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) as being otherwise; it is not a teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the nature of the five consciousnesses is distracted, this also refers to the tainted (*sāsrava*) five consciousnesses accomplished by those of other vehicles, and does not refer to the untainted (*anāsrava*) five consciousnesses of the Tathāgata.

Thus, one should know that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) of the Tathāgata are all fully complete and are comprised exclusively of the untainted. Therefore, it is said:
This is precisely the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
This fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is furthermore inconceivable, because it cannot be illustrated by any worldly metaphors.
[The text] provides two explanations for the three characters "inconceivable" (*acintya*): this fruit of the transformation of the basis is not only called the untainted realm, but is also named...
Inconceivable, because it transcends the path of discursive thought and verbal expression; this is the general explanation of "inconceivable.
It is subtle and profound, being realized within oneself; thus, it is not something attained through discursive thought, nor is it something that can be illustrated by any worldly analogy.
It is beyond the reach of verbal discourse.
Furthermore, because this is the nature of the wholesome, pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*), it is produced from wholesome seeds and is subsumed under untainted goodness (*anāsrava-kuśala*).

This is the third explanation of the word "wholesome" (*kuśala*). Purity is "white," while defilement is "black"; therefore, they are called "white dharmas. Below, *nirvāṇa* is used as an explanation.

"Good. Because the naturally pure *dharmadhātu* is free from the defiled phenomena of birth and death, because it is most tranquil, and because it is utterly secure, no demonic realms can disturb it. Below, "good" (*kuśala*) is explained by means of *bodhi*:

because the mental states of the four wisdoms function with wondrous efficacy in every direction, and because they possess the most supreme skillful means. Below, both are explained together by means of...
These seeds of bodhi and nirvāṇa all possess characteristics that are conducive and beneficial, and they are all contrary to the unwholesome (akuśala). An objection is raised:

the treatises state that the bases (āyatana) and so forth are not merely indeterminate (avyākṛta), but actually pertain to all three natures (tridhātu-svabhāva). How could the Tathāgata lack the five faculties (pañcendriya) and the three objects (tri-viṣaya)?
When he manifests as a body of birth-and-death (saṃsāra-kāya), this is precisely the characteristic of being tainted (sāsrava) and indeterminate. As it is said:

Regarding the karmas, afflictions, and so forth that have been manifested, these possess the characteristics of being outflowing (*sāsrava*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*). Now, it is said that they are "exclusively wholesome" (*kuśala*);
why is this? The answer states: there are three explanations here, as explained in detail previously.

First, all dharmas such as the bodies and lands of the Tathāgatas' merits are subsumed within cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*). Second, it is taught that the Buddha-lands and so forth are not subsumed under suffering (*duḥkha*) or its origin (*samudaya*).

Therefore, the third category—namely, the contaminated (*sāsrava*), neutral (*avyākṛta*), and unwholesome (*akuśala*) objects manifested within the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousness of a Tathāgata—are all produced from uncontaminated seeds;
thus, these three types of objects are exclusively of a wholesome nature (*kuśala*).
Furthermore, because this has a constant and inexhaustible duration, it reaches the limit of the future without interruption or end.
Fourth, the explanation of the character "constant" (*nitya*). "Inexhaustible duration" is the meaning of "constant. The *nirvāṇa* of the fourfold purity is "constant.
The four wisdoms (*jñāna*) of the fourfold [purity] are "constant" *bodhi*. Question: Since *bodhi* is obtained from that which is produced, it is not...

If intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirvāṇa*) were originally eternal, then because it arises from causes—and since that which arises from causes must necessarily cease due to those causes—it possesses both arising and ceasing;
how, then, could it be said to be eternal? Furthermore, the mental states of the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-citta-varga*) all belong to the categories of form and mind.
If one does not perceive form or mind, and they are not impermanent, why is it said that they are neither interrupted nor exhausted? Answer:
Although the mental states associated with the four wisdoms arise from causes, by the power of their original vows, the sentient beings to be converted have no end in time.
Extending to the limits of the future, it is uninterrupted and inexhaustible; thus, it possesses the meaning of permanence.
Furthermore, because it is blissful and free from affliction, both types of transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) are termed "bliss."

The five explanations of the two characters "peaceful" (*āśvasta*) and "blissful" (*sukha*): it is "peaceful" because there is no oppression; it is "blissful" because there is no affliction. The three phrases regarding purity refer to the peace and bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
The three phrases regarding the four wisdoms refer to the peace and bliss of *bodhi*. Regarding "permanently free from the nature of harm":

being free from the nature [of harm] means one is personally without oppression or affliction; being free from harming others means bringing peace and bliss to sentient beings. These two natures are able to [benefit] oneself...
It is peaceful and blissful, and it can also bring peace and bliss to all sentient beings; for this reason, both fruits are termed "peaceful and blissful.
This is because the two fruits of the twofold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) attained by the two vehicles are all subsumed within these [two fruits].

The sixfold analysis explains that what is called the "body of liberation" (*vimuktikāya*) for the Great Sage (*mahāmuni*) is termed the "body of liberation" when referring to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), but is termed the "dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*) when referring to the Great Sage.
Although the two vehicles attain the fruit of the twofold transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), they do so only by severing the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because they have not yet severed the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and lack the various merits for benefiting sentient beings, it is said that they possess no "extraordinary dharmas" (*viśeṣadharma*).

They merely abandon the bonds of afflictions (*kleśa*) and escape the death and rebirth of the segmented existence (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*); therefore, the body they attain is merely called "liberation" (*vimukti*).

If, however, it is the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, the five stages of dwelling are exhausted and the two types of death are extinguished; the four wisdoms are perfected and the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the one [Great Mirror Wisdom].
Having realized all phenomena and attained equal and perfect enlightenment, he silently realized the principle of wordless quiescence; therefore, he is named the Great Muni.

This Nirvāṇa and Bodhi—the two fruits of the transformation of the basis—realized by this Muni, which are eternally free from the two obstacles and are not the liberation body (vimuktikāya), are called the Dharma Body (dharmakāya).
This is because it possesses immeasurable and boundless great merits, such as the powers (bala) and fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya).
Because it is adorned by the Dharma, it is called the *dharmakāya*. What is meant by "body" (*kāya*)? It is said:

because this essence of bodhi-wisdom is fully endowed with a vast accumulation of immeasurable meritorious qualities, it is conventionally designated as a "body" in the sense of being an "accumulation.
What is meant by "accumulation"? It is said: this *dharmakāya* has five dharmas as its nature. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that it is pure *tathatā*.

Together with the four wisdom-aspects, these are called the five dharmas. Taking the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as nirvāṇa and the four wisdom-minds as bodhi, these two combined are termed the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). It is not that the single pure dharma-realm alone is called the dharma-body;
rather, through the two types of transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), these five dharmas are subsumed, for all five are [the dharma-body].
Because they are subsumed within the *dharmakāya*, the immeasurable and boundless qualities of great merit are, in brief, said to be ninefold. The verse says:

Immeasurable liberations, The spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), The absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the sublime knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), The analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), The purity of the various marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*), As well as the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), The non-guardings (*ārakṣa*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), And the permanent abandonment of all...
Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); the sublime dharma of non-forgetfulness; the qualities unique to a Tathāgata’s great compassion; and the sublime wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

As for the powers (*bala*), these are the ten powers of a Tathāgata: first, the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*); second, the power of knowing the ripening of one's own karma (*karmavipāka-jñānabala*);

third, the power of knowing the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis (*dhyānavimokṣasamādhisamāpatti-jñānabala*); fourth, the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties (*indriyaparāpara-jñānabala*)...
1. The power of knowing others' faculties; 2. the power of knowing various inclinations; 3. the power of knowing various elements; 4. the power of knowing the paths leading everywhere;
5. the power of knowing recollection of past abodes; 6. the power of knowing death and rebirth; 7. the power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows.

"Fearlessness" refers to the four fearlessnesses: first, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path;

and fourth, fearlessness regarding the teaching on the end of suffering. The term "and so forth" includes the remaining seven matters, as explained at length in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and the fourth chapter of the *Vyākhyāyukti*.
Thus, the Dharma-body has three distinct aspects (up to: which cause each [being] to obtain various benefits and matters of bliss.

The seventh section specifically clarifies the divisions of the Dharma-body, consisting of seven parts. First, it correctly clarifies the three aspects of the Dharma-body; this takes up the single Dharma-body.
The three bodies (trikāya) are distinguished according to essence (svabhāva), characteristic (lakṣaṇa), and function (vṛtti). The svabhāvakāya is the essence; the sambhogakāya is the characteristic;
and the nirmāṇakāya is the function. As the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śloka* states: "The svabhāva, dharma, sambhoga, and nirmāṇa [bodies] evolve in their respective distinctions."

That scripture and treatise state: "Although the essential nature of the pure *dharmadhātu* upon which all Tathāgatas rely is without differentiation, there are three kinds of distinct characteristics and different modes of transformation; therefore, it is called 'differentiated.

The verse refers to the 'dharma of intrinsic nature' (*svabhāva-dharma*), which is precisely the Tathāgata’s initial *svābhāvika-kāya*. Because its essence is eternally unchanging, it is termed 'intrinsic nature.'"
Because it is the basis for all qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), it is also called the *dharmakāya*. The verse says "enjoyment" (*saṃbhoga*);
this refers to the subsequent *saṃbhogakāya*, because it enables oneself and others to enjoy the manifold great joy of the Dharma.
The verse says "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*); this refers to the final *nirmāṇakāya*, which manifests in order to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Because it manifests various kinds of transformative activities. Question: What constitutes the essence of the *svābhāvikakāya* (Self-Nature Body)? Answer:
It is the very essence of the Tathāgata’s intrinsically pure *dharmatā*. This is because it is the basis upon which the two bodies—the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*—rely.
Since it is free from names and free from signs, transcending both speech and thought, it is fully endowed with infinite, true, and eternal virtues; it is the [nature] of all phenomena.

Because it is the nature of equal reality. Furthermore, why is it called the *dharmakāya*? It is said: because it is that upon which all meritorious qualities (*guṇadharma*) rely. The Great Master Pūrṇa (Pur-rin) said:

"That which serves as a standard and sustains [the mind] is 'Dharma' (*dharma*); that which is relied upon is called 'Body' (*kāya*). How is this known? The *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Light) states:
"The name 'Dharma' signifies that which is to be followed as a standard. All Buddhas follow it and thereby attain Buddhahood. *Mahā-*... [text continues]

Deyan said: "Profound stillness is the cessation of thought; profound silence is called 'severance. That it can serve as the basis for the manifestation of form and appearance—by this one knows [it is the Dharma-body].

Question: "If profound silence is called 'severance,' why do you say it is the Dharma-body? Answer: "The Dharma is truly nameless. It is for the sake of sentient beings' capacities that it is explained through expedient means;
to designate the essence of profound silence, we forcibly call it the 'Dharma-body. Question: "The essence of profound stillness should be identical to empty space."
He said: "All that possesses marks are, in fact, non-marks. To perceive the five tones as echoes from a valley is to know that there is truly no sound;

to understand all phenomena as dream-forms is to see that they are not form, yet emptiness and existence are non-dual. The Middle Way is thus clearly manifest; one must not, hearing of 'non-existence,' claim that emptiness is a state of annihilation.
"What is called the Sambhogakāya (Enjoyment Body)? He replied: "It is that which is able to fully provide for the enjoyment of both self and others."
Because of the various great dharmic joys, there are two kinds: first, self-enjoyment; second, other-enjoyment.
What is meant by self-enjoyment? It is said: that which is unknown to others, known only by the Buddha himself, and realized only by the Buddha himself.
This refers to the cultivation of immeasurable provisions of merit and wisdom throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, thereby adorning the *dharmatā*.
From this arise immeasurable, true merits, through which one attains the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and realizes the complete *saṃbhogakāya*.
Pervading the ocean of *padma-garbha* worlds, it remains serenely and eternally, constantly and spontaneously enjoyed in its vastness.

Because it is the joy of the Dharma. Furthermore, for what reason is it called the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body)? It is said: because it is obtained through cultivation over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), it is called the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Only this is real; all subsequent [bodies] are *nirmāṇakāyas* (emanation bodies). Pūrṇa-ruci says:

"Recompense" (*saṃbhoga*) refers to karmic fruition, as it is the fruit obtained from cultivating causes over three great eons (*tri-kalpa*). As for "body" (*kāya*), it is termed "body" based on the two meanings of reliance and continuity.
The meaning of "reliance" (āśraya) is that it serves as the basis for conditioned merits. The meaning of "continuity" (prabandha) is that it extends without interruption until the end of the future.
This refers to the fact that the boundless, true merits that have arisen continue in a serene flow until the end of the future;
this is precisely the meaning of reliance and continuity. What is meant by "enjoyment for others" (parasaṃbhoga)? It is said to be this very [state].
The Tathāgata, by means of his wisdom of equality, manifests a body of subtle and pure merit;

for the sake of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), he displays supernatural powers and preaches the Dharma, resolving their manifold doubts and enabling those Bodhisattvas to enjoy the bliss of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Because this [body] has ten aspects and appears to those with the capacities of the ten stages, these two types [of enjoyment] are combined and termed the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Body. What is meant by the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)? It is said: that which suddenly exists where there was nothing is called "transformation. The gathering and transformation of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is termed a "body.

This is the Tathāgata, who, through the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), manifests immeasurable transformation bodies according to the various types of beings for bodhisattvas prior to the stages, as well as for those of the two vehicles and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). He preaches the Dharma to them according to their capacities, causing them...
Each and every one attains benefit and happiness through the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) previously mentioned, which benefits both self and others.

This transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), however, is exclusively for the benefit of others. It consists of three types: first, the great transformation body; second, the minor transformation body; and third, the transformation according to type.
The Great Transformation Body possesses a body one thousand *zhang* in height and presides over a great trichiliocosm; it is the body for those whose capacities are vast and superior.

The Small Transformation Body is the golden body sixteen *zhang* in height, which presides over a single four-continent world; it is the body for those whose capacities are the two vehicles and ordinary beings.
As for transformation according to the species, he manifests as a monkey among monkeys and as a deer among deer; or, appearing as a dog or a common person, he manifests a body three feet in height.
The manifestation of the old woman in the eastern city within the palm of her hand also belongs to the category of "conforming to types" (*yathā-jāti*).
As with the three bodies mentioned above, they are all the Dharma-body, which has as its nature the five dharmas realized by the Muni. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"If the self-nature body did not exist, there would be no Dharma-body; it would be like the absence of the visual faculty. If the Dharma-body did not exist, there would be no enjoyment body."
For example, like visual consciousness. It should be understood that herein, the support (*āśraya*) and the supported (*āśrita*) serve as the illustrative analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*) of a similar property.
If there were no enjoyment of the body by the bodhisattvas who have already entered the great stages, there would be no enjoyment of the dharma-joy (*dharmasvāda*).

If there were no enjoyment of the dharma-joy, the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) would not be perfected. This is just as, for example, there would be no seeing of forms if there were no transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Bodhisattvas on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and Śrāvakas of inferior resolve who have first set out on the path would all be rendered without [the possibility of] such attainment;
therefore, it is certain that there must be three bodies (*trikāya*). Furthermore, it is said:

"For what reason is the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) not identical to the Essential Body (*svabhāva-kāya*)? Because of six reasons: first, because the form body (*rūpa-kāya*) is visible; second, because it is immeasurable..."
1. Because the distinctions among the Buddha’s assemblies can be observed; 2. Because the nature of what is seen is observed to be indeterminate according to one's dominant resolve (*adhimukti*);
3. Because the nature of what is seen is observed to fluctuate as it is perceived individually; 4.
Because various assemblies, such as bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and devas, are observed to be interspersed; 5. Because the ālayavijñāna and all [other consciousnesses]...

Because it can be seen that the transformation of consciousness and the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) are not logically consistent [with your position], it is unreasonable to claim that the Buddha’s enjoyment body (saṃbhoga-kāya) is identical to the nature body (svabhāva-kāya).
For what reason is the emanation body (nirmāṇa-kāya) not identical to the nature body? It is because of eight reasons.

Namely, since beginningless time, the bodhisattvas have attained non-retrogressive concentration (avaivartika-samādhi), yet they take birth in Tuṣita Heaven and among human beings; this would not be possible [if the emanation body were identical to the nature body].
It is not reasonable that these bodhisattvas, from long ago, have constantly recollected their past lives yet were unable to correctly understand the treatises on writing,
calculation, arithmetic, seals, and arts and crafts, nor their engagement with the enjoyment of sensual objects. Furthermore, it is not reasonable that these bodhisattvas,
having known for a long time the teachings of both poorly expounded and well-expounded doctrines, would go forth among the non-Buddhists.
This is not tenable. Furthermore, it is not tenable that bodhisattvas, having long since been able to thoroughly know the correct path of the three vehicles, would practice false asceticism.

Moreover, it is not tenable that bodhisattvas would abandon hundreds of millions of Jambudvīpas and instead attain perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of the true Dharma in only a single location.

If, apart from manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment, one were to perform buddha-activities in other places solely through an emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), then one should attain perfect enlightenment only in Tuṣita Heaven.

Why then is it not established that Buddhas appear simultaneously throughout all of Jambudvīpa? It is not so established because there is neither scriptural authority nor logical reasoning for it. Although...
There are many emanations, yet this does not contradict the statement that "only one Tathāgata appears in the world," because a single world-system is comprised of four continents.
Just as two wheel-turning kings do not appear simultaneously, so it is here. Regarding this, there is a verse:
"The Buddha’s subtle emanation bodies, equal in entering many wombs, manifest the turning of the wheel of perfect enlightenment in all its aspects. This is for the purpose of...

It would be illogical for one to bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, to aspire to practice, and to realize great enlightenment and ultimate nirvāṇa, because such aspiration and practice would be fruitless, resulting in the fault of futility.

Since the Buddha’s enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are impermanent, how can the sūtras state that the Tathāgata’s body is permanent? It is the *dharmakāya*, upon which these two depend, that is permanent.
Therefore, because the body of natural outflow (*niṣyanda-kāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) are constantly enjoyed without cessation,

and because they manifest repeatedly without ever being permanently interrupted— just as one constantly experiences pleasure or constantly bestows food— one should know that the Tathāgata’s body is likewise eternal.
Regarding the inclusion of the three bodies (*trikāya*) within the five dharmas: [it is said that] because they lack functions such as sense organs, they are not said to exist.

Second, regarding the inclusion of the three bodies within the five dharmas, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "There are five kinds of dharmas that encompass the stage of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi-bhūmi*).

What are these five? They are: the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-viśuddhi*), the great perfect mirror wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), and the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*)."

The wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) and the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). According to one interpretation, pure *tathatā* (suchness) and the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) comprise the self-nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*).

The wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) and the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) comprise the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), while the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done comprises the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
This is because the Sūtras state that *tathatā* is the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), and the Śāstras state that by transforming the ālayavijñāna, one attains it.

The *svābhāvika-kāya* (Self-nature Body) is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), which is attained through the transformation of the eighth consciousness; thus, one should know that the first two [wisdoms] subsume the Self-nature Body.
The Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) is as described in other treatises: it is able to manifest various Buddha-bodies in pure lands according to the inclinations of the bodhisattvas.
The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) is also as described in the treatises: it is able to manifest within great assemblies...

All sovereign activities consist of preaching the Dharma and severing doubts; furthermore, it is taught that by transforming the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), one attains the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Therefore, one knows that the middle two [wisdoms] subsume the Enjoyment Body. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Was to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) initiates all transformative activities (*nirmāṇakarma*).
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Was to Be Done initiates various [activities] throughout all realms.
Because there are immeasurable and inconceivable transformative manifestations, we know that the latter [of the two] subsumes the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Furthermore, since all three bodies of the Buddha are subsumed within the excellence of "wisdom" among the ten meanings, we know that all three bodies possess wisdom.

There is also the interpretation that the first [of the two] subsumes the *svābhāvikakāya*, as the four wisdoms are its essential nature, with which they are associated and co-existent, and which serves as the basis for the bodhisattvas on the stages...
The subtle aspect of one portion manifested by the *sāmbhogika-kāya* subsumes the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).
If it is the coarse aspect of one portion manifested for the sake of Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), it subsumes the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). Question:

Why does pure *tathatā* (suchness) consist only of the Nature Body (*svabhāva-kāya*) and not include the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*)? Answer: Because all the sūtras state that pure *tathatā* constitutes the Dharma Body (*dharma-kāya*).

The *Buddhapraśaṃsā-śāstra* states that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is without arising or ceasing; the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra* states that the Buddha’s self-nature body is eternally constant by nature;
and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the merit of receiving, upholding, and expounding that sūtra.
The *dharmakāya* is the cause for realization, whereas the other two bodies are the causes for birth;

thus, various sūtras and śāstras state that the *svabhāvakāya* (essential body) is common to both Buddhas and sentient beings, pervading all phenomena like space, not belonging to form or characteristics, and not belonging to conditioned things because it is neither a material nor a mental phenomenon.
Since the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is a material or mental phenomenon, [it is not the *svabhāvakāya*]. Question:
If that is so, why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that by transforming the ālayavijñāna one attains the svabhāvakāya? Answer:

By transforming the seeds of the two obstacles within the eighth consciousness, the dharmakāya is manifested; it is not said that the dharmakāya is identical to the ādarśajñāna (great perfect mirror wisdom).
Furthermore, regarding the statement that the dharmakāya is "endowed" within the excellence of the wisdoms, this means that the four wisdoms have the dharmakāya as their support.
Because the *dharmakāya* is that very reality (*tattva*), it is not said that all three bodies possess real wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*).
Although the *svabhāvakāya* (self-nature body) possesses infinite, true merits, because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it cannot be described as a substance such as matter or mind;
therefore, it is not subsumed under the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). One should rather say that the true merits arising from mirror-like wisdom, and...
The perfectly round, pure, and eternally pervasive form-body subsumes the self-enjoyment [body]. The subtle and pure body of merit arising from equanimity subsumes the other-enjoyment [body].
The various types of bodily forms manifested according to the categories of beings by the class of wisdom that accomplishes tasks [subsume the transformation body].
This subsumes the *nirmāṇakāya*. Question: How is it known that the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) subsumes the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*)? Answer:

The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states that the great perfect mirror wisdom is the enjoyment Buddha (*saṃbhogabuddha*), because by transforming the preceding seven consciousnesses, one attains true enjoyment.
Question: If mirror-like wisdom is designated as the enjoyment Buddha, does it also involve the transformation and abandonment of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)?
And one attains enjoyment. Why, then, is it said that it is the transformation of the *ālayavijñāna*? Answer:

Although enjoyment is attained through the transformation of the *ālayavijñāna*, this treatise specifically teaches that by transforming away the *ālayavijñāna*, one manifests the *svabhāva-dharmakāya*.

Therefore, regarding the attainment of enjoyment, it is omitted and not mentioned here. Furthermore, it is taught that the *svabhāva-dharmakāya* is without arising and without cessation; its nature is non-... [text ends].
It undergoes transformation, like empty space; it is attained through the cause of realization, not through the cause of birth.

Being signless and unconditioned, it is neither form nor mind, and therefore is not subsumed within the Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Since the Perfect Mirror Wisdom is contrary to the self-nature Dharmakāya, [it cannot be identical].

If it were not the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), to which body would it belong? Moreover, the enjoyment body subsumes the Tathāgata’s immeasurable, uncommon, conditioned, and true merits accumulated over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, as well as the realization of the extremely pure, eternal, and omnipresent form-body (*rūpakāya*).
Within the category of the four wisdoms (*jñāna*), all that possesses actual matter and mind is subsumed under the enjoyment body. Question: Regarding the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*)...

The *sāmbhogika-kāya* (Enjoyment Body) and the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (Emanation Body) also possess both form and mind. Why, then, are they not subsumed within the *ādarśa-jñāna* (Mirror-like Wisdom)? Answer:
Both the *parasaṃbhoga-kāya* (Body for Others' Enjoyment) and the *nirmāṇa-kāya* are manifestations displayed as skillful means (*upāya*) for the benefit of sentient beings;
they do not have the four wisdoms as their true essence. Although it is said that because wisdom is preeminent, the three bodies are fully subsumed [within wisdom], they are merely similar to wisdom.

Manifestation is not actual wisdom (*jñāna*). Alternatively, it is based upon fundamental actual wisdom that arises through skillful means (*upāya*), and is conventionally designated by the name "wisdom," though its essence is not real.
Therefore, it is said that because wisdom is preeminent, it fully encompasses the three bodies (*trikāya*); this does not mean that all three bodies possess actual wisdom.
Thus, the sutra speaks only of two types of wisdom that can manifest two bodies, but it does not say that the two bodies are themselves [wisdom].
Regarding the two wisdoms: thus one knows that both wisdoms are subsumed within self-enjoyment. Question:

Since the four wisdoms actually possess both form and mind, and are all subsumed within self-enjoyment, how can the other-enjoyment body and the transformation body—which lack actual form and mind—expound the Dharma to benefit sentient beings?
Answer: Although these two bodies lack actual mind, [they still manifest through the power of the wisdoms].

Regarding mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), there are manifested mental and mental-factor phenomena. Question: Since mental and mental-factor phenomena fundamentally lack physical form or substance, how can they manifest?
Answer: The Unsurpassed Greatly Awakened One is able, through inconceivable supernormal power (*ṛddhi-bala*), to manifest phenomena that lack physical form or substance.
If he were unable to manifest such formless phenomena, how could the Tathāgata manifest [himself]?
Regarding greed, hatred, and so forth: since the Tathāgata has long since severed the three poisons, how could śrāvakas and ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) all know the mind of the Tathāgata?
For even bodhisattvas on the stage of Equal Enlightenment cannot know even a small portion of the Tathāgata’s true mind;
how much less, then, could those below that level know it? Therefore, one should know that [the minds of] śrāvakas and...
That which is known by ordinary beings and others is merely the transformative mind of the Tathāgata.

For this reason, the Sūtra states that when the Tathāgata manifests the bodies of immeasurable classes of sentient beings through transformation, he is simultaneously able to manifest the minds of those immeasurable classes of sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s transformative wisdom (nirmāṇa-jñāna) manifests as the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.

It is also said that these transformations depend upon another's mind; that is, taking the real mind of another as the substantial essence (bimba), one further manifests the provisional objective parts (nimitta-bhāga) of mind and mental factors, which then serve as the objects perceived by sentient beings. Thus, we know that what is known and perceived by sentient beings...
Those who perceive [these] are all seeing the semblance-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the Tathāgata’s dharmas; they are not the true Tathāgata.
This is because the true Tathāgata cannot be known by the mind nor seen through signs. Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Upon the wisdom of the Tathāgata, these coarse signs—the mind, mental factors, and all such merits—manifest so that those in lower stages may be able to clearly perceive and understand them. If..."
In that case, how could those of the two vehicles or ordinary beings know the distinctions among all the Tathāgata’s qualities, such as his mental states and mental factors?
Furthermore, how is it that the Tathāgata, having already attained Buddhahood long ago, can still manifest various transformation bodies endowed with desire, hatred, and so forth?
Other sūtras also state that he transforms immeasurable classes of beings, causing them all to possess minds; they further speak of [his] transformations...
The body is also called "possessing mind" and is also called "without mind. It possesses a mind that depends on another, but lacks a mind that depends on itself;

therefore, it is said that the transformed mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) and so forth appear based upon the actual mind. However, these are merely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the actual mind, which appears as if possessing functions such as cognition and deliberation.
Like fire in a mirror, it has no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and arises in dependence upon various conditions, just like other states of mind.

Although it is stated elsewhere that there is no "transformative mind" (*nirmāṇacitta*) and so forth, because such things lack practical utility (*artha-kriyā*) as do actual minds, whereas transformed matter (*rūpa*) and so forth do possess real functional efficacy as do actual matter and so forth, they are therefore said to exist universally.
This is because the coarse characteristics (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*) of transformative minds and the like manifest clearly and are easily [perceived].
Because they understand it. This extends even to monkeys, who can know the mind of a Tathāgata; yet, if it were the Buddha’s actual mind, even the great Bodhisattvas could not comprehend it.

Furthermore, it is said that mental transformations (*citta-nirmāṇa*) are of two kinds: first, those associated with one's own body, which refers to the manifestation upon one's own mind of various distinct images of minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); second, those associated with the bodies of others, which refers to causing...

The other's mind also manifests various distinctions of images of minds and mental factors; these are both aspects of the object (nimittabhāga) appearing as if they were the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga).

According to one interpretation, the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can cause one's own mind to understand phenomena that are not its own sphere; this is called "transforming what belongs to oneself" (*svabhāgavikurvaṇa*).

To bestow grace upon sentient beings—causing those who are ignorant to understand profound and subtle dharmas, and causing those who have lost mindfulness to regain right recollection—is called "transforming the minds of others.
However, the mind itself is not transformed, because it lacks physical form. As the treatise states: "Because the mind has no form, it cannot be transformed.
Furthermore, it is said that a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is devoid of mind and mental factors; this refers to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) and...
It is said that these are produced by the power of concentration (*samādhi*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). However, their power of concentration is inferior;
they cannot manifest formless phenomena (*amūrtadharma*). The inconceivable concentrations of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, however, can manifest all things.
Otherwise, how could a Bodhisattva manifest desire, hatred, and so forth? How could Śrāvakas and even animals know the mind of the Tathāgata? How...?
The Sūtra states that the emanations of immeasurable classes are all endowed with mind. How, then, can it be said above that these emanations possess mental karma?

And how can the Sūtra say that they depend upon the minds of others? It is simply that while the emanated forms share the same functional utility as real forms, the emanated sense faculties and the mind do not.
It is merely that appearances manifest; they do not constitute actual functional utility. Furthermore, this statement is made with reference to the lower classes of beings.

If that were so, why does one not transform insentient things (*asattva*) to cause mental appearances to manifest? Since insentient things are already the objective-image (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the mind and its associates, how could one further cause mental appearances to arise within them?
If mental appearances were to manifest, they would be designated as sentient beings (*sattva*) and would no longer be subsumed under the category of the insentient. This is because...
Therefore, the *nirmāṇa-citta* (transformative mind) is described as having only two types.

Thus, although the three bodies (*tri-kāya*) all fully possess the merit of transformative characteristics for the purpose of benefiting and bringing happiness to others, there are three sets of merits of the three bodies.
That is to say, the *svabhāva-kāya* (essential body) possesses the true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true purity.

There are four kinds of qualities: it is *nitya* (permanent) because it is neither born nor extinguished; it is *sukha* (blissful) because there is no accumulation [of suffering]; it is *ātman* (self) because it is supremely sovereign;
it is *śubha* (pure) because it is free from defilement. It is "free from all impurities" because, from the very beginning, it has never been associated with any defiled phenomena.
It is "the basis of all virtues" because it is fully endowed with immeasurable intrinsic qualities.
Therefore, because its self-nature is suchness (tathatā) and equal, there are no distinctions of characteristics or functions between form and mind.
Since these distinctions of characteristics and functions are manifested in the gate of arising and ceasing, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:

"This aspect of the True Suchness of the mind reveals the essence of Mahāyāna; this aspect of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind can reveal the self-substance of Mahāyāna."
Because they function as marks [of realization]. As for the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body), it is comprised of the four wisdoms;
therefore, it is able to fully possess immeasurable, perfectly pure, eternal, and omnipresent sublime qualities of form, mind, and so forth—true merits that are enjoyed solely by itself.

As for the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (other-enjoyment body) and the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), they manifest exclusively in accordance with the inclinations of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and ordinary beings.
Manifesting as if they were form, mind, and so forth, these transformed marks and qualities cause sentient beings to obtain great benefit and happiness, and to attain great enjoyment.
Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Do these three bodies each possess distinct qualities?

The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body has the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of pure *tathatā* as its characteristic; it is a truly existent goodness, inherently pure, and remote [from defilement]..."

Because it is free from all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), because it is the basis for all meritorious qualities (*guṇa*), and because it is the true nature (*tattva*) of all meritorious qualities, it is called "endowed with all meritorious qualities. There is no distinction between form and mind regarding these meritorious qualities;
the Buddha’s Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) is fully endowed with the true meritorious qualities of all phenomena, such as form and mind, and serves as...

Regarding the merit of the manifested forms (*nirmāṇakāya*): the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) possesses exclusively all the meritorious qualities of manifesting forms, mind, and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that all three bodies possess merits numbering more than the sands of the Ganges.

Furthermore, the *svābhāvikakāya* (self-nature body) is primarily subsumed under self-benefit (*svārtha*), yet it belongs exclusively to benefit for others (*parārtha*) because it manifests for the sake of others.

Regarding these four bodies and two types of benefit, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Moreover, the *svābhāvikakāya*—being quiescent and blissful—is correctly subsumed within the merits of self-benefit;
yet, as a sovereign condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), it benefits sentient beings and thus also belongs to benefit for others. (Because of itself...)

The *svabhāvakāya* (nature body) acts as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for all sentient beings, causing them to obtain benefit and happiness. Because the *svabhāvakāya* arises in common with the Buddhas, it serves as a dominant condition for sentient beings, assisting them in its manifestation;

that is to say, when sentient beings abide in samādhi, they are able to see all Buddhas equally. Furthermore, it serves as the basis for the merits that benefit both [self and others] in the two other bodies (*kāyas*).
It is comprised of the two benefits. The Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) possesses two aspects: first, the aspect of enjoying the Dharma for oneself;

this refers to having cultivated practices for one's own benefit throughout three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), thereby perfecting the actual body of realized form and so forth, which allows one to experience subtle and sublime joy for oneself.
Second, the aspect of enjoying the Dharma for others; this refers to having cultivated practices for the benefit of others throughout three incalculable eons.

[This is] the practice. Having perfected the physical emanations (nirmāṇakāya) that realize [the goal], he manifests various forms and teaches various dharmas for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages (mahābhūmi), causing those bodhisattvas to experience the great joy of the Dharma.
Due to these two aspects, this body is sometimes said to be comprised solely of self-benefit, sometimes said to be comprised solely of benefit for others, and sometimes said to be comprised of both.

None of these are contradictory. As for the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it manifests various transformed forms solely for the benefit of others; therefore, it is subsumed under the category of benefiting others.
Furthermore, while the self-nature body (*svabhāvakāya*) abides in the dharma-realm land (*dharmadhātu-kṣetra*), the dimensions of its dependent bodies are likewise without fixed limit.
The fifth [point] concerns the mutual dependence of the bodies (*kāya*) and the lands (*bhūmi*). Regarding that which is supported by the *dharmakāya*: it relies upon the *dharmatā-bhūmi*.
Since there is only the single *dharmatā*, how can one distinguish between "body" and "land"? It is said: From the perspective of the meaning of that which depends [upon it], it is called "body";

from the perspective of the meaning of that which is depended upon, it is called "land. Furthermore, when it has the nature of being the body, it is termed the *dharmatā-kāya*; when it has the nature of being the land, it is termed the *dharmatā-bhūmi*. That is to say—
This is the true nature of the three lands and the three bodies (*trikāya*). Buddhas and sentient beings possess it equally;

for while sentient beings have not yet realized it, the Buddha has already realized it. Therefore, it is said: "Although there is no difference in the essence of these bodies and lands, they are distinguished because their attributes (*dharma*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ.

That is to say, when the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) belongs to the Buddha, it is the *dharmatākāya* (Dharma-nature body); when the *dharmatā* belongs to the Dharma, it is the *dharmakāya* (Dharma body).

Regarding the "nature-land" (*dharmatā-kṣetra*): because the nature varies according to its manifestations, it is described in this way. In the *Qingliang Shu* (Commentary by Qingliang), a question is raised:

"Are the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*) and the Dharma-nature land distinct, or not? If they are distinct, they cannot be called 'Dharma-nature,' for the nature is non-dual. If they are not distinct, there would be no distinction between the supported and the support.
The answer states that the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says: "The Dharma-body is constituted solely by the pure Dharma-realm (*viśuddha-dharmadhātu*)."

Furthermore, the dharma-nature (dharmatā) itself constitutes this oneness. Although its nature is of a single flavor, it is divided into three distinctions according to the characteristics of the body [of the Buddha] and the land [of the Buddha].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When reckoned among sentient beings, it is called buddha-nature; when reckoned among non-sentient things, it is called dharma-nature.
Though conventionally described in terms of subject and object, in reality there is no difference. These bodies and lands of the Buddha all belong to true suchness (tathatā).
Neither is subsumed under form (*rūpa*). Question: It is certainly known that there is no difference between the body and the land; however, can their dimensions be described? Answer:
Although their dimensions—whether large or small—cannot be described, their measure is nonetheless boundless according to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
Since the three bodies, such as the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and the three lands have infinite phenomena as their nature, how could they themselves have limits? For example:
Space can pervade all places, whether material or immaterial; this serves as a general metaphor for both the body and the land. The formal argument is:
the form and measure of space are boundless because it pervades all places, just like space itself. The self-enjoyment body likewise relies upon the self-enjoyment land;
that is to say, the pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, which is the eighth consciousness at the stage of fruition. This...

This is the causal basis (*āśraya-hetu*), for it is upon this that the sudden transformation depends. From "by what was previously cultivated" below, this is the causal factor of practice (*caryā-hetu*).

From "from the initial attainment of Buddhahood" below, its resultant characteristics are distinguished. First, its vertical extension is clarified; from "perfectly round" below, its horizontal breadth is clarified.
This refers to that which is manifested by the stainless pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), resulting from three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of the past.

Throughout kalpas, he cultivated ten supreme practices as the conditions for a pure land. Therefore, when he first attained Buddhahood, by means of that purified consciousness, he manifested a purely immaculate Buddha-land that is circular and boundless, adorned with myriad jewels, and which continues uninterruptedly until the end of the future.
The self-enjoyment body relies upon this land; this land is the Flower Treasury Adorned World (*Kusumatalagarbha-vyūha-lokadhātu*).
"Also. As for "Pure below," this clarifies the dimensions of the body and the land. This pure land is immeasurable, and the dimensions of the body are likewise so.
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The body has immeasurable colors; each color has immeasurable marks; each mark has immeasurable secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
The supporting fruits upon which it rests are also immeasurable, with various adornments. According to what is manifested, there are boundless [appearances]."
It is inexhaustible. Why is this? Because it is all produced by the guidance of immeasurable roots of goodness from throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Regarding the section on "merit" below, it clarifies that the body and the land pervade all places. Question:
Merit follows the body upon which it relies, and wisdom follows the *tathatā* (suchness) realized; since the body and the land are both without limit, so too are merit and wisdom.
Is there a limit to its magnitude? Answer: The meaning is as stated in the text. The Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) likewise relies upon the Land of Enjoyment for Others.
This refers to the pure consciousness associated with the Wisdom of Equality, manifested through the power of great compassion.

Because, during former causal stages, one cultivated practices for the benefit of others, which served as the conditions for the Pure Land, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, one does not abandon the benefit of others; accordingly—

This is appropriate for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). By means of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) and the power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they transform it into a pure land.
Its dimensions—whether large or small, superior or inferior—are not fixed. The Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) relies upon this land;
since the land upon which it relies has no fixed measure, the size of the body that relies upon it is likewise so. As for the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it relies [upon a land]...
The transformation land refers to that manifested through the power of great compassion by the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Furthermore, because one cultivated practices for the benefit of others in the past as the conditions for purifying both pure and impure lands, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, it appears according to the stage of the bodhisattvas before one.

It is also suitable for śrāvakas, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and others. By the power of great compassion, it manifests as buddha-fields that are pure or impure, large or small, with indefinite dimensions. This transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) dwells in these lands; since the lands are not fixed, the dimensions of the body are likewise so. Question: What is the essence of the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*)? Answer: It consists of the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*bodhi*) and the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*).
